Forward, Wilhelm Kütemeyer!

Continue your afterword to The Concept of Irony!

Continue it today, in 1947!

If you can erase eighteen hundred years, it should not be difficult for you to erase the final eighteen years that have passed since that afterword.

Or do you want to offer the age you despise so much the miserable spectacle of repentance-preachers fighting among themselves?

Approved repentance-preachers.

Authorized repentance-preachers.

Licensed repentance-preachers.

Seen through Kierkegaard’s eyes, this is surely one degree more pathetic than the officially approved preacher in a church pulpit.1

To Günther Krauss, who wrote that he could not really call Kleist’s women Marian:

Kleist’s women are, first of all, not “ladies” like Goethe’s Iphigenia.

That removes the main obstacle to connecting Kleist with the Virgin Mother.

Mary is the woman among women.

And is the Maid of Orléans really not Kleistian?

Once the Ecce ancilla—“Behold the handmaid”—is properly understood, the whole problem appears differently.

And the Ecce ancilla is surely the center of a Marian view of history.

Shakespeare, on the other hand, is in no sense Marian.

But Annette, the wise-foolish virgin, belongs with Kleist.

Is it not sad that the two never met?

Though this would have been one of those encounters that German circumstances never permit.

What does it actually mean when Sohm says that law is tied to the past?

Is this an absolutization of nullum crimen—no crime without a prior law?

Or what is it?

With Hobbes, the meaning, and its connection with nominalism, is immediately clear.

Is it equally clear with Sohm?

Predictability?

(The delight in acceleration.

The accelerator of accelerators against his own will.

Was that what drove me,

carried me,

and deceived me?)

Sohm’s touching error:

law protects the weak.

Customary law, by contrast, supposedly serves the strong.

A social-political illusion belonging to an age in which statute law was still regarded as a means of social justice.

An age in which law had not yet become pure planning.

Law, Sohm says, depends on form.

But is form merely something determined in advance?

Rigid external form?

Something already formed rather than something that forms?

Form that has become rather than form still becoming?

11 October 1947

Is this return to my own body, to my one true possession, merely an individual tendency in me?

An “ancient” inability to accept the modern dissolution of everything into forces, waves, and radiation?

Or is it a movement of the age in which I myself am participating?

Order and location:

house and farm,

city and country,

land and sea,

my body,

my clothing,

my house—my home,

my land.

Or consider language.

Reflexive relations involving the body can really be imagined only in painful forms:

I hit myself.

I torment myself.

I kill myself.

But:

I caress myself,

I stroke myself,

sounds comic and ridiculous—or physically horrifying.

I can kill myself.

That is the only essential bodily relation between “I” and “myself.”

But I can neither conceive myself nor give birth to myself.

This is where the problem of suicide would have to begin.1

A person does not commit suicide because he hates himself.

Nor because he loves himself.

Explanations in terms of self-love or self-hatred explain nothing.

The answer can lie only in the immediate symbolism of the physical act of suicide.

The bodily act of killing is essential to it.

The question therefore becomes:

can this act take on a form?

Can it become a rite?

Of course it can.

But what does any of this have to do with civil war?

G. Krauss wrote to me about the death of Otho in Tacitus, Histories II.49.

That is civil war.

Civil war is bellum with a justa causa, a just cause, on both sides, but with an iniustus hostis, an unjust enemy, on both sides?

Law—that is, the form of formally recognized war—consecrates death in war.

To what extent does the reality of civil war or social war remove the criminal character of suicide?

A formally recognized war justifies killing.

The form does this.

Not the iusta causa.

Civil war lacks that form.

Civil war is not simply formless war.

On the contrary, it makes use of legal and judicial forms.

But it is the most horrifying destruction of form through form.

Anyone forced to take part in civil war is placed under a compulsion to kill that cannot be justified by any formally valid order.2

By killing himself, does such a person merely anticipate the killing that would otherwise be done by the enemy?

Or is it the entire condition of civil war—the self-destruction, the suicide of the makros anthrōpos, the great collective human being—that, although it neither justifies nor excuses the suicide of the individual participant, nevertheless absorbs it through the specific force of the situation?

If my name appears on a proscription list, why should I not be permitted to kill myself?

I kill myself only so that I do not give the enemy the triumph of murdering me.

It is not I who take my life.

The enemy takes it from me.

I determine only the modus moriendi:

the manner of my death.

I take back my human dignity, which the enemy intended to take from me.

And I deprive my enemy of the pleasure of giving me an undignified death.

That is what distinguishes this kind of suicide in an acute civil war.

It is the final expression of the human being’s free power of self-determination.

It does not interfere with God’s sovereign power.

It interferes with the murderous claims made by my human enemies.

Sunday, 12 October 1947

Inside the space of a war that has no recognized form, different standards apply from those that apply elsewhere.

This is the absolute state of exception experienced by an individual pushed into the most extreme defenselessness:

the outlaw who refuses to be stripped of his human dignity even when he is treated like an animal or like vermin.1

Being a peripsēma, an outcast, does not make suicide into a sacrament.

Only the position of the fighting warrior in civil war raises the question in this way.

Here “civil war” stands for war without a formally recognized legal structure.

A war lacks such form when one side strips the other of its rights.

Bellum civile.

Bellum sociale.

Bellum internum.

No one can surrender the right to defend himself against an enemy.

Leviathan, Chapter 14.

Consider what it actually means to be:

hors la loi—

outside the law.

Must a person really be required to submit to that?2

13 October 1947

Keeping company with Hauriou instead of Bodin and Hobbes.

The clean, ordering intelligence of his conceptual thought.

A vision of essences.

Entirely juridical.

The deeper questions of origin are pushed toward the edges, but without falling into positivism.

Someone must dare the prior command, the obéissance préalable.

My † on the Hohe Molmert:

“Toward divinity one thinks letters silent from the beginning; it keeps secret what you carve into the cliffs. Come into your own where you inherit your shipwreck.”

An oracular, numinous lifting-up through these verses by Däubler to his sister Edith.

So the good Hauriou, with his balances and equilibria, with his relational thinking—especially the relation between power and freedom—is nevertheless what we in Germany called a liberal-authoritarian compromise.

In other words:

National Liberal.

But his sense of form is magnificent.

And his ability to contemplate without prejudice, to see juridical essences directly, is enchanting.

He never gives us form without principle or principle without form, as German National Liberalism did.

His books can be read with intense contemplation because they are themselves the product of intense contemplation.

That is a great pleasure.3

This kind of contemplation can hold me even when I am tormented by worries and even fears.

The lines of the thought are drawn so clearly and cleanly that they pull the reader along.

Even while my poor ears are being dirtied and abused by the piano-playing below me, these precise lines can absorb me completely.

This kind of cleanliness is a sign of moral qualities that are rare among us.

The terrible loneliness of such a jurist in Germany.

The chatterers of every camp regard me as an enemy.

14 October 1947

You speak of the beyond.

Of overcoming merely sensory nature.

Of overcoming merely physical life.

And every breath you take proves you a liar.

Because every breath is an unconditional submission to physical existence and to its all-encompassing terror—a terror that rules spirit, soul, and body alike.

“My hand was still permitted to touch the Cross.”

Great consolation.

Bentham’s “Expectation”:

planning,

predictable planning as a form of existence,

and the disappointment of an expectation based on that planning as the only sin.1

22 October 19472

Paul Valéry calls Descartes’ philosophy “intellectual coups d’état.”

Brilliant.

That also describes my own excessively decisionist way of thinking.

Carpe diem.

Seize the day.

Veniet hora.

The hour will come.

What comfortably static measures of time all these are.

Today we no longer live in days or hours.

We live in fractions of seconds and splinters of moments.

Nothing but packages.

Atomic packages.

Bundles of shares.

Clumped packages of power.

Formerly this kind of power appeared as the dynastic power of a family.

Today it appears as the power of a corporation or organized group:

an elite,

a sworn community,

a coniuratio,

a vanguard,

a political-criminal association,

or a cooperative.

The distinction between the personal and the real—between relations based on persons and relations based on things—is one of the primal principles of law and of all social life.

These are the “two principles” whose opposition itself forms the primal principle.

Everyone who possesses property thinks in real terms.

That means territorial terms for as long as the soil of the earth remains the most important res, the most important thing.

Everyone else thinks in personal terms:

community as an association of human beings rather than an association built around things.

The personal and real sides of the state.

The real side is the spatial side.

The human being in space.

Today all of this is undergoing an enormous transformation because space itself seems to be becoming a work created by human beings.

Juridical conceptual realism.

A contradictory figure:

the nominalist republican.

If even the res publica is no longer meant realistically, what remains of a republican at all?

Rome = res.

A depopulated res publica.

But worse still:

a res publica without a res.

A republic without a thing.

A mere state of consciousness.

23 October 1947, Elberfeld

There is no quantization in the Being of Parmenides.

Gerhard Nebel said this.

Prayer of Duns Scotus:

“In You there is no quantity.”

27 October 1947

If we define the aggressor purely in terms of possession and first action, then in the future we will no longer have to say:

the aggressor is the one who fires the first shot.

Instead we will have to say:

the aggressor is the one who drops the first atomic bomb.

The duty, then, is to wait until the first atomic bomb has actually been dropped.

That is the “juridical” solution to the problem.

29 October 1947

I found a classic example of the sociology of the elite understood as a politico-criminal association: Balzac’s preface to The History of the Thirteen. Everything is there: the secret society, the sworn brotherhood, the elite, the dream of loyal followers, magic, power—all of it romanticized.1

Why should this not count as one of the paths that prepared the way for the H.[itler] regime?

This romanticizing of crime!

Of interest for The Concept of the Political: these Thirteen were “political enough to conceal the sacred bonds that united them, strong enough to place themselves above all laws” (and I would add: “and to make completely uninhibited use of every means that legality placed at their disposal”).

The romanticizing itself—“the dark and mysterious poetry of this story”—is an effective force in the further development of this kind of elite.

Compare H.[itler]: “My life is a novel.”

This kind of preface is almost a literary genre of its own. But only someone who knew not merely the preface but also the works it introduces in detail could say anything really useful about that.

30 October 1947

Is this still political Romanticism?

With the first leaders, yes—for example, Lassalle and Hitler.

With the masses, it becomes political myth.

These leaders experience only the novel, the great personal drama.

The tone Lassalle uses with Countess Hatzfeld and Hitler’s tone toward the German people are essentially the same. One need only compare the correspondence from May and June 1857!

Listen:

“To demand explanations when I have stated the necessity of the matter so clearly is so disgraceful that I am disgusted by my own weakness in continuing to write to you” (letter of 2 June 1857).

The German itself is essentially the same, and so are several other things, especially the rapid, improvised acquisition of culture and ideas.

“Humanity has two scourges. I know them too well to love them, and I know them too well to hate them.”

Perípsēma—the refuse, the offscouring—from the ghetto and from the homeless shelter.

Did Eduard Rosenbaum have any idea what he was saying when, in 1930, he claimed that Lassalle had been the first National Socialist?

The road that led us—Lassalle?

An essay by Kautsky on this subject can ruin the most beautiful autumn day.

In any case, the subject belongs to the larger complex: the idea of genius in the nineteenth century; Max Stirner; the Wilhelmine types; and finally Brother Straubinger as an object of cult worship, with the Nobel Prize as the cult-mythic laurel wreath.

31 October 1947

Franz Kafka could have written a novel called The Enemy.

It would have shown that what produces anxiety is the enemy’s lack of definition.

There is no other kind of anxiety. The essence of anxiety is precisely the sense that there is an enemy somewhere without knowing clearly who or what that enemy is.

Reason, by contrast—and in this sense, high politics—has the task of identifying the enemy.

And identifying the enemy always means identifying oneself at the same time.

Once the enemy has been clearly defined, anxiety comes to an end. At most, fear remains.

But how are we supposed to pull anything out of this state of uncertainty and give it a definite form when we no longer possess any concepts in common?

One of the defining features of civil war is precisely that the enemies no longer share a common language of concepts. Every concept then becomes an intrusion across the enemy line.

3 November 1947

The mistake of F. A. Kramer (Before the Ruins of Germany, Koblenz, August 1945), Reck-Malleczewen, and the others:

Such a tiny man, such an enormous sinner!

The more insignificant this Brother Straubinger is, the more remarkable the whole thing becomes. The more purely he functions as an empty amplifier, as nothing more than a device for projecting sound, the more uncanny becomes the current of power that carries him and the words that bellows so loudly.

The more he was merely a sponge soaking up some substance, the more remarkable that substance itself becomes.

And the more the explanation is reduced to individual psychology, the more it turns into self-revelation on the part of the person doing the explaining.

Eventually that self-revelation itself becomes uninteresting.

Those who destroy what is nothing destroy only themselves.

The suction of nothingness.

“Deep calls to deep.”

Everyone classifies himself through his enemy—through the person or thing he is willing to recognize as his enemy.

That applies to Brother Straubinger.

But it applies just as much to those who declare him to be the one and only enemy and keep him alive through the idea of collective responsibility.

4 November 1947

Now I hardly dare even draw breath, for fear of distracting the mysterious hand that is guiding things.

5 November 1947

No comforting lie about life deceives me any longer.

The expression “life-lie,” viewed in the history of ideas, developed directly alongside the philosophy of life and was eventually drowned out by the noise of faith in life.

“The ocean is free, and freer still are springs.”1

Let us see whether one springs up.

In any case, to speak today of the “freedom of the ocean” is no longer entirely honest.

In 1926 there was an attempt to draft a convention “on questions relating to the pollution of navigable waters by petroleum” (Gilbert Gidel, The Public International Law of the Sea, vol. I, 1932, p. 480).

And then came the conventions for saving the whale!

So the great Leviathan itself is now under nature protection—and we are still supposed to call the ocean in which it swims a free ocean.

There can be no movement without empty space.

There can also be no law without free space.

Whenever a space is brought under rules, ordered, and enclosed, there must remain another space outside it—a free space that remains outside the law.2

How terrible a world would be in which there were no foreign countries left at all, only one single domestic realm.

No road leading out into the open.

No room in which free forces can measure themselves against one another and test their strength.

One World.

7 November 1947

The religion of those who wait:

waiting for the Messiah who has not yet come;

waiting for the Messiah who has already come but will nevertheless come again;

waiting for the Comforter and the Holy Spirit;

waiting for the classless society and the eternal kingdom.

The Trinity as an expression of this waiting.

What Bruno Bauer calls Judaization is the establishment of waiting as a permanent condition: a waiting room designed to last indefinitely and made more and more comfortable as time goes on.

“Thus judgment is awaited!”

The traveller wants to lie down among those who are waiting and wait there for a little while.

Just as Nacht can be read as N + acht—N plus “eight”—so NORD = N + ORT.

Once again: the identity of order and location.

(Written to Herbert Nette, 7 November 1947.)

Metabolē, change or reversal; tropē, turning; phora, movement (Statesman, chs. 13 ff.).

“A small part of the race remains.”

“Many strange and astonishing sufferings.”

That, then, is the kind of metabolē in which we are sitting today.

Understood cyclically: a world-age of reversal and counter-movement.

The movement into the opposite.

9 November 1947

My impression from reading Arthur Koestler, Baumgartner’s speech, and so on:

Everything today is working toward the retroactive realization of the assumptions behind the earlier wild protests.

“A people without space”?

Indeed—today, in 1947.

“The solid national community”?

Indeed—today, in the most concrete form imaginable: collective guilt.

These opposing camps now give one another their meaning.

Anyone who commits an injustice today can be sure that tomorrow’s injustice will provide his justification.

So one anticipates these later justifications in advance.

Be bold enough to do that here too.

There is a connection between these criminalizations after the fact and these justifications after the fact.

“He who accuses excuses himself.”

In Hermann Hefele one finds the following pair of opposites, embedded in an entire labyrinth of antitheses that cross and recross one another thousands of times:

from morality to legality

—that is, from the subjectivity of individual conscience to the objectivity of the collective will.

This is then supposed to correspond to:

Guelphism against Ghibellinism;

Classicism against Romanticism;

Roman against Germanic;

state against empire.

Today a Bavarian parliamentarian speaks of “the lack of instinct in legality.”

I reread the preface to the first volume of Sohm’s Church Law, from 1892.

Sohm appears to say quite clearly:

“Purely legal treatment has merely (!) formal value. Law does not take its content from itself. It receives that content from other powers—in the field of church law, from the religious powers of human life.”1

There is something disturbing about the general, neutralizing way this is stated.

Does the entire problem simply come down to a general opposition between “mere form” and content, which is supposedly something more than mere form?

If so, then this would no longer be the painfully specific problem of church law.

And who are these “religious powers”—not merely intellectual or spiritual powers?

Does church law receive its content from a potestas spiritualis, a spiritual authority?

That would almost be hyper-Catholic.

In short, the thorn is still there.

Francis Bacon, in Of Seditions and Troubles (chapter XV of the Sermones Fideles, 1644), warns princes against joining themselves to a political party.2

His warning example is Henry III’s joining the League, which later turned against him.

The auctoritas principis, the authority of the prince, thereby becomes something secondary and dependent.

There is something similar in Bodin.

I was startled by the sheer, unsupported arrogance with which Kelsen criticized my theory of the neutral guardian of the constitution and tried to discredit it as unscientific.

10 November 1947

On Sohm:

The essence of art also depends on form.

So why can one not say:

the essence of art stands in contradiction to the essence of the Church?

Does it contradict the essence of spirit that musical scores and written poems exist?

Fixed intervals?

Firm lines?

12 November 1947

On Hobbes:

Rudolf Kassner’s comments from April 1942 in the Europäische Revue seem extraordinarily illuminating.

  1. Hobbes is the true philosopher of the Baroque.

The Baroque puts up a façade in front of the new, Faustian world and makes that façade swell with importance.

There is a separation between rule and power:

Louis XIII — Richelieu Emperor — Wallenstein

Hobbes’s separation between outside and inside, with the strongest possible emphasis on the outside, does indeed have something of this putting-forward of the façade.

  1. The relation to death.

“Desire of power, that ceaseth only in death.”

Always the fear of death.

Even Leviathan is a mortal god, a Deus mortalis.

Kassner is entirely right when he says:

“Hobbes’s view of power is neither that of the Greek Sophists, nor that of Machiavelli, nor that of Goethe’s Mephistopheles. None of them, when thinking of power, thinks of either death or sin; they remain in the real (? sic!).”

With this “ceaseth in death,” something loosens in the connection between being and power.

Hobbes does not recoil from death in horror.

But he sees it.

He seeks protection in power—but only protection from death at the hands of other human beings.

Power must not be allowed to kill on its own authority.

That is the decisive point.

Poor metabolists that we are—poor creatures of change!

Any fool can make himself important by declaring us diabolists.

Life is the façade in front of death.

That is Baroque.

Leviathan itself is a façade: the façade of rule placed before power.

That mysterious curtain on the title page of Leviathan.

But it is not a “mere” façade.

Not mere illusion or appearance.

Prestige, glory, honour, representation, omnipotence—but still, in the end, an external omnipotence.

Back then, in the Baroque age, the superiority of the inner over the outer was not yet taken for granted as it is today.

The whole psychology and sociology of “unmasking” was a dismantling of the Baroque façade in order to expose the naked core of power beneath it.

Republic = verta = laying bare of force (virtus).

And so it becomes clear:

Hobbes is the only completely radical and completely consistent theorist of the state based on law and security.

For him, the image of Leviathan is a Baroque façade.

Behind it lies the need for security among competing powers and, ultimately, among competing individuals.

For the individual, precisely because he is an individual, is forced to set himself down, distinguish himself from others, assert himself, and practise a politics of power.

Strangely, Behemoth is not as suitable a façade as Leviathan.

Why?

Is the land animal too solid?

A very important question!

Because the façade is false.1

13 November 1947

To Ernst Jünger:

Strange that Elisabeth Langgässer should cross your path now.

In her book The Indelible Seal she makes Donoso Cortés speak.

I cannot continue reading until I know what she is doing with him.

When you have read the central passage in her novel, please also read my two essays on Donoso. Both are reprinted in Positions and Concepts.

Incidentally, on p. 83, sixth line from the bottom, Donoso continues:

Then the Russian soldier can walk through Europe l’arme au bras—rifle in hand.

That matters to the vividness of the image.

What Tocqueville foresaw for Europe in relation to America, Donoso foresaw in relation to Russia.

I would like, one day, to show you the original passages.

I have no hesitation, today, as a sixty-year-old man, after everything I have experienced with people and books, speeches and situations, in calmly stating that Donoso’s great speech on dictatorship of 4 January 1849 is the greatest speech in world literature.

I make no exception for Pericles or Demosthenes, Cicero or Mirabeau or Burke.

But this is an immense subject.

I mention it only because your reference to Elisabeth Langgässer’s novel touched an extraordinarily sensitive point in me.

(In the same letter: Friedrich Georg Jünger should write a poetics under the influence of Hindemith’s theory of musical composition.)

An indirect—and for that reason more reliable and deeper—influence of Kierkegaard on Léon Bloy, by way of Denmark, similar to Bruno Bauer’s influence on Nietzsche.

Joy is an acceleration of the circulation of the blood, Hobbes says.

That is Walter Pater’s “as many pulsations as possible” from 1868.

15 November 1947

The splendour of this earthly world is completely independent of human suffering and torment.

A single second of conscious pleasure, or pleasurable consciousness, can outweigh years of the most terrible suffering.

And the reverse is equally true: a single second of pain and anxiety can wipe out years of undisturbed happiness.

The two cancel each other out completely.

Arguments like these prove nothing and decide even less.

The Russian nihilist can point to one poor, tortured child and use that child to condemn the whole earthly world.

And, in the opposite direction, one could restore the value of the whole world by pointing to the happiness of one child.

So where does the decision lie?

The Baroque—Hobbes—still has a substantial public sphere.

Spinoza is not Baroque.

The Baroque therefore still possesses legitimacy and not merely legality; rule and not merely power.1

The emperor defeats Wallenstein.

The Stuarts defeat Cromwell.

Louis XIII does not need to fear Richelieu.

Only the destruction of dynastic legitimacy beginning with Louis-Philippe clears the road for naked power.

Napoleon I still attempts to establish legitimacy and is, in that sense, still Baroque.

Napoleon III is merely an actor, living off the fruits of earlier ages to the accompaniment of operetta music.

The separation of régner and gouverner—of reigning and governing—is already a kind of first cell division from which naked power and legality emerge.

The democratic legitimacy of the American Constitution is destroyed by Marxism.

Law does not become power.

It becomes something far more dangerous:

positivist legality.

What does rational natural law mean within this development from Baroque legitimacy to positivist legality?

Hobbes’s rational law already knows only legality.

Everything else has already become mere façade—above all, the image of Leviathan.

<…>

16 November 1947

To live off another person’s guilt is the lowest possible way of living at another person’s expense.

To live from fines, penalties, and blood-money is the dirtiest possible way of taking booty.

But this is how they have always lived:

from the confiscated property of proscribed enemies and enemies placed hors la loi, outside the law.

The booty of civil war.

The particular idea of booty that belongs to civil war.

The profiteers of civil war.

The victor’s claim to compensation.

There is no triumph in civil war.

It was already considered offensive that, during Caesar’s triumph in September of the year 46, Cato’s suicide was displayed in an image (Ed. Meyer, p. 38), even though the triumph was presented not as a triumph over defeated Roman citizens but as a fourfold victory over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus, and Numidia.

On James Burnham’s The Managerial Revolution:

These are discoveries we made twenty or thirty years ago.

All the better.

But here is a question.

If freedom depends on the existence of opposition, who organizes the opposition when everything is organized and even what remains unorganized becomes nothing more than a protected nature reserve?

So:

who organizes the opposition?

Does the opposition organize itself freely?

Then the ruling elite no longer has it under control.

Or is the ruler himself supposed to organize his own opposition, as under Kemal Pasha?

Then the whole thing is rigged.

The decisive fact remains that the pressure toward conscious organization, bureaucracy, and planning becomes total.

That is Burnham’s starting point too.

That is what is current, realistic, suited to the age, and free of illusions.

Why, then, does he suddenly turn toward this contradictory optimism about opposition?

How tiny, how minimal, the room left for opposition becomes under total planning!

This is still the old idea of opposition that belongs to the spatial imagination of a maritime empire whose ruling class can divide the wealth of the earth among itself—with a free ocean still available!

Once things become serious and bare survival is at stake, games like that come to an end.

The most astonishing example of historical dialectic is one that today’s Hegelians have failed to see even though it stands directly before their eyes:

within an empire based on sailing ships—essentially an empire without machines—the machine and the Industrial Revolution arise.

The philosophy of the “I” is an enormous lever for prying the world off its hinges.

If I am transcendental consciousness—and surely I must be, since otherwise I could not even deny that I am—then why should I not myself be the Ens Perfectissimum, the most perfect being?

Why should I not apply to Myself all the arguments of the ontological proof of God?

The ontological proof of God would then prove that I am God.

The splendour of this earthly world is easy enough to argue for.

See above, 15 November 1947; below, 21 November 1947.

<…>

17 November 1947

The only thing I inherit is my own body.

The only thing I possess is this one, unnameable instant, lost the moment it arrives.

<…>

Max Stirner, p. 244:

“In the end I must withdraw even the half-adequate language I have been using, language I intended to use only for as long as I was still digging around in the entrails of law and at least allowing the word itself to remain.

But once the concept disappears, the word itself truly loses its meaning.

A right can be granted only by a spirit—by God, humanity, or divinity.

I demand no right, and therefore I need recognize none.

With absolute right, right itself disappears. The rule of the very concept of right is abolished.

I am simply powerful.

If I am powerful, then I am already authorized by that fact alone.

Right is a fixed idea granted by a ghost.

Power—that is Myself.

Right is an act of grace bestowed by the judge.

Power and force exist only in Me, the powerful and forceful one.”

That—and nothing else—is the splendour of this earthly world.

Hobbes would say:

As long as a man enjoys honour among other people, as the famous Rilke did, he will find this earthly life splendid despite every bodily suffering.

But wait and see how the world looks to him once he has been dishonoured and stripped of his rights.

The moment we succeed in reaching the contemplative position, we are forced to find the world not merely bearable but magnificent.

There it is:

the Ens perfectissimum.

The best of all possible worlds.

Beautiful to look at and terrible to be.

But anyone who does not want merely to contemplate the world but to change it must necessarily find the world in need of change—which means bad.

I am disgusted by the pathos of moral outrage that arises when someone wants to create the world anew so that he can indulge his will to power and destroy his enemies.

18 November 1947

Werner Kaegi, “Problems of the Rule-of-Law State” (Universitas, August 1947), argues that the abolition of the right of resistance—the great showpiece achievement of the modern state—has now been reversed beneath the shadow of Leviathan, and that the problem of resistance has perhaps never been more urgent.

“As the level of the rule-of-law state falls, the level of the right of resistance rises; when resistance within the constitution fails, resistance outside the constitution appears.”

Yes indeed.

But, I believe, His Lordship wrote this more bravely than he would have acted on it.

Compare Hobbes’s reply to Bishop Bramhall (pp. 436, 454, 1750 edition).

Where was His Lordship when he wrote this?

Germany in 1938?

Or Switzerland in 1948?

So once again: the problem of legality and legitimacy.

Has he understood the problem of legality at all “in the shadow of Leviathan”?

Has he himself ever been in a situation of resistance?

Resistance against whom?

And what, concretely, did he think and do then?

Has he ever stopped to consider the responsibility he assumes when he encourages people to resist while being unable to protect them?

Ernst Jünger:

The positive counterpart of pity is protection.

That applies even more strongly, more directly, and indeed absolutely to the right of resistance.

You grant someone a right that he is then supposed to obtain and fight for by himself.

In that case, please also leave it to him to decide whether, when, and how he will exercise it.

These “legal thinkers” simply abstract away from the eternal connection between protection and obedience, persecution and resistance.

One can give the ambiguous term “rule-of-law state” a precise meaning by saying:

The rule-of-law state is a political community that replaces the right of resistance with a legal route of appeal through established institutions.

What is involved is the elimination of resistance.

In concrete terms:

feud and revolution.

In more modern language:

sabotage, high treason, treason against the state, collaboration with the enemy.

So begin by demanding the abolition of those criminal laws.

That would be disarmament!

The rule-of-law state abolishes the idea of the internal enemy.

That makes sense only if the actual enmity really comes to an end.

See Otto Brunner.

If this connection between the rule-of-law state and the ending of civil war is forgotten or concealed, then all the dangers of “pre-modern” life are summoned back into existence.

Few people today are capable of facing those dangers.

Most do not even want to be capable of facing them.

Under such circumstances one should not proclaim general theories about a resurrected right of resistance.

Typical of the Swiss and others who sit safely far from the firing line while laying down ethical and legal demands for everyone else.

19 November 1947

Before God, everything that lies in the future has already happened.

What strikes us as the present is like a ray of light from a distant star that disappeared long ago:

light still travelling onward even though its source has already gone out.

The justice of the divine order of the world therefore consists in its ignoring what we ourselves experience as our present.

When God allowed hundreds of thousands of Jews to be killed, he already saw at the same time the revenge they would take upon Germany.

And what he sees today in those who take revenge and exact retribution will be experienced by human beings in some unexpectedly different future present.

The mechanism by which day turns into night, light into darkness, solid into liquid, and so on becomes most abstract in the opposition between yesterday and tomorrow.

The past:

fixed, unchangeable, completely closed.

The future:

full, infinitely undetermined, even empty.

This mechanism is so stupidly mechanical that it must be wrong.

What follows?

The future is not open and the past is not closed.

The past is not full and the future is not empty.1

On Barion’s letter of 11 November 1947:

Concerning Sohm’s thesis:

Law refers to the past, not the present, and binds us to the past.

Law is a worldly rule made by human beings for human beings—that is, a rule agreed upon in nominalist fashion.

It is a rule fixed in advance, something already given.

All of that already belongs to the rule-of-law state:

anteceding law, the regula, the rule laid down beforehand.

But that is only one possibility—the one I called “normativist.”

Decisionist law, by contrast, comes into being only at the moment of decision.

And the law of every concrete order exists in a permanent present.

So the binding force of the past applies only to the regula.

<…>

Is Luther’s binding of Christianity to Scripture—“The Word they still shall let remain!”—not itself a binding to the past?

Is it not narrower and more rigid than the regula fidei, the rule of faith, of Catholic dogma?

Does every act of turning something into dogma also turn it into law?

20 November 1947

The purer and more absolute contemplation becomes, the more this world becomes, for the contemplative person, the best of all possible worlds.

That is the meaning of the ontological proof of God discovered by cloistered monks and no longer understood by those who are not monks.

For to be pure and absolute means, above all, to be able to contemplate without disturbance.

And the stronger and more absolute activity becomes, the more the world appears to require change—which means that the world appears worse.

In <…> Utopia, activity comes to an end.

But the invention of utopias is itself a product of activity.

Optimism toward the future.

Pessimism toward the past.

Pure contemplation belongs to no human being.

It would be God’s affair.

But anyone who builds his concrete human existence upon contemplation becomes godlike and finds the world good.

Human being:

whatever you fight against, that is what you will become.

The people are the patient ones.

The completely patient ones.

Those who do not even rebel when they are exploited in their own name.

In the eyes of the contemplative person, the activist is a wild animal.

In the eyes of the activist, the contemplative person is a sophisticated social parasite, a reactionary idler and saboteur.

And the God of the contemplative person is a product of Epicurean boredom—at worst a password used by the fifth column, at best an excuse for people who have simply remained sitting where they are.

21 November 1947

On Utopia, to Miss Marie Stewens:

(Reference to “state novels,” Robert Mohl and Kleinwächter, Ernst Bloch; prompted by André Maurois’s essay on James Burnham’s The Managerial Revolution of 1941, from the Revue de Paris, published in German in the Neue Zeitung on 1 August 1947.)

What is specific to Utopia, as distinct from every possible kind of ideal construction, wishful dream, or fantastic programme?

It lies in the fact that Thomas More, who invented the word Utopia, stood in the middle of the great spatial revolution of his age.

From that position he made the leap into non-space, the u-topos, the “no-place”—a leap that an ancient Greek could never have made.

The astonishing thing in More is this removal of topos, of place, from consideration.

But that is only the first and most superficial, negative side of the matter.

The deeper point is this:

when space and place are set aside—when thought is uprooted from place—it also becomes abstracted from the connection between location and order, a connection that would have seemed eternal to an ancient person.

Every order is law located somewhere concrete.

Law is law only in the right place, on this side of the “line.”

More deliberately leaves all of that behind.

Place and space no longer matter.

They are no longer given by God or nature.

They become accidental, arbitrary, freely chosen by human beings—even made by human beings for human beings, constructed upon a levelled surface where location itself no longer matters.

So by Utopia I do not mean arbitrary fantasy or some ideal construction.

I mean a system of thought built upon the abolition of spatial limits and the removal of human coexistence from any necessary connection to place.

In other words, it rests upon what one might call the “retreat of the barrier of nature,” which turns man into the master of nature.

Man creates his own world according to rational principles.1

As technology advances, Utopia in this sense rises into ever more daring dimensions.

Eventually it reaches the final natural barrier:

human nature itself.

It then imagines a political community composed of human beings who have themselves been systematically standardized.

That is the logical consistency of Brave New World.

Its enormous importance lies precisely in this deliberate alteration of human nature by human beings themselves.

Pay attention to this particular question:

the relation of Utopia to human nature.

Education.

Breeding.

Eventually, the manufacture of the homunculus.

In More there is still the classical humanist assumption about human nature.

In Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe, there is already the construction that begins from the isolated individual.

In Swift, human beings themselves are fantastically altered:

giants, dwarfs, horses.

In Aldous Huxley, standardized human beings are deliberately manufactured by scientific means.

In other words, this is total planning.

It includes even the natural facts of the human body and mind within its removal from place.

Utopia therefore means:

the consistent uprooting of things from place in the most total sense possible, until even humanity’s own place within the nature that has so far been given to it is abolished.

The connection between order and location is broken.

Plato’s Republic is a Utopia insofar as every Idea represents a removal from concrete reality.

Pierre Linn had already shown in 1938 that the totalitarian state is the logically consistent ideal state: Platonically rather than Aristotelian-Thomistically consistent, once the difference between Idea and reality is settled in favour of the Idea and the Idea is made real.

But Plato does not yet think in an exact scientific manner.

Nor globally.

His thought still remains tied to place.

Yet his idealism opens the road toward Utopia.

Again and again it is Aldous Huxley’s enormous, crushing, practically and theoretically overwhelming Brave New World that defines for us today both the idea of Utopia and the idea of the New World.

Thomas More brings the removal from place at the beginning of the geographical revolution of space.

Huxley brings the removal of humanity itself at the beginning of the technological revolution of space.

For we are only now entering the age of technology.

More comes from the England that is preparing to conquer the new world of the sea.

Huxley comes from the point at which the modern industrial and technological world begins opening into a new world whose adventures will be greater and more terrible than those of the old adventurers of the pirate age of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

(Then a question about the word: corny.)

22 November 1947

So, my dear Max, nothing is above You.

Strictly speaking, your sentence “Nothing is above Me” cannot even survive translation into this form of addressing another person.

The I rejects such forms of address.

Being addressed as “you” already threatens it in its uniqueness.

Still:

what magnificent solidarity!

Millions of us can shout together in chorus:

Nothing is above Me!

And:

I am I!

Perhaps you can say this about yourself.

And perhaps millions who roar along in your chorus can say it too.

Unfortunately, all I can say about myself is that I do not know whether I am I, or whether nothing is above Me.

I do not know what this I of mine actually is.

Whether it is a fixed star or a will-o’-the-wisp in a swamp.

Or both.

Are you one unique I?

Or are there a thousand, countless selves inside your I?

I know none of this.

I do not know who I am.

If you know who you are, so much the better.

Make use of your knowledge.

You say:

“Living, I consume myself.”

I too consume myself.

That much is certain.

My body consumes me and I consume my body.

I do not know which of us is consuming the other.

You celebrate your I with jubilation.

Why do you show us only its euphoric, high-spirited side?

Surely your I has other sides too, you cheerful Euphorion of yourself.

In any event, good friend, I am gradually coming to know you, and I do not wish to interrupt your feast of life any longer.

What is remarkable about Max Stirner is not this philosophy.

It is the desperation of his struggle against the frauds and ghosts of his age.

The honesty of this bankrupt ego, who does not call upon other people to liberate themselves so that he can place himself at their head;

who does not surrender himself to some substitute religion;

whose entire strength consists only in the weakness of everyone else.

The typical superiority of Brother Straubinger—to whom Stirner also belongs, as a boor, a swaggerer, a student roughneck—so long as this Brother does not try to become a leader but remains a drummer.

The people are the powerless.

23 November 1947

The totality of mobilization consists in this:

even the unmoved mover of Aristotelian philosophy has now been set in motion and mobilized.

Then the old separation between unmoving contemplation and moving activity comes to an end.

The observer himself begins to move.

And once that happens, he can no longer identify and prove the Ens perfectissimum, the most perfect being, with the old certainty.

Then we are all activist observers and observing activists.

At most, one possibility remains imaginable:

that in this way we might one day produce the Ens perfectissimum ourselves.

Then the rule becomes:

Whoever is not on the road experiences nothing.

24 November 1947

What is miserable about Machiavelli is the half-heartedness involved in speaking about power at all—turning power into an object of discussion.

Power is and remains a secret.

Public power is the most impenetrable secret of all.

Anyone who possesses power knows this.

Anyone who wants power ought to know it.

A consistent Machiavellian speaks like a Tolstoyan.

But a philosophy of the will to power is the summit of the most miserable1 bad taste and existential stupidity.

On Otto Veit’s efforts concerning “natural law”:

Compare the chain of antitheses on pp. 395–96 of issue 3 of Merkur, with positive law as the opposite term.

I regard concepts like these as revivals from legal history—perhaps even anachronistic revivals—produced by jurists philosophizing helplessly.

The distinction suited to our own time is:

legality and legitimacy.

Donoso Cortés already understood this.

At the very beginning of his great speech on dictatorship of 4 January 1849, he attacks the politician Cortina for turning unconditional adherence to legality into a principle.

For Cortés, dictatorship is no longer legal, but it can be legitimate.

The age of unconditional legality is over.

The practical question is merely whether dictatorship will come from above or from below—today one would say from the Right or from the Left.

So the real question is the legitimacy of dictatorship:

“When legality is enough to save society, legality; when legality is not enough, dictatorship.”

And almost automatically, already in this speech of 1849, the corresponding concept appears:

legitimacy.

“Dictatorship is a legitimate government like any other government.”

There is also a philosophically very important document showing that today’s real issue is precisely this opposition between legality and legitimacy.

In more than one respect, it is almost a classic document:

Georg Lukács’s essay “Legality and Illegality” of July 1920, which Lukács later included as a chapter in History and Class Consciousness (Malik-Verlag, Berlin, 1923, pp. 261–75).

Lukács says there—in agreement with Lenin’s work on left-wing radicalism as the childhood sickness of revolution—that those committed in principle to illegality still attach an inherited, Romantic importance to “the law as law.”

The class-conscious proletarian, however, must regard the question of legality or illegality as a purely tactical question, one that changes rapidly with circumstances.

The question must be answered, with complete “freedom from prejudice,” according to “considerations of immediate usefulness”—Lukács himself emphasizes those words.

Lukács too arrives at the antithesis:

“Legality — Legitimacy.”

The revolutionary struggle of the proletariat is “legitimate.”

At the end he says, literally:

“The proletariat of Central and Western Europe still has a difficult road before it. In order to reach consciousness of its historical calling, of the legitimacy of its rule, it must first learn to understand the merely tactical character of legality and illegality and rid itself both of legalistic cretinism and of the Romanticism of illegality.”

So there can be no doubt about the present importance of the distinction between legality and legitimacy.

Nor can there be any doubt that the title of my 1932 book, Legality and Legitimacy, was well founded.

But there can equally be no doubt that people who possess such dialectical clarity about legality and illegality will lose all sense of humour on this point once illegality is practised against them—once the illegality is directed against legal and therefore changing <…> .

In the otherwise remarkably complete chain of antitheses that Otto Veit constructs from the opposition between natural law and positive law, this particular antithesis is missing.

Why?

Because the distinction between natural law and positive law is outdated.

The issue is no longer “nature.”

Today that would produce, at best, a biological law—and we have all had quite enough of that.

The issue is history.

Whether sacred history or history made by human beings.

History made ever more consciously, ever more deliberately, ever more according to plan, as historical consciousness and total planning grow in intensity.

History developing into the conscious and total planning of things to come.

25 November 1947

At half past three in the morning, I came across the letter Popitz wrote to me on 1 November 1930 about The Concept of the Political.

I was filled with happiness at the immediate presence of his voice, his gaze, his gestures—and at the happiness of that friendship.

The most beautiful thing about Popitz was his capacity for friendship.

I owe him a testimony.

But how am I supposed to give it while people are silencing me by refusing even to mention me?

Be still.

The testimony has already been given.

Do not fall for the fraud committed by life when it imagines itself superior to the dead.

“The dead” means nothing more than those who are absent from us, elsewhere, on the other side.

How pathetic it is when those who happen to be present at this moment want, with a patronizing gesture, to offer alms to those who happen to be absent.

It merely shows that they are no longer capable of any beyond.

Turned into termites, reduced to biology, reduced to positivism:

presumptuous mealworms.

So do not be angry with me, dear Popitz.

I have returned to my homeland.

You had to die together with Prussia and the state.

Il n’y a plus de Prusse.

There is no Prussia anymore.

I am leaving history and entering into my substance.

Donoso Cortés, tanned into leather for a dining table by Dietmar Westemeyer and cut up into decorative trim for a novel by Elisabeth Langgässer.

Poor Donoso!

Meanwhile Brother Straubinger, after his death, succeeds in carrying out his most astonishing fraud yet:

he is turned into the representative of all the ideas he himself merely used as instruments of deception.

This is the result of the blind thirst for revenge of emigrants returning in fury.

Brother Straubinger even succeeds in attaching his name to that of Richard Wagner, linking his crime to the most modern music, and entering Wahnfried as a hero.

The consequences are impossible to foresee.

A turning point in intellectual history of unbelievable importance.

If, from now on, everyone who is moved by the music of Tristan is forced to think of H.[itler] and connect his image with that music—

then perhaps he really was the logical conclusion of the nineteenth century after all!

For the genuine bureaucrat, legality provides the basis for an almost ascetic refusal to adopt personal “values” or make “value judgments.”

This is analogous to—perhaps often identical with—the ascetic restraint Max Weber demanded of the scholar.

Positivist asceticism, with private reservations kept inside.

A value judgment is by definition subjective, unscientific.

In any event, the sharpest possible separation between what ought to be and what is.

Quite right.1

In Germany, every attempt at unity has so far ended in particularism, secession, separatism, and itio in partes—a splitting into opposing camps:

the reception of Roman law;

the Reformation;

the Peasants’ War;

nationalism and socialism.

Until finally the fanatical drive toward unity produced a fourfold division imposed from outside.

26 November 1947

In this movement, the most subtle, most theological distinctions of the spirit found their Acheron—their descent into the underworld.

In every movement?

Certainly in this one.

Thanks to Langbehn’s sensitivity, the many remarks Jakob Burckhardt made in the 1880s, and Bruno Bauer and Johann Georg Hamann?

Every movement of distance, however subtle, eventually finds its Acheron.

So be careful.

Here lies the very real truth of sayings of the Lord such as Matthew 5:28 and 5:44.

This is the basis of the monstrous disproportion between a thought and the realization of a thought:

between the microscopic sound that triggers something and the enormous amplification that follows.

Something completely alien always inserts itself into the “execution” of an idea.

A “mass.”

Perhaps to Otto Veit:

I have read your essay on “The Intellectual-Historical Situation of Natural Law.”

You yourself drew my attention to it, and so I may say a word about it.

After your letter, I must.

Not in order to twist people’s heads around by suddenly forcing them to look in another direction <…>, but [to admire] this attempt to frame the problem.

I am sure you will allow me to count, in questions of natural law, as a reasonably well-informed critic;

in questions concerning the intellectual situation of the age, as an expert made somewhat wiser by repeated misfortune;

and in my personal relation to the author, as an open-minded reader and listener filled both with personal respect and intellectual curiosity.

Otherwise I would have no right to speak and would not wish to speak.

I admire the encyclopedic completeness with which an almost boundless problem has been framed through an entire chain of antitheses.

Anyone who understands every single link in that chain—and there cannot be many—will share my admiration.

Yet one antithesis is missing.

And I believe it is precisely the antithesis that saves the subject from becoming too much an exercise in legal history:

legality and legitimacy.

That is the present form taken, in legal concepts, by the problem of obedience and resistance.1

27 November 1947

(To H. P. Ipsen:)

I have now been spat out by Leviathan three times.

So I am a kind of Jonah.

I now understand the unconquerable reluctance of that biblical prophet when God ordered him to preach repentance.

For my part, I prefer to remember the observations I made inside the belly of the fish.

Naturally, one of them concerns the question that was always asked whenever an interrogation turned into something resembling an academic discussion:

How was all of this possible?

My answer was always:

The key to answering your question lies in the concept of legality.

The Russian major understood the answer.

Carl Tobias:

a good pseudonym.

Primal positions based on basic states of existence.

28 November 1947

The fate of technology—that is, the fate of human beings who surrender themselves to technology—follows from the fact that technology first turns everything into a weapon.

But then the weapon itself ceases to be a weapon and becomes a pure means of annihilation.

A weapon is still a means by which forces measure themselves against one another.

The new thing is simply a means of destroying whatever has been declared worthy of destruction.

Coniuratio, the sworn conspiracy, as distinct from other sacred forms of oath:

“Whoever wishes the republic to remain safe, follow me.”

The oath ritual:

velut initiatis militibus—as though the soldiers had been initiated into a mystery.

Livy 10.38.2.

On this, Franz Altheim, “Lex Sacrata,” Welt als Geschichte 6, p. 420 ff.

So:

coniuratio = open civil war?

At its core, the narrower sworn brotherhood.

The confederates bound by oath.2

Max Weber’s forecasts:

  1. America — Russia.

Letter of November 1918, Collected Political Writings, 1921, p. 493.3

  1. Ahead of us lies “a polar night of icy darkness and hardness.”

“When this night slowly begins to lift, who will still be alive among those whose spring now seems to bloom so luxuriantly?”

Politics as a Vocation, p. 66.

Lecture, winter 1918–19.4

  1. “When the period of exhaustion is over, peace—not war—will have been discredited: a consequence of absolute ethics.”

Ibid., p. 57.

  1. “Anyone who wishes to act according to the ethics of the Gospel should, above all, not speak of revolution. Surely that ethics does not teach that civil war is the one and only legitimate war.”

Ibid., p. 57.

Of course!

Once war is no longer legal and legal wars come to an end, legitimate wars begin!

29 November 1947

How could I have allowed myself to be annoyed for even a second by Hans Barth’s petty human subordination and his article on Leviathan?

Among the shadows cast by the name Leviathan, one of which falls across my little book, there is also this touching little darkener.

He too eagerly carries over his tiny piece of blackout equipment, just as the old woman carried her piece of wood to the pyre of Jan Hus.

So here too, in response to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung:

O sancta simplicitas!

O holy simplicity!

Still, let us remain humane.

Let us not deprive the old woman of what gives her inner support, nor Mr Barth of his moral foundation.

Let him keep the background against which he defines himself through us Germans.

Say nothing against the Swiss!

How unbearable I found the polished, self-righteous tone in which Fritz Ernst spoke about his fellow Swiss, the statesman and historian Johannes Müller (Corona VII, 1937).

And yet that essay contained the wonderful sentence, concerning Johannes von Müller’s conflict with Jérôme in May 1809:

“No one knows in advance what he is capable of carrying, or what he will be willing to endure. The decision belongs to the mystery of the incalculable moment.”

How does a Swiss know things so true?

And why does he refuse to let them apply to us?

Or is this kind of generosity and wisdom merely an internal Swiss ethic that does not apply to Germans?

30 November 1947

Under the influence of Barion’s letter of 11 November, I feel a strong temptation to write a continuation of B.[enito] C.[ereno] on another level:

B. C. on Trial.

Perhaps its mood could be combined with elements from Franz Kafka’s novel The Trial.

Is this how B. C. should end?

In a Kafkaesque trial?

Horrible.1

B. C. charged with piracy before a court that refuses to permit any discussion of the “foundations” on which the case itself rests.

Will he step onto this carpet woven out of concepts?

Will he remain silent?

The problem of every political trial?

Before an admiralty court, he has a chance.

Before a special tribunal created to combat Spanish imperialism, he has none.

1 December 1947

Magnificent, Aldous Huxley’s comment in Time Must Have a Stop on the dying Hotspur’s lines from Henry IV, Part One, Act V:

Thought is the slave of life; life is time’s fool; and time, which surveys the whole world, must one day stop.

Thought is the servant of life.

But that philosophy of life is only the first sentence.

The thought continues:

life itself is the fool of time.

And time itself eventually ends.

Why should I not surrender myself to the comfort of these lines and to the Patinir-blue gentleness of this Advent evening?

I am not, after all, the owner of possessions belonging to this life whose servant my thought would then be.

I have no possessions.

I have only a domain:

as far as my eye and my thought can reach.

Others possess the domain of the hands, the manus.

Only darkness <…>.

I recognized myself and my own way of thinking in every sentence of Aldous Huxley.

What does this communication mean?

Certainly more than an exchange of letters.

Only do not try to turn your thinking into a possession.

2 December 1947

Popitz’s birthday.

This Prussian civil servant had something of Thomas More about him.

More too possessed the humanist gift for friendship.

Popitz could never have written a Utopia.

But perhaps he could have invented one.

More invented the genre of “Utopia.”

For that very reason, he himself could never afterward have written “utopias” in the ordinary sense.

The inventor cannot imitate himself.

Machiavelli could never have been a Machiavellian.

People of the Thomas More type no longer write utopias today.

What did Popitz invent?

No new literary genre, because he was not a man of letters.

But he had something of Thomas More’s humanist holiness.

He did not push himself toward martyrdom.

He gave way for as long as giving way was possible.

And when death became unavoidable, he remained cheerful.

Speaking of the title of Annie Kraus’s essay, I am reminded that an acquaintance of hers, Dr R., appeared in Berlin in April while I was still imprisoned and tore me to pieces.

But you know, Paul Adams, that I have never been one to spoil another man’s fun.

So let us not disturb him further in the enjoyment of his satisfactions.1

A true Brahmin feels pity for the tiger that eats him.

And a true sociologist feels understanding—or rather, “understands”—the proscription lists on which his own name appears.

And now I am reading in Baader that it can be proved to every human being that his greatest pleasure, even the worst one, is ultimately nothing more than an answered prayer.

Strange protective masks are growing inside us, allowing us to pass through Advent undisturbed.

3 December 1947

Today every physicist knows what in earlier times was clear only to good theorists of knowledge:

the object being observed is changed by the very act of observing it.

If that already applies to observation conducted with the exact methods of natural science, how much more must it apply to the kind of observation through which a trial court establishes the facts of a case:

through questioning witnesses,

statements by the parties,

open or unspoken presumptions,

and the assumed “foundations” of the trial itself, which no one is permitted to discuss.

The changes made to the object, the distortions of perspective created by the forms of the trial, must then become enormous.

In abnormal times, dealing with abnormal events, the result can only be falsification.

It becomes worst of all when amnesty does not arrive in time.

Minima non curat praetor.

The judge does not concern himself with the smallest things.

Maxima non curat praetor.

Nor with the greatest things.

Not too small and not too large.

Above all:

not too high and not too deep,

not too near and not too far.

Here too, in everything:

the “middle.”

Law exists only in the right place.

Why are the classes moyennes, the middle classes, the true sociological home of jurists?

What is the sociological home of the theologians of Scholasticism?

And what, therefore, did the removal of theology from legal science mean—especially in international law?

4 December 1947

Endlessly stirring up the rubbish bin again.

German pedantry as an obstacle to every reasonable amnesty.

At bottom, none of this interests either victor or defeated.

It interests only that third person who is both involved and uninvolved and wants to enjoy his entirely personal revenge.

Let him enjoy it.

5 December 1947

Amnesty too belongs to the primal foundations of anything that can properly be called law.

The dissolution and abolition of thing-like reality is at the same time the abolition of what has been posited and of law itself—which are the same thing—and the transformation of the world into pure action.

Fichte’s astonishing genius.

They are all geniuses.

The concept of genius is the great disaster.

Most revealing of all—most brilliant about brilliance—is Kierkegaard-Haufniensis in The Concept of Anxiety, pp. 97–100.

Richard Wagner’s genius too.

Pure action.

O God, all these brilliant arch-priests of the primal I that does nothing but act, that consists of nothing but activity.1

The “primal positions” contain the essence of finite things (!) in an eternal form.

They make up the ideal material from which God created the world.

Thus Böhme, Fichte, and so on.

Zeller, p. 727.

In criminalization there is a mismatch within the legal definition of the factual offence:

“war of aggression” is therefore the condition for making the legal consequences indefinite.

The “outlawing” of “war” replaces the atavism of war with the atavism of outlawry!

6 December 1947

To R. Stoedter:

You say that the mills of time are grinding more slowly than they did after the First World War.

In some respects that is true.

But in other respects they are grinding faster by exactly the degree to which the Second World War was deeper, more total, and more global than the first.

For example, the prohibition of alcohol—which was introduced without retroactive force—created less confusion and corrected itself more quickly than the abolition of war, which has been applied retroactively.

Another reliable measure is how deeply discrimination penetrates once it is based upon criminalization.

7 December 1947

The will to—

the right to—

and the academy for—

these are the three symbols of a world turned upside down, divided against itself and uncertain of itself.

8 December 1947

There is no fame anymore.

Instead there is more and more distribution of fame:

fame allocated through ever-new special awards that are discredited almost as quickly as they are given.

There are Nobel Prizes of every kind.

How childishly delighted the otherwise so critical André Gide becomes when he receives the Nobel Prize.

Like a schoolboy.

Better Drieu la Rochelle than that.

One key concept:

legality.

The other:

genius.

Together they provide the complete answer.

And for the idea of genius, the most important thing is Kierkegaard’s discussion in The Concept of Anxiety.

Enchanted by the superiority of the French esprit:

Rivarol says:

“An army used to enslave others is already itself enslaved, and the hammer receives as many blows as the anvil.”

Against the hammer-and-anvil ideology of the will to power!

9 December 1947

Again and again:

the Deus Absconditus, the hidden God.

Its opposite, incidentally, would certainly not be a Deus Publicus, a public God.

An inexhaustible source of opportunities for deception.

Tormenting uncertainty.

This, and nothing else, is also the starting point of Descartes’ question:

Who protects me from the spiritus malignus, the evil spirit?

And a powerful one!

Dreams cannot be translated.

Dreams cannot truly be put into words.

Every time you analyse a dream, you are analysing the words used by the dreamer rather than the dream itself.

You analyse the language the dreamer constructs out of his dream.

That is why dreams cannot be translated into foreign languages.

Translate your dream:

Cogito ergo sum—

sum, sum, sum—

buzz, buzz, buzz, little bee.

10 December 1947

The need for stimulation is the need for increased tension and release.

Accelerated movement.

Again and again:

Hobbes’s accelerated circulation of the blood.

In other words:

movement.

Whoever says movement really means intensified, accelerated movement.

Normal movement, like normal tension, is rest.

Read Gerhard Nebel’s essay “On Islands, Rivers and Mountains.”

So this was written in 1941, at the same time as my Land and Sea.

Why does that make me so sad?

Because he is young and I am old?

Is my little book not just as beautiful?

Just as original?

But only injustice ever happens to me.

I am hors la loi.

Outside the law.

An outlaw.

A foolish emotion.

11 December 1947

The opposition between is and ought is already dictatorship.

Kelsen’s intellectual lack of instinct.

You cannot—but you ought to!

That is why his democratic worldview is simply a false front.

O happiness of the gnat that still keeps hopping—

is that not supposed to be funny?

To Barion:

Keywords:

  1. Machiavellian.

  2. The boomerang from 1947 back to 1937.

We speak as infinitely experienced theorists, diagnosticians, and experts in conceptual ballistics in genere.

But I know very well that only a few judges, only a few prosecutors, and only a few people who become the objects of this ad consequentias producere—this carrying of every position through to its consequences—are actually capable of realizing it fully.

Still, even in our own case, we should remain before ourselves at the full height of our theoretical standard.

On Ebeling’s thesis that the essence of church history contradicts the essence of the Church:

nothing but—I do not want to say lies—but nothing but incompatibilities.

The final result of all these incompatibilities is that the essence of the Church becomes simply the “Wholly Other.”

It then contradicts everything human beings do under the name of an “essence.”

Indeed, it loses all connection with it.

The complete and absolute incompatibility of original Christianity with the entire world and—with particular emphasis from Kierkegaard—with everything human.

The “inhuman” quality of Christianity, as K. calls it.

But I would add one more point to my argument.

The Lutherans do bind themselves to the written Word.

B. replies that this is not a binding to the past because the understanding of the Word remains free at every moment.

But the same is true of the fixed words of the legislator, especially if—as Sohm himself said—the law is wiser than the legislator.

13 December 1947

More than ten years ago I came across the sentence:

“They have violated the spirit.”

It still comforts me today.

14 December 1947

Creation out of nothing is pure creation, creation unclouded by any admixture of material.

Every other act of creation is partly determined by the material from which it works.

But what is nothing?

Nothing can be said about that.

For most people, “nothing” is in reality merely the unlimited.

Creation would then mean:

setting boundaries and giving form.

The worldview of the potter.

I am losing my time and gaining my space.

Time must have a stop.

Away with the 1,800 years—or, for all I care, 18,000 years!

Enough of Utopia!

Aldous Huxley closes the age of Utopia.

Thomas More opened it.1

More can now be canonized, while Huxley—

“A nation”2

“can only be condemned out of her”3

“own mouth.”

15 December 1947

Deus sive Natura.

God, or Nature.

Natura sive Genius.

Nature, or Genius.

Genius = Nature, in the Romantic sense.

What a cabinet of curiosities! Та4

16 December 1947

I am losing my time and gaining my space.

But the moment I say this, piano tinkling from a radio next door begins sounding through the wall and teaches me that a space crossed by somebody else’s sound waves has already been destroyed as one’s own space.

The inaudible waves crossing my room are not consciously heard.

But I am conscious of them as something inaudible.

It is as though I were walking through a hail of invisible projectiles while experiencing this condition as peace and as my own space.

Our consciousness is not designed for this kind of knowledge.

But we cannot adapt ourselves to the new consciousness without destroying ourselves.

The elder Huxley already imagined that a sufficiently powerful intelligence could have predicted, for example, the state of the animal life of Great Britain in 1868 if only it had known the “cosmic vapour” in which the present world lay potentially contained—just as one might have predicted the breath visible on a cold winter day.

Bergson, Creative Evolution, p. 41.

“In a doctrine of this kind, one still speaks of time, one pronounces the word, but one hardly thinks about the thing itself.”

Creative Evolution, p. 42.

He sees the destruction of time.

The extraordinarily clear, lively, compact style of Gerhard Nebel may partly result from his work and experience as a schoolteacher speaking before intelligent young people.

Something similar is clearly true of unusual stylists such as Bergson in Creative Evolution and Oswald Spengler.

Successio, succession, as a specifically temporal process is itself only a change within spatial presence:

one contents of space replaced by another.

Successio imperii, succession of empire:

the identity of a space even when its location changes.

Byzantium to Rome.

The First, Second, and Third Rome.

Space can be transferred.

Space is an event.

Only events create space.

Space is property and duration.

“The only thing I inherit is my own body” means:

I possess no space.

I live in empty—or free—space.

Empty space and free space are the same thing.

There is no empty space.

But neither is there any completely full space.1

17 December 1947

Karl Marx says that the emancipation of the J.[ews] took place by turning Christians into Jews.

In the same way, assimilationists of Kurt Hiller’s type imagined not only emancipation but assimilation.

In the end, the whole village is supposed to mauschel—to speak and behave in what the antisemitic stereotype calls a “Jewish” manner.

<…>2

So what remains of the doctrines of Marx and Freud is a method and a technique for observing facts.

The “worldview” falls away.

But what was this “worldview”?

Nothing more than the generalizations, exaggerations, demonizations, and constructions of enemies that arose from the ambitions and social situation of a particular social group and elite.

The office of G. & K. appeared to me like Kafka’s Castle.

How is it that simple sacramentals—the sign of the cross, the ringing of bells—seem more essential to me than the official sacraments?

Have the former not yet been captured so completely?

Are they less capable of being captured and occupied by a hierarchical ruling authority?

Is this popular Christianity alongside institutional Church Christianity?

18 December 1947

Very clear:

the purity of Bruno Bauer’s original Christianity;

the purity of Kierkegaard’s existential life;

all of this is threatened, precisely in its purity, by a particular kind of enemy.

More specifically:

the slightest3 deviation from the purest4 purity is worse, more dangerous, more hostile than the open, brutal, clumsy opponent.

The microphysics of the political.

Compare Thomas Hobbes’s fury against clerics and professors, fighters for <…>ism.

The characteristic enemies of this kind:

professors,

j.[ournalists],

clergy,

priests.

Kierkegaard’s deadly hatred too:

of journalists.1

Intellectuals against one another.

A sociology of the intellectual as the “most dangerous” enemy.

The subtler an idea is, the more catastrophic its execution.

“Even the most sublime ideas are always carried out by savage beasts.”

Le peuple, the people, are—according to Rivarol—those who are au début de la vie, at the beginning of life.

The blank pages.

Democracy:

appeal to the blank page.

The man in the street.

The journalist:

the page that writes—and writes itself.

Dietrich Reinking, scholar of international law, Lutheran and loyal to the emperor (1590–1664), was arrested by the Swedes in Stade in 1645 and kept for four months in strict imprisonment.

Arthur Wegner, History of International Law, 1936, p. 192.

19 December 1947

To Gerhard Günther, in reply to his question about demonological literature:

Several times in my life I have gone on a similar search and eventually become stuck.

Baader contains several striking passages, but it is impossible to push much further.

Perhaps that lies in the nature of the subject.

I do not have Saint-Martin.

The literature of lower magic is barren and repellent.

What interests me far more is the hidden demonic force inside concepts from intellectual history that, on the surface, appear perfectly respectable in the salon and the lecture hall.

Above all:

the concept of genius.

Here the connection with the events of 1925–45 is immediately obvious.

Beyond that, all I can say is that, so far as I know, René Guénon is today the best-informed author on the subject.

On the katechon:

I believe in the katechon, the restraining power.

For me, it is the only way to understand history as a Christian and to find meaning in it.

Paul’s secret teaching is no more secret—and no less secret—than Christian existence itself.

Anyone who does not himself know, in concrete experience, something of the katechon cannot interpret the passage.

To Adso one must add Haimo of Halberstadt (Migne X.117, col. 779), who is Adso’s source and much clearer than Adso himself.

Today’s theologians no longer know this.

At bottom, they do not even want to know it.

What I really wanted to ask you was:

Who is the katechon today?

Surely one cannot regard Churchill or John Foster Dulles as the katechon.

The question is more important than the question of Jünger’s Chief Forester.

For every age of the past 1,948 years, one must be able to name the katechon.

The position has never been vacant.

Otherwise we would no longer exist.

Every great emperor of the Christian Middle Ages believed, with complete faith and conscious certainty, that he was the katechon.

And he was.

It is simply impossible to write the history of the Middle Ages without seeing and understanding this central fact.

There are temporary holders of this task.

Passing ones.

Fragmentary ones.

I am sure that we could even agree on many concrete names right down to the present day, once the concept itself became clear enough.

Donoso Cortés failed theologically because this concept remained unknown to him.

20 December 1947

Delusion everywhere.

That is almost harmless compared with:

deception everywhere!

Fraud everywhere!

Once every other deceiver has been discovered, and a human being finds himself alone, thrown back entirely upon himself, the stage of the worst deception begins:

self-deception.

That is where the age opened by Descartes now finds itself.

It was a spiritus malignus, an evil spirit, whose bottomless deception Descartes regarded as possible.

He shuddered before that possibility.
