“Primal positions”: they appear not in Fichte the father but in Fichte the son, in his metaphysics, where, as Eduard Zeller observes, “in substance they recall Böhme, as does his—Böhme’s or Fichte’s?—nature in God,” and so on.

Good old Zeller likes to lapse into Swabian.

I do not want to push biology so far that I import the son’s ideas into the father.

Nevertheless, your observation strikes me: in the later Fichte the father—whom the son consciously wished to continue—the act of positing by itself determines the basis of contemplation.

For me, as a Christian Epimetheus, that is especially revealing.

Then a reference to G. Nebel, On the Elements.

(In our present misery we occasionally need such stimulants.)

As for your essay, I naturally have no right to judge it quoad rem, on the substance itself.

But perhaps I may at least enjoy encountering the spirit of Joseph Schumpeter again after so long, and observing that his power to stimulate thought has not weakened at all.

My last conversation with Schumpeter took place in 1926/27.

At the end of my Concept of the Political, published in 1927, you can still find an example of that influence.

Even after being refracted several times through translation and quotation, I can still recognize his voice.

It is a great pleasure to argue with him.

One can feel that in your essay too.

(In a postscript I asked about Sauermann.)

Early this morning, around six, in the darkness and half asleep, I heard a factory siren and at the same moment saw the wide-open jaws of a large fish.

I would like to investigate this immediate simultaneity between an acoustic impression and a visual image.

It would probably tell us more than research into radar problems.

It would offer a glimpse into our inner sensory world.

People who no longer hear church bells but only factory sirens—are they supposed to believe in the God worshipped in churches?

They are more likely to believe in a very hard iron Moloch, and to seek salvation in the melting process of a furnace.

But as long as they hear both side by side—bells and wailing sirens—they will be helplessly torn between them.

They will waver.

They will be unable to decide.

And they will hang steel bells in their churches.

20 February 1948

Stay with Hobbes and do not move on to Bacon, even if Bacon really did have a hand in Shakespeare’s finest plays.

(I read Ernst Lewalter’s Bacon, 1939, last night.)

How small Bacon’s end seems.

How comfortable his life!

Not when compared with nineteenth-century jurists, certainly, but when compared with Hobbes: the solitary refugee without office or social position.

Bacon’s rise and fall resulted from court intrigues.

His defeat came through a miserable bribery case in which he played a pathetic role and then sadly humbled himself.

He was thoroughly well supplied with social, economic, and intellectual comfort.

He had debts, but he was never a fugitive.

His wisdom is court wisdom of the cleverest kind, but it does not come from existential fear.

He sends no signals to refugees and evacuees.

His despair does not seem to me as deep as that of Thomas Hobbes.

I have no wish to exaggerate the depth of Hobbes’s despair either.

But from my own situation I can understand that depth.

That is why I can admire and praise him.

With Bacon everything disappears into an impenetrable region where I cannot follow him.

The question is whether what lies there amounts to anything more than the secret arts of court life, and whether his mysteries are anything more than the secrets of a lodge.

Lewalter’s book is badly constructed and badly obstructs its own strongest quality: the light of a man who has a feeling for sources.

He wants to be interesting as a writer.

So instead of letting this fabulous material appear and work by itself, he arranges it.

He illuminates it with fake problems like “Shakespeare or Bacon” in order to interest the educated reader, and in doing so only produces an even greater disappointment.1

21 February 1948

Magnificent journey through the Bergisches Land.

The most precious receptiveness.

Gliding along on impressions and memories like a sailing boat driven by the finest wind toward the coasts of wonderful concepts and formulations.

“Finding definitions is part of the work of discovery,” says J. S. Mill.

And so I returned to Düsseldorf on 17 February 1948, and my memories of the years 1912–1914 were no longer merely subjective feelings.

They became approaches toward objective forces located there—forces that seized me at the time and, through their own power, determined which people I encountered and which events happened to me.

Those forces and radiations are still there, even beneath the ruins.

They cling to the ground.

They are part of the ground.

And that ground seizes me when I step onto it.

Hegel says in his Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Glockner edition, pp. 508–509:

Against the overwhelming power of armored knights, a technical means was discovered: gunpowder.

“Humanity needed it, and immediately it was there.”

There you have it.

So where does the atomic bomb come from?

Humanity needed it, and immediately it was there.

Let us hope the countermeasure appears as well!

And if, according to Hegel, the “higher courage” involved in firearms consists in the fact that one “shoots into the general,” at the abstract enemy rather than at particular individuals, then does dropping an atomic bomb raise both courage and abstraction into the transcendent?2

The so-called Second World War did not begin on 1 September 1939.

“The monstrous collapse of the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929 in reality meant the same thing for the coming world economic crisis as the Defenestration of Prague in May 1618 meant for the Thirty Years’ War. Yet official circles in America were already expecting a new prosperity in 1930.”

Thus Ernst Trendelenburg.

G. Ferrero called American optimism one of the pillars of European civilization—alongside English respect for law, French courtesy, and the German sense of duty.

Wicked optimism.

22 February 1948

It is almost tangible: the “superman” imagined in the nineteenth century is the machine, the motorized apparatus.

Only of the machine is it practically and literally true: supplet naturam—it supplements nature.

Faced with this enormous fact, the genius of Thomas Hobbes is astonishing.

Today, while reading Le Corps Politique (1653, Elzevir), chapter VIII, I was once again moved by his clean individualism and his consistent sense of reciprocity.

How noble and decent:

“C’est contre la loi de Nature que de vouloir presser les autres de prendre son avis ou conseil, si les autres le refusent … on peut avec raison tenir pour suspects semblables conseils.”

“It is contrary to the law of nature to press others to accept one’s opinion or advice if they refuse it … such advice may reasonably be regarded with suspicion.”

This whole chapter 4 is a model example of the identity of natural law and international law in relations between sovereigns.

Here, unsolicited advice is an insult and therefore an injustice.

It would be a task worthy of me to compare Hobbes’s extraordinarily tactful individualism with Spinoza’s and Max Stirner’s.

What keeps Thomas Hobbes so firmly together, while Stirner talks himself to pieces through ironic boasting about the ego, until the reader turns away tired and bored?

At best Stirner is amusing and roguish.

Toward the end the rhetoric becomes embarrassing—“I may say of myself”!!

The voice becomes a boy’s crowing.

Excellent observation by Günther Krauss: in the Oraison funèbre de Louis de Bourbon, the territory of the German Reich appears as land that can simply be occupied.

Today we are being divided as Poland was divided.

What a subject for international law!

And am I not supposed to become depressed when people come asking me for tips for memoranda in the style of Budde?

Perhaps it would be useful to reserve the word Landnahme—“land-appropriation”—for the occupation of land regarded as free for the taking, and to use “territorial transfer” for changes of territory within an already bounded legal order.1

23 February 1948

The key to the intellectual history lies with Rudolf Sohm—and with Below and Max Weber.

That also means that the German university is still Protestant.

It now seems very important to me that Rudolf Smend was the second examiner for Günther Krauss’s doctoral dissertation in Berlin in 1934.

Both Smend and Carl Brinkmann wrote to me in 1947/48 in a tactlessly forgiving tone.

I possess every charter and exemption certificate that the World Spirit can issue, and anyone who does not grant me that immediately cannot be my friend.

Performances of Mendelssohn, reverence for Heine, admiration for Thomas Mann: three cult forms of subjugation.

That would be a subject for Theodor Haecker, the great polemicist—for the old Theodor Haecker, meaning the young one.

24 February 1948

To Mrs. Jünger:

The portrait of Niemöller that you sent me is a revealing document.

As I happened to read in a newspaper, his OdF card—his official recognition as a “Victim of Fascism”—has been withdrawn, by Dr. Epstein, chairman of the OdF.

This is a useful lesson in the concepts underlying the whole system, especially the concept of the “victim.”

I found several letters from your Berlin friend Niekisch, especially one dated 25 September 1933 concerning my Concept of the Political.

What he said about it then differs so radically from what he says about it today that it seems like a break in all continuity of thought and personality—indeed, almost like mental illness.

After all, discontinuity is ultimately a form of mental illness, however great the human capacity for transformation may be, and however wildly Bacchic and fantastic the festival of metamorphoses becomes.

(The same accidens; compare 13 February 1948.)

26 February 1948

The final declaration that the gods have been deposed—the sentence that is not victorious, but is superior to every conceivable victory; the proudest sentence ever spoken by a human being as a human being, greater than every “God is dead”—comes from Lucan, the poet of civil war, and concerns those defeated in civil war:

Causa victrix diis placuit sed victa Catoni.

“The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.”

In other words:

history is no longer a judgment of God.

Vitoria’s seven—seven!—legal titles for the Spanish conquest of America are electrifying.

Even the order in which a Christian monk presents them is astonishing:

jus commercii — the right of commerce; jus praedicandi — the right to preach, or propagate the faith; jus protegendi Christianos conversos — the right to protect Christian converts; jus Christiani principis a Papa delegato et instituto — the right of a Christian ruler delegated and established by the Pope; jus interventionis contra tyrannidem — the right of intervention against tyranny; jus liberae electionis — the right arising from free election; jus protectionis socios — the right to protect allies.

The first two—commerce and propaganda—flow into one another and occupy nine-tenths of the whole argument!

At the end, the Spanish government is reassured that it will suffer no financial losses; that Roman imperialism did very well with these Christian titles; and that a facta conversio already exists—the accomplished fact of a Christianization already begun—which makes just wars effortless to justify.

The conclusion of the Primus titulus, the first title—septima conclusio: Hispani quando et in quo casu possent saevire in barbaros tamquam in perfidos hostes: the seventh conclusion, concerning when and under what circumstances the Spaniards may act violently against the barbarians as perfidious enemies—reveals the entire sinister logic of the “just war.”

The enemy is transformed into a convicted criminal.

The justus hostis, the legitimate enemy, becomes the perfidus hostis, the treacherous enemy.

The victor becomes the judge.

The defeated side is completely stripped of rights.

And all of this forty years after the fait accompli of violent conquest!

It is fortunate that this whole aura surrounding Vitoria was never analyzed by Karl Marx or Lenin.

That would have been very bitter.

I keep asking myself:

what does Vitoria actually want?

He plainly does not want to alter the political or economic outcome of the Conquista.

So what does he want?

He wants control of the argument so that he can retain intellectual leadership.

27 February 1948

To understand Silete Theologi—“Theologians, be silent”—one must know the great debate between Las Casas and Sepúlveda at Valladolid in 1550.

It stands in the entrance hall of the international law between states that stretches from Sepúlveda to Bodin.

Let us set aside the quality or persuasiveness of the arguments on either side and instead look at the existential situation of the men making those arguments.

Then one sees that this was the first great dispute in international law between a theologian and a non-theologian.

The theologian is not interested in the consequences for foreign policy—and for that reason he can easily practice a radical ethics of pure conviction.

He sees only the relationship between state and Church, not the relationship between one state and other states.

That is why he talks past his legal opponent.

The non-theologian sees the specifically political and state-centered side of the question, and the direct exercise of power.

A fascinating struggle between direct and indirect power.

(Today the type represented by James Brown Scott and Jackson would like to inherit the potestas indirecta, indirect power.

What an estate!

What heirs!

What a probate court!

More likely the Church will inherit them first.)

28 February 1948

But Sepúlveda is not yet a jurist.

He is still a humanist in the Erasmian style, even if he is not an Erasmian pacifist.

So when he argues against the theologian, his argument remains literary, philosophical, general, and based on a worldview.

Against the argument that the Indians are human beings, he argues that they are not.

Genuinely humanist.

In other words, he turns them into criminals and nonhumans instead of asking, like a jurist, whether they are enemies—and specifically whether they are enemies on an equal level, justi hostes, legitimate enemies—or what else they might be, and who has the authority to decide.

He argues just as unhistorically as Las Casas.

The connection between the concrete historical situation and the legal question does not become clear until Bodin, where it culminates in the concept of sovereignty.

With Sepúlveda, Silete Theologi was not yet due.

He really did not yet have the right to say it.

Public law can only be historical law.

It was a misfortune that Savigny was a private-law jurist.

A second misfortune: the thinker of public law, Hegel, was a philosopher.

And so, within the double opposition between private and public law on one side, and jurisprudence and philosophy on the other, everything could quickly be talked to pieces.

Compared with Hegel, Savigny was the concrete thinker—that is, the positive thinker, that is, the historical thinker.

But he had already been pushed aside into the purely historical.

Compared with Savigny, Hegel was the thinker of public law, but he had been pushed aside into philosophy.

And so intellectual leadership passed into the hands of the men of letters.

For me, as a jurist of the jus publicum Europaeum, the European public-law order, Bodin and Hobbes provide a better vehicle and better companions than the polarity of Savigny and Hegel.

1 March 1948

In party-political Germany, the festival of metamorphoses has for several decades been turning into a festival of false beards.

Most people think they have undergone a metamorphosis when all they have done is remove a false beard.

2 March 1948

My style rests on the inner completeness of each individual sentence, section, and so on.

Like the words in a Latin sentence, they can to a considerable degree be taken out and rearranged.

Incidentally, this is the opposite of a “mosaic.”

It is conceptual realism.1

I observe the events in Prague as a seismologist observes an earthquake.

Everything is unfolding in such a way that the model character of the German development of 1929–33 becomes obvious.

My book Legality and Legitimacy is the only scientifically adequate record of this typical sequence.

So now Beneš finds himself in Hácha’s role and discovers what that feels like.

Many more analogous exchanges of historical roles are still to come.

How can it be that neither a sociological nor a mass-psychological nor an economic study, but rather a legal and constitutional investigation like Legality and Legitimacy, captured the model character of events most accurately?

Because conceptual realism, properly applied as it is in the science of public law, is superior to every other kind of scientific contemplation.

Maurice Hauriou is more important to his age than all the others.

Who can resent my pride in my conceptual realism?

But what tragedy there is in the situation of the Czechs.

Under Masaryk and Beneš they had, with full awareness, chosen the West.

And now they are being taught that the problem of the Großraum, the greater political space, remains relevant regardless of changing political regimes.

If even the small Czech nation suffers so badly from making its choice too early, what would happen to us Germans if we rushed to choose between East and West and practiced a false decisionism?1

Resistance movements against yesterday’s enemy!

On that basis one can create new privileges, impose inferior status <…>, enjoy <…>.

Magnificent resistance against a dead enemy!

Magnificent resistance against an opponent who can no longer fight back, against a powerless man whom one can kick while he lies on the ground!

Gueydan:

le maquis est une création posthume.

“The Resistance is a posthumous creation.”

“I would only like to know whether this book—Legality and Legitimacy—as a scientifically adequate picture of a model situation and a model development did not achieve more, both in diagnosis and prognosis, than all the sociological, mass-psychological, philosophical, and other studies of those interesting years, years that already contained all the seeds of what followed.

I am very proud of my discipline, the science of the jus publicum Europaeum, and I am looking for a young person in whom I can awaken the same pride.

You have no reason to be ashamed of your discipline.”2

5 March 1948

Cuius regio eius justitia:

whose realm, his justice—and his judiciary.

Incidentally, the old formula cuius regio eius religio—whose realm, his religion—really means no more than what Hobbes says:

cuius jurisdictio eius religio.

Whose jurisdiction, his religion.

So do not be surprised by the submissiveness of the judiciary.

By abolishing the distinction between enemy and criminal, we have destroyed not only law but also the judiciary as a concrete order, as an ordo.

E. K.:

You are still fighting Versailles.

And now perhaps you will win that struggle in the same way that the Unknown Soldier of the First World War posthumously won the First World War that had been lost—while losing the second.3

Astonishing remark by Count Yorck to Dilthey, which I encountered again in Heidegger’s Being and Time:

“For the natural scientist, alongside science itself there remains only aesthetic enjoyment as a kind of human tranquilizer.”

A key to the essentially aesthetic culture of the nineteenth century, especially the Goethe cult in Germany.

For Yorck, Ranke is a great telescope, and so on.

How often I have seen all this and exposed myself to the hostility that such insights provoke in Germany.

On the concept of utopia:

What Heidegger calls our essentially spatial “Being-in”—our Being-in-the-world—is not denied in utopia.

On the contrary, it is affirmed with particular intensity in favor of some other Being-in, somewhere else.

That is the lie of utopia, which is becoming visible today.

One is entitled to ask whether a man who wrote such a utopia can really be a saint in the Christian sense.

That question is even more pressing than the question—raised, for example, around the canonization of Robert Bellarmine—whether someone who has written an autobiography can be canonized.

Heidegger becomes kitschy and banal when he squeezes every possible meaning out of words like “uncanny” (Being and Time, p. 188), and when the “everyday interpretation of existence in ordinary speech” is good enough for him not merely as evidence but even as an ontological-existential tool of interpretation.

His criticism of das Man—the anonymous social “they”—is perfectly ordinary criticism of the age.

A polemic against “the loud chatter of the common sense of the They.”

It remains a polemic.

And it remains on the level of a Protestantism that is not even especially deep, combined with moral seriousness of character.

By contrast, sentences such as “Silence is an essential possibility of discourse” are very beautiful—twice on p. 164, and again on p. 296.

There is also a primal Protestant feeling in the section on “ambiguity.”

But fundamentally all of this remains ethical and characterological, not ontic, and not even really ontological.

Perhaps to Rolf Stödter:

Under the impact of the model situation that I clearly recognized—and clearly described on p. 33 of Legality and Legitimacy, and that is presenting itself again these days in Prague:

G. Jellinek thought jurisprudence would lose its field in the Heraclitean flow of things, and Rolf Stödter agrees with him without reservation.

But this is merely positivist illusionism based on the status quo nunc, the present status quo.

It means abandoning every form of conceptual realism, even though conceptual realism is the very essence of legal thought.

Model realities are caught and given form within institutions.

So too are the dialectical oppositions to what Maurice Hauriou understands by equilibrium, équilibre: a state held in suspension.

But when one relates things to the death of Christ, one does not arrive at balances.

One arrives instead at connatural points of tension—fixed angles formed within existence itself.

A crown, for example, comes into being: a knot connecting a man and a family, followers and soil, withdrawn from the flow of superficial time without becoming something timeless and eternal beyond history.

This is a historically embodied formation, not an institution.

“Institution” is already too rational.

It already points toward constitution.

A man, a family—since when did we begin calling that a race?—a piece of earth, a historical moment, an event such as the Battle of the Lechfeld: these grow together into a connection that appears as a crown and can be borne by a human being.

La juridicidad es la lepra de los pueblos latinos—“Legalism is the leprosy of the Latin peoples.”

I read that in the essays of Pérez Bueno from 1921.

He wants to modernize Spain.

It is the Spanish counterpart to the French saying:

la légalité tue—legality kills.

At least he still says juridicidad, juridical-mindedness, rather than legalidad, legality.

6 March 1948

Space is magic.

Time is sorcery.

Speed is nothing but witchcraft.

Time flows.

Space stands or lies still.

Movement abolishes space by turning it into an empty container for the movement taking place within it.

7 March 1948

O mors, ero mors tua; morsus tuus ero, inferne.

“O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite.”

From the Lauds of Holy Saturday.

Innocens Deus occisus.

The innocent God slain.

This is my Christianity.

My love for the old images of the Crucifixion.

The wood of the Cross.

Holy Week.

8 March 1948

The mysterious mythology of Bacon.

For example: the fish Remora; the mention of Pan, who enters into no marriage and marries only his own Echo; the idola specus, the idols of the cave; and so on.

This is a major subject.

Important for Shakespeare and for Hobbes, who appears to lack this mythic sense completely—but who probably only suppressed it consistently, since the Leviathan is itself one enormous mythic image.1

How strange that Hobbes did not emerge in public until he was already a mature man.

What was going on inside him when he was young?

But let us stay with Pan, who can marry only his own Echo.

This is a symbol of post-Christian paganism returning to nature, of Goethean humanism, indeed of the whole German ideal of Bildung, insofar as it is aesthetically defined.

All the efforts of these ego-armored connoisseurs end in marriage to their own echo.

Why does G. F. Jünger omit this detail from his otherwise magnificent portrait of Pan?

Why does he forget Pan’s marriage to his own Echo?

Ah—but what drives these discoverers of Pan is only cultivated learning, not true panic terror.

The ego too can marry only its own echo.

It is incapable of any other marriage.

It is equally incapable of any other property—and of possessing its own grave.2

Marriage and property are both, for the ego, phenomena belonging to das Man, the anonymous “they.”

Now listen carefully to this sentence from Martin Heidegger:

“The They-self says ‘I—I’ most loudly and most frequently because, at bottom, it is not authentically itself and evades its own authentic potentiality-for-Being.”

(Being and Time, p. 322.)

9 March 1948

The magnificently desperate power of abstraction in Thomas Hobbes.

His desperate vis superba formae, the proud power of form, in the nominalist concept.

Conceptual power of the highest kind.

These are the great jurists of the age, just as Kepler and Galileo are its great physicists.

J. Vialatoux is merely an apologist.

He drives everyone else into the dead end of an either-or and then presents himself as the victor with “Love.”

In that case, give me Hobbes.

10 March 1948

W. Dilthey (Collected Writings, II, p. 150):

Bodin’s own view must still be established.

Mine too.

De nobis ipsis silemus, jurisconsulti.

Let us jurists be silent about ourselves.

Utopia: the puppet paradise of a Mozart composition.

Papageno’s little bells and the dancing Moors.3

Dilthey says on p. 323:

“From the social and ecclesiastical dreams active in the lives of the peasants, spiritualists, Anabaptists, and Savonarola (!) there runs a line of connection to the political novels of Thomas More and Campanella.”

This is intellectual-history clairvoyance.1

You can forgive a good man like Robert Mohl for using a phrase such as “political novels,” but not Wilhelm Dilthey.

He ought to have defined exactly the nature2 of the novel and of the novelistic:

the journey of a problematic individual toward himself.

G. Lukács, Theory of the Novel, p. 75.

Irony toward the realization of the ideal.

The element of irony is very strong in some utopias,3 for example Samuel Butler’s Erewhon.

In Campanella it is completely absent.

In Samuel Butler it is strongly biographical and is therefore, in that respect too, more genuinely a novel.

Erewhon is a utopian novel, not a pure utopia.

What is specifically utopian?

Humorless planning.

The irony and humor in More, Butler, and Huxley are English additions, not the essence of utopia itself.

The English, as individuals, are incapable of a pure and unconditional utopia because they are incapable of surrendering themselves unconditionally to a collective order simply as such.

For them utopia is a vehicle for criticism of the age, irony, and so on.

For the French utopians, it is bitterly serious and polemical.

11 March 1948

Today suicide contains a renunciation of the grave.

Or, to put it the other way around:

it is a conclusion drawn from the realization that the grave has been taken from us, that we no longer have a grave.

12 March 1948

What is a “crime against humanity”?

Are there crimes against love?

Murder is a crime.

Rape and , and so on.

But if we subtract all these concrete offenses, what remains as a pure crime of “inhumanity”?

A crime against God—humanity, or the Great ?

Godlessness turned into a crime?

A fine piece of Hitlerism.

What is the structure of the thing that can be protected or attacked by such a crime, when the crime is defined not through a precise description of an act but exclusively through its general hideousness?

Crimes against decency or reverence are, by comparison, still precisely defined.

I was disgusted yesterday evening when Max Weber bombarded me with heaps of material from the sociology of religion and a few crudely inadequate concepts such as opportunities for appropriation, journeyman-intellectualism, and so on.

How sad and ugly:

this boiling irrationality that continually convulses as it tries to cover itself with rational fig leaves.

The force of his honest scholarly self-discipline is an ethical merit.

But it is not yet a scientific achievement.

The essence of utopia is humorless planning.

Placeless = humorless.

Thomas More: an architect of socially rationalist constructions, softened by humanist learning and English humor.

Humor is wet.

Humor is maritime.

Every utopia should be tested by asking how it deals with graves and cemeteries.

Most of them will say nothing about them.

In a genuine utopia, only crematoria are permissible.

Utopia hollows out heaven.

13 March 1948

The great acts of placing and displacement now taking place in Prague.

The end of the younger Masaryk affects me deeply and completely personally, at that point within private life where the existential contact takes place between the great whole and the individual human being placed at the disposal of the World Spirit.

With Masaryk’s suicide, the European age in which one could choose between West and East comes to an end.

The elder Masaryk had been a true European katechon, a restraining force: the katechon of Western liberal democracy.

With an astonishing degree of historical consciousness—infinitely greater than anything the German politicians, philosophers, or historians of the time could summon—old Masaryk chose the West after the most thorough reflection.

He knew Russia and the East better than most Germans, Poles, or Serbs of his time.

He loved that Russia.

But his intellectual decision was for the West.

He married an American woman, and that marriage became a symbol larger than their private lives: the symbol of his choice of the West.

The son born from that marriage, who has now killed himself in Prague, was the guarantor of that Western choice, together with Beneš, whom Masaryk had designated as his successor.

And so this age now ends with the son throwing himself from a window of the Czernin Palace.

This is more than the earlier Defenestrations of Prague: that of the New Town councillors in 1419,1 and that of the imperial councillors in May 1618.

This is the Czechs’ own suicidal fall from the window, following the fall of the Germans and the many suicides of April 1945.

What wars will this third Defenestration of Prague set in motion?

I feel that this is one of those moments in my life when the personally private and the all-encompassing universal meaning of events coincide, and when God’s ordering shadow touches my small individual life.2

I must tell my daughter this so that I have a witness.

Just as Joseph de Maistre’s parents told their child, while he was playing, in 1772:

“Child, a great disaster has occurred. The Pope has dissolved the Jesuit order.”

How do I grasp the depth of this moment?

How long can I manage to remain at this depth?3

14 March 1948

I quickly read the Grewe–Küster discussion, Nuremberg as a Legal Question, Stuttgart 1947.

I suspect Grewe knows the legal opinion I wrote in the summer of 1945 on the international-law crime of aggressive war and the principle nullum crimen sine lege—no crime without a law.

However unpleasant Küster sometimes seems, and however cautiously Grewe conducts himself, a great deal becomes visible.

Not only questions and arguments that are properly legal.

Something infinitely more important as well.1

This discussion is evidence that we in Germany are sitting at the very core and center of the modern problem, and that we must work through this entire terrible problem within ourselves and with ourselves, without help from East or West.

We must carry out this whole monstrous “trial” inside ourselves—as an internal German matter and at the same time as a matter concerning the whole world.

Both disputants have the intellectual stature and the beginnings of what would be needed.

That is very important.

We must produce the enemy within ourselves so that we do not stand facing an empty void.

Because none of the arguments coming to us from outside can bind or convince us.

That becomes tangible precisely in Küster’s style.

We have been defeated.

Thrown to the ground.

Subjugated.

Quartered.

Trampled.

But in no essential respect have we been annihilated—not morally, and not legally.

We are occupied, but we have not been conquered.

Only someone who knows his booty better than the booty knows itself can truly conquer it.

So who in East or West could conquer us?

The military, technical-industrial, and economic giants who hold us on the ground and keep us subjugated do not even want to know us or learn about us.

They throw us to the émigrés to be devoured.

And the émigrés do not want to know us either.

They merely want to prove that the positions they held twenty years ago were right and to collect their compensation.

15 March 1948

The tu quoque—“you too”—reveals the murky kind of cleverness characteristic of people like Küster.

He continually mixes together the very things that he continually and cleverly claims to distinguish.

Naturally, an inhuman person has no right to reproach another inhuman person for also being inhuman.

But we, as observers and judges, certainly may conclude that it would not be justice if someone who himself commits inhuman acts appointed himself judge over another person and sentenced him to death as an inhuman being.

The moment I begin speaking of “inhumanities”—beyond the already recognized offenses of murder, robbery, and rape—I leave the sphere of institutional human law and legal positivism.

I enter the Hobbesian state of nature.

And there the tu quoque opens the judicial stage of the bellum omnium contra omnes, the war of everyone against everyone.

Then everyone becomes not only everybody else’s potential murderer, but everybody else’s criminal judge as well.

The murderers of one side sit in judgment over the murderers of the other and refuse to hear tu quoque.

The status naturae.

The state of nature.

16 March 1948

Two beautiful confirming quotations come running toward me like messengers:

  1. Max Weber’s diagnosis and prognosis:

“Under all circumstances, the unavoidable fate of the legal profession, as a consequence of technical and economic development, is an increasing tendency to regard whatever law happens to be in force as a rational technical apparatus—an apparatus without any sacred content and therefore capable at any time of being rationally redesigned for particular purposes.

This fate can be concealed by the growing tendency, arising for general reasons, to submit to existing law, but it cannot actually be averted.”

Who besides me spoke about this before 1933 and tried to do something about it?

  1. Friedrich Engels, in the posthumously published essay “Force and Economics in the Formation of the German Empire,” written in 1888:

Bismarck had “proved” to the German bourgeoisie “that he knew better than they themselves did what was good for them.”

That is my beloved Bruno Bauer quotation of 1849!

Wrote Veronica a postscript about my Legality and Legitimacy.

Compare 2 March 1948.

17 March 1948

Balzac:

The Art of Being a Victim.

Quoted by Günther Krauss.

18 March 1948

Wave and particle, representation and nominalism appear at the same time in intellectual history and apparently belong together in some topological and wave-like sense.

Veritas in verbo (dicto), non in re.

Truth lies in the word—in what is said—not in the thing itself.

Presence and conceptual realism.

Nominalism:

not presence, but making something present within consciousness—something absent, or better, something that is not actually there.

Dictatorship and nominalism:

the dictamen, the command or authoritative pronouncement.

Veritas in dictamine, non in re.

Truth lies in the command, not in the thing.

“Objective necessity.”

The re- in representare seems to contain an overcompensating urge to intensify, an urge that accompanies the feeling that something is not real.

It does not simply mean “back.”

But perhaps it originally connects with tendencies toward restoration.

19 March 1948

Sociology from the standpoint of the dispossessed:

the antechamber takes possession of the salon;

the caretaker takes possession of the villa;

the former inmates of the prisons become the new rulers;

the enemies win and now appear as victims, demanding compensation and bonuses for martyrdom.

The reverse would be sociology from the standpoint of those who have arrived.

But the successful rarely practice sociology.

Sociology apparently is an “oppositional science.”

The intellectual curiosity it presupposes is already highly suspicious.

The victor feels no intellectual curiosity.

21 March 1948

From Germany’s point of view, the Second World War was not merely a war on two fronts.

It was also a war combining two kinds of war.

H. tried to wage two different wars—and it was clumsy beyond belief to imagine this could work:

a nondiscriminating war against the West;

and a discriminating war against Russia and the Slavic peoples.1

For that reason, the true answer came from the East, from Russia.

The master of the Nuremberg Trial was the Soviet Union, which made use of American moral outrage.

Russia’s role in the Nuremberg Trial—I mean only the great main trial before the International Military Tribunal, which was intended as the fundamental trial—became clearly visible in the way the Katyn case was handled, in Rudenko’s shot at Hermann Göring, and at various other moments in the proceedings.

The only real question is whether Germany belongs to the Russian or the American Großraum, the greater sphere of intervention.

The Czech question too concerns the Großraum problem in international law—in other words, the question of the intervention sphere.

Apart from that:

an empty stomach has no ears.

22 March 1948

The great Cisneros founded the University of Alcalá, opened in 1510, without a law faculty.

Nam a civilibus et forensibus studiis adeo natura sua abhorrebat, ut multi serio affirmantem audiverint, quicquid illius disciplinae pectore concepisset, se si fieri posset libenter evomiturum.

“For by nature he so recoiled from civil and courtroom studies that many people heard him seriously declare that, if it were possible, he would gladly vomit out everything of that discipline that he had taken into his breast.”

Alvar Gómez de Castro, De rebus gestis a Francisco Ximenio Cisnerio, Alcalá, 1569.

On his mépris de la chicane, his contempt for legal hairsplitting: Marcel Bataillon, Érasme et l’Espagne, 1937, p. 14.

The university had a chair of nominalist philosophy.

Duns Scotus stood beside Thomas Aquinas on equal terms as a classical theologian—in contrast to Salamanca.

The three careers that led to wealth in Spain at the time:

iglesia, mar, casa real—

the Church, the sea, the royal household.

25 March 1948

I am now more than Thomas Masaryk.

27 March 1948

Found a note from 14 December 1913, Düsseldorf:

Sohm is a Marcionite.

Also, from Harnack, History of Dogma, 4th ed., I, p. 651 n.:

Basil, in Epistle 210 ad prim. Neocaes., explains a troubling passage in Gregory Thaumaturgus by saying that the remark was made not δογματικῶς, dogmatically, but ἀγωνιστικῶς, in the course of struggle or argument.

And Jerome, Ad Pammachium, Epistle 48, chapter 13, proclaims the right to write γυμναστικῶς—gymnastically, as an intellectual exercise.

30 March 1948

What is Hermann Kasack’s The City Beyond the River?

An afterlife?

No.

It is the emptying-out of the former world on this side, produced by the shock that has shattered bourgeois existence, by the loss of security, and by the removal of the industrial-economic foundation.

That is still a very long way from gaining access to the world beyond.

It is merely the shadow of the world we already had here.

Even Wilhelm Ahlmann appears in Kasack only as a puppet, not as a figure with any substantial inner life—not even as the shadow of his soul.

Deeply disappointed by the second part of Kasack, p. 290 onward.

Here he becomes a caricaturist—with a license number.1

To Pascual Jordan:

I observe the following:

the weak individual becomes completely <…> strong the moment he receives political power.

He becomes <…> invested.

What is this disproportionate increase in power that occurs with every political position?

What is this monstrous increase in effective potential that comes with the decision of an “objective power”?

It is completely “irrational.”

More fantastic than all the already fantastic disproportions between microphysical acts of control and gross macroscopic effects in physics.

“This comes from God,” pious people say.

These are divine forces and powers, thrones and dominions.

But one soon sees that “objectivity” can also be filled by forces that are anything but divine.

The monstrous disproportion between the power of the individual and the objective power remains the same.

Where are the managers located?

The elite?

The innermost central power group?

Is there an image from physics that can describe this?

Or must one suspect that the whole of your modern physics is itself only a precisely constructed, experimentally mounted reflection of sociological reality—the reality that today enters our existential consciousness through concepts such as “elite,” “innermost central power group,” and so on?

1 April 1948

The deepest, deadliest, and most common of all sins:

continuing the struggle against an enemy who has already been defeated.

Fighting yesterday’s enemy, who no longer exists, so that one does not have to face the real and present enemy of today.

This is the ugliest form of continuing the war.

At the same time, it is the most contemptible form of cowardly evasion and the most dishonest form of pacifism.

Keep kicking at the crimes of the defeated, armed with all the licenses granted by the current victor.

The victor secures immunity for his own crimes by appointing himself judge over the crimes of the defeated.

2 April 1948

Eventually they will make Christ himself an O. d. F.—a “Victim of Fascism”—and tolerate his cult on that basis.

That is the friend-enemy distinction.

How touchingly static and mechanical this is:

δός μοι ποῦ στῶ.

“Give me a place to stand.”

The point is no longer to lever the world off its hinges, but to “change” it—that is, to infect it.

The poû stō, the place on which to stand, is nothingness.

Utopia.

Read several notes from the spring of 1933.

Conclusion:

Stare decisis.

Let the decision stand.

A cloud of memories.

An electron-world of numinous meanings and feelings.

A Pleiades of significations.

A Milky Way of symbolically glittering concepts.

To Heinrich Weinstock, with a copy of my lecture of February 1941:

The introduction to Thucydides is in fact a Historiographeia in nuce—a theory of historical writing in miniature.

(Remember my note on Tocqueville, and Hobbes’s introduction to his translation of Thucydides.)

Hobbes, with his overpowering objectivity, belongs to that glorious chorus.

3 April 1948

(To Wilhelm Grewe, concerning the discussion of Nuremberg as a legal question and his accompanying letter:)

I have read your remarks with the greatest care and have come to the conviction that something infinitely more important becomes visible here, far beyond the expert precision of your argument:

namely, that we in Germany still stand at the center of thought, and that we must work through the most terrible problems entirely within ourselves, without any help from West or East, Right or Left.

We are carrying out a trial within ourselves:

subjugated,

quartered,

trampled underfoot,

and yet “annihilated in nothing.”

The intellectual achievement and style of your argument show me that neither West nor East can today boast that it knows itself, us, and the present world better than we know that world and ourselves.

That is the general impression I received from reading your argument.

Your remarks are, of course, framed within a discussion and therefore contain all the considerations, restrictions, reservations, tactical advantages and disadvantages, and everything else that such framing necessarily brings with it.

You have managed to secure a considerable amount of room for your own line of thought.

But in the end the whole thing still appears as a discussion.

And it is neither my place nor appropriate for me to take part in it.

I do not count occasional curiosities as participation—for example, the involuntary recollection that the passage from 2 Samuel 12:5 cited by your opponent on p. 73 is used by Hobbes as an example of a tyrannical desire to kill and of a violation of the principle nulla poena sine lege, no punishment without prior law.

So I remain outside the discussion.

I therefore want only to indicate two things about what you say.

First:

I consider your question about the Gerichtsherr, the actual authority standing behind the tribunal, on p. 10 to be essential, and I think one can insist upon it even in this introduction.1

It would be revealing to ask historically, sociologically, and psychologically who the real master—or masters—of this proceeding actually were.

That question forced itself visibly enough upon the whole world in the treatment of the Katyn case.

It may also touch upon the strange fact that the supposed aggressor liked to imagine that he could still wage a old-style war toward the West, while toward the East he believed he could afford a discriminatory war <…>.

Two fronts also meant <…> two kinds of war.

And second:

I consider it a great and decisive methodological achievement that you separate the question of criminalizing aggressive war as such from the question of the other crimes—inhumanities and war crimes—and that you state this distinction consciously, clearly, and forcefully, raising it to the level of a basic principle on p. 99.

Without that distinction there can be no scientific discussion of the trial, either as a whole or in its individual parts.

Nor can there be any legal understanding of an offense as new and difficult as aggressive war, with all the new problems involved in precisely defining the prohibited act, identifying the circle of possible perpetrators, and determining the relation between earlier definitions of “aggression,” which had been conceived in purely terms, and the substantive problem of responsibility for war and the justa causa belli, the just cause of war.

And then there is the entire problem of <…> forcing one to jump <…>, which is far too to be thrown out into the street.

The problem of creating new crimes and new penalties must trouble every thoughtful jurist who knows what has already happened in the legal history of civil war.

Beginning with “heresy” and “tyranny”—along with fine related offenses such as flattery and favoritism.

Then the modern dissolution of criminal law into the extermination of pests and troublemakers.

And finally the biological criminalization of illness in Samuel Butler’s Erewhon, something we hardly dare laugh at anymore after our own experiences.

The victorious Northern states committed horrifying atrocities in 1864.

But apparently they neglected to declare the slaveholders retroactive criminal offenders.

In future civil wars, people will probably not make that mistake.

That you separate this great problem—the criminalization of aggressive war as such—with complete clarity from other kinds of crime is an important achievement. Given the present situation, doing so requires as much tact as intellectual and moral courage.

I say this to you openly and without hesitation, especially as I remember our mutual friend Wilhelm Ahlmann, although, as I said, I cannot take part in your discussion myself.

So, with thanks, I confirm that I have received what you sent me. With every good wish for you and your work,

Yours, [C. S.]1

4 April 1948

On 4 April 1948, while sunk in the most helpless depression, I was suddenly and comfortingly distracted by the discovery of an astonishing phrase. Goethe’s genius for language—which never stops astonishing me—had tossed it off casually, almost in passing, in a letter to Johann H. Meyer dated 6 June 1797.

He says that in Wallenstein, when all is said and done, everything depends on the mass of the army itself—yes, the army as a mass—which no longer remains with Wallenstein “as soon as he changes the formula of service.”

I could hardly believe my eyes or ears.

I have never come across anything more exact on the subject of legitimacy and legality, because the phrase captures both things at once: the sheer weight of the mass, and the apparently formal nothingness of a mere formula.

So there it is:

Change the formula of service!

(And incidentally, Goethe is magnificent on the question of exposition: an exposition must not simply communicate the facts. It must be designed to convey the full breadth of an existence and the mood surrounding it.)

There is an orchid that makes itself look ugly, like a blowfly, in order to protect both itself and the honey it produces from actual flies.

Did that do you any good?

Actually, yes.

What is all this talk supposed to mean?

No one will give up the criminalization of the enemy if it proves to be an effective weapon.

But in the hands of the West it is not an effective weapon, and cannot be one.

If the West handles its atomic bombs as amateurishly as it handles this weapon—the criminalization of the aggressor—they will be more likely to fall on its own roof than even to touch the real enemy.

5 April 19481

To G. Nebel:

I can read Kasack’s The City Beyond the River only as far as Part II, Chapter XIII, p. 290. Then it suddenly turns into caricature and anti-literature. A pity.

The first part very successfully brings Kubin’s The Other Side and Kafka’s The Trial into the world of 1943–44.

Why do all these gifted writers refuse to listen to Ernst Jünger’s warning against every polemical word?

If polemic is no longer directed immediately and completely against a strong enemy who is fully present and has you directly by the throat—as with Léon Bloy or the young Theodor Haecker—but instead against a dead enemy, it immediately begins to squint sideways and is poisoned by the corpse-toxin of the dead enemy.

Later, when I have recovered from the shock of my disappointment, I will continue reading. I hope I will then also be able to judge the appearance of Wilhelm Ahlmann properly.

Léon Bloy’s influence on Ernst Jünger is an extraordinary problem.

Jünger could approach Bloy, the “pariah,” with his savage hatred of Protestants, Prussians, and Germans only by overcoming the strongest possible revulsion.

But Bloy’s diaries are also a prototype for the whole form of the “diary.”2 I could even say that they helped create the form.

With one stroke they leave behind all that Romantic and impressionistic rummaging through the soul. They make it impossible to confuse “radiations” with “reflections,” and they give the aphorism a concrete situation instead of letting it flutter away into emptiness.

Bloy’s secret was symbolic interpretation.

What is magnificent for me—unexpectedly so, beyond anything one could have calculated—is that Ernst Jünger can appear, in this respect, as Léon Bloy’s heir.

Theodor Haecker had long since lost his strong claim to that great inheritance.

But the profiteurs de Léon Bloy—the people who profited from Bloy—such as Claudel, or still more Maritain, threw the inheritance into the street. In return they received the miserable sinner’s wages of satisfying their hatred of a Germany that had already been trampled underfoot.

The baseness of that hatred makes both of them ripe for the curse of today’s pèlerin de l’Absolu—the pilgrim of the Absolute.3

6 April 1948

To H. Barion, referring to W. Grewe and the discussion of Nuremberg as a legal question:

I ask him to read it,

“so that you will understand why it matters to me that my memorandum on the criminalization of aggressive war was already complete in the summer of 1945, before the indictment was brought.4

It stands as a record of the considerations that any lawyer with the necessary expertise could and should already have made at that time—and which one discriminated German lawyer actually did make, without concealing them from anyone, not even from the CIC [Civil Internment Camp].”

That seems important to me.

For the sake of the German name, and for every lawyer anywhere in the world who thinks scientifically. Also for the honour of the legal profession itself.

Defamed, discriminated against, dismantled, contaminated, underprivileged on every side.1

7 April 1948

In a dream I say to the Englishman:

You are free?

You are ripe!

Riper even than the Frenchman.

Ripe for the final coup de grâce, like Tsar Nicholas of Russia.2

Your last move was to accept the unconditional surrender in Schleswig-Holstein, although you had no right to do so. You did not bring about that surrender. The Russians and Americans did. It was not you, but the Russians and Americans, who were masters of both the conflict and what was at stake in it.

The whole argument becomes murky when I think of H. S. Chamberlain.

Wonderful, the Shakespeare passage Günther Krauss copied into his diary Captivitas:

“It is enough for us to know that we are the king’s subjects. If his cause is wrong, our obedience to the king clears us of the crime.”3

“Here lies” is the final part of his story. —Daniel Defoe.

Certainly:

Here lies.

But where does Hitler lie?

Where do those people lie whose ashes an uncomprehending hunger for revenge scattered across the whole world, in the most un-Christian ignorance of the song:

The ashes will not rest, they scatter through every land?4

Could they, through the stupidity of their enemies, have escaped the grave?

Very good, Günther Krauss’s question:

Defeated in the name of Christianity, we ask ourselves where this Christianity is actually to be found.

8 April 1948

To Arnold Gehlen:

I respect the fact that there is a general fear of a contagion de l’infortune—a contagion of misfortune.

That respect even gives me a kind of belated satisfaction in my present status, and allows me to draw something useful from my existence as a peripsēma—an outcast, something cast away.

I say satisfaction in my status, because I can no longer claim the honour that once belonged to that status.

On your question about when the idea of “vested rights” was born:

Taken as a whole, the end of vested rights naturally begins when law is transformed into positivist legality.

“Acquired” then simply means légalement acquis—legally acquired—and a single stroke of the legislator’s pen can turn not only whole libraries into wastepaper, but whole paradises of securely acquired rights into piles of rubble.

Modern lawyers have long since begun speaking instead of a situation établie—an established situation—or something similar.

The heart of the problem lies in the relationship between legality and legitimacy.

See my 1932 essay5 and the question above from 2 March 1948.

9 April 1948

Arnold Toynbee (International Affairs, November 1947) attempts the feat of finding a third position, a third force, a third path between capitalist America and communist Russia without becoming fascist.

He wants to make Western Europe an independent third factor without allowing Germany to recover its strength.1

Europe must not try to become strong again, because Germany might then become strong again.

Better for Europe to perish than for Germany to rise again.

All of this is stated perfectly clearly while remaining peaceful, Erasmian, and never quite spoken outright.

What an immensely cultivated and twisted mind!

In the service of a twisted disposition!

What he calls Western Europe—and from which Germany is excluded—is a bourgeois society in the same social position as the German bourgeoisie in 1919: an intermediate stage between capitalist prosperity and the impoverishment of the underprivileged peoples of Asia.

Germany belongs completely among the underprivileged.

So according to Toynbee, Germany has only one option left:

Russian communism.

He is the Spengler of the postwar age after the Second World War, just as Churchill became the Clemenceau of the Second World War.

No katechon.2

10 April 1948

So Claudel has discovered that Germany is the protection and shield of Western Europe against eastern communism (Le Présent, 19 March 1948).

Others had already discovered that when it was not yet too late.

If even Luther in Wittenberg could be called “the soft-living flesh of Wittenberg,” then how should one address Herr von Goethe in Weimar?

Hobbes used to say that it was lawful to use bad instruments for one’s own good.

“If I were thrown into a deep pit,” he said, “and the Devil lowered his cloven hoof down to me, I would grab hold of it and let him pull me out.”

From the biographical introduction to the 1750 edition.3

Still Toynbee:4

They are all guilty of the same thing.

They want to prevent their neighbour from growing stronger.

First France tried to hold down biologically stronger Germany.

Then Germany tried to hold down biologically stronger Russia.

Now England, too, wants to hold down Germany and Russia at the same time.

With almost mathematical and physical certainty—and in any case with moral and philosophical-historical certainty—the result will be the liquidation of all of them by Russia.

The most relevant reading today is a history of the age of the Diadochi, the beginning of the Hellenistic period.

For example, Plutarch’s biography of Demetrius Poliorcetes:

wild immoralities and violent reversals of fortune, like Adolf’s life—“my life is a novel.”5

More interesting than the history of the Caesars, who already sit on top of a fully organized machine of power.

The fantastic theatricality of it all.

The pluralism of these successor-states, no longer capable of unity.

Because unity simply for the sake of unity is something for the sort of people Hegel describes when he says:

the uneducated person thinks abstractly.

Which today means:

globally.

11 April 1948

Ernst Jünger says, on the occasion of Arnold Toynbee being brought into the great American defence council, that philosophers of history are now more important than atomic physicists.

Of course.

As the man who diagnosed the discriminatory concept of war and the transformation of war between states into civil war, I am not surprised.

One becomes even more conscious of Spengler’s genius when comparing him with Toynbee.

But Spengler talks too much about Cretans, Hittites, and periods he never experienced himself, but constructed only through parallels, analogies, and similarities.1

His universal world history is an imperialist annexation of the past.

Excavation becomes triumph and conquest.

Tocqueville is more modest, purer in contemplating his own fate.

Toynbee is both things at once, an English and superior synthesis, but without genuine strength and concerned above all with preventing Germany from rising again.

Perhaps this type of historian has existed only since Versailles in 1919:

philosophers of history belonging to decline.

Neither victors nor defeated.

Here a third kind of participant writes history.

And Toynbee’s construction of a “third” between West and East—a weak third force whose only purpose is delay—corresponds exactly to this position: the third party sitting between the two sides, the weaker third, the defeated victor.

Very sad.

And for us—and for me personally—very dangerous.

No true Erasmus.

No pure Alexandrian.

Simply attached to the great power, not on the command ship itself but being towed behind it.

Where, incidentally, is Eugen Ott?

Isn’t it time he appeared?2

(Addition, 8 September 1951: after reading Der Spiegel on Erich [actually Richard] Sorge: oh God, oh God.)

12 April 1948

Europe is a balance between land and sea, between oceanic and continental existence, with ports opening both onto the ocean and onto inland seas.

The transition from sailing ships to machines destroyed that balance.

The airplane belongs to the sea in its function as a vehicle, but its advantages ultimately go to the space of the land.

The law governing the seizure of ships and cargo on the high seas arose under the conditions of sailing navigation. It cannot simply continue unchanged in the age of airplanes and radar.

That would be like taking rules written for the use of pistols and applying them to atomic bombs.

Russia is land.

But the United States is not sea.

The ship called England is not being towed behind a salvage tug.

It now sits inside the force field of a remote-control system.

13 April 1948

To Ernst Jünger, asking him to pass on my greetings to E. Peterson in Rome:

You write about Arnold Toynbee and the relationship between philosophers of history and atomic physicists.

Of course.

With discriminatory—or “just”—war, meaning the transformation of war between states into civil war and the declaration of the enemy as a criminal, the importance of philosophers of history and augurs necessarily rises.

Undermining an opponent through civil war, and shaking his confidence in his own historical meaning, becomes correspondingly a stronger weapon than the atomic bomb.1

I recently read Toynbee’s diagnosis from November 1947, in a lecture published in International Affairs.

He asks about a third force between West and East and rejects the idea that Europe should become strong again, because Germany would then become strong again too.

“In a European Union excluding the USA and the Soviet Union, Germany must sooner or later, by one means or another, come out on top,” etc.

For him this “German crux” is “an insurmountable obstacle to the construction of a European Third Power.”2

So he would rather let Europe sink and search for a third force without any force.

I had a very interesting conversation with him in 1938.

Incidentally, he has none of Spengler’s flashes of genius.3

On the Dreyfus affair, you should sometime read Léon Bloy, Méditations d’un Solitaire, 1916, p. 211:

“There are fortunate periods for the Devil.”

I feel about the affair much as you do.

Until now I thought this was because lawyers had narrowed the whole issue down into procedural questions surrounding a trial.

But the Nuremberg trials do not seem to possess the same power to electrify people.

14 April 1948

Georges de Lagarde, Recherches sur l’esprit politique de la Réforme (1926):

a rather facile champion of order who becomes annoyed by the contradictory claims of the Reformers.

He has a legal mind.

A good sentence:

“The sovereignty of the state is now”—after Christianity has become entirely inward, the Church has become a state church, and Sohm has been proved right—“truly exclusive, truly ‘territorial’” (p. 304).

Territorial.

The totality of the temporal.

Transfer this to the entire earth, and what results is not merely a wider but, through the dropping of the atomic bomb, also a deeper temporality, territoriality, and totality.

15 April 1948

Sohm II, p. 233.

A list of the contaminated, used to determine which groups were to be discriminated against after victory:

Even in the third century, not only actors, charioteers, gladiators, hunters, sculptors—when they made images of the gods—executioners, brothel-keepers, and magicians, but also schoolteachers, because they worked with pagan literature, and above all soldiers and people who exercised the state’s power to punish, were excluded from membership in Christianity.

Yes: Christianity.

“A soldier could not at the same time be a Christian; a public official of the pagan Roman world empire could not at the same time be a member of the people of God.”

Take less than 1 percent freedom.

Stir it thoroughly into a 40 percent claim to social responsibility.

Add less than 9 percent Christianity.

And do not forget to reserve the remaining percentage for an exception that cancels out everything you have just added.

Then you have turned wood-pulp paper into a new German constitution.

A newspaper clipping from the FAZ of 29 September 1953 pasted in.

On the left: the astrological sign of Jupiter, drawn in red.

On and beside the clipping:

“On the book by James P. Warburg, Germany, Key to Peace, [Cambridge] 1953.”

Rikus:

Wood and stone are not matter but the breath of creation.

The modeller works with clay and earth, kneading them freely, arbitrarily, with brilliant, speculative, fantastical freedom.

The sculptor in wood and stone works by overcoming resistance and making use of it.

(But after speaking of the breath of creation, this image no longer fits its own form!

Phrases.)

17 April 1948

Read Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen, whose manuscript G. Nebel gave me yesterday in Wuppertal.

I accepted it, although I had reservations about receiving it from anyone other than Jünger himself.

The entry for 14 December 1943 in Kirchhorst, referring to my letter about the breakdown between protection and obedience during air raids:

“Among all the minds I have known, C. S. is the one who can define things best.”

Yes.

But my concepts are not affected by the opposition between image and concept that Jünger otherwise maintains.

I do not know whether, as a natural scientist, he fully understands me here.

Very good, Jünger’s historically concrete description of my individual situation:

“As a classical legal thinker”—I do not like the word Rechtsdenker, legal thinker; “classical” is the right word—“he belongs with the Crown, and his position necessarily becomes crooked wherever one batch of the demos replaces another.”

Very important and correct that he mentions the Crown, and therefore legitimacy.

A correct intuition of the suggestions I gave Condé and Franco:

make a crown.

“When illegitimate powers rise, a vacuum remains where the first jurist of the Crown once stood, and any attempt to fill that vacuum comes at the cost of one’s reputation. These are simply occupational misfortunes.”

Yes.

And many thanks for the correct diagnosis!

18 April 1948

Apart from that, I personally dislike many compound words formed with the German genitive form Rechts-—“of law.”

Rechtsdenken, legal thinking.

Rechtsraub, robbery of rights (4 September 1943).

You cannot leave out the linking s, yet somehow you cannot properly leave it in either.

There is an interesting duality in Jünger’s diary, perhaps one he himself has not noticed.

On the one hand:

style is law and justice (17 February 1942; similarly, though only implicitly, 16 July 1943).

On the other:

only authors trained in the natural sciences write good prose (around 1943–44).

Once you make the usual methodological separation between the natural sciences and the humanities, this really is a contradiction, and a symptom of beginnings that have not been thought through to the end.

First: let me anticipate the obvious cheap criticism of this diary.

There is too much private material.

Too much Burgundy.

Too many orchids.

Too many women doctors.

Too much luxury.

And too many military situation conferences.

There is always a danger in mentioning luxurious states of mind and small personal encounters.

A dash of Pepys runs through the whole thing, either to the reader’s personal delight or to his outrage, depending on the prejudice with which he approaches Jünger himself.

How can the book be protected from that cheap kind of criticism?

Or would it actually be useful—painful though it might be—to let cheap malice spit itself out?

I can already hear the screamers from the red gas-hell.

Second, a more serious criticism:

I have reservations about some of the pious and Christian passages, especially those connected with his reading of the Bible.

It is difficult to find the right style here and completely avoid a certain smell—whether the external smell of the sacristy or the inward smell of a private devotional chamber.

Even Léon Bloy sometimes falls into that smell.

Here Jünger is inexperienced, too innocently military.

He lacks the practical self-corrections needed against those invisible, tasteless clouds of poison gas that have attached themselves to every word and turn of phrase in this whole sphere.

From one side they come from hypocrisy, bigotry, sugary piety, sacristy routine, and Bible routine.

From the other they come from the irony of critics, parody, and Enlightenment mockery.

And the two sides penetrate each other irresistibly.1

19 April 1948

Third:

the memoir-like character of these diaries.

Memoirs from Beyond the Grave.

Or:

Memoirs from Beyond the Flood.

Futurist phonetics.

Phuturist fonetics.

After us, the dismantling.

Optimism at the end:

did we get away with it once again?

Again and again:

the magnificent confrontation of a German with Léon Bloy.

That alone would raise this diary to the level of the greatest document of contemporary European intellectual life.

Fourth:

these diaries are not memoirs.

They are nothing but materia prima, raw material for a book.

The commercial and journalistic exploitation of something that has not yet been given form!

Photocopies of palimpsests instead of genuine editions.

(Like <…>.)

20 April 1948

Not everyone is capable of asking the burning question about the meaning of modern technology and the machine.

The first and absolutely necessary condition for even approaching the heart of the problem is the ability to distinguish two things:

the general philosophical dialectic of the master-servant problem—and of the end-means problem—from the mythical and religious meaning of the question.

And then one must also be able to see both at once and connect them.1

That requires tremendous conceptual strength.

So far I have found it in no one who has ventured into this dangerous field of forces.

Friedrich Georg Jünger shows beginnings of it.

But when it comes to the philosophical dialectic of the matter, his conceptual strength fails him, because he would rather fall in love with the mythology of antiquity and become a pagan.

You wish to worship the natural gods; you will be forced to worship the civic ones.

To Helmut Rumpf:2

Many thanks for sending me your essay, which I read with great intellectual pleasure.

It contains powerful seeds, and the strength of its concepts and presentation is refreshingly direct.

I would very much like to see that strength tested in a monograph or systematic work that grows out of a real abundance of material, rather than only in an interesting newspaper essay on a subject as enormous as “freedom.”

I have still not answered your letter of 23 February.

I want to tell you quite openly why.

You tell me of your conversion to the Catholic Church, and one cannot simply receive such news in silence.

But neither is it easy to say anything substantial about it.

For me, the Catholic faith is the religion of my fathers.

I am Catholic not only by confession, but by historical descent as well—if I may put it this way, by race.3

I have watched a number of friends and acquaintances turn toward Catholicism and finally convert to it, beginning with Theodor Haecker in 1916 and continuing all the way to fellow prisoners in the camp in 1946.

Often, especially when I had unintentionally helped lead someone toward the practical conclusion, I felt like a brother who sees a long-lost friend return as the bridegroom of his sister.

For that reason, as in other cases of conversion, I find it impossible to make anything except the most private comments on an event of this kind.

Should I use some conventional family phrase of congratulations in your case?

That would suit a lawyer speaking to another lawyer least of all.

Still less could I try to “construct the case” and interfere with the unfathomable mystery of such deeply individual events.

But despite the great difference in our ages, we now share the same dangerous field: the science of public law.

So perhaps I may tell you in what direction my thoughts moved when I read your letter.

You have become a Catholic, but not a theologian.

As far as I can see, you remain a lawyer.

For a lawyer who wants to understand his own particular scientific task, that raises a more difficult question than it first appears—and a more difficult question than your letter itself seems to suggest.

As lawyers today, we stand between theology and technology, caught in an exhausting alternative that may, in the end, abolish us precisely as lawyers.

Of course, you can simply turn yourself into a legal technician.

Then all difficulties disappear.

But you, like the German university as a whole, and like the German university as an intellectual institution, come from Protestant origins.

What that means in concrete terms can be seen in the key figure of the intellectual history of the last century: the great legal scholar Rudolf Sohm and his immense influence on people outside the law—historians such as Georg von Below, sociologists such as Max Weber, and so on.

So, if you have the time, immerse yourself in the posthumously published second volume of Sohm’s Church Law.

But perhaps you do not want to.

Your letter sounds very decisionist in a few places.

Good.

Even then I would say to you that, as lawyers, we have a very specific inheritance entrusted to us.

Maurice Hauriou,1 who fulfilled this task in his own time, stands closer to us than the neo-scholastic formulas of earlier centuries.

The problem of legality and legitimacy reaches something more essential than all the traditional commonplaces of natural-law doctrine.

And of natural-law doctrine it remains permanently true what E. Troeltsch said about it in Social Teachings, p. 173.

(And I remember his plan to think about the empire of the Middle Ages.)

I would rather stop here.

So once again, many thanks for what you sent me, and please send me anything further that you publish.

With sincere greetings and good wishes,

Yours, C. S.

What was most deeply degrading—what was truly humiliating—in the suffering of the crucified God?

What was the worst desecration?

Simply:

having to appear before the judge.

That is Léon Bloy’s answer.

And this answer, which is correct, could have arisen only among a nation of lawyers and in a language shaped by lawyers.

21 April 1948

This posthumous second volume of Sohm’s Church Law is extraordinary.

Page 303:

the retroactive force of political removals from office.

The trial of the dead Pope Formosus in 897.2

That is actually more consistent, and closer to the ideal of judicial procedure, than renaming streets and public squares, replacing graves in the Pantheon, and all the other retroactive removals of people from offices, minor positions, and graves.

Modern cremation, of course, makes trials of the dead much harder.

How moving Sohm can be when he writes.

For example, he says (vol. I, p. 456):

“What have we seen?

We have seen how church law arose within the Church of Christ, and how the entire nature of the Church was thereby transformed …

the realm of the Word became a realm of law.”

How was this possible?

Because people needed outward, formal order.

Protection.

A bulwark against hostile powers.

“But the very means of protection itself contained a falsification of the Christian faith.”1

Again and again:

the problem of the titulus absolutus.2

The loss of place.

Only from 1179, under Alexander III (p. 284 ff.), does absolute ordination become valid.

In the ancient Catholic Church, ordination is by its very nature appointment to a specific office.

It must not be “absolute.”

Why not?

Because one is bound for life to this particular church?

Place and order?

Because the saint belonging to that church chooses and “ordains” the candidate.

Ordo.

Ordinatio.

Appointment.

The assumption of a mystical marriage between the cleric and the local saint (Hefele I, p. 419; Sohm, p. 301, note 32).

The formally established office begins only in the fourth century with the organization of dioceses.

The idea of being placed somewhere.

  1. Church property as the property of an institution rather than a corporation: Sohm I, p. 77. The legal subject is the building itself—aedes, domus, etc.

  2. The titulus—Sohm II, p. 284.

In both cases:

the local saint.

  1. Rome as the eternal episcopal seat of the pope.

The pope is given a place in Rome.

See above, p. 2, 13 August 1947.3

How almost harmlessly, normally Protestant Hobbes appears when placed within the general Protestant doctrines of state and law.

How well-behaved his Leviathan is!

Why does everyone throw himself at Hobbes?

Why not, for example, at Marsilius of Padua or Rudolf Sohm?

What did Hobbes actually say and do?

He courageously drew the consequences and organized them into a system.

He was a thinker who accepted the given realities as given.

But he was no enfant terrible like Max Stirner.

Nor was he an opportunist.

Nor a liar.

Nor someone who supplied fig leaves.

But neither was he someone who ripped the fig leaves away and then forced his way into what they had concealed.

Again and again I am moved when I see the extraordinary conceptual power of this man, reaching into the centre from every direction.

22 April 1948

The flight from freedom, in concrete terms, is nothing other than the flight into technology.

I must say this to Otto Veit sometime.

The path into freedom would therefore have to be the path out of technology.

Does he really dare to say that?

To become a European Gandhi?

Or to make Samuel Butler’s Erewhon real?

New paganism:

people invent gods, goddesses, Mount Parnassus, and Elysian fields.

Then they have to become furious—and we will soon see at whom—when someone points out to them that none of this is real.

You wish to summon the natural gods; you will be forced to accept the civic ones.

This is foolish and sad.

Above all, sad.

Why were we given this urge to invent and imagine?

Wrote to H. Barion:

I read Sohm’s chapter on the Titulus (Church Law II, p. 284 ff., §29) with enormous excitement.

It is a treasure house for the problems of declarations of invalidity, the revocability of acts of government, the irrevocability of administrative acts, retroactive effect, vested rights, and so on.1

Church law—and the history of church law—really does prove richer, at least for a public-law scholar, and more powerful as a source of paradigmatic forms and models than the thoroughly privatized study of traditional Roman law.2

That chapter in Sohm also contains revealing views onto modern problems.

In particular, no one can deny the contemporary relevance of the proceedings against the dead Pope Formosus.

Seen in the light of that trial, a number of questions from recent years receive their proper illumination.

The now common practice of burning the bodies of political enemies does, however, have the disadvantage of making trials of the dead in the style of the Formosus proceeding practically more difficult.
