But Kempner and I managed to have a conversation.

I have no desire to engage with Annie Kraus’s many words about “humility.”1

We poor goyim are simply stupid.

That has now been settled for the next thousand years and established with full legal force by an international military tribunal.

Res judicata.

A decided matter.

Military tribunals are the highest <…>.

And reading so much “On Stupidity,” dedicated with reverence to Gertrud von Le Fort, genuinely hurts me for Annie Kraus’s sake.

She behaves like a little throttling angel.

Yet she does not really belong in the company of the prosecutors and accusers.

And if I was responsible for her somehow ending up among them, then I regret it.

So now I see her riding toward me on the high horse of Christian humility without being able to change so much as a single line of The Concept of the Political.

Because I still have not discovered whether enemies really exist or whether there are only fools.

And despite all these years of talk about existence and existentialism, I have still never found any existential category other than the distinction between friend and enemy.

One rather striking conclusion of The Concept of the Political might be this:

treating the enemy as a criminal can itself become just as criminal as treating him as a bottomless fool is foolish.

Or am I to be held responsible because Germans have a tendency to substitute their distinction between I and non-I for the distinction between friend and enemy?

A fine dedication between Germans:

Con-versanti in re illicita Co-existentibus in re illicita.

To one involved in an unlawful situation. To those co-existing in an unlawful situation.

5 November 1948

Today “natural law” is nothing more than the phosphorescent product of decay left behind after two thousand years of talking the subject to death.

The mere possibility that a thought might someday be communicated—even if that possibility remains completely unconscious—already falsifies the result of thinking.

So what are we supposed to make of everything that has been spoken?

Or, worse, written?

Or, worse still, printed?

And what are we supposed to make of diaries that were already intended for publication at the moment they were written?

The height of madness:

a just war combined with a liberum veto for the great powers on the World Security Council!

What an order!

The unrestricted veto places the great power above the peace order.

It makes the great power the final authority on questions of peace and therefore also on the justice of war.

7 November 1948

Anthropology since Pascal:

grandeur et misère.

Man is enormously great and enormously small, very much and very little.

In short:

an oversized giant-dwarf.

Situation.

Recognize the situation!

Existentialist imperative No. 1.1

  1. European legal scholarship is the last refuge of law.

  2. European legal scholarship is in exile.

  3. We belong to the government-in-exile.

11 November 1948

At the deepest level:

the terrible drive to live,

the terror of the instincts,

the compulsion to go on living—

the élan vital is a criminal arrogance—

that is the Leviathan.

Julien Green described it well.

Hobbes and Rousseau both seek protection from it.

Hobbes does so by intensifying the problem.

Rousseau does so by removing the problem.

Hobbes turns Leviathan into a machine, an apparatus, a collective.

By doing so he opens the technological age:

protection and security through technology.

Rousseau turns Leviathan into a rabbit with poison in its tail, venenum in cauda.

What concerns me most deeply is the transformation of the beast of prey into a machine:

the connection between technology and Leviathan—that is, between technology and a predatory sea-creature.

Hegel’s genius shows itself in the fact that he saw the connection between the sea and industrial technology (Philosophy of Right, § 247).

But Hobbes’s genius is greater still.

It shows itself in the fact that he symbolized all of this in his Leviathan.

Son of this consecration, son of this knowledge, son of this transformation—always son.

How beautiful.

It even leaves open whether I am the son of a father or of a mother.

Probably the father is meant rather than the mother.

But this cannot be decided either on the father’s side or the mother’s side.

Least of all can the two be combined in some gynandrous mixture.

It must remain unspoken.

The scientific word for this is:

result.

15 November 1948

From presence to presentation, and from there to representation.

Why is there no re-presence?

Why only representation?

Yet we do have re-education.

All of these are suspicious re-volutions.

Artificial beginnings.

Forgeries produced by making something “genuine.”

Things “made good again.”

Artificial virginity.

Re-presentification.

30 November 1948

This world unleashed.

Machine:

the unleashed activism of a world unleashed.

2 December 1948

They issue emergency-contribution stamps—that is, tax stamps—and require people to stick them onto letters before those letters can be sent.

The post office refuses to carry letters and other mail if the tax stamp is missing.

The postal service is transformed into a tax-enforcement agency.

The postal monopoly is used to collect taxes.1

A blatant détournement de pouvoir—misuse of power.

It is a simple method of forcing obedience:

exclude people from the positive services provided by the administrative system.

Why not use the same method to obtain money for residences suitable to the rank of the new ministers?

Here we have a dangerous gateway into the total administrative state.

“The serpent, it is said, can cause its whole body to enter at the opening through which its head will pass: with regard to legal tyranny, it is against this subtle head that we should guard.”

That is what defenders of the rule of law—Bentham among them—were saying more than a hundred years ago.

Today they have become helpless.

They have lost even their instincts.

“Beings destined to perish are in agreement with their enemies.”

Their clouded intellect is no longer capable of recognizing the nature of an administrative state.

But if I were to say these simple truths aloud today, a pack of my colleagues would immediately reopen the hunt against me and shout:

The characterless scoundrel is stabbing the brave people of Berlin in the back while they are fighting!

So it is better to remain silent.

Christ died the death of the person stripped of rights:

the death of a slave.

Christ’s crucifixion took place hors la loi—outside the law.

The Jews and pagans acted together.

Who placed the Holy One outside the law?2

Pilate did not act as a judge toward Christ.

He did not sentence him to death.

At the urging of the Jews, he simply handed him over to the administrative measure of crucifixion.3

I can find no formal wording of a death sentence in the Gospel text.

Rex Judaeorum—King of the Jews—is not the wording of a judgment.

Pilate was not a judge.

How could a judge who, acting as a judge, sentenced an innocent man to death say at the same time:

I am innocent of the death of this man whom I myself have sentenced to death?

That would be a completely meaningless and useless protestatio factis et actis contraria—a declaration contradicted by one’s own deeds and actions.

We cannot reasonably attribute that to an educated Roman of the period.

4 December 1948

How sad and hopeless.

I say:

l’obscurité protège mieux que la loi—

obscurity protects better than the law.

And at best people find it clever.

People think in concepts, not in situations.

Unfortunately, “situation” itself has become an especially interesting concept.1

That explains the many disappointments one experiences precisely with those people by whom one initially felt so well understood.

How can someone who has never been defamed understand someone who has?

Where do these conceptual footbridges lead, the bridges that appear to span the abyss?

On this narrow bridge we are merely dragging the stolen calf with us, like the knight Tondalus, and in the end we meet only ourselves on the thin plank stretched over the abyss.

Advent in the Lenne Mountains is overwhelming:

the total presence of pure waiting and expectation.

12 December 1948

Here is a Thomist or neo-Thomist in 1948 who fears the world will be “de-spiritualized” unless we remain Thomists.

O God.

I know spiritualization.

I know the ending in spirit, in the Northern Lights.

I know the return to blood and soil, which Michelet was already preaching in his Bible of Humanity.

I know the chthonic thinkers and the followers of Pan.

Is contemporary Thomism now supposed to offer itself as a juste milieu, a comfortable middle way between spiritualism and materialism?

As the golden mean between blood and brain?

The Yogi and the Commissar?

No:

the Martyr and the Grand Inquisitor!

14 December 1948

My rejection of positivism came with age.

Would it have made more sense in my youth?

Compare this with the young Hegel’s rejection of “positivity.”

Positivity = legality = Judaism = despotism = the cramp of the “ought” and of the norm.2

Hegel polemically opposes a non-positive religiosity to positive Christianity.

Georg Lukács points this out in The Young Hegel (Zurich, 1948, pp. 46 ff.) without mentioning that, for the young Hegel, this positive Christianity explicitly means the religion of law and Judaism.

The young Hegel is searching for a religion that is subjective and yet public.

Here his famous Janus face is already visible.

Hegel’s contradiction as the deepest principle of all things and of all movement:

everything—life itself, the Absolute—is a union of union and non-union (Nohl, pp. 347–348).

“Neither the one nor the other contains the truth; the truth lies in their movement.”

(Phenomenology.)

Not the identity of opposites, but the identity of identity and non-identity.

Infinity is not the opposition already overcome once and for all.

It is the continual overcoming of the opposition.

(Jena Logic.)

Those are the sentences Lenin liked.

So:

Hegel said, “The great scholar of constitutional law sits in Paris” (letter to Niethammer, 29 August 1807).

Where does he sit today?

Today the great teacher of international law sits in Moscow.

From there he directed the Nuremberg Trials.

15 December 1948

Give your enemies no way to understand you.

As long as they do you an injustice, they have not understood you.

That is the great satisfaction that becomes nourishing food for someone who is persecuted unjustly.

They—my enemies—are forced to slander me.

What would they themselves be if I were not what they claim I am?

They would stand exposed in their own true existence.

That revelation is what terrifies them.

That fear forces them to lie.

16 December 1948

Overwhelming joy at reading these lines in Shakespeare:

For as thou urgest justice be assured Thou shalt have justice more than thou desirest.

And immediately before them, signs of a Christian knowledge that has become esoteric, in the wonderful distinction between flesh and blood—between flesh and Christian blood—between the fleshly world and the flowering world.

Overwhelming joy.

This elemental metaphysics plays with the tools of an excessively sharpened legalism.

O upright judge, O learned judge! A Daniel, a second Daniel!

This Shakespeare truly belongs on the blacklist and ought to be banned from German schools.

Is that you, Shake-Spear, whom I meet?

My fellow member in the black-list card index!

Ave consilescens in arcano!

Hail, you who grow silent in the secret!

We give them no way to understand us.1

18 December 1948

One must have a memory for effects that unfold over very long periods.

Thus the Spanish Inquisition was an answer, given six hundred years later, to the originators and instigators of the Saracen invasion of the eighth century.

Here the great Hegel fails.

He thought that something which lies far enough in the past is no longer true for that very reason.

“Christ died for our sins so long ago that soon it will no longer be true.”

(Rosenkranz, p. 541.)

Now I understand Otto Weininger’s fear of that kind of remark.

This is the unjust combmaker Hegel, who unfortunately exists as well and who is now supposed to become Lukács’s chief witness (Lukács, p. 590).

In the whole history of the world there is nothing so free of any need for redemption, so completely immune to even the slightest impulse toward redemption, as Hegel’s philosophy of the identity of being and non-being in a union that is not merely union, complexio, or coincidentia oppositorum.

It is the union of union and non-union.

The identity of identity and non-identity.

Eternal process.

Eternal unrest.

Anyone who understands that no longer needs redemption.

20 December 1948

News of the death of poor Gustav Adolf Walz.

That is how German scholars are driven to their deaths.

Ecce quomodo moritur justus, et nemo considerat.

Behold how the just man dies, and no one takes notice.

But I will remember him in a Christian consideratio.

The room causality leaves us for maneuver is the room of our freedom.

It is also the room occupied by counterfactual statements about the past.

What an idle game it is to try to calculate freedom!

I cannot know in advance what a free person will do with his freedom.

And afterward I can no more know what he would have done with it if he had acted differently.

Yet this miserable realm of “if” and “would have” is the realm of our freedom, of our writing of history, and of our criminal justice!

Konrad Weiß:

I must fan the meaning of the world (others are the guardians of the world);

How is the earth proclaimed inwardly?

The path of saying does not separate itself from disaster.

(The Fate of the Christian Epimetheus.)

I want the judgment.

More than that!

If not love, then I want the clear, purely born will,

and it shall call to account the meaning that once was great.

Punished with banishment, persecuted in every word, threatened with death—this has been his fate from the beginning.

And still he must walk the path and bring the threat into clarity.

And as a German one is then expected to listen to the banalities of a follower of Spengler such as Toynbee—or to the even murkier enthusiasm for Toynbee displayed by ambitious German schoolmasters and obedient subjects.

22 December 1948

Reading Georg Lukács’s The Young Hegel presents me with a great task:

to make the Christian Epimetheus visible, the figure from whom Hegel’s Heraclitean Epimetheus is merely a falling away.

Of course even this fall is still a thousand times more magnificent than the UN-Toynbee and the positivists of the West.

Naturally, saying that the world was created out of nothing does not explain how the world came into existence.

Nothing means:

nothing.

And if it is supposed to mean something else, then it is no longer nothing, and the whole thing becomes a puzzle made of deceptive words.

“Creation out of nothing” has no meaning other than this:

to make the origin of the world from God incomprehensible, and to leave it within that incomprehensibility.

The infinite superiority of nihilism over positivism.

Hegel is a nihilist, not a positivist.

Nothing is stronger than something.

24 December 1948

The bootlickers of the West declare the bootlickers of the East to be barbarians and subhumans.

The man licking a polished patent-leather boot feels culturally superior to the man licking a felt boot.

And so on.

The whole thing shamelessly calls itself liberation.

Caliban has a new master.

And now, with complete freedom of speech and of the press, he is permitted to insult his murdered former master and every enemy of his present master.

What progress.

25 December 1948

Unity of time, place, and action:

that is it.

But it can only be achieved in a sacred or magical way.

Otherwise it turns into a classicist arrangement made up of carefully prepared, made-to-measure tailoring.

In Shakespeare it is not unity itself but the sheer speed of the action that absorbs place and time into itself.

There is already something utopian about that.

Breaking free of the land draws maritime heroes into an adventurous world.

Blessed is the rare adventurer!

He does not fall out of space into time.

He falls into action.

Into action and drama.

And finally into a perfect beyond.

“The enemy is our own question embodied. And he will drive us, as we drive him, toward the same end.”

[Däubler,] “Song to Palermo.”1

What do these lines mean, and where do they come from?

That should be an intelligence test for every reader of my little work The Concept of the Political.

Anyone who cannot answer the question from his own knowledge2 should be careful about commenting on the difficult subject of that little book.

A well-meant piece of advice to people3 such as Kurt Hiller, Hans Barth, and William Ebenstein.4

The spade of our enemies is our own question embodied.5

10 January 1949

The enemy gives us our laws (Communist Manifesto, 1847).

The law of the state remains law only as long as the independent individuality of the individual remains a reality.

That is what a “constitution with fundamental rights of the individual” means.

A constitution cannot contain two different kinds of fundamental rights:

individual rights and collectivist rights belonging to organizations and associations.

Where does the individual find protection today?

In his party.

In his association.

Not in the state against the party or the association.

And where does the poor man find bread?6

14 January 1949

Klages and the consequences:

thinking is non-life.

Counter-life.

The murder of life and hostility toward life.

So once again we have discovered a new enemy of humanity.

The potential for hostility contained in thought is infinite.

Because we cannot think except through oppositions.

Le combat spirituel est plus brutal que la bataille des hommes.

Spiritual combat is more brutal than the battle of men.

Of course.

On se lasse de tout, excepté de penser.

We grow tired of everything except thinking.

Bad enough.

Kill them!

They are thinking!

Unfortunately, even that promising slogan requires a minimum of thought.

Otherwise the thinker could easily deceive the non-thinkers and make fools of them.

The thinker who is beaten to death would merely be the person who thinks differently.

And the supposedly non-thinking person doing the killing would be another thinker of a different kind.

Only if human beings were reduced completely to animals and plants would thinking finally come to an end and paradise on earth be achieved.

Oh, the animals of the forest and the flowers of the field!1

Where are they now?

In the zoo.

In the Jardin des Plantes.

In the nature reserve.

Thinking places non-thinking under nature protection.

Non-thinking will place thinking under historic preservation.

In the nineteenth century, the historical past tried to place the present under historic preservation.

Sad, and no longer even capable of hostility:

the end in the museum.

Leviathan in the aquarium.

Behemoth in the zoo.

The helplessness of the principle of equal opportunity.

Neutrality between Right and Left.

Parity between radically opposing fronts.

The just judge is torn apart by both sides.

15 January 1949

The most thankless political role is that of guardian of a democratic constitution against undemocratic parties that use democratic methods.

That was my situation, Schleicher’s situation, and also Johannes Popitz’s situation during the Prussian coup of 20 July 1932.

But not even General Schleicher and Johannes Popitz lived to experience the full tragedy.

The tragedy is this:

After 20 July 1932, the radicals of the Right first came to power in Germany by democratic methods.

They mistreated those guardians of the constitution and, insofar as the guardians were still alive after 20 July 1944, they hanged them.

Then, twelve years later, in 1945, the radicals of the Left, now the chief victors within a global coalition, took the lead in the struggle against those same guardians of 1932.

Now the guardians of the Weimar Constitution were eliminated from the Left in the name of that very constitution.

A double defeat.

It was as if, in the years ahead, Germany were going to be forced into unity first from the West and then from the East.

In Germany today, those excavating and restoring the Weimar Constitution are forced to deny and persecute its only loyal helpers:

the men of 20 July 1932.

The entire restoration will fail because of that.

Today they write into their constitutions exactly what follows from my book Legality and Legitimacy.

It would have been better if they had read and understood it properly back then, in the summer of 1932.

I read an author who develops what is supposedly a purely scientific theory—say, the descent of man from the ape, or the psychoanalytic explanation of dreams and neuroses.

But all I ever see is the author.

The material is varied, ambiguous, impossible to survey, never complete, and therefore ultimately impossible to control.

That leaves it open to every kind of mythic shaping.

All the clearer and more undeniable, by contrast, becomes the image of the author and of his historical situation.

From Darwin’s Origin of Species nothing emerges except an image of Darwin, his psychological type, and his sociological situation.

The same is true of all the books and writings of Sigmund Freud.

In both cases, the supposed scientific certainty is merely the reflection of the confidence of a rising social class that knows it is defeating a dying one.

The animal developing from ape to man is the nineteenth-century plébéien qui arrive—the plebeian on the rise.

The European situation after 1848 made this possible for the first generation.

Hence the enormous success of The Origin of Species in 1856.

And then came Viennese psychoanalysis, from around 1912 onward!

A particular social group strips away inhibitions and disturbances inherited from earlier situations and settles into a greater sense of security.

The situation after 1848 made that possible for the second and third generations as well.

Rites of de-ghettoization.

Myth is the interpretation of the symbol.

Where is the symbol here?

17 January 1949

A human form!

The satisfied purring of the brain:

Man, become a spark!

Earth, become radiation!

Firefly, glow!

Spirit, become absolute!

World, become total!

Absolute prince.

Absolute ablative.

Absolute fool.

Total power.

Total lunar eclipse.

Totalitarian and anti-totalitarian idiot.

Deficiente vino el mundo no es fino.

Without wine, the world is not fine.

Hostility is supposed to be excluded from the very nature of man?

“Man” is supposed to mean:

peace, harmony, and concord?

Brothers are supposed to be eternal friends?

And Christians or Jews are supposed to believe this?

Then they can no longer believe that they are descendants of our common ancestor Adam, the first man.

Adam had two sons:

Cain and Abel.

A beautiful beginning for universal brotherhood!

18 January 19491

Once again, one of Däubler’s great calls reaches me:

“Now the laws, seen through at their very root, will shatter.”

The expansive force of such German Alexandrines!

The rhythm springs forward through powerful compounds.

Clusters of words act like enormous accumulators storing spiritual radiation.

Against the cunning of existence, every form and every expression must remain indirect.

Kierkegaard.

That is the secret of the potestas indirecta, indirect power, which became indirect when earthly power appeared directly.

The cunning of power?

Hobbes meant what he said directly and honestly.

19 January 1949

Again:

one must remain incomprehensible to one’s enemies.

But when I understand them, do I turn myself into them?

Or do I turn them into me?

22 January 1949

Gottfried Benn says wonderfully:

I do not believe that growing old means resignation.

Growing old means being allowed to risk the utmost.

Correct.

Very good.

At most I would add:

I have nothing left to lose except my corpse.

And I would rather not leave that in the hands of my enemies.

26 January 1949

We are the invisible ones.

That is why we cannot be grasped and cannot be organized in an age of total organization.

Hence the hatred directed at us by the holders of power and by their opponents.

Hence all the shouting about sabotage and betrayal.

We are neither legal nor legitimate.

Nor are we some shadow state preparing itself to seize power.

Our worst persecutors are those who immediately scream “betrayal of the spirit!” if you do not belong to their clique, and who organize a campaign of persecution if you ignore them.

How harmless were those who, at the beginning of 1933 in Germany, thought they could smell a new spiritual dawn, compared with those who, in 1945, took spiritual revenge on Germany because they had supposedly smelled nothing and foreseen everything.

We are the invisible ones.

If the Catholic Church becomes an asylum for us, it proves itself to be the Church:

the dialectical synthesis of visibility and invisibility.

27 January 1949

Ernst Jünger grows more and more mature.

Soon he will be ripe for the Nobel Prize.

Crowned with those laurels, he will then stroll arm in arm with André Gide and T. S. Eliot through the Jardin des Plantes.

And Ernst Robert Curtius will write an essay about him, although that famous professor from Bonn otherwise seems to follow the principle of writing essays only about citizens of victorious states.

The new elite.

To Mrs. Jünger:

I have found a kind of asylum among admirers of Däubler.

But one whistle is enough.

All it takes is one scoundrel to drive me out again.

Chaos is greater than cosmos.

Cosmos is small-space.

Chaos is great-space.

This belongs under the heading:

Chaopolitans.

The cosmos is created out of chaos.

Constitution of the Chaopolitans:

Article 1: All Chaopolitans are equal.

Article 2: Quod licet Jovi non licet bovi.

What Jupiter is allowed to do, the ox is not.

Article 3: Freedom is inviolable.

Its content is determined by the laws of liberation.

29 January 1949

Schelsky’s second world:

a world created by human beings for human beings, made up not merely of tools but also of man-made materials.

Technology is the age of plastics.

The most horrifying of all utopias.

13 February 1949

Authority and asylum:

the two belong together.

The only asylum ever granted to a German was granted by the Vatican.

Why, then, does it want to be invited to international conferences?

Historia in nuce.

History in a nutshell.

Friend and enemy.

The friend is the person who says yes to me and confirms me.

The enemy is the person who calls me into question.

Nuremberg, 1947.

But who can really call me into question?

At bottom, only I can call myself into question.1

The enemy is our own question embodied.

In concrete terms, that means:

only my brother can call me into question.

Only my brother can be my enemy.

Adam and Eve had two sons:

Cain and Abel.

15 February 1949

I can renounce only what I actually possess.

Any other renunciation is fraud and imposture.

I cannot renounce American money.

I cannot renounce Stalin’s power.

Only someone who possesses the world can renounce the world:

only the lord of the world.

Only the emperor who has conquered it.

The Ludus de Antichristo knew this.

So first you would have to conquer the world.

And then hostility would become serious.

Nothing enrages the lord of the world more than someone renouncing his world.

He will try to exterminate you.

On this point, he cannot be deceived.

19 February 1949

There is such a thing as a highly civilized, highly educated, but purely physical state of well-being.

It is merely a question of diet and the care of body and mind before one reaches this paradise.

Everything now called civilization and culture aims toward this condition.

Intellectual spices belong to it.

Moral and anti-moral spices.

Psychological and spiritual spices.

Then the circulation of blood through our organism floats in harmony with every cosmic vibration:

an equilibrium of all forces, currents, waves, and radiations.

“In the enchantment of this paradisal atmosphere, every demand made upon life and every hope for the hereafter is satisfied.”1

This is the total presence of this world.

The present god.

In his immediate presence, past and future alike disappear.

Regret and anxiety end by themselves.

Self-preservation dissolves into a state of blissful existence.

A moment barely greeted before it is lost, an unspeakable moment, Lenau thought.

But in eternal recurrence it returns eternally.

And with the instruments of our science, we will drive Lenau’s Romanticism out of it.

We will turn longing into reality.

We will organize the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

The greatest happiness of the greatest number.

Anyone who interferes with this is an enemy of humanity and a criminal.

The criminalization of the disturber.

22 February 1949

Today the judiciary finds itself helplessly thrown back and forth between general legal clauses and coercive measures imposed by generals.

That is merely one expression of our intellectual position between theology and technology.

Ho Ho Ho through Ro Ro Ro.

The New Covenant: compare 17 August 1948.

The great sentences of Hegel, greater even than Schiller’s rhetoric:

Encyclopedia, § 248:

“for what goes so far astray is still spirit.”2

Phenomenology, pp. 139–140:

the turning point at which self-consciousness steps out of the colorful appearance of the sensory world here below, and out of the empty night of the supersensory world beyond, into the spiritual daylight of the present.

Question:

What did those brilliant private tutors actually mean by “spirit” in those days?

En quelque façon nul—

in some sense, nothing.

H.-P. Ipsen writes about this in his essay “German Jurisdiction under Occupation Authority” in the Festschrift for Laun.3

Montesquieu’s formula has depths it did not knowingly intend.

It opens up the enormous dialectic of power and powerlessness, being and nothingness, commanding and obeying, master and servant.

This is the dialectic developed in Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit, Part B, “Self-Consciousness,” and which in practice eventually reaches its climax in the formula recently discovered in the Weizsäcker trial:

resistance through cooperation.

An “appeal to the self-restraint” of the person in power is not yet an institution.

Once it becomes an institution, the ruler’s power has already been limited.

In the meantime, all that remains in practice is the poor hope that an occupation which has lasted four years is no longer really an occupation but has become something else—something better or something worse.

Psychologically, all that remains is the touching expectation expressed in a Baroque poem, J. Ch. Günther’s “Aria of Consolation”:

At last, at last envy can die, At last Herod too can die, At last David’s shepherd’s cloak Can dye its hem in purple. At last time makes Saul Too weak and tired to persecute.1

I see with horror that the standpoint of the just war destroys every such hope.

It instantly sweeps away every argument—whether the principle that one may not contradict one’s own previous conduct, or an appeal to specific or general provisions of the laws of land warfare.

And in the victor it immediately suffocates every impulse toward reciprocal thinking.

That is why I regret that Rolf Stödter dismisses this subject very briefly in his otherwise thorough book (p. 107).

C. M. O. van Nispen tot Sevenaer (The Hague, 1946) confirms my fears.

Barandon’s Hamburg radio lecture on the Bochum dismantling trials of February 1949, meanwhile, shows that even an old and cautious diplomat can become tactless through sheer excess of caution.

24 February 1949

Until now, Germans have generally been able to distinguish only between I and non-I, not between friend and enemy.

The result was that they confused every non-I with the enemy.

Then, once they realized how absurd that was, they believed they could put everything right again with a “kiss for the whole world.”

How could the precious salt of self-irony ever flourish under such conditions?2

(To Otto Veit, thanking him for sending the speeches of 29 December 1948:)

But the I is not the friend.

And the non-I is not the enemy.

This is not about epistemology or metaphysics.

It is about concentrations of power within which one has to hold one’s ground.

“One”—yes, one, you dreary pedant, with your cheap, smug, pseudo-philosophical criticism of the word one!

25 February 1949

What was brewing between 1900 and 1914?

Deify the body and embody God!

I see in you the God Whom shuddering I recognized, To whom my devotion belongs!

The beautiful body and the healthy animal:

the new God.

And all of it standing in the foreground before the great machine.

Nietzsche’s spirit became flesh.

Incarnation.

At last, a God!

Rilke cried in August 1914.

I would like to identify the point at which the legal scholar’s normative concept of law and the natural scientist’s causal concept of law meet again deep below the surface, after neo-Kantianism in Germany had separated them so sharply.

What did that separation mean?

The German art of evasion.

German double meaning.

The law in which Rousseau and Michelet believed was incapable of such divisions.

What a falsification of the myth of law and of the lawgiver.

The Législateur is powerless, en quelque façon nul—in a certain sense, nothing—just as only science can still be powerless today.1

We are all en quelque façon nul.

Only science today is still capable of pure powerlessness and therefore of purity.

Even Kurt Hiller’s agitated flailing around over the word “enemy”—in his article against Paetel in Die Weltbühne of 4 October 1932—gives some sense of the wonderful dialectic of which the concept of the “enemy” is capable and in need.

Age grants me, as a touching compensation for physical and social misfortune, the most beautiful migrations of cranes—not only of the spirit but also of the imagination.2

Unfortunately, it is precisely honest and helpful people who underestimate the extent and intensity of the extra-legal persecution being carried out against me by some of my older colleagues.

It would be wrong of me to bring people who want to help me into contact with the existential hatred and will to destroy that drive those persecutors.3

27 February 1949

“That immediate giving of laws is therefore the tyrannical outrage that turns arbitrary will into law and ethical life into obedience to it—obedience to laws that are merely laws and not at the same time commandments.”

Hegel, Phenomenology, p. 323.

“As a particular law, the law has an accidental content.”

(Compare the remarks on Hegel of 22 February 1949 and 14 December 1948.)

Everything “double-meaning” and double-faced.

Hegel’s double face is the authentic German face.

His double meaning is the German way of making sense.

1 March 1949

“The men of the German National Assembly in Frankfurt wanted to found a Reich whose very existence would have been equivalent to a European revolution.”

They failed.

Instead, another Reich was founded whose very existence became equivalent to a world revolution.1

The poor little men in Bonn, meanwhile, are straining themselves to found a non-Reich whose existence is supposed to mean the avoidance of every change to the status quo.

In other words:

the preservation of a status quo that has long since become chaotic—so chaotic that even calling it a status already sounds like a bad joke.

They would like, after the fact, to pretend that none of the possibilities that once existed were ever real.

Désaveu.

Disavowal.

Bonn:

the great disavowal.

I wonder whether there is a single reader of my Donoso essay who clearly understands all this, or even dimly senses it.

Oberheid, who read the essay, cannot understand my language.

Worse:

the moment he hears my language, he can no longer understand anything at all.

Wilhelm Schmitz ought to be given the essay to read.

Even so, it is good that the Donoso essay now exists in print in German.

It had to be deposited in the asylum offered by the Dominicans.

Not everyone has the right to offer me asylum.

One genuine asylum today means more than many written constitutions.2

3 March 1949

The state was the present God for them.

For the Prussians, that is.

They took an anti-theological French experience with theological seriousness.

The state was the Prussian sacrament.

Still better than the cinema or a party rally.

Still better than a meeting of the UN or UNESCO.

No one will ever call those things the present God.

That would not even make a good bad joke.

But the Prussian sacrament was also better than the humanitarian one—better by exactly the degree to which a tragedy by Kleist is greater than one by Goethe.

A profoundly German invention:

resistance through cooperation.

From Arminius to Weizsäcker.

German loyalty.

German wine.

Hegelian ambiguity and dialectic.

“For war presupposes in those who make it, if not equality of strength, then at least the belief in such equality; from this arises in each side the desire and hope of defeating the other.”

In the state of nature, everyone can possess that hope.

So writes d’Alembert in the Analysis of The Spirit of the Laws, Serving as a Continuation of the Éloge of M. de Montesquieu—the introduction to the five-volume Montesquieu edition, Paris, Chez Jean-François Bastien, 1788.

Today they no longer have the slightest idea what they are doing when they say that fighting has become meaningless because weapons have become so unequal.

And that is supposed to amount to the outlawing of war?

D’Alembert, in this Analysis, still follows Thomas Hobbes completely.

Typical eighteenth century.

Very fine, Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws, XII, chapter 5:

“One must be extremely cautious in the prosecution of magic and heresy.”

Or XII, 6:

“crime against nature.”

Yes:

against nature.

“Tyranny can abuse even the horror that one ought to feel toward it.”

I see:

tyranny loves to exploit that horror.

Moral outrage—or moral rearmament—is now nothing more than a pretext for confiscating property, creating jobs and salaried civil-service posts, and exterminating the enemy.

The crime against humanity is simply the new edition of the old crime against nature.

If we keep this level of readability, I think we have the right voice for the rest of Glossarium: unmistakably Schmitt, but with almost none of the unnecessary friction that a modern reader would otherwise feel.

What a flood of throwbacks to the past—this liberation of Germany through the psychoses of 1945!

4 March 1949

Do not forget the striking parallel between foreign and domestic affairs throughout the whole development from 1919 to 1939.

Abroad: France and England refused the Weimar democratic government even the smallest amount of rearmament. Schleicher had to make way for Hitler when he tried to increase the Reichswehr from 100,000 to 300,000 men. Yet afterward, those same powers allowed Hitler to rearm without restraint from 1935 onward.

At home: from 1925 onward, the Reichstag refused to grant emergency powers to governments that depended on its own confidence. It preferred to let the Reich President issue emergency decrees under Article 48. But then this same Reichstag suddenly gave Hitler the insane powers granted by the law of 24 March 1933.

What does this mean?

That is the only important question, and the starting point for any honest answer.1

It means many things. Among them, that figures like Hitler are genuine executors: collectors of unpaid debts; releasers of forces that have been dammed up too long; agents who finally carry out ideals whose realization has long been overdue.

You moral people, filled with outrage: one day you will be taken at your word.

6 March 1949

For the first time, establish jurisprudence as an independent intellectual authority, instead of what it has been until now: a function of political, social, or professional developments and interests.

Justice is not a profession, a subject, a specialty, or a function.

The administration of justice is.

Today, the administration of justice means deciding disputes—in other words, maintaining public safety and order through the police.

The claim that justice itself can be cultivated as the profession and official duty of ordinary human beings is a lie.

Perhaps one could imagine an order whose members were prepared to accept martyrdom for justice.

But they would not be lawyers.

7 March 1949

What exactly are you doing in Plettenberg?

I am making the transition from existence to essence.

I am de-existentializing myself and my being.

Is that not admirable?

Does that not deserve some higher form of Nobel Prize?

At the very least, a meal at the Prytaneum—or a CARE package?

Hobbes had already lived through the experiences and confirmations that Erasmus still had ahead of him.

Erasmus knew nothing yet of St Bartholomew’s Day massacres, Gunpowder Plots, or amity lines.2

8 March 1949

Back to Goethe?

First we would have to restore Goethe’s space and abolish the reality of the human space we live in today.

What was Goethe’s real space?

What was his existential picture of the world?

The concrete answer lies in the line:

“Above my cap, only the stars.”

That is the concrete sense of space experienced by Goethe the man, at its highest intensity.

But what is the real human space today?

Above our caps, airplanes buzz past—sometimes enemy aircraft, sometimes others.

Movement through time and space:

When we move through space, nearby things rush past quickly. Things farther away move slowly. Eventually the most distant things appear motionless, like fixed stars.

When we move through time, the seconds, minutes, and days of the present seem long to me, while distant periods fly past.

The year is short.

The hour is long.

I want to be thought of, I who am entirely thought.

10 March 1949

So far, the Song of the Sixty-Year-Old, both as a whole and in its details, has been understood only by people who have themselves physically been inside a prison cell.1

In that sense, it belongs under the heading “The Man in the Cell.”

The inner time of the verses is also cell-time—prison-cell time, not monastic-cell time.

Anyone who has never physically known the space of a cell will even misunderstand the word “performance-space.”

Today we are all inside the honeycomb cell of the bee.

We even call that freedom.

Everyone is horrified when their workplace is taken away.

The right to one’s honeycomb cell is treated as a basic right, a right of freedom, a human right.

The present method of turning every literary idea into journalism, of making one’s own correspondence commercially productive, of keeping diaries that are already intended for publication at the moment they are written—all this destroys every good possibility of genuine correspondence.

Instead of a conversation in writing, all we get are scattered and one-sided notes, already glancing sideways at the printing press.

Horrible.

Pepysism + opinionism.

Ro-Ro-Ro-Pepysism.

The opposite danger is the transformation of conversation into a chain of causality, in which question and answer become cause and effect.

Then all resonance and radiation stop.

12 March 1949

I am the messenger in the chain, a messenger am I in the chain.

(Pro quo legatione fungor in catena, ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει)2

(The end of the Letter to the Ephesians, Eph. 6:20.)

Therefore.

13 March 1949

Gottfried Benn’s letter, which moved us so deeply when we read it in manuscript several months ago, has now been published in issue 12 of Merkur.

And look what happens: licensed publicity destroys everything.3

The questionnaire is not some Balkan invention. It is a Bolshevik-American invention.

There was something in the manuscript of Benn’s letter that I barely noticed and paid no attention to at all.

Now that the letter has been printed unchanged, this one thing suddenly stands at the center of everything, illuminating everything, putting everything in its true light, dominating the whole text:

My questionnaire is in order.

Good boy, my dear Benn.

Your questionnaire is in order!

Probably even the American questionnaire with its 143 questions, each to be answered yes or no.

How touching.

How often have we asked:

Whose questionnaire is actually in order today?

Answer:

That of the nihilist Gottfried Benn!

At last, a questionnaire that is in order—even the questionnaire of a German nihilist who has been publishing books for more than thirty years!

Some nihilists!

Or are they perhaps such superior virtuosos in obeying the enemy’s legality?

Can they really make use of the legal order imposed by the enemy with such daring?

Unfortunately, that is not how it sounds.

Practical conclusion:

Anyone who dances on this stage has already been judged, directed, and brought into line, no matter what he says.

Just like poor Bernanos on the UNESCO stage in Geneva—when he was not elected.

14 March 1949

A Luxembourg newspaper (Journal d’Esch, 13 December 1948) calls the German judges who were being prosecuted in Luxembourg

“products of an authoritarian barracks culture that wanted to breed herd animals and cannon fodder for large-space politics, while filling the emptiness of its leading personalities and the vacuum of its intellectual world with the hysterical screaming of psychopaths and the cult of violence that has always given weaklings their rigid military bearing.”

What an echo of Hitler!

Pan marries his Echo.

Listen—and suffer.

The hysteria of the small space sounds just as shrill as the arrogance of the large space.

The spirit of the person being insulted immediately enters the person doing the insulting.

That is what now fills the intellectual space.

How the mill clatters beside the rushing stream!

Echo of an echo.

No one speaks a true word anymore.

Echo answers echo.

What am I doing if I publish the Donoso essay anonymously?

Am I doing with my legitimate child what Rousseau did with his illegitimate ones when he left his newborn children at the door of the foundling hospital?

Not at all.

I am merely removing a conspicuous badge from the child’s coat so as not to provoke the fury of its enemies.

I take off its red headscarf because we are passing close to enraged bulls.

That does not mean I deny my child or abandon it.

I am simply behaving as the situation requires.

For the first principle of a good father is also:

Know the situation!

15 March 1949

Being incorruptible is not much; being impossible to deceive is the goal.

We are all under suspicion of ideology.

And those who impose this suspicion on us now have entire occupation armies at their disposal.

That sad discussion about democracy and elites:

a sociologist’s son,1 a schoolmaster’s son, and a former schoolmaster stage a bad beginner’s exercise.

Sad.

16 March 1949

The anti-fascist concept of the “victim”:

not so much a substitute for religion, or a substitute religion, but rather a substitute morality.

A moral foundation for receiving privileges while standing in line and when jobs are being handed out.

A moral justification for elbowing better-qualified competitors out of the way under a manipulated system of legality.

18 March 1949

What remains of the deeds of this regime?

Franco’s Spain.

Is that nothing?

Brilliant remark by Danzenbrinck:

All three peoples—the Greeks, the Romans, and the Jews—killed their greatest man:

Socrates, Julius Caesar, and Jesus Christ.

But the greatness and moral superiority of the Romans can be seen in the fact that they did not kill their man through a judicial procedure.

22 March 1949

The trend from unanimity to majority (Guggenheim, International Law, p. 222).

Who could fail to laugh?

Supremely democratic.

And who is such a donkey that he does not tell himself:

What we are experiencing today is precisely the next step:

from (manipulated) majority to unanimity.

25 March 1949

Prohibition of alcohol as a form of hostility toward the Catholic sacrament of the altar.

Wine is neutralized into “alcohol.”

The wine drinker is turned into a criminal.

26 March 1949

What is a prohibitionist?

A person who is no longer European and who, because he feels that he himself no longer has the right to drink wine, wants to forbid everyone else from drinking it too, in order to destroy what is sacred.

31 March 1949

The sequence of continuing injustices:

the injustice of Versailles intensifies into the injustice of Hitler, and that intensifies into the injustice of Yalta, Moscow, and Nuremberg.

The law governing these ever-escalating chain reactions.

Judicial procedure as the final peak.

3 April 1949

Watch out, friend Barth.

Suddenly the Wholly Other will arrive—and in a wholly different way.

You will be surprised.

Then suddenly this world will become the Wholly Other in relation to the world beyond.

Then you and I will speak privately, face to face, and put your “Wholly Other” to the test—that Wholly Other which you imagine you have taken out an exclusive lease on against everyone else.

4 April 1949

Read Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit as a Hölderlinian book.

And wish for enough time, inspiration, and intelligent listeners to reproduce this wonderful Hölderlinian mode of expression as what it truly is:

first in language, then in thought, through all those magnificent passages about presence, about the lonely lord of the world, about the Lethe of the higher world, which consists in acquittal—not from guilt, but from crime.

That is the content of everything I am doing.

I am incapable of any other work.

For myself and for my people, I am searching for acquittal from crime.

And all around me, everything is being constructed and organized only to create new crimes and new forms of criminalization.

What drives me toward this Phenomenology of Spirit despite my deathly exhaustion?

When I am incapable of any other movement, I can read this supposedly difficult book and lift my shattered spirit through it.

Who draws me away from everything else and toward this book?

We were guilty because we acted.

That followed automatically, eo ipso.

But who made us criminals?

Those who condemned us on the basis of a criminalization of aggressive war that they themselves had created.

A judge who passes judgment on the basis of a criminal category he himself has invented is already judged.

He cannot acquit, even if he tries.

He can only condemn.

By doing this, he has removed the real criminals from the reach of justice, while depriving those who were merely guilty, but not criminals, of the drink of Lethe offered by the higher world.

He has made forgetting impossible.

And without forgetting, no earthly life is possible.

Acquittal from crime.

That is what matters.

It does not matter whether this acquittal means condemning those who invented the new crime.

10 April 1949

Truly, they sit upon their justice as though sitting upon plunder.

Their justice is simply one part of their spoils.

That is why they guard it as they would stolen goods and refuse to allow any objective discussion of this law.

Rapinam arbitrantes justitiam—regarding justice as plunder (cf. Phil. 2:6).

And rightly so.

These are the people we have to deal with when we try to become clear about the idea of just war.

The new doctrine of just war turns justice itself into spoils.

It too is an act of plunder.

The great turn toward Hölderlin was not matched by any turn toward the true Hegel—who is the same as Hölderlin, of the same spirit.

Philosophical power had died out.

So now they become poets.

But is that not much more?

Germany missed something important in Hegel at that time.

Historically, Hegel became effective only in Leninism and Mussolinism.

The Germans no longer knew anything about him.

In the nineteenth century they had chosen Schopenhauer instead.

Today Hegel is a sacred cat in the idol-temple of foreigners.

And who would dare to tear him away from the power of malicious priests like Georg Lukács?

And even if this sacred theft succeeded, where would we take him?

The German professors would tear the rescued image from your hands so they could store it safely in their picture warehouse and make it harmless.

So he is better left as a sacred cat among the idolaters.

At least there he has an effect instead of growing mold in an atmosphere of scheming boredom.

12 April 1949

In Germany, spirit acts with the greatest strength and immediacy.

That is why its vessels shatter:

Hölderlin, Kleist, Grabbe, Nietzsche.

That is also why our great geniuses who grew old in respectability are suspect:

the old Goethe and the old Hegel.

Both knew what they were doing when, in old age, they no longer dared to reveal how unfinished they remained.

The monastic orders are guards whom we station at their posts.

We must not make them drink with us when we hold our great feasts of culture and education.

Pleasure lies in the eyes, not in the belly.

13 April 1949

The knowing spirit that knows itself;

against it, the pissing body

(compare Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit, p. 263).

To embody the spirit and spiritualize the body—

to paint out the continuation would be tactless.

In proceedings such as denazification, every good legal argument only makes me sad.

Because this is not about law.

Nor is it about reason.

Nor logic.

It is not even about denazification.

It is about clearing profitable jobs for new occupants and giving legal cover to the dirtiest forms of unfair competition.1

14 April 1949

Current pseudonym:

Joseph of Arimathea.

He brings the body of the Lord to safety, but cautiously and secretly, even though he has official permission from the occupying authority:

occultus propter metum J.[udaeorum]—

secretly, for fear of the Jews.

John 19:38.

15 April 1949

I place the whole of exact natural science under suspicion of ideology.

For me there is no grosser form of self-deception than the theory of atoms—atomic nuclei, protons, neutrons, and so on.

16 April 1949, Easter Sunday

I had hardly written that when Pascual Jordan’s Physics in Progress appeared.

Very progressive indeed.

Like Einstein, he demands a world government and makes fun of the fear of technology.

Just as promptly came Heinrich Triepel’s On Style in Law, which proceeded to dispose of itself.

He wants to extract “aesthetic charms” from law.

That is what he calls style in law.

Not even an account of the specific idea of form in law.

Beware the bitter drink of satisfaction that comes from being unjustly persecuted.

That drink is brewed from the justified criticism of failures like these.

Justice is not only conflict.

It can also become a stimulant to injustice.

But the Crucified leaves me to myself.

20 April 1949

Good Gerhard Nebel.

He discovers love at the heart of Ernst Jünger’s nature.

That really is touching.

Good Gerhard Nebel: the gold that your rich interpretation of love pours over your picture of Jünger comes from your own wealth, your own abundance.2

All these methods—

the economic interpretation of history, psychoanalysis, sociological unmasking, suspicion of ideology, relativity theory, and the most extreme abstraction—

all of them really are “means for the complete apprehension of alien realities.”

That is Pascual Jordan’s phrase for the abstractness of relativity theory.

22 April 1949

On the birth of Hans Fleig’s daughter:

Among the three wishes I still have for my earthly existence is the wish to get into an argument with Hans Fleig about filiaque instead of filioque.

Every girl rises out of the ocean of possibility like a new world, a true ἀναδυομένη—a figure rising from the sea—as friend, wife, mother or grandmother, sister or cousin.1

But the relation between father and daughter is the most astonishing, mysterious, helpless, and beautiful of all imaginable human relationships.

A son is, at best, a duplicate—homoousios or homoiousios, of the same or similar substance.

A daughter is the Wholly Other.

Above and beyond every individual fate stands this most sublime and intense of all bonds.2

Wonderful essay by Hans Fleig in Die Tat, 15 April 1949, on “Democracy and Finance.”

I felt the professional happiness of the augur.

Pure happiness, with a pure smile.

Finance, mot d’esclave.

Finance: a slave’s word.

A thousand questions and answers meet there, introduce themselves to the reader, and then immediately withdraw again with discretion.

That is how I imagine a lecture by Descartes before Queen Christina.

23 April 1949

Do not imagine that these humbly grinning intriguers will help you when the killers of Christ persecute you—this time in Christ’s own name, presenting themselves as victims of Christian persecution so that they can collect compensation claims worth three hundred percent.3

Humanly speaking, it is shameless to demand from a person the degree of humiliation, self-denial, and hopelessness contained in the command to follow the Impaled One.

I am now one of the impaled.

Result of this Holy Week:

homo humanus must regard impalement, and the command to allow oneself to be impaled, as a crime against humanity, a crime contre nature.

That will come too.

There are still plenty of well-paid prosecutor’s jobs to be filled here.

The bitterness of being impaled has been forgotten and lost today.

It survives only in Konrad Weiss’s Cumaean Sibyl, in the poem “Fulfilment.”

Yes—

where does the weak man get bread?

24 April 1949

I know the Psalm and read in the Bible:

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.

I know modern philosophy too, and read in Heidegger:

Man is the shepherd of Being.4

But I also know the human economy of scarcity, the scarcity of humanity.

I have known it for years.

With this new shepherd, I shall want for everything.

Even a piece of bread, if man becomes my shepherd.

Yes—

where does the weak man get bread?

Better the hostility of Adolf Hitler than the friendship of these returning emigrants and humanitarians.

He EK-sists.

He has his being in the There.

His Being is Da-sein—Being-there.

He is no longer, as before, in himself and for himself and in-and-for-himself.

No.

He is there.

Da!

Now that is what I call Dadaism.

Law becomes statute.

Then it becomes threat—threat of punishment.

O my old corpse, I have measured you and taken all your dimensions.

I know your power and your limits.

You good, old, familiar Deus Venter—God the Belly.

Pain and pleasure.

We have known all this for sixty years.

You are no deceiver.

The higher faculties are the deceivers.

The brain is the liar.

House, shepherd, clearing:

these are Heidegger’s essential words.

That is where he is genuine:

a lump of gold in the garbage bin of polemics and a lump of philosophical butter in the German language’s word-milking shed.

25 April 1949

Have they still not understood that today a Grundgesetz—a “Basic Law”—is in itself something much more disgusting than an “organizational statute”?

The foreign word is the milder one.

The native German word now names only rubbish.

With a foreign word, you hop over the abyss.

With a primal word like Grund—ground, foundation—you hop straight into it.

Now everything becomes primordially German:

thorough and lawful,

grounded and law-bound.

Now we legally go to our ruin—zu Grunde—

with our own Self forever in our mouths.

Poor, good, decent Weizsäcker.

You offered the others an act of treason against your country, and doing so cost you more than it would cost a decent mother from a good family to offer herself in order to save her daughter from rape.

And now, after the rape has taken place, the rapist accuses and convicts you of procuring.

Poor, decent Weizsäcker!

To be sentenced to prison by these people is not even an honor.

You do not resemble God.

You resemble the worm to whom lust has been given.

The powers of this world and their regimes exist for you merely to obtain a liter of schnapps.

What, in the end, was more indecent:

to support Hitler in 1933,

or to spit on him in 1945?

The neurotic is afraid of losing his fear.

False presence.

Fear of moving.

Fear fixes itself in the very moment of fear.

Terrible inertia.

Status quo.

The law is supposed to replace the father.

That is how it is conceived.

The shamelessness of obéissance préalable—obedience in advance—once the connection between protection and obedience has been torn apart.

Legal positivism kills its father and devours its children.

The ordo dispensatorius, the ordering power that grants dispensations, raises some people—who in themselves are all equal1—above others:

quibusdam praelati videamur.

We appear to be placed above certain others.

Alios aliis dispensatio occulta postponit.

A hidden dispensation places some behind others.

So Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job 21.15.

It is this dispensatio occulta, this hidden distribution of rank and favor, that interests me and that I can feel at work.2

Troeltsch, p. 173:
Norm
Absolute Natural Law		 Divine Power
Theocracy		 Norm
Relative Natural Law
Kratocracy
Earthly Power
Fourfold Structure

Four elements, closely joined, Have built the unified culture

(namely the unified culture of Christian Democracy).

Divine power and earthly power Are brought together by natural law; But natural law only relatively so, For absolute natural law goes completely wrong.

Two elements belong to positivist law—order.

Two belong to normative law—what ought to be.

This, gentlemen, is the one true relativism:

the relativism of relative natural law.

It allows the Christian to find this vale of tears to be properly ordered, and to relativize sin and the Fall.

This theory of relativity has no shortage of practical Einsteins.

Democracy is kratocracy—the rule of power.

Homo homini homo.

Man is man to man.

The problem of judicial procedure when dealing with the enemy.

Enemy = state of nature.

Hobbes gives the simplest answer.

Kant’s great note on the trials of deposed sovereigns (Doctrine of Right, II, General Remark) is one of the great sources for the philosophy of law concerning political trials and the doctrine of tyrannicide.

The historical examples are Cromwell’s trial of Charles I (1645) and the French National Assembly’s trial of Louis XVI (1792–93).

Kant treats both trials on the same level, although today we can clearly see their historical differences.

The Calvinist English require a formal judgment because their doctrine of tyrannicide demands one (compare Troeltsch, Social Teachings, p. 694).

The French Jacobins, by contrast, conduct their trial according to a democratic natural law and as representatives of the sovereign nation.

Kant says:

using the form of a trial, carrying out a formal execution, killing the political enemy while claiming to exercise criminal justice—

for him, this is the true sin against the idea of law.

It is a crimen immortale, inexpiabile:

an immortal, unatonable crime.

Perhaps Kant is fundamentally thinking of the state of nature.

Once the sovereign has been removed, he and the people stand opposite one another in a state of nature:

one enemy facing another.

To claim powers of criminal justice and criminal jurisdiction—which belong to the civil condition—over an enemy is indeed a crime.

By using the form of law and legal procedure, law itself is degraded into the victor’s spoils.

It is the most shameless form of robbery and plunder.

The enemy is no longer respected even as an enemy.

Even the law of war disappears.

Why should the Russians, Poles, Czechs, and Serbs not take revenge on the Germans?

They did so in their own way, but within a state of nature.

To that extent, the whole affair can at least be imagined as something that might later be covered by an amnesty.

But can solemn judicial trials also be covered by an amnesty?

Can murders carried out through judicial forms be forgotten?

They must be forgotten if justice is ever to become possible again.

Form is the essence of law.

But is form not the essence of everything?

Then what happens when form is intensified in law?

It becomes law itself:

its visibility,

its external form,

its public character.

What is most formal is the substance of law—or better, its actuality.

Law has no other specific substance.

There is only law that is actual.

That is all “positive” law really means.

What was outrageous about Hitler’s secret orders—even orders for “executions”—was their lack of form, visibility, and publicity.

Outbursts of rage and casual phrases thrown out in passing were treated as “orders” of criminal justice.

Here we have the opposite image of the crimen immortale Kant describes.

In the killing of the supreme ruler, the dialectic seems to reach its highest point.

Who can reach the supreme ruler through a formally valid procedure?

Does every conspiracy not necessarily lack visibility and publicity?

The Calvinist solution—making the magistrats inférieurs, the lower magistrates, the formal bearers of resistance—is obviously inadequate.

At best it is an emergency solution, determined entirely by the political usefulness of these lower magistrates in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

So only the a Deo excitatus remains:

the man raised up by God.

Stauffenberg was not that man.

Ek-sistence, Da-sein in the clearing, ecstatic standing within the openness of Being—

only the supreme ruler has this.

How are you going to kill him without destroying the house in which we all live?

Without darkening the clearing in which we ek-sist?

Only the blind Samson can do that.

And he cannot do it through a judicial procedure.

He can do it only in an elemental act, once his hair has grown back.

He destroys the entire house—

and himself with it.

26 April 1949

Language is the house of Being.

So is law, because of the essential unity of law and language recognized by Savigny.

The criminal ruler destroys the house of law from above.

But the murderer of the ruler destroys the house of law at its foundations.

What is magnificent in Heidegger is the “primordial” quality of his language, his constant attempt to return to beginnings.

That is why he keeps discovering nothing but space.1

Everything becomes space for him:

thinking builds the house of Being;

language is a house;

ἦθος means a dwelling place, the place where one lives—

therefore, space.

I lose my time and gain my space.

Incidentally, there is no better preparation for reading Heidegger—and especially for reading him critically—than reading Konrad Weiss.

It is more important than reading Hölderlin.

The right of heroes.

“In the state there can be no heroes: heroes appear only in an uncultivated condition.”

Who says that?

Should not every humanitarian pacifist enthusiastically agree?

Hegel says it.

And he says it as a completely consistent consequence of his concept of the state.

The pre-state condition—with the Augean stable and the beds of Procrustes—is the space of heroes.

So Hegel is civilized after all.

Who is civilized?

The person who contrasts the state of nature as a state of war with the “cultivated” condition and prefers the cultivated condition, regarding it as higher.

The pirates beyond the line were still heroes.

The connection between Hegel and Hobbes is obvious.

So these passages belong together:

Philosophy of Right, §93:

the right of heroes in the state of nature,

with the addition:

“Little can be achieved by kindness against the violence of nature.”

And §247:

the maritime basis of industrialism and civil society.

27 April 1949

Not only:

fame praesenti—

hungry from present hunger,

but also

fame futura famelicus—

hungry already from future hunger.

And not even only that, but:

taedio futuro taediatus—

already bored by future boredom.

29 April 1949

Who is being described here?

  1. Compare 26 May 1948.

  2. “La politique de l’impossible, la théorie de la folie furieuse, le culte de l’audace aveugle.”

The politics of the impossible, the theory of raging madness, the cult of blind daring.

Who is being described?

Tocqueville says:

La Convention a créé la politique de l’impossible, etc.

The Convention created the politics of the impossible.

(Mélanges, p. 189.)

Or:

  1. “Vainqueurs, ils traiteront les vaincus de conspirateurs et demanderont qu’on punisse leurs complots.”

Once victorious, they will treat the defeated as conspirators and demand that their plots be punished.

Who is being described?

Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, p. 255.

The revolutionaries declare their own power legitimate against the legality of the state.

Arnold Toynbee’s essay of April 1949, on communism as a useful catfish:

everything he writes—every sentence, every tone of voice, every formulation, every outlook—carries the fatal, stale, sickly-sweet aftertaste of euthanasia.1

Seventy years ago Ernest Renan honestly said:

La France se meurt, ne troublez pas son agonie.

France is dying; do not disturb its agony.

Toynbee is incapable of such directness.

And yet one still hears the message beneath everything:

Ne troublez pas l’euthanasie.

Do not disturb the euthanasia.

It is comfortably disguised in English fashion.

And Ch.[urchill] appears as the Clemenceau of the Second World War.

So that this euthanasia will not be disturbed, Germany is supposed to perish in the most horrific dysthanasia—

a terrible, prolonged death.

1 May 1949

For a scholar of the humanities there can be no doubt that the opposition between corpuscular and wave theories and phenomena in modern physics is nothing other than the opposition between classical and romantic, with all its shades and forms.

And at an even deeper level, it is the opposition between land and sea.

On the waves, everything becomes wave.

In other words:

the whole of modern physics is still operating before it has even reached the proper level of categorical questioning.

Spiritually, it is naive.

Let us hope it is also naively good-natured, and that it drops its atomic bombs not on our heads but on someone else’s.

Truly:

docui, sed frustra.

I taught—but in vain.

Even my thirty years of repeatedly pointing people toward Hobbes was useless.

And how movingly decent this Thomas Hobbes is!

He saw everything simply and clearly and said it plainly.

Everyone repeats him without any awareness of intellectual history.

I am reading Emery Reves, The Anatomy of Peace, 1945:

the core is Hobbesian thought, inflated in the American manner.

There can be no peace among sovereign powers.

Only the unity of the world can bring world peace.

Unity and peace through law, not through treaties and pacts.

Paci non pactis sed poenis—

peace must be secured not through agreements but through penalties

(legibus = penal laws).

De Cive, VI.4.

But when the same thing is said with American superficiality, Albert Einstein, Thomas Mann, and all these pacifist-imperialists shout their agreement.

They smell the whole world as prey.

Who could be stupid enough not to see the fraud?

And who is bold enough to say that he sees it?

Poor, good Hobbes.

La trahison des clercs—the betrayal of the intellectuals—is something truly experienced only by the Catholic layman.

Konrad Weiss and I experienced it.

And it is even more depressing than betrayal.

It is the abandonment of a child.

The Christian Epimetheus must also be corrected against Bachofen’s interpretation.

Bachofen turns Epimetheus into a dull creature of matter, in contrast to the masculine, fiery, solar Prometheus.

But if so, how can he be his brother?

Everyone takes the side of Prometheus.

Next to the heroic Prometheus, Epimetheus then becomes a somewhat dim-witted reactionary.

That is how Carl Spitteler presents him.

But in truth the two are brothers—

like Cain and Abel.

This Abel gives all the gifts away to the animals, leaving nothing for human beings.

He thereby causes the “biological inferiority of man.”

In his loving eagerness to give, he opens Pandora’s box.

He falls for the deceiving woman sent by Hermes.

In Schiller we must search for the concepts of tragedy that give us the key to this whole problem of acting and becoming a doer.

Every action is already a crime.

Every action is a betrayal of the idea.

Every person who acts is a tragic criminal and, at bottom, is mystically aware of this about himself.1

The false Demetrius as the archetype of every person who acts.

The “necessity that the acting person must appear to be something”—that is how Max Kommerell puts it when speaking of Schiller’s active figures.

The “doomed life.”

The activity of appearance.

And the figure of Demetrius as someone condemned by history to evil.

The German spirit of cultivation and education is weak and treacherous.

All the old generals and ministers became traitors.

But first they had enthusiastically cheered him on, just as they had cheered the National Assembly in Frankfurt in 1848, only to let it die in Stuttgart afterward

“like a prostitute in a tavern.”

He was supposed to be the son of their revenge for the lost First World War.

This Kaspar Hauser, this soldat inconnu—unknown soldier—was adopted by Mother Germania as a false Demetrius.

From 1933 to 1941 she kept saying to herself:

Though he may not be the son of my heart, he shall at least be the son of my revenge.

But the faithless Mother Germania did not keep playing her part once she saw that the road was leading to the abyss.

He, however, pulled the whole house down with him.

The only one who remained faithful to him to the end was the Catholic from the left bank of the Rhine, Joseph Goebbels—

a Walloon.

These are materials that form an indispensable precondition for every future attempt to interpret the phenomenon of the years 1933–45.

2 May 1949

The pure dialectic of this German purity.

The pure man of action is the most impure thing imaginable.

For the act, merely by being an act, already contaminates the thought.1

The person who acts, simply because he acts, is already guilty and impure in some mysterious way.

If he becomes nothing but action, pure action, then the purer he becomes as a man of action, the more impure he becomes.

So, in the Goethe year of 1949, we discover Schiller.

5 May 1949

Dialectic of the idea of the victim:

The defenseless are victims to such an extent that today they no longer even count as “victims” under compensation law.

A victim in the sense of present-day law is someone whose suffering creates a claim to compensation or restitution.

But it belongs to the essence of a true sacrifice that it receives no compensation and no restitution.

Otherwise it is only a transaction.

Sometimes a very profitable one.

The true victims in Germany include, for example, the Party members with membership numbers above two million.

They are victims both of the Nazis and of the persecutors of Nazis.

It is at their expense that the others are elevated into the status of victims and granted privileges.

7 May 1949

Dialectic of democracy:

The phrase “discriminating concept of war” was genuinely dialectical and therefore very good.

Within this system of thought, to accuse someone else of “discriminating” means nothing other than to discriminate against him yourself.

The original sin of democracy is called:

discrimination.

Naturally, no democratic system can escape this Fall.

The platform of democratic equality is only the springboard for new inequalities.

That is Tocqueville’s real fear.

Complete equality is never truly real.

It is true for only one fleeting second:

the moment when the old privileges have been abolished and the new ones have not yet openly consolidated themselves.

It exists only in that almost impossible-to-grasp instant when the old discriminations turn into the new ones.

The fairy-tale interval in which neither the Nazis persecute the Jews nor the Jews persecute the Nazis.

9 May 1949

Again, Schiller finds the exact formulation.

What he wanted to deal with in Demetrius was

“the effect of belief in oneself and of the belief of others.”

Only the act creates the character.

The nation-awakening power of great downfall, and other oracles from Kommerell’s lecture of 9 November 1934.2

That lecture, and the passage in Erich Voegelin’s The Idea of Race in Intellectual History, 1933, pp. 140 ff., on the ninth letter of On the Aesthetic Education of Man.

From “the pure ether of his demonic nature” flows not only the source of beauty, but also the right to act.

What is crime?

That which calls up against itself a force of validity greater than the strength of the person who acts.

So Kommerell, p. 16.

10 May 1949

Five years ago in Portugal I heard Churchill’s speech:

The old flag flags.

Yes indeed.

The old flag flies.

It sounded Wilhelmine to me.

At the time I remembered the lines:

Et le vent furibond de la concupiscence Fait claquer votre chair ainsi qu’un vieux drapeau.

And the furious wind of desire makes your flesh flap like an old flag.

The old flag.

Le vieux drapeau.

Poor Churchill.

To speak of you with a vent furibond de la concupiscence—a furious wind of desire—would really be giving you far too much credit.

All you can still do is shout “unconditional surrender” at the poor Germans while Roosevelt and Stalin blow into your old flag and puff it up.

11 May 1949

I am still shattered by Sussmann’s requiem for Däubler—

that obscene piece of effeminate presumption, intrusion, and nesting inside the collapsing house of a medium-like spirit vibrating to the rhythms of the stars;

prepared by Jakob Hegner.1

The noble knight of the sorrowful figure of the imperialist Worker, with the Pour le Mérite and a claim on the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ecco 1949.

15 May 1949

“In my possession.”

What?

In whose possession?

What is it?

A picture postcard from 1933, intended to hand Heidegger over to the present rulers for persecution.

In whose possession?

In the possession of one Günther Anders.

Important enough to publish in 1949 with Suhrkamp.

Everything becomes clear through the same owner’s essay on Kafka.

What, then, is Nothing?

The much-quoted Nothing?

It is an abyss.

Obviously, it is an abyss.

What is an abyss?

An abyss is something that yawns.

Therefore:

a yawning Nothing.

Yawning,

abyss,

boredom.

17 May 1949

Max Weber still coined his highly scientific sociological concepts in foreign-language forms:

charisma, traditional, rational, and so on.

Martin Heidegger coins his in primal German, with the air of beginnings and beginners.

Every expression is an externalization.

That much is clear.

The only question is:

externalization into what?

Into what is foreign, or into the self?

Farther outward, or deeper inward?

The Asinus mysteria vehens—

the ass who carries the mysteries.

Do not despise this donkey!1

Not every beast is capable of this role, much less worthy of it.

Modern Jews are not donkeys.

Donkeys are not modern Jews.

Have a good Christian painter paint you a Jew and, next to him, a donkey.

Then meditate on the picture.

Meditate on it for several years.

18 May 1949

A remarkable shift:

Êtes-vous heureux?

Are you happy?

Nous sommes puissants.

We are powerful.

Instead of asking:

Do you possess auctoritas—authority?

They answer:

We possess potestas—power.

It is shameful to answer:

We possess potestas indirecta—indirect power.

Or perhaps there is a superiority that rises even above this shame?!

20 May 1949

Level 1:

There are people who are not ashamed to have accepted the Nobel Prize.
