Still lower, level 2:

There are people who are not ashamed to have accepted the National Prize that Hitler created as an alternative to the Nobel Prize.

Lowest of all, level 3:

There are people who receive compensation because they were given a prize not by Hitler but by Stalin, and who then put themselves forward and recommend themselves as candidates for the Atlantic Nobel Prize.

Miracle of the Deutsche Mark:

Thomas Mann appears in Germany again!

21 May 1949

Power is Being.

Being is power.

That lies behind every word spoken about Being.

So is power evil?

No.

Only the power of evil is evil—

which means the power of the Other.

One’s own power is always good.

It belongs to the essence of true power that it can be lost only through one’s own fault.

Once power has been possessed, losing it can only be understood as giving it up.

For true rulers there is only one form of death:

suicide.

Max Kommerell puts it exactly:

In many deaths all nobility dies here for one guilt: that it possessed power and did not know how to keep it.

Kommerell as the most important heir to the spirit of Schiller and to Schiller’s greatness, hidden beneath bourgeois myths.

23 May 1949

We have our δός μοι ποῦ στῶ—

our “give me a place to stand.”

It is our suffering.

Our non-participation in the crimes and counter-crimes.

Our uncontaminated solitude.

Our loss of legal rights at the hands of a world that falsifies law into mere legality.

Our existence hors-la-loi and hors-la-contamination—

outside the law and outside the contamination.

We have our airfield,

we beggars of the air,

poor and strong.

A line from Goethe for the Goethe year:

We have nothing with which to compare it.

Above all, compare this very line, which has been made so painfully embarrassing.

The most important sentence in Thomas Hobbes remains:

Jesus is the Christ.

The power of such a sentence continues to operate even when, within the conceptual system being built, it is pushed to the edge or apparently even placed outside the system altogether.

This pushing-aside is analogous to the way Christ is turned into a cult object by Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor.

Hobbes states openly and argues scientifically for what Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor actually does:

he neutralizes the effect of Christ in the social and political sphere.

He removes the anarchic force from Christianity.

But in the background he still leaves Christianity with a certain legitimating effect and, in any case, refuses to give it up altogether.

A clever tactician gives up nothing unless it has become completely useless.

Christianity had not yet reached that point.

So we can ask:

Who is closer to Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor—

the Roman Church,

or the sovereign of Thomas Hobbes?

Reformation and Counter-Reformation turn out to move in related directions.

Tell me who your enemy is, and I will tell you who you are.

Hobbes and the Roman Church:

The enemy is our own question made visible as a figure.

Abstraction from the causa—the cause.

What does that mean?

To separate the wolf’s hunting instinct from its hunger:

abstract hunting instinct and abstract hunger.

To separate the drive toward knowledge—the search for truth—from the drive toward satisfaction through arriving at the correct answer.

Between Stalin organs and phosphorus bombs, for us Germans there remained only the fearful choice.

Upon the foreheads of the victims of fascism shines their transfigured light.

Only hopes without ulterior purpose have the power to draw toward themselves what they hope for.1

In German, you cannot even say “thank you” politely without risking giving an insulting kind of “thanks.”

Terrible.

In German:

politeness = pretense.

Goethe’s pure lyricism is wonderful.

But how sad and depressing it becomes when a lyric poet takes himself onto the public stage, externalizes what is effortlessly present into dialectical-dialogical representation, and tries to make us take a dramatic interest in the prima-donna problems of a Tasso-like existence.

26 May 1949

From 1933 to 1936 I felt so infinitely superior to those <…> poor thieves who were seizing power that even then my personal problem became identical with the general ontological question of the relation between spirit and mass, idea and interest.

“In such cases, the idea has always embarrassed itself,” Friedrich Engels said.

He seemed to fear this humiliation.

He tried to avoid it.

I did not fear it.

I did not even think about it.

That is why it cannot kill me today.

The general concern for humanity and the general convention called “humanism” can probably be explained physiologically.

It comes from the feeling that human physical nature itself is now being mortally threatened by technology and natural science.

The homme machine—man as machine—is becoming serious now:

syringes,

injections,

prostheses.

And so they cry out in desperation:

Humanity!

Which means:

Stop the thief!

But how can this concept, violated and debased long ago, still help us?

It serves only as a pretext for moral outrage.

A pretext for constructing “crimes against humanity.”

In other words, only a basis for new criminalizations and new declarations that the political enemy stands outside the law.

Even with the best will in the world, one cannot deny it:

the final word spoken by this most noble princess, this incarnation of German idealist spirit in Tasso and of German genius-worship—

her final word is, after all:

Away!

(Tasso, Act V, Scene 1.)

That is the final word of German Idealism as a whole.

Kleist experienced it.

He went to his death, into the sensual pleasure of the grave, with a poor woman.

But the lady leaves the stage with a decisive:

Away!

And she does not return.

31 May 1949

The depth of the phrase:

Qui n’a pas l’esprit de son âge, de son âge a tout le malheur.

Whoever does not possess the spirit of his age suffers all the misfortune of his age.

But âge here means “age” in several senses:

one’s personal age,

one’s stage of life,

one’s historical age,

even an entire world-age.

French leaves all of this open.

How beautiful.

Where does this strange universal agreement on the word “humanism” come from?

It comes from anxiety about the last remnant of nature that technology has not yet destroyed and replaced:

the human body itself.

The last remaining piece.

Fear that the body will now actually become a machine,

a function,

something whose parts can be altered or exchanged through drugs, vitamins, and replacements.

And so, full of fear, they cry:

Man!

But the man they are calling upon has already been lost.

PreviousBook I · 1947NextBook III · 1949–1951

Book III

16 June 1949–14 August 1951

16 June 1949

Hobbes was the archetype of internal emigration. All the great figures of the seventeenth century withdrew into esoteric thought. In that sense, he was authentic.

The clear precision of Hobbes’s language confirms his own philosophy of language in his own case: homo verbo fit potentior—man becomes more powerful through words.1

But the English rejected Hobbes and cast him out.

Hobbes calls the Israelites a gens prophetarum avida—a people greedy for prophets (De Cive, Part III, ch. XVI, § 15, p. 312 of the Elzevir edition of 1647).

Above all, there is the classic passage on p. 343:

Non enim potest civis privatim determinare quis amicus, quis hostis publicus sit—a private citizen cannot decide for himself who is a friend and who is a public enemy.

That passage belongs at the beginning of every study of the individual’s direct standing under international law.

17 June 1949

The twin brotherhood of pacifism and Malthusianism; the united front of abortionists, advocates of cremation, and pacifists; the bodily sensibility of the women of the Anglo-Saxon elite.

Homer Lea, The Day of the Saxon, 1912.

A magnificent sentence: the world today is smaller than the Tower of Babel.

Said in 1912, long before the airplane and radio!

Homer Lea, a harbinger of the revolution in space.

The earth is smaller than the Tower of Babel, and within this cramped space the confusion of languages becomes all the more deadly.

America + Russia; colonial war + civil war.

That is the reality behind the return of the just war.

18 June 1949

The basic line of thought:

from chaos to cosmos; from the state of nature to the state.

But at the point of transition there is always the man of force, the man who makes the transition happen: Hercules, who kills the monsters and is then left behind as the final monster himself.

That is what this “state” is.

“When culture arrives, the heroes disappear,” says Hegel.

But this culture has become stale to us.

This peace is beginning to bore me.

So we call for heroes.

And they come!

Look how they run and <…>.

What was the heart of the interstate jus publicum Europaeum?

The overcoming of civil war and the exclusion of colonial war!

And what does the return of the just war, brought about by America and Russia, mean?

It means turning war between states back into colonial war and civil war.

23 June 1949

Only hopes that are free of intention can attract what is hoped for.

Free of intention—that is, giving up every deliberate hope: sperans contra spem, hoping against hope, a hope that expects nothing.2

Expectation from no sources of law.

In the past, recognition as a state under international law—that is, under the jus publicum Europaeum—meant recognition as a justus hostis, a lawful enemy.

Today, after the introduction of the just war, it no longer means that.

So it means nothing at all.

The Mexicans are right with their Estrada Doctrine and with Article 9 of the Bogotá Charter of May 1948!

25 June 1949

The German language is full of mysterious acts of generation and self-generation.

For example, I describe a real situation when I say:

Today, means become immediate.

They do not become ends in themselves, because there are no ends anymore.

They simply become immediate.

There are only drives and functions.

So what are we supposed to do?

Give up every intention and surrender ourselves to the current, without even deciding whether the current carrying us along is like a river such as the Nile, or an electric current made up of waves and lines of force.

Every German word produces a shifting echo.

It lacks an image, searches for an image, and wavers between images.

27 June 1949

Kleist sought the sensual pleasure of the grave, the bed of the Empress.

His suicide was not heroic conduct directed against his own personality (compare Hegel, Addition to § 70 of the Philosophy of Right).

Nor was protest against the political situation the decisive thing. His act was not meant to claim some higher right.

After the ending of Penthesilea, it was really only consistent.

The deed itself was simply the ripe fruit growing from the tree of a feeling that knew with complete certainty.

28 June 1949

Just look at this porcelain-factory world of Goethe’s Tasso or his Iphigenia!

It simply has to end with an “Away!”

Everything here is so infinitely refined and cultivated that people can only whisper in blank verse and live on nothing but nectar and ambrosia.

At last, the genius falls out of character and receives the well-deserved classical command:

“Away!”1

“We have nothing with which to compare it!”

Indeed we do not.

A beautiful subject for the Goethe Year, with E. R. Curtius as the custodian of high culture, defending the humanist cult-image of Goethe with all the zeal of a churchwarden and all the quotation-covered pedantry of a schoolmaster.

30 June 1949

The death of Empedocles—the heroic plunge into the sun-fire inside the earth—and the unleashing of atomic energy, that is, sun-fire stripped of its covering:

they are the same thing.

This is the philosophy of light and spirit found in German Idealism.2

In its name, the world is now waging an idiotic moral and “just” war against us, the very people who sensed the disaster coming.

In 1870–71 Nietzsche wanted to write a tragedy called Empedocles.3

Empedocles is driven through every stage—religion, art, science—and then turns the final stage, which dissolves everything, against himself.

Without lightning, no light.

Without fear, no lightning.

Without darkness, no fear.

Only someone already born for openness and light can experience narrowness and darkness as oppressive.

But the worm born in darkness and born for darkness feels perfectly at home there and does not even recognize darkness as darkness.

So says Baader, whom that fraud Lüth dares to invoke against me.

Baader, of course, got it from Jakob Böhme.

2 July 1949

The bodily and spiritual sensibility of the Gnostic:

crystalline purity; the filth of blood overcome in pure radiation; sterility; Malthusian = pacifist.

Birth control.

Carrion-Comfort.

What do they want?

The masses want to live well and have a little fun: to live and have a fun.

And that is what you will be given:

food and organized leisure, calories and cinemas.

Panem et circenses—bread and circuses—would still be too substantial for this massa perditionis, this mass of perdition.

What they need is carrion-fun.

3 July 1949

Attack is the best form of defense.

But with today’s outlawing of the aggressor, the reverse becomes even more important:

defense is the best form of attack.1

By claiming defense, you mobilize the entire system of collective security and outlawry.

Everyone is declared to have been attacked along with you, and the just-global, globally-just world war can begin.

Touching, to call that “preserving peace.”

All of this is already in Orwell’s 1984.

Jünger’s The Worker is a style of language, not a style of thought.

It is scientific observation—or more precisely, the observation of beetle fauna by an insect researcher.

Not a trace of ontology.

It is an entomological study of the forms taken by historical phenomena, producing aphoristic conclusions.

What is genuinely visionary in substance becomes an old-fashioned opening to a novel.

For example, in 1932 he writes:

“For Ahasuerus, who begins his wandering again in 1933, human society and its activity present a strange spectacle.”

That could have been written by Balzac.

It has great charm.

But for how much longer?

4 July 1949

But under no circumstances mention my name!2

Emigrants are unpredictable and are usually, in some respects, morally disturbed.

They sit on their rights as though they were sitting on captured booty and defend them like stolen property.

Through their rights, their conviction that they are right, and the 300-percent exploitation of their righteousness, they have been driven outside themselves and beyond ordinary human proportions.

They wage the just war, the most horrific thing human self-righteousness has ever invented.

Their rights and their moral outrage prevent them from returning to themselves and to reason.

I do not know whether this also applies to Karl Löwith.

But today one has to allow for such possibilities, and I have no desire to direct the hatred of this human type toward my poor person on top of all the persecutions I have already survived.

I am filled with taedium fugae—weariness of flight.

And as for publishing, I follow the ancient saying:

non possum scribere de eo qui potest proscribere—I cannot write about the man who has the power to proscribe me.

What does it actually mean to speak of the juridification and institutionalization of Christianity in the Roman Church?

It means only this:

realization.

For what is law?

Hegel’s answer is:

law is spirit making itself real.

Nature simply is what it is (remark to § 29 of the Philosophy of Right).

Law is the existence of the free will.

It is freedom as Idea.

It is spirit itself, not merely spirit as an individual.1

By rejecting realization—that is, works—they remain pure.

The act itself is already a crime.

A misdeed.

And then the result is called:

tragedy.

The Roman Church is historical reality.

Seen through Idealism, that makes it eo ipso—by that very fact—a misdeed.

It is the katechon, the restraining power.

So presumably it must also be the greatest criminal of all.

Seen through Idealism, every historical act is a misdeed.

Seen through Idealism:

law = injustice = an act of imposition = arbitrariness.

And then they call this tragedy!

Sohm’s thesis does not apply only to canon law.

7 July 1949

Jesus Christ in America.

A correction to John 8:7–11.

He said to the Pharisees:

“Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone!”

But when they heard this, they shouted:

“The tu quoque argument is inadmissible according to the doctrine of our great Prosecutors!”2

And they stoned the woman and tried to hit the Lord as well.

But he passed through the middle of them and went away.

8 July 1949

When Georges Bernanos’s Le chemin de la Croix-des-Âmes fell into my hands (Gallimard, 1948), I was happy to encounter him again and eager to discover what he had thought and said during the years 1940–44, while we were sitting inside the jaws of Leviathan.

I read his dispute from April 1944, where he encounters a Viennese emigrant named Karpfen, who now calls himself Carpeau[x], and who gives poor Bernanos several lessons in humanity.

So how does the old biographer of Drumont answer the new Christian and Frenchman Carpeau[x]?

Uncertainly and cautiously.

With reservations.

He is visibly very worried about being regarded as an antisemite.

At that point, Karpfen has already won.

He is no longer a carp but a pike.

“The Jewish genius,” says Bernanos, “is a genius for contradiction. If that were not so, people would long ago have stopped speaking about a Jewish race, and there would be no more question of restoring Palestine to the Israelites than Tuscany to the Etruscans.”

How harmless and old-fashioned that sounds beside the fact that the new Messiah, Isidore Isou, had already completed his Agrégation d’un Nom et d’un Messie, and that Gallimard, their common publisher, was already printing and publishing it while good Bernanos was still alive!

But very well.

For Bernanos, Catholicism is a race.

What does he say to his new racial relative Karpfen?

He says:

As a Jew, you suffer from religious pessimism.

We French do not abandon hope.

We remain with espérance.

The Germans, however, are also pessimists, just like the Jews:

metaphysical pessimists.

So Jews and Germans are brothers.

Their hatred of one another is merely the hatred of hostile brothers.

“The Jewish people and the German people remain bound together by a mysterious affinity.”

So he says, p. 420.

How sad this mixture of nationalism, traditionalism, and political theology is, mixed together with the remains of that extraordinary beginning from 1920, from the period of his friendship with Valléry-Radot!

How painful to see all the indirectness in this man who was once the very embodiment of directness.

What remains of the brave, completely direct Bernanos who so inspired us in 1930?

An emigrant and journalist, staggering between his old role and his new audience.

An emigrant who wants to return home but knows perfectly well that no celebration awaits him there.

The only welcome waiting for him is to be absorbed into one of the fronts of the civil war.

He has suffered the bitter fate of the successful modern writer.

Today’s bourgeois public enjoys applauding bold theses.

Its intellectual curiosity likes being excited by direct, provocative statements, and it happily gives praise that commits it to nothing.

The author is expected to take a risk.

Above all, he is expected to risk saying honestly something that the public itself is incapable of honestly believing.

That is what he is paid and rewarded for.

But if he begins to take his own success too seriously, he is shown the door, more or less politely.

In every sentence of these articles in Le chemin de la Croix-des-Âmes, you can feel what Bernanos himself feels.

He feels that he has emigrated and been dismissed.

Qui quitte sa place la perd—leave your place and you lose it.

It is sad to see him still appearing in Geneva in 1947 in his old role, while Isidore Isou had already publicly mocked him and spat on him.

And it is sad, as a German, to have to admit that it was probably a good thing not to have heard all these declarations from good Bernanos during the years 1940–44.

Bernanos speaks of the “front of the cathedrals.”

Well:

the French cathedrals are still standing.

The German cathedrals have been destroyed.

That was the real “front of the cathedrals.”

Of course, much of what he says is extremely accurate:

“It is not true that peoples are deceived. It is not true that the wolves disguised themselves as sheep in order to seduce them. They always acted like wolves and spoke like wolves. … The seizure of Czechoslovakia is a crime, but Munich is another crime” (March 1942, p. 212).

And Nuremberg?

Hiroshima?

Morgenthau?

<…> perhaps in the autumn of 1938), poor Georges.

On Isidore Isou:

They talk endlessly of elites, Yet most of them hardly know: There are only Isra-elites now Across this planetary globe.

“A great people in upheaval does nothing but carry out executions” (Rivarol).

9 July 1949

The Movement was a mixing bowl.

Its purpose was to separate what had been mixed together.

That never happened because its conceptual starting point was pitiful.

It was completely paralyzed from the beginning by the unresolved mixture contained in the concepts of race, people, and community.

Race was Anglo-Saxon:

a front against the East.

Volk, people, was Slavic:

a front against the West.

Reich was Christian-Germanic.

What was really meant—in the esoteric core—was race:

an attempt to ingratiate oneself with the Anglo-Saxons and gain admission to the distinguished global firm, first as an authorized manager and then as a director.

Not willed, and faithful alone, No thing can deceive me.

But these people are the reverse:

nothing but will, and no faithfulness.

That is why they are always deceived, and why everything conspires to deceive them.

The deception they complain about so loudly, the betrayal they themselves provoke, is nothing more than the inevitable answer to their own willfulness.

It is simply the echo of their inability to remain faithful.

Bach is musical oratory.

Beethoven is ethical speech.

Rossini is untroubled being, the happiness of a chirping bird.

But what is Wagner, the great magician of Tristan and The Mastersingers?

Rossini could still find lodging with Rothschild.

Wagner could no longer do so.

11 July 1949

We have known it for a long time:

wherever people talk constantly about race and proclaim the racial principle, there is usually not much real race left in substance.

People talk most about what they lack.

That is natural and obvious.

And it is only in this sense that we speak so much today about man and mankind, peace, freedom, and humanity.

Now suppose that today I publicly state only the first sentence of this simple observation and speak only about the fraud of race.

I receive universal applause.

People are even prepared to forgive me.

I am granted an amnesty.

But if I also say the sentences that follow, the ones about mankind and humanity, then I am thrown into prison in the name of mankind and humanity.

12 July 1949

Nuremberg was the great collapse of justice.

There was only one genuine academic jurist sitting there:

Donnedieu de Vabres.

That was the trahison des clercs, the betrayal of the intellectuals.

But let us give nothing back, least of all this word “traitor.”

We were forced to accept the behavior of successful Russian professional revolutionaries and Jewish emigrants as the standard by which normal German behavior was to be judged.

And then—only now do the clercs really appear, because before this point one can hardly speak of clercs in the European sense—the antifascist Catholic clergy adapts itself and tries to fit into the ideology of this completely non-European type:

the lamb howling with the wolves.

But these shepherds are not lambs.

They ought to know how miserably “treacherous,” how suicidal their behavior is when the shepherd joins the wolves in howling.

Radbruch and Jaspers were the humanities pin-ups of liberated Germany in 1945.

They were very proud of their success.

Today they indignantly regard it as the renazification of Germany when people begin to find them boring and take their pictures down.

Rather than accept being taken down like old pin-ups, they would apparently prefer to see a few more Germans hanged.

Ready for any denunciation, they declare that they will fight to the very end.

And fight they will.

They are no more likely to lose their pensions today than they were in 1933.

So onward into battle for freedom of speech and human rights.

13 July 1949

This is really not a trahison des clercs.

Who are these clercs anyway?

Are they even capable of betrayal?

No.

Instead, look at Winston Churchill, that respectable whisky drinker.

He is responsible for unconditional surrender.

That is the betrayal of the old whisky drinkers.

We poor continental Europeans will hardly ever manage to surpass that betrayal.

14 July 1949

A civil war can end only with an amnesty, not with the judgments of political courts.

The damage done by those courts cannot be repaired afterward through pardons.

Here there is only one solution, as in the final book of the Odyssey:

the lightning bolt of Zeus, and then amnesty.

But amnesty is a two-sided, reciprocal act.

That is something completely different from mercy or a pardon.

Amnesty can only be sworn mutually.

These are the horkia, the sworn agreements and covenants at the end of the Odyssey.

The parties swear to end the feud.

15 July 1949

There they go, walking around talking about Europe, in France and in Germany.

In France, André Gide gave the famous answer to the question of who the greatest poet was:

“Victor Hugo, alas.”

In Germany, nobody would understand me if I answered:

“The greatest modern German poet is Theodor Däubler, alas.”

In Germany, the disciples of George, the disciples of Rilke, even the Wiechert fanatics and the baggage-carriers of Thomas Mann would leap into my face and roar:

“You miserable Nazi pig, get yourself denazified first!”

Proud that they are not among those being accused, only among those doing the accusing.

Shame.

17 July 1949

The secret of Goethe’s fame.

What is he celebrated for today?

I know.

He is universally celebrated because he was clever enough to preserve the fullness of his heart.

He became silent in time.

Tell it to no one except the wise.

Nobody likes to make a confession in prose.

At most, let us say it sub rosa, in private, when the Muse yields herself to us as willingly as she yielded to this great poet.

In 1794 Goethe rejected Gagern’s appeal, “A German Nobleman to His Countrymen,” with these words:

“Unfortunately, one must usually remain silent so as not to be thought mad, like Cassandra, when one says aloud what is already standing at the door.”

He did not merely remain silent.

He became mute.

He is hiding some kind of mutilation that all of us are hiding.

It is already too much to say this much about becoming silent.

“There are problems for which Themis has no scales.”

In the Goethe Year of 1949, I discover Schiller:

the fragment Demetrius.

And with that we are back in Nuremberg.

Many people compare the Nuremberg Trials with the Dreyfus trial.

Maurice Bardèche does so, for example, in Nuremberg ou la terre promise, Paris 1948.

What is the great difference between the problem posed by Nuremberg and the problem posed by the Dreyfus trial?

In the Dreyfus trial, the dispute concerned only facts and factual findings.

The moral judgment and the jurisdiction of the court were already settled.

At Nuremberg, the problem was whether the matter could properly be judged by a court at all.

The problem concerned the very foundations.

“There are problems for which Themis has no scales.”

These were not even questions of law.

They concerned the limits of what human beings are entitled to declare to be law by means of a trial.

Maxima non curat praetor:

the judge cannot deal with the greatest things.

The Greeks killed Socrates through a judicial process.

The Jews killed Jesus Christ through a judicial process.

The Romans, the people of law, did not kill their greatest man, Julius Caesar, through a judicial process.

That is to their credit.

But Nuremberg is far too small to be compared with such great names:

too small on the side of the judges, too small on the side of the prosecutors, too small on the side of the accused, and too small on the side of the defense.

So let us leave it alone.

Let us leave judgment on this judgment to time.

To time—not to posterity, and not to history.

Only to time.

Tempus docebit.

Time will tell.

19 July 1949

Title:

Material for Clearing a Juristic Existence and Making a Life in Legal Scholarship Visible.

No Radiations—although matter is supposedly nothing but condensed radiation, and radiation nothing but sublimated matter.1

I am a polite man.

For me, politeness is the first human virtue.

I like addressing other people, and I also like being addressed.

But I live among a people that lies whenever it tries to be sociable and polite, and that has turned language into a means of entangling itself more deeply in its own monadic silence.

Tragic.

In German, one lies when one speaks socially—when one speaks not to oneself but to another person.

To address another person is already to show off.

An immeasurable loneliness.

I am looking for an open conversation, even if not a public one, about how a civil war can be brought to an end.

Instead, I find only accusers and defenders.

I find only people looking for material that will incriminate or exonerate someone, driven either by the zeal to persecute or by the fear of being persecuted.

A persecution psychosis has been legalized and institutionalized for more than four years.

That is why it has now become almost impossible to overcome.

20 July 1949

Reading the Bonn Basic Law fills me with the cheerful amusement of an old man who has seen everything.

I am almost frightened by the force with which Werner Weber attacks the work.

Bella gerant alii.

Let others wage the wars.

22 July 1949

Between 1933 and 1944, I no longer experienced this kind of ruler as fate.

I experienced them only as a plague imposed upon us.

Only after 1945 did the element of fate become visible to me, when the German resistance figures finally revealed themselves.

Humanity.

Bestiality.

We say:

the municipal central cattle yard.

We quietly leave out the slaughterhouse.

How tactful.

But of course the slaughtering is silently understood.

And it would be inhuman—indeed bestial—to say the word “slaughter” aloud.

23 July 1949

In Der Monat, No. 10, July 1949, an American-occupation German magazine devoted to “Education,” Professor Robert M. W. Kempner publishes extracts from Alfred Rosenberg’s diary concerning Hitler’s struggle against Christianity.

What does any of this have to do with the Jews?

Kempner does not say how he obtained the diary.

Presumably it forms part of the spoils on which the just victors are sitting as though on captured loot.

And now we are expected to be impressed by:

  1. how Rosenberg saw Hitler;
  2. how Robert M. W. Kempner saw the two of them.

Meanwhile, under Article 139 of the Basic Law of the present regime, I am forbidden to say openly and publicly what I think of:

  1. Hitler;
  2. Rosenberg;
  3. Hitler in relation to Rosenberg;
  4. Kempner;
  5. Kempner in relation to the relation between Hitler and Rosenberg.

Meanwhile let us celebrate The “Hochland” high in Bavaria, Fertilized from afar by Moscow.

I observe the following:

there are people who, in solemn laws and even Basic Laws—fundamental laws—guarantee me the inviolability of human dignity and at the same time will not even grant me the right to die of old age.

They can spit in my face under the protection of law and yet do nothing to prevent me from dying of the most miserable and completely concrete hunger.

Can one believe such a thing?

Let him die if he learns the truth.

And long live those Basic-Law people,1 who enacted such products of the constituent power—the constituent Gewalt, power and violence—of the German people, with the approval of the occupying powers, subject to Article 139.

Do not say anything against fertilization from afar.

The moment you drink coffee, you have already been fertilized from afar.

Excuse me:

I have not.

We discovered America.

America did not discover us.

And that remains true despite all the colonial-ethical noise made around Vitoria.

Klamaux.

Today, 23 July 1949, a follower of Klages with a talent for graphology looked at Spranger’s handwriting and diagnosed:

an infertile, malicious egoist, the most ridiculous Sinistro .

He looked at Smend’s handwriting:

a dangerous intriguer.

Then he looked at Ernst Jünger’s handwriting and said:

this man has a strong weakness for the fair sex.

26 July 1949

A time will come when people discuss the following question:

Why did Donoso Cortés want to enter the Jesuit order rather than the Dominican order?

That question is certainly more important and more interesting than whether Heidegger was an atheist, whether Gerhard Nebel was a Christian, or whether Ernst Jünger has genuinely converted or is merely showing off a little and pretending to do penance.

It is a pity that these Nobel Prize people—truly “human beings” in the sense of homo homini homo—cannot even allow a fellow human being like Knut Hamsun to grow old.

They will not even allow him the right to die of old age.

The older generation does, after all, possess certain prior achievements and advantages.

The younger people have to strip those advantages away from them.

On that, the young agree.

Only the traitors to the spirit, the masters of every original opportunity—people like Thomas Mann, the eternal candidate for every Goethe medal, every Stalin medal, every Nobel medal and every antifascist medal—receive ever louder applause.

Even so, I would rather be a scapegoat than that kind of virtue-goat and Nobel Prize goat.

A candidate for every prize and at any price, even the Nobel Prize.

Oh, you fools of the Movement!

I gave you a chance.

You used it to set me up as a target in your shooting gallery.

Now the anti-shooting-gallery has arrived and proudly announces that it has found a shooting-gallery target in me.

The cycle of the antiphon.

28 July 1949

Maxime Leroy, in his biography of Count Saint-Simon, Paris 1925:

between two religious and philosophical simplifications—the eighteenth century and Chateaubriand’s return to traditional beliefs—Saint-Simon tries to discover the true religion appropriate to his own time.

He tries “to find in science the themes of a new religious enthusiasm”:

a secular religion.

In a period “violently deicidal among its scientific elites,” the scientific sublime is supposed to raise man above himself.

This scientific sublime is supposed to let man read, in Newton’s heavens, the decisive lesson of order:

a lesson addressed to students trained in Cartesian certainty.

This was written in 1925.

Without the faintest idea of what was coming.

In French:

“Will the scientific sublime, by lifting man above his task, not allow him to read in Newton’s heavens the most decisive lesson in order ever given to pupils of Cartesian certainty?”

O God—

God killed by science!

The man of 1950 asks himself with horror:

What lesson in order are we supposed to read in the heavens of modern astrophysics?

It is no longer much of a lesson in order.

It looks more like a manifesto of chaotic explosiveness.

4 August 1949

Look at that wonderful sun!

The sun does not protect me.

It does not help me.

Under just such wonderful sunshine, an American soldier kicked me in the back.

N. S.1

It is certainly safe enough for a legal ward, but not safe in the full old Roman sense of pupillus.

At most, it is “ward-safe” under the present implementing regulations of the German Civil Code.

In view of Herr Friesenhahn:

there are not only human rights.

There are also donkey rights.

Inalienable donkey rights.

One basic right of every donkey, for example, is the right to have a dead lion available so that he can kick it as much as his heart desires.

Every genuine donkey constitution guarantees this right, and the authorities make sure it is thoroughly turned into positive law.

Because what is at stake here are the most basic drives of the true donkey.2

Do not forget the age in which you live.

Do not deceive yourself.

From time to time, remember the reality around you and the kind of people who embody it:

people who find the phrase “upsurges of human existence” to be the proper expression for their highest moments.

Upsurges of humanity!

The cry for the just war is probably one of these upsurges.

(More on the situation: 13 August 1949.)

6 August 1949

How eerily the definition of religion given by Reinach, Durkheim, and other emancipated Jews applies to themselves and turns back upon the very people who gave it.

For them, religion is a system of scruples from which one must free oneself.

It is the definition of newly arrived freedmen trying to rid themselves of the memory of the ghetto and stealing the sacred cat of scientific respectability in exchange.

The same applies to Marx and Freud.1

After reading Rudolf Diels’s Lucifer ante Portas:

In Germany, you become a scapegoat if you are normal and behave normally.

Especially if you possess normal intelligence.

This abnormality of the normal is deeply rooted in the German situation.

Germany:

the land without normality, and therefore full of norms and normativity.

This is where its kinship lies with the Jews of the transitional age.2

12 August 1949

The justus hostis, the lawful enemy, from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century:

de-demonization, Renaissance.

The Leviathan treated objectively and without fear as a great animal, as it appears in Shakespeare (Leviathan, p. 38, n. 1).

Today’s bellum justum, the just war:

re-demonization, existentialism, fear.

The Leviathan threatens to devour us.

The evil enemy.

13 August 1949

The concrete German constitution of 1949 rests on the separation of West and East.

From outside:

for the western half, the Marshall Plan; for the eastern half, a Stalin Plan.

A plan is the constitution!

The internal constitution:

in the western half, the returning emigrant, the Morgenthau Plan, decides what “character” means and who possesses character.

In the East, Johannes R. Becher decides.

For the schools, compare the Cominform.

I shudder at the corpse-poison of this cadaver that refuses to die:

Thomas Mann.3

Organized leisure?

Filling empty time.

That assumes that what is to be filled has already been prepared and divided into compartments and drawers.

It assumes the typing and standardization of the people whose leisure is being managed.4

14 August 1949

The German tu quoque is a touching appeal.5

It is:

  1. an appeal to equality before the law, nothing more.

So <…> from equality under the law:

aeque enim transgredientes aequaliter puniri jubet aequitas naturalis—natural equity commands that equal transgressors be punished equally (Hobbes, De Cive 13, 14).6

It is an appeal to the idea that everything which is supposed to become sacred to us from now on must also be sacred to our persecutors.

But evidently it plays no role at all for our persecutors.

As I said:

touching.1

  1. an appeal to a saying of Christ:

“Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone!”

(Compare 7 July 1949.)

17 August 1949

Language is the house of Being.

My dear friend and my respected enemy, the issue is no longer the house.

The issue is the coat and the shirt.

My shirt is closer to me than my coat.

My coat is closer to me than my house.

The survivor is the Over-Man.

I inherited no house, no coat, no shirt.

The only thing I inherited was my own body.

The people entitled to inherit whole hereditary farms still have not understood this.

They still want to inherit entire estates.

Nothing is more interchangeable than Right and Left.

And precisely because they are so interchangeable, Right and Left suddenly and unexpectedly become an absolute shibboleth, sending some people to heaven for all eternity and others to hell for all eternity.

So now there is a mighty empire in America occupying and ruling us in Europe.

As a member of occupied, ruled, and totally defeated Germany, I have had direct experience of the power of this mighty American empire.

I was arrested.

My most intimate possession, my library, was taken from me.

I was put into a cell with convicted criminals.

In short:

I fell into the hands of this mighty American empire.

I was curious about my new masters.

And yet to this day, after five years, I have never once spoken with an American.

I have dealt with no Indians, no Puritans, no Mexicans, no Aztecs, no Incas.

I have dealt only with German Jews:

Herr Löwenstein, Flechtheim, and others like them.

They were not new to me at all.

I had known them perfectly well for a long time.

A strange master of the world, this <…> poor modern Yankee with his ancient Jews.

Always only German or Austrian Jews.

Original masters of the world.

Global makers of order in the style of Truman:

Herr Roosevelt-Morgenthau-Löwenstein-Ebenstein.

I am disgusted by a world made by human beings for human beings.

20 August 1949

“Science will overcome death.”

That was Condorcet’s faith.

By science, he meant natural science—we know this <…> well enough.

By death, he meant physical death, which he overcame, that is <…>.2

Does a faith like that have any right to accuse Christianity of inhumanity?

Horrific.

Not love, but science.

The experimenters want to overcome death through their experiments.

For that, they first need experimental subjects.

The overcoming of death will come later.

By then we will have been dead for so long that this victory over death will no longer interest us.

Madness.

An entire great people is turned into the whipping boy for an obviously hysterical emigrant ethos, and it accepts the role while wagging its tail.

I really am a shepherd of Being.

The fact that Ernst Jünger can now absorb Léon Bloy into himself is, for example, one effect of my shepherding.

The fact that Theodor Haecker converted to Catholicism did not happen without me standing guard.

I am a shepherd of Being.

I also carry the shepherd’s fate.

The murderers try to kill the shepherd.

What am I supposed to do?

I remain the shepherd.

I become the bearer of the fate of the Miorița.

I have escaped many murderers.

I was always farther away than the place they were shooting at.

At the moment when they acted, they did not even notice me.

God made me invisible.

Inconspicuous.

The shepherd of Being is inconspicuous.

21 August 1949

Genocide, the murder of peoples:

a touching concept.

I have experienced an example of it in my own person:

the destruction of the Prussian-German civil service in 1945.

Automatic .

They drive these people to suicide.

But against me they are committing the most shameless ideocide.

22 August 1949

In his death mask, every human being wears a mysterious smile.

That superior smile says:

I am now beyond your firing range.

Your persecution can no longer reach me.

Hic et nunc—here and now—none of you can get at me anymore.

You no longer have any power over me.

Proposal for new crimes based on human rights:

Anyone who publicly insults another human being while at the same time preventing that person from answering publicly.

Also:

Anyone who publicly attacks a person in the press while knowing that the person has no access to the press and cannot defend himself there.

Such a person violates the human right of personal freedom.

He violates the right to freedom of speech and freedom of the press.

He violates the due process of law that belongs to the reciprocity .

The naivety of other new crimes can be seen from the typical examples used to explain them.

Take “crimes against humanity”:

for Aroneanu, a crime against humanity is a crime committed by Germans.

Or take genocide.

The destruction of Prussianism is permitted.

German civil servants are not a protected group, and so on.

The automatic arrest of such groups is permitted and is even treated as a good deed in the service of humanity.

Ideocide is the crime that has been attempted against me for twenty years.

Yet these criminalizers, who otherwise shout so loudly, remain silent about that.

Meanwhile the figure of Scaeva, the figure of the soldier in civil war, is becoming decisive.

The only decisive figure.1

What do Ernst Jünger’s Radiations show us?

That he wears the Pour le Mérite of interstate war, but not the Pour le Mérite of civil war.

Civil war has no Pour le Mérite to award.

The heroes of 20 July 1944 were not partisans.

Ernst Jünger is not a Scaeva.

He wore the clasp to the Iron Cross.

What raises him above the Biedenhörner?

His awareness of the problem?

On p. 450, he calls me:

“Crown jurist without a crown.”

I answer:

state-soldier without a state.

Or worse:

state-soldier in a one-party state.

Where does he retreat?

To gardeners and botanists (p. 565)?

Where do I retreat?

Compare my essay on Vitoria with Ernst Jünger’s Radiations!

The only question is:

where are the Scaevas today?

I had thought Malraux was one of them.

I told Jünger:

Malraux is the Ernst Jünger of civil war.

Jünger answered, somewhat jealously, that he had reserved that position for himself.

But there simply is no bearer of the Pour le Mérite of civil war.

Civil war is decided only by the type represented by Scaeva:

minor vobis causae vestrae amor quam mihi mortis—

you love your cause less than I love death.

The amor mortis, the love of death, existed only in Spain.

That is why Spain alone has so far survived its civil war.

Amor mortis?

Once, perhaps, in the trenches.

Today, back in Paris behind the lines, the words are:

“I do enjoy taking part in the life of human beings.”

Paris, 10 May 1943, p. 328.

Jünger is a Privatier, a private gentleman of independent means.

Unfortunately, he never became a privateer.

23 August 1949

Nos actes nous suivent, nos théories nous suivent, nos paroles nous suivent.

Our actions follow us.

Our theories follow us.

Our words follow us.

They follow us, pursue us, and summon persecutors against us.

That is why we will not die.

We remain alive.

Non omnis moriar.

I shall not wholly die.

But we cannot choose the forms and conditions in which we continue to live.

There are great surprises.

For example, I now see myself continuing to live in the Bonn Basic Law of 23 May 1949 in a completely unexpected way.

Meanwhile we are awakening from the utopian fairyland of a linear and two-dimensional idea of time.

We are awakening from Renaissance and Humanism.

We are awakening from the artificial paradises of homo humanus, humanistic man.

We discover that we are not naked.

We are not pure Greek human beings.

We are not classical figures.

We are not inhabitants of paradise.

The nakedness of classical man was a metaphysical fraud.

It was the fiction of a paradise of humanity.

Today we are being taught that the earth is not paradise.

The paradises of relative natural law are sinking as well.

Who is the true criminal, the true originator of Hitlerism?

Who invented this figure?

Who brought this episode of horror into the world?

To whom do we owe the twelve million dead Jews?

I can tell you very precisely:

Hitler did not invent himself.

We owe him to the genuinely democratic mind that dreamed up the mythical figure of the Unknown Soldier of the First World War.1

So come on, Prosecutors!

Come on, you criminalizers and builders of crimes against humanity and genocide!

Come on, you people who abolished the principle nullum crimen sine lege—no crime without a law!

Here are great trials to be conducted, guilty people to be discovered, questions to be asked, interrogations to be carried out, indictments to be constructed, and death sentences to be harvested!

Come on!

Come on, you persecutors!!

The Pax Romana belongs together with the Lingua Latina:

with a language whose words and sentences hold things and the right order together at the same time.2

The Anglo-Saxon language, by contrast, floats like something maritime.

The decisive thing in a language is its sound.

Why do the English pronounce Latin as though it were English?

Since Henry VIII.

That is:

since the beginning of their exodus onto the open sea.

A floating, maritime language is incapable of world rule.

It produces no Pax.

It produces only the abolition of war between states and its transformation into global civil war.1

26 August 1949

One good side effect of the excommunication of Communism in July 1949:

freedom from that dreadful Cauchemaritain.

They forge the chains of an inescapable causality and then want to become the masters of the prison created by those chains.

A few clercs, however, are given permission to rattle the chains so that the sound creates the impression of a movement toward freedom.

The posthumous “if” and “if only” of this system is the space allowed for their freedom.

It is the foundation of criminal responsibility and of historical predictions made after the event.

The united front of the abortionists is ready to strangle me!

What do you call verses with seven stresses?

27 August 1949

A horrifying aspect of eternal recurrence:

the eternal return of the elites within the eternal circulation of elites.

The eternal return of Herr Hausenstein!

What is European rationalism?

There are many definitions.

Here is a truly great one:

European rationalism is immunity to the intoxicating drugs of the enemy.

28 August 1949

From this point of view, we can measure the infandum scelus, the unspeakable crime contained in these two sentences:

  1. Religion is the opium of the people.
  2. Christianity is Judaism for the people.

Both sentences come from the period before 1848.

Their echo took almost a century to arrive.

1 September 1949

Instead of “decision,” I could also say “imprinting” or “stamping”:

coins are stamped.

Communion wafers are stamped.

Coined money is more than labor.

But they still would not understand me.

Rathenau and Goebbels agree on one thing:

if this or that were to happen—for example, if Wilhelm II or the Russians were to march through the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin as victors—then “world history would have lost its meaning.”

My good people!

World history has lost its meaning many times already.

It loses its meaning constantly:

the meaning that you give it and assume it possesses.1

That this Hans Peters was such a character was something we genuinely did not know before 1945.

He probably did not know it himself.

At that time, after all, he was still wearing the German Hitler uniform.

4 September 1949

Do you think you can impress me with the “starry heavens above me”?

That would not even have been possible in Fichtean terms.

I snort your stars!

A pinch of consciousness!

Bless you!

Besides, modern astrophysics has turned your entire starry heaven into an explosive mixture of hydrogen and helium.2

16 September 1949

Exul in patria sua—an exile in his own homeland—is, comparatively speaking, more than <…> privileged in patria sua.

I hear a patriotic <…>.

That is the difference between Ernst Jünger and me.

He still lives from the Pour le Mérite.3

He lives from merit, from the opus operatum, the accomplished work.

My own opus operatum has been lost to me as a possession.

It has fermented into time itself.

<19> September 1949

In the past, bedbugs disturbed you in your room.

Today, the radio disturbs you.

A matter of taste.

The only question is:

which of the two damages the substance of a shepherd of Being more deeply?

Which is the deeper alienation, the deeper uprooting?

Our enemy repeatedly fails before three mysteries:

the Incarnation of the Son; the birth from the Virgin; the resurrection of the flesh.

Of these three mysteries, only the second contains the beginning of history:

through the Virgin’s consent to the will of the Lord.

21 September 1949

Enmity arises constantly by itself.

It arises, changes, and disappears.

Things become bad only when people settle down inside enmity, establish themselves there, and institutionalize it.

But the worst situation comes when people allow the struggle itself to drive them into new enmities.

In other words:

when war no longer grows out of enmity, but enmity grows out of war.

And that—the creation of new enmity—is typical of the relapse into the doctrine of the just war.

Omnis actio humana specificatur ex objecto.

Every human action receives its specific character from its object.

That is to say:

the meaning of the just war lies in the booty.

The booty is the object.

What can serve as booty?

People, land, and power.

The three so-called elements of the state—

people, territory, and state power—

therefore become, in different ways, the object and goal of war.

In medieval theory, a just war meant that the victor had a lawful right to enslave the subjects of the enemy and take their land.

Today, under higher and more centralized forms of control over the masses, it means above all the right to determine the constitution and political regime of the defeated country.

The humanization of war, like humanity itself, has two edges and two poles.

At the positive pole, it means containing and softening war.

At the negative pole, it means dehumanizing the enemy, which reaches its most extreme form in a war of annihilation.

The humanization of war means, above all, removing God from war and reducing it to a purely human relationship.

That means giving up all the balances, restraints, distances, inhibitions, and considerations that arise from transcendent forces and powers.

On the basis of pure humanity, of nothing but homo homini homo—man being human to man—the humanization of war does not last very long.

Instead, man becomes the being of all beings.

He becomes God and animal at once.

And then the enemy simply has to be treated as an animal, because he cannot be turned into a god.

23 September 1949

Mass action against an enemy can work only with crude and deadly labels.

There is always a shibboleth.

People wearing a cross as their sign kill people wearing a crescent.

People wearing a white star kill people wearing a red star.

Very simple.

During the Sicilian Vespers, anyone who could not pronounce the word Ciceri in Italian was beaten to death.

Who had time to ask questions?

The right to be heard was respected.

More precisely than one could possibly wish.

God will recognize his own.

All you have to do is wear the correct sign.

Today many new crimes are being invented, with categories such as wars of aggression, crimes against humanity, genocidia:

new kinds of crime.

Are the old crimes no longer enough?

Murder, robbery, rape, plunder, and so on?

Has mankind become so obsessed with criminal law that the criminalizers are actually right?

Anyone who knows the history of law ought to regard them with suspicion.

Montesquieu already warned against this.

In the nineteenth century, Samuel Butler, in Erewhon, showed us a few of the possibilities and suggested what else might become imaginable here.

Should we now join this newest occupation and help the criminalizers ourselves?

Let us leave that alone.

Above all, let us hope that one day these modern criminalizers are not themselves criminalized.

Do not do to another what you would not want done to you.

These criminalizers always forget that.

We should not forget it.1

24 September 1949

Despite all our falls into sin, we poor jurists still remain connected to language.

Language is the house of Being.

And the language of lawyers over the past hundred years is just as ugly as the architecture of the past hundred years.

Savigny was the last.

Sohm’s language is still honest.

And yet, despite everything:

the real horrors will probably come only when the philosophers attach themselves to us and begin interpreting and explaining our stock phrases, milking every last drop out of our words.

Heidegger is not a shepherd of Being.

He is a milker.

He milks the German language.

I can already hear Heidegger explaining to us the deep meaning, the Being-meaning, of the legal phrase:

“I leave it to you!”

Here come the fundamental negations charged with all the force of historical revolution.

Here come the Pure.

Here come the Free.

Here come the Beggars and the proletarians.

But what is all of that compared with the lay people rising in revolt against the clergy?

In truth, we are still living inside this revolt of the laity.

Cela recommencera toujours et cela restera toujours la même chose.

It will always begin again, and it will always remain the same thing.

Once again, carried by the inner image that cannot be possessed, we will land in new worlds, and the civil wars already raging there will make the Conquista easy for us.

Any conqueror who landed on earth today with new means—horse and iron—would need only to play the Russians against the Americans and West against East.

The planet is ripe.

Its present rulers are ripe in exactly the way the Aztecs and Incas were ripe.

No savage gods would be needed.

T<.> does not need them.

Horse and iron would be enough, together with the logical consequences of our own philosophy of history.

Parallels:

  1. We would discover a moon whose existence we had never suspected.

Horrible.

  1. A moon whose existence we had never suspected would discover us.

Our bourgeoisie would adapt itself immediately, and we would quickly be defeated.

Law is infinitely more than morality.

That should be obvious to us.

Instead, Jellinek speaks of law as a “minimum.”

An ethical minimum, even.

25 September 1949

Our task now is to make sure that jurisprudence does not die the same death as the myth of the Legislateur, the great lawgiver.1

The katechon, the restraining power, is lack.

It is hunger, need, and powerlessness.

It is those who do not rule.

It is the people.

Everything else is mass and an object of planning.

The wonderful power of non-oppositional negation.

The social constitutional state.

.

If the ruler strikes you on the left cheek, offer him the right one as well.

But that does not mean you also have to lick his boots.

Not even under the presumption that his acts are lawful, and not even under the doctrine of obéissance préalable, prior obedience.

26 September 1949

The structure of Nietzsche’s argument:

If redemption existed, it would have arrived long ago.

If development had a goal, we would have reached it long ago.

If there were an end, it would have arrived long ago.2

If there were a God, I could not bear not to be God myself.

This is the argument of impatience.

The argument of losing patience.

What does that really mean?

A demand for absolute presence?

The claim that full presence already exists and has already been reached?

An inability to wait?

The will to have it now!

All pleasure wants immediate eternity.

That is:

it tastes of more.1

It is becoming clear that I am the only one who, throughout this whirlwind of metamorphoses, has remained faithful to himself and to his friends.

The only one who understood how to remain faithful.

I refused to let myself be appropriated.

And the people who are convinced that they are right, because they failed to bring me under their control, call that:

lack of character.2

1 October 1949

Why do you refuse to undergo denazification?

First:

because I do not like being appropriated.

Second:

because resistance through collaboration is a Nazi method, and it is not to my taste.

The revolution of the managers requires, above all, that the managers themselves manage a philosophy of history about the revolution of the managers.

And that is exactly what will cause the revolution of the managers to fail.

There are people who renounce this world without possessing it, without ever having possessed it, and even without any prospect of ever possessing it.

What do these people who renounce the world actually want?

They want the people who really do possess it to renounce it and give up possession.

Then the property has no owner.

And booty can be taken without risk.

Part of my own kind of honesty is that I renounce nothing that I do not genuinely possess.

But could you not renounce the possibility or the chance of possessing it?

Then I would be renouncing something I do not know.

Anyone who has never possessed the world cannot know it.

And in all honesty, one should not renounce what one does not know.

Important for Hobbes and the age of Cromwell:

the conscious abandonment of the katechon tradition of the Roman Empire.

Incidentally, there is nothing of it left in Vitoria either!!

No Third Rome, as in Moscow!

No more succession.

And yet:

in France, down to Napoleon I, there is still empire and Caesarism.

For Hobbes, in any case, the Roman Church is the ghost sitting on the grave of the Imperium Romanum.

Bacon and Hobbes criticize the Roman Empire on the grounds that it was never truly universal.

It was not an Orbis, a world-order.

Homo homini homo—man is human to man—means:

the final obstacle preventing man from becoming human is man himself.

And indeed he is.

So let us exterminate him, this final obstacle!

Lenin’s ideal was an electrified earth.

Our superiority over Lenin and Leninism rests on the fact that:

  1. we genuinely have no ideals.

He himself claimed to have none, and claimed that this was his superiority.

  1. if we did have an ideal, it would be a de-electrified earth rather than an electrified one.

Because we love our earth.

When someone suffers a defeat, you do not see exactly how weak he is.

You see how strong the other side is.

But when someone wins and then collapses helplessly, you see how weak he really is.

And you see why the other side was so strong:

the other side fooled him into winning in exactly that way.

Fooled him into being shattered by victory in a way no defeat could ever have shattered him.

(Kierkegaard, The Concept of the Chosen One, p. 295.)

Ecco.

France and England!

Not humanitas, but humilitas.

Not humanity, but humility.

2 October 1949

Regnare enim dicitur non qui agendo, sed qui loquendo, id est praeceptis et minis regit.

A person is said to reign not when he rules by acting, but when he rules by speaking—that is, through commands and threats.

Therefore, proprie et accurate loquendo—speaking properly and precisely—the rule of God is not regnare, not reigning in this sense.

I now understand Caesar’s Caesarian joke about Sulla:

he was too uncultivated to be a Dictator.

Anyone who cannot speak cannot command.

The world lives by Rhema, by the spoken word:

rhemasin peithomenoi, en panti rhemati.

The best thing in the world is a command, not a law.

A command is direct speech.

A law is general.

That means:

indirect.

5 October 1949

It is beautiful and comforting today to read Kierkegaard and then look reverently at our modern professors of Kierkegaard, theologians and philosophers alike.

The fierce preachers of repentance in 1945, who attacked us with such passion, blamed us because we had failed to let ourselves be beaten to death for law and truth.

According to them, that was what we were actually obliged to do.

But I never noticed any of these preachers of repentance citing the text by Kierkegaard that deals explicitly with precisely this question under the title:

“May a Man Allow Himself to Be Beaten to Death for the Truth?”

Kierkegaard’s conclusion is:

he may not.

I do not want to discuss the substance of this difficult problem here.

The problem itself really is difficult.

It is especially difficult inside a modern, well-organized, smoothly functioning state.

Thomas Hobbes, the great philosopher of the modern state, believed that only one kind of person is obliged to become a martyr:

the person who calls on others to resist and himself preaches martyrdom.

Kierkegaard is just as clear and just as concrete.

He knows the modern preachers of repentance perfectly well.

He says these preachers do not want to be beaten to death themselves.

They want to play the teacher who beats the pupil.

But to be a true preacher of repentance, Kierkegaard says, does not mean beating other people.

Above all, it means being beaten yourself.

Or at least striking in such a way that you yourself will be struck in return.

That means preaching against today’s victorious enemy of truth, not preaching against those who have already been defeated.

There is only one genuine test of whether somebody is a true preacher of repentance:

“The more beatings the preacher of repentance receives, the better he is.”

That is Kierkegaard.

But our preachers of repentance in 1945 did not receive beatings.

They received CARE packages, Goethe Prizes, and invitations to give lectures in foreign countries where the food was better.

Kierkegaard’s wonderful essay dates from 1847.

Theodor Haecker translated it in 1916, during the First World War.

The passage quoted above can be found on p. 303 of that translation.

Haecker also added an afterword in which he predicted that the Christian churches would have no difficulty joining themselves to democracy as well.

6 October 1949

In this whole vast dispute over the justice and injustice of the Nuremberg trials, I can afford to wait and let the eager public speakers of the day exhaust themselves. I am old and ill. But I possess the bow of Philoctetes.1

9 October 1949

Heideggerisms:

Time brings forth the newspaper. The newspaper brings forth the times. Man is the shepherd of Being. Shepherd boy, shepherd boy, one day they will sing to you there too.

Christ und Welt has printed a nice little piece of mine, with an advertisement for Nivea cream inserted into it. That is as it should be. Under the tsars, Russian nihilists wrapped their bombs in bouquets of flowers. Why should I not surround my equivalent concerns with Nivea advertising? Or, the other way around, appear merely as the frame around an advertisement for Nivea cream, so as not to provoke my persecutors?

10 October 1949

World War One and World War Two, They say all good things come in three. Man makes his plans for world history; What hideous judgments there will be. In the end they become mere rumors, which I then cultivate into myths. But God reduces man ad absurdum; in the end, man’s plan is simply stupid. Only you could be so stupid! The only thing missing is Deus sive Natura, the Spinozist God, or Spinozist Nature. Ah, what a ! <…>2

11 October 1949

The more man busies himself making plans, the more completely his plan collapses. And God’s plan, when it finally appears, reduces friend and enemy alike ad absurdum.

The word Anschluss already belonged to the vocabulary of mechanized politics. It neutralizes every legal idea and is no better than the word Gleichschaltung—“bringing into line.” Is “Christinform” really much worse than Christian socialism?

27 October 1949

A wretched violator of asylum named von der Heydte is tagging along in the great international debate about Vitoria like an asinus mysterio vehens—an ass carrying the sacred mystery in a procession. One should not argue with people who profited from the collective psychoses of 1945.1

The sense of safety that comes over him when he faces someone who has been politically and legally disarmed and publicly stigmatized gives him the courage for tactless insults and stupid, brazen showing-off. It makes his Knight’s Cross-decorated chest swell.

But stop.

Be careful.

A man classifies himself by the enemy he chooses.

1 November 1949

Beware of every polemical impulse!

How weak and embarrassing these lines by the otherwise thoughtful Friedrich Ernst Peters sound:

They say “spirit” and mean a ghost. The age of criticizing the age is over.

How beautiful and joyful, by contrast, are rhymes that truly come off!2

Geschrei—“shouting”—unexpectedly rhymes with Schalmei—“shawm.” And for my sweetest relaxation, Reim—“rhyme”—rhymes with Heim—“home.”

Rhyme is the great test.

Atheistic existentialism kills rhyme. But tragicism and rhyme are incompatible as well.

As long as even a single true rhyme becomes real, chaos has not yet arrived and nihilism has not yet won.

As soon as a genuine rhyme rings out, the soul leaps free of chaos.

Rhyme cannot be isolated. Everything is encounter, echo, and answering echo between words. Everything is the highest freedom and the highest order.

3 November 1949

The history of ideas contains not only secularizations but also theologizations.

Nietzsche’s “Beyond Good and Evil,” for example, is a theologization of the beyond the line. It gives the historical fact of the amity line a radiance from which a rich intellectual harvest becomes possible, after the bare fact itself had already produced enough material booty.

Thoughts and convictions are destroyed in two ways.

First, critically, through dialectical negation.

Second, uncritically, through apologetic affirmation.

The second is the surest method of destruction.

6 November 1949

Columbus came to America without papers and without an entry visa from the Aztecs or the Indians.

Discoveries take place without the visa of the people being discovered.

That is actually part of what discovery means.

E.[rnst] J.[ünger] had neither feeling nor understanding for my situation as an outlaw. He did not even see it.

The appalling thrift of this completely self-enclosed monad who makes use of every last idea that occurs to him.

Not a window and not a door opening onto another human being.

Ernst Jünger’s miserable little voice.

“I would rather not see the poor throat that produces it,” Peterheinrich [Kirchhoff] said.

The poorest, narrowest voice I have ever heard in my life.

A man defending himself is more vicious than a man attacking.

When he is defending himself, he feels that he is in the right. That makes him cruel and gives him the clear conscience he needs to punish the defeated enemy—or even to “educate” him, meaning to inject a different soul into him.

7 November 1949

How rich we were in ideas! How full of sudden insights! How extravagantly we wasted ourselves in conversation!

I rejoice in that waste when I look at these people today who make use of absolutely everything: these miserly petty capitalists, these penny-pinchers with their ideas, these men who ration out their witty remarks.

I am the only one capable of judging this polished economy of spirit.

[later deleted:] And Paul Adams is the only person I could tell this to.

13 November 1949

The medieval ghetto was not based on a fear of germs.

The existentialist existence of Mr. Jaspers, by contrast, rests on germ-phobia.

There is a difference.

As a member of bourgeois society, I am dead.

Now the Parsi dance begins over my grave.

But that is still quite harmless.

There are no graves anymore. We are cremated, and our ashes are scattered into the air.

The ashes refuse to disappear. They drift as dust through every land.

15 November 1949

Anyone who lays down broad general clauses and works with deliberately vague concepts must keep a very firm grip on things.

Otherwise the vagueness turns back on him with terrible force.1

Ernst Jünger has become a prima donna, a complete monad, with Léon Bloy hanging on his façade like a blind window.2

So when a block this heavily armored in its own ego shows even the faintest glimmer of interest that is not purely solipsistic—in this case, an interest in Bernanos—I am moved, and I lend him a book about Bernanos that does not even belong to me.

I knock, and—listen!—a bell rings, and a door opens into other worlds.

And so the door is opened to me.

16 November 1949

Today E.[rnst] J.[ünger] seems to me like his own father—the father he became to himself in Paris in Strahlungen.

He is wreckage washed ashore from the Wilhelmine age.

So is Thomas Mann.

What people take for restoration is merely wreckage that has been rescued from the shore. Nothing more.

Who rescues it?

Who plunders it?

“God bless our shore,” pray yesterday’s persecuted and today’s persecutors.

To handle vague concepts, to keep things suspended, to evade alternatives imposed from outside—only someone who is openly very strong, or secretly very strong, can do that.

Germany wants to keep its own position between East and West deliberately undefined.1

A word like Großraum—“large space”—is too clear.

Better to say Entwicklungsraum—“development space.”

In an age of deliberate, systematic blurring, when every concept is consciously mixed up with every other, it is foolish to use precisely defined words.2

The same applies to the definition of the political, whose core is the distinction between friend and enemy.

All powers agree on one thing: they persecute the discoverer of such words and concepts.

The secret behind the hostility toward the discoverer.

The people who are to be discovered demand that I first obtain an entry visa from them.

But that cannot work.

Columbus did not have a visa from the Aztecs or the Incas either.

So they simply beat me to death.

The fate of Miorița: the good lamb and the good shepherd.

Man is the shepherd of Being.

Miorița-thinking.

People cannot tolerate being recognized, much less discovered.

No one likes to be completely understood.

That is why a person sees the man who has understood him as an enemy.

Everyone—even the righteous black-marketeer—is convinced that the better you know him and the more completely you understand him, the more you must love and admire him.

What follows from all these undeniable truths and obvious realities?

It follows that Don Capisco—Don “I Understand”—has every chance of being declared hostis generis humani, an enemy of the human race.

25 November 1949

I live in a dreadful exile, exul in patria mea—an exile in my own country.

The Germans are a people of metaphysicians and technicians, but neither jurists nor moralists.

Reading a few extracts from a book by Amédée Ponceau (Timoléon: Reflections on Tyranny) moves me to tears.

A voice like Ponceau’s would be impossible in Germany.

It is an almost miraculous consolation to hear such a voice coming from France.3

Ernst Jünger is like many famous figures who stand on the public stage of literature or art.

They concentrate all their strength on their public appearance. They call that concentrating on “their work.”

They gather themselves for the moments of their public vocation, even when those moments are spent sitting alone at a desk.4

They do not waste themselves in private life, in conversation, or in any exchange that cannot be turned directly into something useful.

They practice a well-founded economy with their strength and their radiance. They let nothing go to waste.

They make use of everything that can possibly be made useful, without giving any of themselves away.

As a result, their entire presence lies in their public work.

Their whole existence is absorbed into publicity.

You should see them on stage or read their books.

There is little point in dealing with them outside that setting.

You are “handled” by them. You are identified, sorted, and put to use according to their methods for extracting value from whatever can somehow be used.

As a little sweet, you are handed a sentence they printed years ago.

They are absent whenever they are not appearing before their audience or working for that audience.

Truly: genuine workers in the publicity machine.

Nothing but workers.

What remains is not even silence.

It is zero.

When absolutely everything that can possibly be used is put to use, there is no remainder at all.

Someone puts on the fog-cap of a half-mythological disguise. He retreats into suggestive landscapes and spaces. He paints Böcklin-like landscapes in historical and political colors.

He no longer speaks of Jews, but of Parsis, although everyone can see that he is talking about himself and the Jews, and so on.

He no longer speaks of Nazis, but of the Demos and the governor.

No longer of the SS, but of Mauritanians.

No longer of himself, but of Commander Lucius.

In this way he can speak about himself and his age, use every attraction of a roman à clef, and still, in the end, say nothing definite enough to pin down.

Everything remains wonderfully noncommittal.

The eager reader, who now wants to know what the author actually thinks about the Jews or the Nazis, is left just as fooled as the author remains free of commitment.

A very practical method of protection through coded language, and highly recommended in times when the fronts change quickly.

One speaks very wisely and at great length, yet never commits oneself.

One says enough to fill a thick book and still ends up saying nothing dangerous, only painting pseudo-mythological scenery.1

But this is probably the correct method for publishing on current affairs in a state where everything requires a license.

Non possum directe scribere de eo qui potest directe proscribere.

I cannot write directly about the man who can directly proscribe me.

The present international debate about Vitoria and the legality of the Spanish Conquest is the sad background music accompanying the destruction of the glorious European overseas empires and the transformation of India and Indonesia into sovereign states and equal members of the United Nations.

26 November 1949

The memorandum by R. P. Bruckberger of 5 October 1949, written at El Abid near Géryville in southern Oran:

“The Third World War Is a War of Religion.”

The recent decree of the Holy Office against communism and its various militant parties is the official declaration of that war.

Faith against faith.

Church against Church.

Universal religion against universal religion.

The Communist Manifesto against the Syllabus.

“The first act of a war is to define the enemy.”

The modern world began with the Jacobins.

“I await the Cossacks and the Holy Spirit,” Léon Bloy wrote.

“What Christ guards, the Goth does not destroy,” St. Augustine wrote at the time of the barbarian invasions.

At Yalta and Potsdam, the Anglo-Saxons pursued a Third Force policy: unconsciousness pushed all the way into lethargy, the congenital condition of every Third Force, the mentality of the No-No Zone.

“Having studied philosophy and theology, the history of the Church and of nations, and papal documents for more than twenty years, and having read and reread Bernanos, Péguy, and Drumont, I believe I know what I am talking about.”

In 635, the most distinguished Christian in Damascus handed the keys of Damascus to the Muslims.

“For my part, I prefer Charles Martel.”

The Catholics are the anarchists and nihilists of the communist order.

The new chivalry.

He thinks the Russians will abandon the schism the moment they spit out communism.

The entire conceptual armory for this struggle has been lying ready for more than twenty years.

He does not know it.

I would like to say to him: περίψημα.

But what is the point of a layman opening his mouth!

Laicus taceat in Ecclesia nisi clamat acclamationes praescriptas.

Let the layman keep silent in the Church unless he is shouting the prescribed acclamations.

Answer:

Silete theologi extra ecclesiam!

Theologians, keep silent outside the Church!

30 November 1949
