So Prussia has been destroyed, erased, exterminated.

Les États s’en vont. Les Conseillers de l’État restent.

States pass away.

Councillors of State remain.

States disappear; State Councillors endure.

3 December 1949

Dabitur donum fortitudinis.

The gift of courage will be given.

“These are all dona—gifts,” Father Franziskus Stratmann said beautifully.

Above all, courage.

And then one thinks of the Ernst Jünger of the First World War.

4 December 1949

Write it in your book, in your miserable book.

Write:

This is the disgrace!

They no longer even know what disgrace is.

There is no fixed point anymore—fixed point!!—no δός μοι ποῦ στῶ, no “give me a place to stand,” nothing by which this immeasurable disgrace can be measured.

“And tomorrow, gentlemen, we shall create the world!”

So said Fichte, the philosopher .

My reply to him:

Today and tomorrow and forever, my dear Professor Fichte, we would rather be spared the sight of your world being created.

But do you not see the creators of the new world?

6 December 1949

There are crimes against humanity and crimes for humanity.

Crimes against humanity are committed by Germans.

Crimes for humanity are committed against Germans.

That is the whole difference.

And that is what one would have to say in response to Eugène Aroneanu’s essay Le Crime contre l’Humanité, in the Nouvelle Revue de Droit International Privé, 1946.

His definition is:

Crimes against humanity are crimes committed by Germans.

On the subject of crimes against humanity:

Take a close look at this Monsieur Aroneanu.1

His definition:

Crimes against humanity can only be committed by Germans.

“We do not compare the victims. We compare only the judges.”

(P.[ère] Laberthonnière.)

Newspaper clipping pasted in.

The Times Weekly, 15 February 1950.

On the left:

In the total state, equal rights become equal burdens.

Clear enough.

But these burdens do not fall on the elite.

The elite eats butter and fires cannons.

The elite proclaims that labor, not gold, creates value.

That means workers’ wages are paid not in gold but in home-made ration coupons.1

In the total state, equal burden-sharing is only a formal transitional stage.

In reality, it is merely a passing moment in democracy’s dialectical abolition of itself.

The stage immediately after it—a stage already contained within that transition—is one of extreme over-privilege and under-privilege.

These arise automatically when the former, defeated elite is destroyed and preventive measures are taken against the beginnings and formation of new elites.

But what if Hitler was only an echo?

A reverberation?

An after-echo?

What if everything he did was only a response—or less than a response, merely a recoil?

What then, you criminalizers?

What if he was not merely a consequence and a result, but only the immediate echo?

8 December 1949

What are you, really?

The conceited priest of the Ego will answer:

I am not a what. I am a who.

But let us remain factual and modest, as poor human beings should.

So once again:

What are you, really?

I am a Catholic layman, German by people and by state.

What do you mean by that?

I mean that it is better for me to keep silent.

From the right and from the left, from above and from below, every objective power, spiritual and secular, stops my mouth.

10 December 1949

Whenever someone utters the word “humanity,” the elites take the safeties off their bombs and the masses start looking for a bomb-proof shelter.

13 December 1949

To Pierre Linn:

There are grotesque rumors about me.

It is true that I have become a myth.

You, Pierre Linn, ought to know that I am Catholic by breed, and that this means I would become ridiculous, insignificant, null, and nonexistent the moment I left the Church.

What you call a “handler of ideas” is nothing other than the freedom and ease of a spiritual breed.

It is true: I have not changed.

My freedom in dealing with ideas knows no limits because I remain in contact with my unconquerable center, which is not an “idea” but a historical event:

the incarnation of the Son of God.

For me, Christianity is not, in the first place, a doctrine, nor a morality, nor even—excuse me—a religion.

It is a historical event.

Summa contra Gentiles III, 93:

Cum infidelibus nec nomina debemus habere communia, ne ex consortio nominum possit sumi erroris occasio.

We ought not even to share names with unbelievers, lest sharing names create an occasion for error.

(Cited in Privilege and Liberty.)

This concerns the word fatum.

A Christian would do better not to use it.

Unfortunately, the freedom of thought and speech that was almost real in Europe during the years 1925–32 is not among the things restored in this period of restoration—a restoration that had become due after a second world war.2

20 December 1949

Pity is based on identification.

The mystics of pity, Rousseau and Schopenhauer, turn this into a magical identity.

But pity that is conscious of itself can only be self-pity and is therefore nothing but self-deception.

I continue to be astonished by Jünger’s method of putting everything to use.

Posterity and posthumous fame are already built into the calculation.

Diaries which, by all earlier standards, could only have been made accessible to posterity are now turned into literature by the author himself while everyone involved is still alive, and published as ordinary books.

The novel Heliopolis appears immediately from a publishing house called Heliopolis.

A book title is turned straight away into the name of a publishing company.

It is as though Hölderlin had published Hyperion through Hyperion Publishing.

The future literary fate of the work is, so to speak, cashed in immediately and in advance.

It would be too harmless simply to say:

Faust would then have appeared from Faust Publishing;

Schiller’s The Robbers from Robbers Publishing;

Freytag’s Debit and Credit from Debit-and-Credit Publishing;

and Dostoevsky’s The Idiot from Idiot Publishing.

No.

It is something else.

It is the unspoken claim contained in the very existence of Hyperion Publishing.1

Ernest Hello says of Victor Hugo:

“The rhymes come crowding forward like slaves overjoyed that their master should do them the honor of employing them!”2

“They run toward him. They give themselves to him. They surrender themselves. They lavish themselves on him with love!”

No!

You do not know what love is unless you have studied the love that rhyme feels for Victor Hugo!3

Rhyme intoxicates the man it adores.

It transforms his life.

It makes his life a perpetual celebration, <…> turns it into a tale from the Thousand and One Nights.

It turns everything it sees into gold.

It fills nature with wonder.4

This magic wand, etc. (p. 76).

Rhyme and V.[ictor] H.[ugo] are inseparable.

He exists only through it.5

<…>

Disarmed of rhyme, Victor Hugo no longer exists.

Because above all he is a painter.

And rhyme in verse is what color is in painting.

It is fantasy, richer than .

Important in the age of unleashed color!

Däubler unleashes rhymes in the same way that colors have been unleashed.

O man, you prey. Yes indeed, it is all about prey. And what rhymes with Beute—prey? Heute! Today! Leute! People! Meute! Pack! Bedeute! Mean!

Expressiones

22 December 1949

As soon as I recognize a plan and see through it, I am able to escape it.

So the plan must remain secret.

It must be impenetrable, like Providence, like God’s decree.

The planner is the earthly god.

The earthly god is not dead.

Where there is nothing left except the earthly god, one must become an atheist.

But the earthly god keeps a close watch.

Secrecy belongs to the very nature of a plan.

If I see through the plan, I can escape it.

God’s Providence must remain beyond investigation.

Human beings who play at being Providence must therefore play the role of God in this respect too: their decisions must remain inscrutable.

So posterity is supposed to judge.

Who is posterity?

Jaspers and Curtius are posterity in relation to Goethe!

What follows from that?

It follows that we know no more about posterity than we know about life after death.

24 December 1949

The Hamburg judgment against the German general Manstein as a gift for Stalin’s seventieth birthday.

The bones of the Pomeranian grenadier served on a silver platter.1

All of this is shameful.

Shameful.

And unworthy of Providence.

And your other Providence as well, you stupid <…> Roosevelt-Morgenthau.

(Stalin’s superiority lies in the fact that, in relation to this Morgenthau planning, he is on the defensive, while Hitler hopes he can still make it over to the other side.)2

27 December 1949

What is man?

A circulation of blood, with one poor will-o’-the-wisp perched above.

28 December 1949

Why is Rossini so much sweeter than Mozart?

It is the mysterious sweetness of restorations, reprises, returns, and rondos.

Is it the happiness of eternal recurrence?

The affirmation of the cyclical?

The affirmation of the present within the endless circulation of past and future?

What stands opposite this moment as the wholly Other?

It is also the wholly inhuman.

But dialectically, the wholly human can only be the wholly inhuman.

Today, unfortunately, cyclicism means nothing more than restoration.

The opposite of Ernst Jünger’s practice of exploiting diaries and letters can be found in T. E. Lawrence.

For Lawrence, the thought that one of his letters might be published after his death introduced a new terror into the act of writing letters.

“There is an American dealer who pays twenty pounds for my letters. Would you write a single letter if that happened to you?”

And Ernst Jünger puts himself in the same category as this T. E. Lawrence.

Ernst Jünger, the exploiter of letters and dreams and diaries!

People persecuted today are divided into five categories.

Let us try dividing the persecutors into five categories:

  1. Those who really did suffer something under the defeated regime.

  2. Those who almost suffered something under the defeated regime.

  3. Those who were persecuted while continuing to receive half their salary.

  4. Those who were persecuted while continuing to receive their full salary.

  5. Those who earned good money and merely felt afraid, without anything actually happening to them.

29 December 1949

The Germans have competence. They often have spirit, and sometimes even genius.

But they almost never have tact.

Despite their hypertrophied musicality.

Their lack of tact connects them with the Jews while, at the same time, separating them from the Jews in hostility.

In fact, in an industrially developed society there are infinitely more people who worship the setting sun than the rising sun.

There are simply more people who get up late than people who get up early.

And those who do get up early today are the ones who are immediately driven off to work.

“Innocence is very far from receiving as much protection as crime.”

Magnificent.

La Rochefoucauld, Reflection no. 488.

Above all, zeal on behalf of innocence will never match the zeal of the criminalizers.

The very young peoples, with no history behind them, and the very old Jewish people, overloaded with history, meet at this one point:

their zeal for criminalization.

“Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily.”

La Rochefoucauld, no. 26.

Magnificent.

The sun is death.

Life exists only on earth.

The sun is a chaotic mixture of continuous explosions.

A modern searchlight.

30 December 1949

What do expressions like this actually mean:

“Then”—meaning if things turn out differently from the way I imagine—“world history would have lost its meaning”?

Or, even more brazenly:

“This or that”—something I personally find horrifying—“is unworthy of Providence”?

They mean nothing other than:

We dismiss God.

This position against God and the gods was not invented in the nineteenth century.

The great historical parallel to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries—the first century—already knew it.

The sentence

Causa victrix diis placuit

“The victorious cause pleased the gods”

is meant in an entirely atheistic sense.

It speaks from below upward and sets man against the cruel—that is, the inhuman—God.

Lucan’s Pharsalia, the epic of civil war, is full of such atheistic declarations.

God is not dead.

Something much worse has happened.

God is on the side of the victors.

God brings himself into line and is always brought into line.

Man, precisely as the defeated party, is the better one.

Further examples from Pharsalia VIII, 484 ff. (the speech of Pothinus), or VII, 440 ff., and the fabulous figure of the civil-war soldier Scaeva; compare 22 August 1949.

Ernst Jünger fails when confronted with the figure of Scaeva.

31 December 1949

Strictly speaking, we are not Chaopolites—citizens of chaos—but Chao-hoplites, soldiers of chaos.

Chaos does not belong to the citizen but to the partisan, the freebooter, the buccaneer, and the privateer.

The development from the seventeenth to the twentieth century:

from the filibuster to the partisan.

9 January 1950

I put this question to you as an old, experienced man of sixty-two:

What is the most unbelievable, the most improbable thing you have experienced in your long and eventful life?

Answer:

The note of 20 August 1949.

My tria mirabilia—my three wonders:1

  1. That the French understand chemistry better than the Germans.

  2. Sociology <…> out of its <…> science into an expression and <God/chain> conforming and of Gleichschaltung; well-adjusted man.

Infandum scelus—unspeakable crime:

Book VIII of the Pharsalia;

Mortisque peribunt Argumenta tuae (lines 868–69).

“And the proofs of your death will perish.”

Manstein is sentenced by the court in Hamburg to eighteen years in prison, just as Pompey is beheaded by that Greek ruler.

The expression infandum scelus appears in the summary of Book VIII in my edition of the Pharsalia, edited by Cortius, Leipzig 1726, p. 231.

10 January 1950

In his birthday letter to me last July, Smend wrote about the downward curve that begins after the age of sixty.

But the only thing that really matters is finding one’s style—and by “style” I mean something different from what Heinrich Triepel meant in his final book.

The only thing that matters is finding the esprit de son âge—the spirit of one’s own age:

the style proper to one’s life, one’s time, one’s world, and one’s own old age.

And surely you have done that.2

To Ernst Jünger:

My warmest thanks for the kind greetings your wife brought with her, together with the bottle of excellent Burgundy and the comforting dedication you wrote on it!

It was a wonderful visit, and a joy finally to have another conversation worthy of the name—a conversation in which a long period of separation simply disappeared.3

Naturally, it has also awakened in me the desire to speak with you again and to look directly at the strange moment created by the publication and first reception of Heliopolis.

We had a very heated conversation late into the night.

For me, the figure of the Parsi woman became the worst stumbling block, while Mrs. Jünger tried in the most touching way to defend precisely this figure.

I drank so much wine that I did not notice how exhausting and upsetting all this must have been for your wife, until Mrs. Schmitt reproached me for it.

I now make the same reproach against myself.

Of course, all of this came from streams in me that had been held back for a long time and, fundamentally, could hardly have come out differently.

I only hope your wife got through it and has recovered by now.

Yesterday we took her to Altena, from where she continued on to Hamm.

In your last letter, of 28 November 1949, you gave me a “friendly warning,” though it was concerned mostly with tactical matters.

We are both old enough, and both find ourselves in situations of such a kind, that tactical questions are really things we should discuss only in casual conversation.

But behind those tactical questions lies the matter itself, and that is something we must speak about properly one day.

I read Karl Korn’s review of Heliopolis in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.

I regard Korn as an intelligent and honest man.

I was pleased by the respect one could hear in the review.

But when I came to the word “private,” I almost froze.

It seems to flow past casually, but unintentionally it works like a whistle that destroys everything.

This word “private” is a dangerous signal.

I know something about that.

It disturbed me deeply, especially because shortly before this I had heard a Westphalian say:

“Ernst Jünger became private long ago and no longer inspires even distrust, except the sort of distrust that animates Mr. de Mendelssohn.”

I am older than you in these matters and probably more experienced as well.

I would like us to find the time and calm for an intense conversation between the two of us, whether in the morning or late at night, like the conversations we often had in Berlin during the 1930s.

Your comparison with battleships decorated with flowers does not fit our situation.

Each of us has a name and a cause, genuine fame and a face.

And each of us can lose all of it.

I will deal with my case in my own way and will not drag you into it.

But your case is completely different—simpler, and yet in some ways more dangerous than mine, even with the whole pack running behind me.

My fear and agitation come from depths and regions that are completely unknown and inaccessible to younger people.

You must grant me the right of an older fellow-traveler, and so you must not read this letter too quickly, dear E. J.

You must know that I remain, unchanged, your supporter.

I greet you with unchanged feeling and with my old loyalty to you and your cause, and remain always,

your C. S.

12 January 1950

The dear Germans—I know them already.

“Then they eliminate them.”

Better to read Lucan’s Pharsalia:

Superos quid quaerimus ultra? What more do we seek from the gods? (IX, 579)

Neither the jurists nor the theologians seem to have understood that all essential and urgent questions have now become questions about the philosophy of history.

A few sociologists would like to take advantage of that.

Aren’t you ashamed of yourself?

You write pleasant letters to former colleagues who trample you underfoot while holding out the prospect of a little charity, so that they can prove their own humanity to themselves!

But I really do write such letters only out of politeness.

My unwavering politeness has become my ruin.

One cannot even accuse me of having played too cheaply.

I knew what was at stake.

I simply could not stop being polite, while first the Nazis and then the denazifiers performed their shoe-slapping dances all around me.

There are people who cannot stop being legal, or cannot stop believing in .

I belong to those who cannot stop being polite.

But you yourself must admit that there is some kind of weakness in this politeness of yours.

What do you expect to achieve with your politeness when Russians and Yankees are dropping atomic bombs, when Morgenthau is devising his Morgenthau Plan, and a hundred thousand Japanese in Hiroshima still have to die even after the Second World War is already over?

What do you expect to achieve with your politeness, poor man?

You are completely old-fashioned, pre-industrial, antisocial, undemocratic—so to speak, impossible to integrate, un-European.

Salus ex Judaeis? Perditio ex Judaeis?

Salvation from the Jews?

Destruction from the Jews?

For now, enough of these intrusive Judaei!

When we became divided within ourselves, the Jews inserted themselves into the gap.

Until that is understood, there can be no salvation.

Benedict—of all names—Spinoza, who was supplied by the synagogue, at that time presumably still intact, with <…> benefices, was the first to insert himself in this way.

Today, those who inserted themselves are experiencing a restoration accompanied by colossal claims for compensation and repayment.

But those who inserted themselves are still worse than the returning emigrants enjoying their revenge.

They ought to be ashamed to take the dollar they are paid.

16 January 1950

All time is interim time.

Every regnum is an interregnum.

Meaning-time is mean-time, etc.

17 January 1950

My concern about Ernst Jünger:

Now he is going to lose even the Pour le Mérite.

One cannot live forever on opus operatum—on the work already performed.1

He constructs his own life as a dangerous one.

The others who really were in danger will not tolerate that, and those who are living dangerously today will tolerate it even less.

In this way he gets drawn into the dispute over who was, or is, in the greatest danger.

How sad.

26 January 1950, in Cologne.

A comforting example:

Scipio Africanus faced with the accusations of the Petilii.

Leave the Forum, go to the Capitol, and see how many people follow you!

We?

(Not me!)

So human beings are now creating a world of their own, an artificial world:

the world of technology.

That is a dangerous adventure.

But is that a reason not to create this world?

God created the world too, and through the fall of the angels and of man it slipped from his grasp, became corrupted and wounded.

Why should human beings not likewise take the risk that their new world may slip from their grasp?

The new New World2 is therefore already among us.

It is in our hands.

It is under construction.

It does not have a bounded piece of earth in which a sacred place can be located.

Its interest in land is an interest in deposits of raw materials.

It cares only about exploitation, not cultivation.

Where does this New World stand?

It removes the ground from under the feet of its previous owners.

It treats the surface of the earth the way a sailor treats the sea, not the way a man walking on land treats the earth.

Its character is not nomadic but maritime.3

Modern industry is a continuation of the transition from land to sea.4

That is why it first arose in England.

Again and again, the astonishing § 247 of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right.

Is there a dialectic in the sequence of the elements?

That depends on how far we can grasp the concept of an element historically and set it into motion.1

If we can, then the sequence is indeed:

land, water, air, fire.

Historical development then moves through this cycle.

Our historical dialectic must begin with these elements, not, as in Hegel’s lectures, with the written material of historical knowledge.

Nor should it begin with economic materialism.

Economic materialism possesses only the time-bound truth of the nineteenth century’s self-destruction and is itself an ideological superstructure built over the Industrial Revolution of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

4 February 1950

Favor victoris.

Favor toward the victor.

What use is a clear and compelling argument in international law in Germany’s favor today?

It always runs into the consequences of the discriminatory concept of war.

That concept gives Germany’s opponents the clear conscience they need to strip the defeated party of its rights.

As every day shows anew, it makes a peace treaty internally impossible.

What remains are only measures of punishment, compensation, and reeducation.2

Every effort to “normalize” relations with Germany—especially relations between the occupying powers and German state authority—runs into this basic source of all the impossibilities of international law.

A discriminatory concept of war does not permit the normalization of the party that has been discriminated against.3

What, then, is a German supposed to do?

The following possibilities exist:

  1. Attack the idea of the just war head-on. Openly demonstrate its historical, legal, and moral perversity; show that it is an instrument of civil war, and so on. Hopeless?

  2. Patiently hollow it out from within by positivist means. Normalize things quietly and unofficially. Sabotage the system by cooperating in the development of the legal foundations of the Nuremberg judgments. Deliberately and systematically play the worm in the rotten wood. Use Portia’s method: take them exactly at their word.

  3. Combine these two possibilities, with different people playing different roles.

How proud and imposingly arrogant this once sounded to us:

“Anyone who comments on himself falls below his own level.”

Very good.

But what about a man who does not merely comment on himself—which would actually do many people some good—but copies himself, complacently imitates himself, and turns himself into a mannerism?

Where does a Heraclitean go if he wants to walk through the same river three times?

A nihilist?

An eighteen-year-old schoolboy said of this:

“This is supposed to be a nihilist—a man as completely convinced of, and coated in, himself as E.[rnst] J.[ünger]?”

5 February 1950

I have read Jünger’s two letters of 10 and 16 January 1950 closely.

Capisco.

I understand.

He says literally:

“If, however, you had followed my advice and my example in the matter, you might no longer be alive today, but you would have the right to pass final judgment on me.”

Good.

Capisco et obmutesco.

I understand, and I fall silent.

So speaks one survivor to another!

(compare 9 September 1958)

He constructs two unreal conditional sentences.

He says:

The survivor is wrong, because perhaps I would no longer be alive.

But before that he says that he himself—although, after all, he too survived—would certainly no longer be alive, physically or psychologically, if he had followed me.

Is this not the sophistry of an ego-mad man who always has to be right?

An aftereffect of his mescaline experiment?1

La guerre sainte, la guerre à la fois diabolique et divine.

Holy war: war that is at once diabolical and divine.

Ch. Journet, L’Église du Verbe Incarné, 1943, p. 360 ff.

Heading:

“Holy War and the Crusade.”

Section:

“Sacral Christendom.”

Cum armis Jherusalem peregrinati sunt.

They made pilgrimage to Jerusalem bearing arms.

He relies on Carl Erdmann, The Origin of the Idea of Crusade, Stuttgart 1935.

Within the problematic concept of “holy war,” J.[ournet] makes a distinction in discussing the Crusades between “the canonical power of the clergy and their non-canonical powers”!

“It will then become clear that ‘holy wars’ are bound to the existence, or the surviving remnants, of a Christendom of the sacral type.”

Exactly.

p. 362.

War, like death, comes from sin:

per peccatum mors.

Through sin, death.

Romans 5:12.2

In the Responsa of Nicholas I to the Bulgarians (866), we read:

“The struggles of wars and battles, and likewise the beginnings of every quarrel, were certainly devised by the deceitful art of the devil.”

War is permissible only in an emergency.

Patrologia Latina CXIX, col. 998, no. 46.

Nevertheless, Joseph de Maistre is not entirely wrong to call war “divine” in the seventh dialogue of the Soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg, because war cannot be explained in purely human terms:

“There is no way to explain how war is humanly possible.”

Exactly.

J. de M.:

therefore divine punishment;

divine in the sense in which hell is divine.

The Deus indignatus—the indignant God—imposes it.

De Civitate Dei, I, chapter 9.

At the beginning of war there is always sin.

But war is just when it is occasioned, not inspired—so he says, p. 363.

A harsh necessity.

But is the idea of a just war not even sadder?

St. Augustine asks this in De Civitate Dei 19, chapter 7.

(This chapter 7 is magnificent and more important than most books about just war; chapter 8 as well, including the distinction between friend and enemy!)

Then Thomas, Summa Theologiae II–II, question 40, articles 1 and 3.

“After reading this description of the just war,” Journet says, “one naturally asks how many wars have ever been completely just. I think one could count them on the fingers of one hand.”

Very good.

Here a new and devastating concept appears:

the one-hundred-percent just war!

J.[ournet] refers to Gustave Thibon, Études carmélitaines, 1939, pp. 63–67:

War is just only when the Christian faces a choice “between war and the denial of his essence as a human being.”

Exactly.

Do these good and righteous people really not see that this turns war into a war of annihilation?!

Ideological war is an idol-war.

Very good.

Here the Christian must be careful not to become the victim of deception—

“and this will not be easy, and only saints will be fully capable of it!!”

Exactly.

G. Thibon, with Journet agreeing, p. 364 note.

The Christian must realize the “paradox”:

inwardly, love and the renunciation of every judgment—

“Christian justice, which judges no one!!”

Exactly—

while “performing the gestures of hatred.”

Very complicated.

And internally paradoxical.

In the end, only saints can do it.

The Cluniac reformers spread the idea of Christian knighthood.

They “transfigured” the Germanic idea of combat.

The distinction between just wars and holy wars appears on p. 365.

A just war does not become holy merely because the pope recognizes the justice of its cause.

William the Conqueror, 1066.

Collaboration, approval, consecration—none of these is enough if the cause concerns secular interests.

Nor, even in a sacral regime, is it enough merely that one is dealing with a crime such as heresy.

Admittedly, wars encouraged and approved by the Church in defense of the faith could be called just wars.

“But we prefer to reserve this name, if the name must be used at all (!), for wars for which the pope himself assumes responsibility and which we shall now discuss.”

p. 367.

So:

holy wars.

p. 367.

Answer, following H. Pissard, La guerre sainte en pays chrétien, Paris 1912:

“Holy wars are just wars (!) which the Church not only encourages but also rewards with its spiritual favors.”

But, Journet says, we do not claim that they are undertaken or directed by the Church.

That is, they do not arise from canonical power.

“They are undertaken and directed by the pope’s extra-canonical power, acting either as head of the Papal State or as guardian of Christendom.”

Exactly.

p. 369.

The pure holy war—that is, a war waged by the pope on the basis of canonical powers—is, according to Journet, impossible.

It has also never occurred.

Not even against the Albigensians in 1208–14.

Pissard takes a different view.

As an honest man, he argues that war was simply the logical escalation of the interdict, the release of vassals from their obligations, and their “exposure as prey,” undertaken in order to execute canonical judgments against heretics who had become too powerful, when the suzerain—not the sovereign!—could not or would not lend the support of his sword.

So Journet, p. 369 note.

“The Church as such does not wage war.”

No one “as such” wages war.

Disgusting, this comme tel—“as such.”

It reminds one far too much of:

“The Party as such stands on the foundation of positive Christianity.”

The great back door.

Carl Erdmann claims that Augustine raised the suppression of the Donatists by Emperor Honorius to the level of holy war.

The author of this war was God himself, and the soldiers were God’s ministri—his servants.

(op. cit., p. 7)

But Augustine always protests against heretics being punished with death.

He fears that the blood of the heretics will fall back upon the Church!!

Batiffol, Le Catholicisme de St. Augustin, pp. 334–35.

Well, look at that.

Gustav Schnürer, L’Église et la civilisation du moyen âge, Paris—he does not give the year—vol. I, p. 115, says:

“The emperors did not proceed against heretics in the capacity of agents of the Church, but in their own sovereign power.”

Exactly.

Comme tel.

“As such.”

En qualité de.

“In the capacity of.”

So all of this already belongs to the sacral order of the Middle Ages.

Heresy is a crime under ordinary law.

St. Gregory is different.

He exhorts Gennadius, the exarch of Africa, “to resist with force for the good of the Christian people.”

Ecclesiastica proelia sicut bellatores Domini fortiter dimicatis!!

You fight the battles of the Church bravely, like warriors of the Lord!!

“This is already, if one wishes (!!), a holy war.”

p. 373.

An appeal to the bloody sword in order to defend Christians against the actions of heretics.

But—

and what do you think comes next?—

but Gennadius is not under Gregory’s orders.

The expedition is undertaken in the name of secular power.

The pope makes no attempt to draw responsibility for it onto himself.

He is not that stupid.

He assumes neither responsibility nor risk.

Good old Gennadius takes those on.

Shameful, this Journet.

p. 373.

The pope merely incites him to war.

“He”—Gregory—“intervenes to incite”—yes, incite!—“the exarch to defend the Church.”

If he speaks of “ecclesiastical wars” and “warriors of the Lord,” this cannot be meant in the strict sense.

And so suddenly it becomes “indirect.”

All from the letters of St. Gregory.

Patrologia Latina LXXVII, cols. 528–29.

Newspaper cutting from Die Zeit, 9 February 1950, pasted in.

Written above it:

“Illustration of the Just War. Die Zeit; yes indeed, Die Zeit.”

Carl Erdmann speaks of the “Gregorian missionary war.”

Another example:

Erlembald, the first knight commissioned by Pope Gregory VII, military leader of the Patarenes in Milan.

Journet, p. 376.

Journet does not think this is correct.

“Even under a sacral regime”—such as existed in the Christian Middle Ages—the warriors and defenders of the faith commissioned by the Church acted “as Christians, but not in their capacity as Christians.”

Exactly.

p. 374, note 2.

Erdmann also says, p. 8:

War against pagans was just only when the pagans became aggressors and implacable persecutors of the Christian faith.

Important:

hostis perpetuus—the permanent enemy.

Unfortunately, this does not appear in Journet!

Important, Journet p. 377 note:

“A religious who, in the case of unjust aggression, does not defend himself acts in his capacity as a Christian, in his capacity as a religious. If he does defend himself, he undoubtedly acts as a Christian, but in his capacity as a human being.”

That is what the Jesuits did on 24 June 1621 when they defended Macao against the Dutch.

See Joseph Duhr, S. J., Un jésuite en Chine: Adam Schall, astronome et conseiller impérial (1592–1666), Brussels 1936, p. 34.

8 February 1950

If nothing remains to me except the choice between a defeated devil and a victorious devil, I choose the defeated one.

I am irresistibly drawn toward the defeated.

I shudder with disgust when I hear the songs of triumph sung by the victorious righteous and read in the Book of Wisdom (5:4–5):1

“The wicked will be astonished by the unexpected good fortune of the righteous.”

I would rather be among the defeated wicked than among the victorious righteous.

Since I know both of them—the victors and the defeated—to be equally wicked, the matter becomes clearer still.

The bestial atrocities of the defeated and the bestial revenge taken for those atrocities really do cancel each other out.

What remains is the misery of these wretched defeated people and the happiness of these triumphant victors.

The case is clear.

Heidegger passes the test of the comeback with the grade “fully satisfactory” on both sides.

Gottfried Benn does magnificently.

Ernst Jünger fails miserably.2

Let us wait and see how I do.

(You are incapable of a comeback at all, because you exist in eternal change and never step into the same river twice.)

So in the end the whole thing comes down to en que—“as a Christian”—and en tant que—“in the capacity of a Christian”—and comme tel—“as such”!

En que—en tant que.

And you expect to save the whole thing with that?!

17 March 1950

What is it, exactly, that we are experiencing now?

The deserters declare the front-line soldiers to be cowards.

The emigrants declare those who did not emigrate to be enemies of their country.

So what we are experiencing is this:

those who ran away declare the forerunners to be mere followers.

(Poor Orwell has still not understood that with his 1984 he is merely a follower of 1894!)

Those who ran away declare those who stood their ground to be mere followers.

21 March 1950

What was really going on during all these years since 1933?

It was an attempt to liquidate civil war on the level of total technology.

It failed because of German Bildung—German cultivated education.

More precisely, because of the strange union between lack of education and technological power.

In Sartre’s L’Être et le Néant, pp. 704–06, one finds a philosophy of holes and anuses perfectly suited to the age, both in its subject matter and in its form, both in thought and in language.

What is one supposed to say about it?

No kind of food should be recommended to those who dream.3

Death is hard.

Into the hole.

Still, there is also a small note there, p. 705:

“One should also note the importance of the opposite tendency, the tendency to pierce holes, which would by itself require an existential analysis.”

Exactly.

Bravo!

Punch a hole in his skull!

That is the counter-movement to the tendency to kick him in his filthy asshole.

p. 466:

C’est se faire muqueuse pure.

It is to turn oneself into pure mucous membrane.

No kind of food should be recommended to those who dream.

The German face.

What is the face of a people supposed to look like when the vengeful emigrant is elevated into its ideal type?

They stomp all over Germany and then wonder why its face looks horrible.1

23 March 1950

There is something I like about Sartre:

the moments when he becomes epigrammatic, in the style and at the level of the great moralists.

He is not really an ontologist like Heidegger at all.

He is a moralist.

His analysis of désir—desire—as fleshly lust belongs to the most modern style of the moralists and reaches its climax in the sentence:

C’est se faire muqueuse pure.

It is to turn oneself into pure mucous membrane.

(p. 466)

Le fait de la mort—“the fact of death”—is bad positivism.

His argument against suicide is delightfully moralistic.

Everything that helps me remain in the space of unobstructed waiting is good.

Everything.

Whether it comes to me as a word of Heraclitus, a sentence of Hegel, a motif from Wagner’s Tristan, or a stanza by Konrad Weiß.

Son of this consecration, you have been dispossessed of yourself.

Listen and suffer.

24 March 1950

Rousseau speaks of the stake with which the first owner marked off his property.

That stake was the first symbol.

It should have been torn from the ground with the cry:

“Beware of this fraud!”

But today there are other symbols of the same kind, symbols that open an age of unfreedom and that would best be torn out immediately.

The blue tax stamp used as a postage stamp is one such symbol.

28 March 1950

Money distorts the world.

It turns everything into merchandise.

1 April 1950

Heideggerisms:

By “publishing”—that is, by having my thoughts typeset and printed—I am already displaced, distorted, ordered, employed:

engagé.

12 April 1950

The retreat of the natural barrier—which followed the retreat of the old boundaries of the orbis antiquus, the ancient world—contains within it the advance of social barriers.

Does technology create free space?

Oh dear.

You can hardly see it.

Every political community, and especially every democracy, has its “underground” part.

Today that consists of the millions who have been discriminated against.

The more their condemnation into this underground realm is carried out in the name of humanity and human rights, and for the protection of true peace, the more final and eternal that condemnation becomes.

In 1926 I wrote and published the claim that one could tell, from every work dealing with constitutional questions, whether its author knew the writing of the young Hegel.

Twenty-five years later, I see how childish this appeal to the education of German teachers of law really was.

I write this today under the impact of rereading The Scientific Ways of Treating Natural Law.

To think that in 1931 I published a book called The Guardian of the Constitution containing a long reference to Hegel.

How naïve!

And people today are still talking about natural law—people who do not even know this essay by Hegel!

Talking about the rule-of-law state without knowing the passage about the spirit of the earth rising upright.

A cutting from an English-language newspaper of 12 April 1950 is pasted in, showing a “High Flying Suit.”

Written above it:

“Ah, no bodily wing will ever join the wings of the spirit.

Le voilà—there he is, the companion!”

21 April 1950

An important current subject:

a sociological problem, a problem in intellectual history, and a problem in other respects as well:

a detailed comparison between the people who profited from the upheaval of 1933 and the people who profited from the collapse of 1945.

28 April 1950

After the suppression of the Bar Kokhba revolt in AD 135, open resistance came to an end.

Only the eschatological and messianic hope remained, kept quietly alive.

“The stable authority of the patriarch, recognized by Rome, replaces the short-lived insurrectionary power of the Son of the Star, and in an Israel now sobered and resigned, the exclusive reign of the Law is established.”

Exactly:

Marcel Simon, Verus Israel: étude sur les relations entre Chrétiens et Juifs dans l’empire Romain, 135–425, Paris, Boccard, rue de Médicis, 1948, p. 13.

That is it:

le règne exclusif de la Loi.

The exclusive reign of the Law.

2 May 1950

The exact title of the book by Karl Binding and Alfred Hoche really is:

Permitting the Destruction of Life Unworthy of Life.

Leipzig, Felix Meiner, 1920.

Every word of that title is totalitarian.

Orwell should already have noticed back then what sort of world we were living in—and that he himself was living in it too:

“Permitting the destruction”!

“Life unworthy of life.”

3 May 1950

On issue 4, April 1950, of Hochland:

In the so-called Hochland the air grows ever more sultry; there they pair Konrad Weiß with Else Lasker-Schüler.1

4 May 1950

Asked Hans Schneider to ask Hans Welzel for the exact reference to the passage in Kant about the judge of heretics.

See p. 19 of Welzel’s work on the erring conscience.

Does Welzel really not see that, at this point, a genuine declaration of enmity suddenly tears apart the whole moralizing fabric?2

5 May 1950

In Bertolt Brecht’s Threepenny Novel—German edition, Desch, Munich 1946? p. 296—the leader of the criminal organization, Macheath, teaches his men:

One must work legally.

It is just as good a sport.

The whole speech he gives on this occasion is an enormous and uncanny illustration of my thesis about the distinction between legality and legitimacy.

Anyone who still does not understand it after this and still comes along talking about natural law belongs among the êtres destinés à périr—the beings destined to perish.

“Brute force has had its day. You no longer send murderers when you can send the bailiff.”

Working legally allows you to take a larger haul, peacefully and at lower cost, and so on.

Working through crime is an obsolete stage of labor:

medieval,

old-fashioned.

10 May 1950

If the donkeys of the present restoration really manage to identify Hitler with Richard Wagner in the artistic sphere, and with me in the intellectual sphere, then we can expect comebacks of an entirely different and far more astonishing kind than the harmless ones we have seen so far—or than the moral rectitude of the denazified could ever dream of.

13 May 1950

Reading Ponceau: anti-Communist bad faith. But is there no such thing as anti-Nazi bad faith?

Is this the great, absolute abnormality—the one unforgivable offense in a world where everything else is forgiven? The one crime that remains after the enormous machinery of criminalization is, inevitably, dismantled?

Good faith alone is not enough. You also need some brains.

19 May 1950

Again and again, you find yourself dependent on words.

All power is command, every command is a word.

Imprisoned in our humanity, we are imprisoned in words. We have no other vehicle.

And God has no other refuge.

Found a note from 24 August 1915 (Munich): the poet’s liberation is purely social. He speaks about himself and finds people who hear [and] understand him. Depending on the case, that is either divine or contemptible.

21 May 1950

There is no ultra-word to match ultrasound; the ultra-man reproduces himself into the void.

23 May 1950

European legal scholarship? Where is it? Who represents it? And if it still has any honor left, it owes that honor to me (Empedocles).1

Whatever you do, don’t write to that Dr. Lewald, that refined and noble strangler.

Non decet scribere ei qui vult proscribere—it is not fitting to write to someone who wants to proscribe you.

Hölderlin’s ode to Vanini, with its ending:

… and your enemies Returned, like you, to the ancient peace. (Holy Nature forgets what human beings do.)

One must work legally (p. 296). One must be able to determine the law before sending out one’s murderers.

There is no need to bend the law. Applying it is enough.

28 May 1950

G.[ünther] K.[rauß] thinks that if he himself had been the Crown jurist of the Crown of Castile around 1530, he could not have defended either the imperial or the papal grant as a legal argument. There was probably no possible justification other than the Aristotelian-Sepúlvedan one.

That means the Pope and the Church abandoned their most faithful and devout protectors.

Perhaps they have to.

There would be a special kind of “tragedy” in that—although “tragedy” is such a kitsch word for something that is, in fact, terribly sad.1

When I read Alvaro d’Ors’s beautiful, devout letter to Father Welty from May 1950, I almost feel sorry for this kind of sincere interest in a Germany that, in reality, sends Mr. Hausenstein to Paris as its first postwar representative and elevates a tactless, repellent fellow like Erich Kaufmann into the guiding spirit of international law.

To Tüngel (Pentecost Sunday):

In your article “The New Biedermeier” (25 May 1950), you say that the problem of how democracy can defend itself against its own principles has “not yet been thought through.”

For the sake of accuracy, let me point out that this exact problem was thoroughly examined in a substantial study published by Duncker & Humblot in 1932 under the title Legality and Legitimacy.

It is not my fault that, back in 1932, it was precisely the democrats who opposed this work and its warnings most fiercely.

Of course, the leading professors of constitutional law at the time also fiercely opposed it, while issuing warnings of their own.

You would probably even enjoy the wording of certain passages—for example, those on p. 33 or p. 96.

If, today, as an old man who has been dismantled along with everything else, I mention this work to you once again, I find myself in something like the position in which, according to an old story, the Sibyl once stood before that Roman king.

But please do not misunderstand me.

I cannot imagine that you would hold it against an old specialist in constitutional theory if, deeply impressed by your article, he slips back into a professional habit formed over forty years and, when he sees an extremely difficult problem being discussed, tries to draw attention to a genuine source.

Yours most devotedly, C. S.

29 May 1950

When the enemy becomes the judge, the judge becomes the enemy.

The German language has no native word of its own for “person,” none for “legal subject,” and none for “family.” It can only say Ich—I, the self.

Think how difficult it is to think legally in a language like that.

German has no native word of its own for “family” either. It knows only Sippe—the clan, the kin-group.

Subject = bearer?2

The criminalization of the aggressor is the legitimation of the status quo.

How monstrously stupid must the opponents of aggression be if the revolutionaries can afford to join them in this criminalization?3

Who sees whom—which today means: who manages to get whom in front of the lens—is surely nothing more than a question of the situation.

I decide who sees whom.

31 May 1950

Marx (and Lukács) speak of reification. By this they mean turning human beings and things into commodities.

But for the thing itself, this transformation is precisely the opposite: it strips the thing of its thinghood.

Marx nevertheless has a feeling for the thing itself. In his critique of Max Stirner he says:

“Private property alienates not only the individuality of human beings, but also that of things. Land has nothing to do with ground rent, and the machine has nothing to do with profit.”1

Correct.

They also have nothing to do with power.

But what happens when they are caught in the web of social relations?

Inhabited land is a more direct instrument of power than an atomic bomb.

Or Capital, Volume I, Chapter <…>, note 33: the history of landed property forms the secret history of the Roman Republic.

Why secret?

3 June 1950

In any case, the question of who has the authority to banish me from the realm of the German spirit has now been happily settled by this article by Dr. Lewald in the NJW.2

Apart from this positive result, the article is merely a document of cultural history. It belongs in the same category as the jurisprudence of the witch hunts.

It has prompted me, very profitably, to reread Count Spee’s Cautio Criminalis of 1631.

Anyone who can write in a legal journal that I, the author of Political Theology, “deified the Antichrist” has placed himself squarely within that historical category.

I have never deified anyone or anything.

At most, for a time, I deified my wife Duschka.

And she deserved it!3

7 June 1950

Paradigms on a world scale.

Great cases in ethics?

Jünger: Heliopolis, In the School of War.

The plank of Carneades.

The suicide of the French fleet at Toulon, November 1942.

Mortisque peribunt Argumenta tuae

And the proofs of your death will perish.

(Above, 9 January 1950.)

In his Journal, under 28 November 1942, André Gide discusses the deliberate scuttling of the French fleet at Toulon.

A classic example of suicide in the face of a choice that is inwardly impossible but forced upon you by circumstances.

Neither East nor West, neither Germany nor England, was possible for the French fleet.

Is that not Germany’s entire situation today?

And if Toulon were to serve as our model, would we not have to commit suicide too?

Gide says of the decision made by the French officers—to sink their ships rather than serve either the British or the Germans:

“It meant placing honor above even the interests of the fatherland … and despite everything, there is in this a preference for oneself over the cause, which leaves the conscience uneasy.”

What a kitsch phrase from such a demanding stylist, a man who is usually merciless when he finds weaknesses like this in the great authors!

“One admires,” he says, “but one cannot approve. In the terrible dead end into which they had put themselves, they had no choice left except suicide or servitude. There was no possible escape, no way out. From the moment our fleet failed immediately to choose dissidence, it became either useless or dishonored. Submission to the terms of the armistice amounted to a delayed scuttling. At the side of the English, this fleet could have rendered very great services”—

that is: they would have stood on the side of the victor. Shame on you for this morality after the event, old man!

—“it now serves only as an example of the harm caused by obedience once personal conscience no longer assents to the orders it receives.”

Every sentence in this argument would have to be analyzed.

It would be worth doing, because the situation of Germany—indeed, of Europe—is the same today.

Here lies the true moral problem beneath the choice between East and West.

What Gide offers is prophecy turned backward. It is the viewpoint of the victor. It means giving up one’s own French existence.

In a situation like this, suicide is the escape: voluntary destruction rather than serving victors with whom one cannot identify.

Gide argues in the most naive possible way, like a historian without dialectics.

His morality depends entirely on perspective.

He moves along the rails of morality with the victor’s good conscience.

When one reads André Gide saying, “Hitler arose from Versailles,” one has to ask:

What, then, will arise from Yalta and Potsdam?

Versailles stands to Yalta and Potsdam as Wilhelm II stands to Hitler!

8 June 1950

The Schleiermacher-Hegel argumentum ad canem—the argument from the dog—says, and apparently expects to count as an argument:

“I would not treat my dog the way I have felt God treating me for years.”

But you are not a dog.

Though you would like to be one.1

12 June 1950

What if someone were to say:

Socialism has as much to do with work in theory, and as little to do with it in practice, as the Christian Churches have to do with poverty?

Or with true Christianity?

The law governing the exploitation of ascetic ideals or philosophies of history.

Those who profit from the struggle against those who profit.

The German language has no native word of its own for “person,” and none for “legal subject.”2

It knows only Ich—I.

Fine.

Even the most fanatical purifiers of German have so far failed to find a German word for these things.

German knows only the Ich.

But look!

Technology is already approaching with a completely unexpected word, and a very German one at that:

Träger—bearer.

There it is:

a bearer of rights, a bearer of office, a bearer of property—which means the destruction of personal property— a bearer of duties.

Yes indeed.

That is where the social sorcery begins: when you flick on the electric light.

That is where man begins to become God.

Fiat lux—let there be light.

Millions of priests perform this act hundreds of millions of times.

And then are surprised by Adolf.

15 June 1950

In Paradise, human beings are naked.

Why?

Because there they have no enemy.

Today, a nude photograph of an enemy leader is a weapon.

More precisely—since the distinction between enemy and criminal has been abolished and there are therefore no longer any “weapons”—it is an instrument of extermination, used to eliminate the pest, the last obstacle standing in the way of universal happiness.

Tormented by intellectual curiosity, and only after considerable trouble, I managed to get hold of Ernst Bloch’s Freedom and Order.

I had remembered his Spirit of Utopia.

What a disappointment.

He does not even engage with Huxley’s Brave New World of 1932.

The intellectual deterioration of these émigrés is terrible. Madame de Staël’s description from 1815 still applies to them:

They have learned nothing and forgotten nothing.

At least the French aristocrats of 1815 returned to their country.

But these poor Jews!!

Who do not want to be Zionists!

22 June 1950

Worse than the criminals are the people who criminalize them!1

23 June 1950

Bravo, Sartre!

That is what the good André Gide writes in his Journal in January 1948.

“It is the antisemite who creates the Jew.”

Gide finds that fair and important.

Now look at the Jews, and then at those pathetic antisemites.

But then comes this:

“The Jews are the gentlest of men.”2

Bravo, Sartre, says Gide.

Just look at sweet Henry Morgenthau.

And Erich Kaufmann.

It is pure chance that we are still alive.

But we would have been killed very gently.

Bravo, Sartre.

“I feel wholeheartedly with you.”

That is André Gide, January 1948.

Still, he adds:

“But there is nevertheless a Jewish question—an anguishing, obsessive question—and it is nowhere near being resolved.”

Well then, my dear André Gide:

What would you have answered on the questionnaire—or under interrogation by Mr. Ebenstein—if he had asked you:

“What is your position on the Jewish question?”

Old André Gide, you never had to sit across from one of these sweet interrogators.

5 July 1950

God is the wholly Other?

So the theologians proclaim.

Well, yes—the theologians of the Christian Churches.

State-employed victims of fascism.

The overprivileged.

Potential Nobel Prize winners.

God, the wholly Other?

God is the wholly Identical.

God is I.

The distance between the typical working legal practitioner and the science of law is much greater than the distance between the typical public-health-insurance doctor and medical science.3

23 July 1950

The cabinet of legal monstrosities:

  1. The latest Allied Control Council Law No. 10 applies only to supporters of Hitler during the Nazi period.

“Control Council Law No. 10 therefore offers the unusual spectacle of a criminal provision which was not yet in force when it could have been violated, and which can no longer be violated now that it is in force.”

(Paul Bockelmann, Zeitschrift für die gesamte Strafrechtswissenschaft, LXIII [1950], no. 1, p. 14.)

  1. The Denazification Law:

Unlimited power of revision.

Reformatio in peius—revision that makes the position of the accused worse—made permanent.

26 July 1950

It was a postmaster who, in 1792, prevented the King of France from escaping and thereby determined the further course of European history.

What follows from this?

It follows that kings must stay on good terms with postmasters if they want to save the monarchy.

Or with their chauffeurs and technicians.

The problem of master and servant, according to Hegel’s Phenomenology.

(Noted on the day King Leopold returned to Belgium.)

27 July 1950

Become a de-de-ifier!

A de-anti-ifier!

The great program of de-anti-fication!

With unlimited powers.

1 August 1950

How proudly I once wrote:

Welcome, good and evil!

And behold:

evil came.

Real evil.

Then I stopped saying welcome.

Then I said:

You damned pack of swine.

8 August 1950

Homo homini Radbruch.

Radbruch is Radbruch to man.

“We don’t kill them, we drive them to suicide.”

That is the formula for ritual murder according to the strictly humanitarian rite.

You do not kill anyone.

You drive the other person to suicide.

Very gently.

11 August 1950

How much longer can he hold out—the crucified Jew?

I took his side, and for doing so I was disgraced by his supposed priests and believers.

No one protects me.

But that is only logical.1

How much longer can he hold out against all this?

I hold out.

But he does not.

He has no intention of holding out.

He is enjoying the trump cards of anti-fascism!

Let him enjoy them.

Without me.

Again and again I have fallen for the deception.

Again and again I have escaped it.

Recommended dissertation topic for ambitious young German male and female students in the West German Federal Republic of 1950:

Carlo Schmid et les beaux arts.

Carlo Schmid and the fine arts.

16 August 1950

De Maistre thought that nothing worse could happen to a decent man than to find himself in the position of having to sit in judgment over the murderer of his own son.

Very beautiful.

Very delicate.

But unworthy of a modern humanitarian.

Today’s humanitarians push forward eagerly to sit in judgment.

The victims rush upon their own victims as prosecutors, judges, and above all as executioners—as Habebald and Eilebeute, greedy for plunder.

It pays to be a victim.

Nothing pays better.

Newspaper clipping dated 3 August 1950 pasted in, with a cartoon about the Korean War. Written beneath it:

“Only someone who knows his prey better than the prey knows itself can conquer it.”

29 August 1950

Ernst Jünger and Monsieur Quine:

Quine has something of the entomologist about him (p. 242 of Bernanos’s novel).

His love of human beings is the beetle collector’s love for his beetles:

an infallible grip that does not hurt its subject, leaves it intact, and yet puts it entirely at our mercy, etc.1

But Ernst Jünger lacks Mr. Quine’s devouring curiosity.

Instead, he has second sight.

My Nomos of the Earth is appearing at exactly the right historical moment.

The time is coming, Nietzsche said in 1881/82, when the struggle for rule over the earth will begin.

It will be fought in the name of fundamental philosophical doctrines (XII, 441).

That is to say:

an ideological struggle for unity.

The Kellogg Pact clears the way.

War as an instrument of rational politics is outlawed, condemned.

War as an instrument for achieving global rule over the earth becomes the just war.

The world becomes an object, says Martin Heidegger.

Heidegger, Off the Beaten Track, p. 205, on nihilism:

The superficial and the clever remain thoughtless for as long as they fail—

fail to do what?

We are all holding our breath.

So:

for as long as they fail—and listen carefully now—

“to think about the site of the essence of man and to experience it in the truth of Being.”

The site.

He carefully avoids naming an actual place.

He does not say Rome.

He does not say Moscow.

He does not say Geneva.

He does not say Prague.

He does not say Lake Success either.

I, on the other hand, pronounce the names like a child.

And that makes me the predestined sacrificial victim of ritual murder, like Kafka’s accused man in The Trial.

I am still alive only because the shades pursuing me are no longer capable of performing rites, and therefore are no longer capable of ritual murder.

That is what saves me.

1 September 1950

Every discussion of the sound of the German word Raum—space—should include Nietzsche’s phonetically astonishing sentence, astonishing even by the standards of Nietzsche’s own prose:

“With firm shoulders, space braces itself against nothingness. Where there is space, there is Being.”

(Kröner, vol. 7 II, p. 58, no. 128.)1

Immediately before it:

“Look into the world as though time were gone, and everything crooked will become straight for you.”

(No. 127.)

Has Heidegger ever quoted that?

13 September 1950

Could it be that every law is ex post?

Really, that should be obvious.

Quid igitur lex? Propter transgressiones posita est.

Why, then, the law?

It was established because of transgressions.

Τί οὖν ὁ νόμος; τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη.

Prosetethē—“was added.”

Does that mean: afterward?

Ex post?

There are translations—for example the German Schott Bible—that actually say:

“established afterward.”

Galatians 3:19.

<…>

30 September 1950

Between theology and technology—

that is precisely where metaphysics belongs.2

It is already there in Auguste Comte’s law of the three stages.

The legal scholarship I speak of at the end of The Situation of European Jurisprudence is, of course, not Mr. Erich Kaufmann or the law section of the Emergency Association of German Science.

My legal scholarship is in exile.

I agree with Schelsky:

only institutions can carry it.3

There are, however, certain companies that carry on the tradition.

“Rome is no longer in Rome; Rome is wherever I am.”

Perhaps, when confronted with Ex Captivitate [Salus], everyone slips away through his own specialist door and coldly kills me by silence.

But you will understand that such a cry of distress, such a final—or first?—appeal to people’s willingness to “hear” was nevertheless necessary.

Otherwise the German spirit would have declared itself in agreement with its own degradation.

The offense must come.

It will probably come in its most poisonous form through German silence.

How is one supposed to explain that in terms of depth psychology?4

S. Freud, volume XVI of the Collected Works, on Moses and the foundation of the Mosaic religion:

a sociological film full of breathless suspense.

It is difficult to say what is more fascinating sociologically:

this Moses,

this religion of Yahweh,

this mythology of devouring the father,

this interpretation of Christianity,

or the author himself.

Wonderful, what Schelsky says about the total school.

Hopefully sees [the] antistrophe:

Kill with C. S.

4 October 1950

Between theology and technology:

that means between two totalitarian realms.1

Theology is necessarily totalitarian in its substance and in its result.

Technology is totalitarian in its method and in its function.

The result is always totality.2

Between them stands the legal scholarship of Western rationalism.

It is not totalitarian.

It is ad alterum—directed toward the other person.

Its institution is the state, which distinguishes public law from private law.

It preserves law.

And law itself is ad alterum: it exists in relation to another.

Audiatur et altera pars.

Let the other side be heard.

Neither theology nor technology knows this principle.

For the theologian, the other side is the enemy—the .

For , the other side simply does not exist.

Jürgen Rausch’s remarks on Ernst Jünger (Merkur, October 1950) are astonishingly perceptive.

He speaks of Jünger’s inner tension and of his distancing way of seeing: an optics that does not recognize what it sees—that is, does not acknowledge it—but hits it.

That is exactly it.

Jünger is an entomologist.

Or not even that.

He is a beetle collector.

He collects beetles and last words:

insects and dying people.

22 October 1950

Should we now cry:

Criminalize the criminalizers?

Far from it.

Even the most terrible self-righteous people are still human beings.

Even the three righteous combmakers are, in the end, still our brothers.

So let us allow them to live.

For if we killed them all, we would simply take their place.

10 November 1950

It is at least a step toward better understanding when A. Mitscherlich (Der Monat, no. 25, October 1950) sets the Kaspar Hauser myth—the complex of modern abandonment—against the Oedipus complex.

“I would say that the human being of our time suffers to a very great degree from a fate that coincides with Kaspar Hauser’s.”

No amount of care or hygiene can hide from us

“that the complex of modern mass man is a complex in the style of Kaspar Hauser.”

That is how I experienced it in the cell.

And for me, Nuremberg was not the city of Dürer or Hans Sachs.

It was not the city of the Meistersinger.

The Party rallies did not even enter my mind.

For me, Nuremberg was the city in which Kaspar Hauser appeared.

The manufacturers of myths and anti-myths in the twentieth century never thought of this myth.

But I discovered it in my cell and spoke about it in many letters.

Yet how suspicious:

Schopenhauer also thought of himself as a Kaspar Hauser.

Every suppressed genius is a Kaspar Hauser.

In the Parerga and Paralipomena (I, p. 162 in the Reclam edition, at the end of the “Remarks on My Own Philosophy”), Schopenhauer speaks about himself and about his philosophy, which had been pushed aside by Hegel, the official state philosopher:

“Accordingly, I became the Iron Mask—or, as the noble Dorguth says, the Kaspar Hauser of the professors of philosophy: shut off from air and light so that no one would see me and my inborn claims could never make themselves felt.”

Then the note:

“But now the man whom the professors of philosophy had killed by silence has risen again, to their great dismay,” etc.

Verlaine’s poem on Kaspar Hauser, translated by Stefan George and R. Dehmel.

In truth, Jesus Christ—the murdered Son of Man, the heir killed by the workers—is the true Kaspar Hauser.

Continued below, 28 February 1951 (p. 84).

The Jews can only be ignored.

But <…>

(not to ignore the Jew is beneath his dignity as a Christian).1

The clerics have taken the wine away from us.

The wine is the discernment of spirits, which they reserved for themselves.

But today we can see that they are not capable of discerning the spirits at all.

Today they run after Americanism.

27 February 1951

Words and sentences from dreams:

Death is the good-for-nothing of our experiences.

It makes them good for nothing.

But death itself is good for nothing too.

For death is not an experience that can be put to use.

Or:

Protestant Security Service.

Analyze that phonetically!

28 February 1951

I am often struck by a paralysis that prevents me from writing.2

The paralysis comes from sudden moments of insight into my true situation—a situation in which the very word “comfort” becomes absurd.

People watch a ritual murder.

They shrug their shoulders.

They quickly look away.

Perhaps they even offer an insulting piece of charity.

They show enormous literary interest in Kafka’s novel The Trial.

But they prefer not to look at the unheard-of trials and procedures taking place in the reality of our own time.

The murder of Christ was a ritual murder.

At the center of the Christian faith stands the belief that our age began with a ritual murder.

Comfort is an absurd word until the Comforter comes.

The Kaspar Hauser myth is the myth of a ritual murder.

The son is ritually slaughtered, like Isaac.

The father is simply beaten to death.

That is the essential difference between the Oedipus myth and the Kaspar Hauser myth.

At the beginning of Christianity:

Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7, Stephen:

You murdered the heir.

1 March 1951

A worker is someone who has the right to a workplace assigned to him by the responsible organization.

Work and labor law.

That is what it comes down to.

The new law of mass discrimination.

Anyone who once rhapsodized about “the worker” ought to be ashamed if, in 1945, he had to discover what this worker really was.

Someone who is unemployed today is closer to work than this legally privileged holder of a workplace, protected by labor law and employment rights.

That is what Jünger should have written a book about, instead of writing about Lucius and his highly educated Persian woman.

People can say many things about me.

They can insult me as the Crown Jurist.

But I did not fall for the myth of work.

I did not write a book called The Worker.

Nor did I mistake a salaried employee obsessed with his pension and benefits for an “imperial type.”

4 March 1951

So what remains?

This remains:

friend and enemy.

Their distinction remains.

Distinguo ergo sum.

I distinguish, therefore I am.

6 March 1951

Delightful: Aristotle’s refutation of “need” as the driving force behind power, Book II, Chapter V (p. 33, Stahr):

“One does not become a tyrant in order not to be cold—

τυραννοῦσιν οὐχ ἵνα μὴ ῥιγῶσιν.”

Hobbes:

If I have no power, I will be devoured.

But there is already the old story:

they go hungry when they do not have power.

7 April 1951

The three-hundredth anniversary celebration of Leviathan in Frankfurt, with Alfred Andersch, Nicolaus Sombart, Anima, Hannes and Freda Winckelmann, Hausenstein.

Andersch strongly emphasized and repeatedly affirmed his belief in human free will.

I told him:

When you speak of free will, you fall into the standard formulas and dead ends of academic philosophy.

You mean something completely different from determinism or indeterminism.

You mean something every decent human being does.

Something you and I have always done:

when we fell in love,

when we became politically passionate,

when we threw ourselves wholeheartedly into something.

In truth, that was not free will.

It was a blindes Vorgebot:

a blind first commitment.

That is the word.

And with the word, we have the thing itself and the situation itself:

the blind first commitment.

22 April 1951

Even more important than the questions on the questionnaires are the great central questions that “they”—that is, Roosevelt and Stalin acting as a single coalition!—put to the Germans in 1945.1

So answer, for example, the following:

Do you consider Thomas Mann or Heinrich Mann the greatest German poet?

Do you consider Heinrich Heine or Zuckmayer the true spokesman of your generation?

Do you consider Robert Kempner or Erich Kaufmann the true representatives of the German sense of law and justice?

To every question of this kind I answer firmly:

Count me out!

14 June 1951

Monarchical-dynastic legitimacy ends in disputes over family law, wars of succession, and harassment over family trees.

Democratic legitimacy ends in the sordid tricks of electoral law and in arguments over proportional representation, electoral districts, and the calculation of that mysterious quantity called “the majority.”

Which is worse?

Obviously the latter.

15 June 1951

What exactly is the population of a modern metropolis today?

Haec omnis, quam cernis, inops inhumataque turba est.

“This whole crowd you see is destitute and unburied.”

  • Aeneid*, VI.325.

Indeed:

inops inhumataque turba.

A destitute, unburied crowd.

They are no longer buried.

Their bodies are burned.

For a while they believed that they voluntarily “had themselves” cremated.

That was the brief transitional stage of a liberal illusion.

Inops inhumataque turba.

That is a definition of the mass.

The transformation of people into a mass begins with the abolition of burial.

Sacramentum Regis:

my three enemies.

Etenim sacramentum regis abscondere bonum est.

“For it is good to keep the king’s secret hidden.”

Tobit 12:7.

16 June 1951

I was just about to become annoyed when I read about the great academic honor that the University of Maryland (!) had bestowed, pari passu, on Cloy and Heuss and Friesenhahn.

Then I happened upon Hobbes, De Cive, Chapter X, p. 177 of the 1648 edition:

“To see the judgment of someone we despise preferred to our own;

to see our own wisdom disregarded before our very eyes;

in the uncertain contest for empty glory, to incur the most certain of enmities—for this cannot be avoided whether we win or lose;

to hate and be hated because our opinions differ;

to expose our plans and wishes to everyone when there is no need to do so, and gain nothing from it;

to neglect our private affairs—

these are evils.”

But being excluded from having a say is not one of them.

O Wisdom, you speak like old Hobbes!

You continue the catalogue in Hamlet’s monologue:

The disgrace, …

22 June 1951

All you have to do is open your ears.

All you have to do is listen.

For example, I hear the word Staatsroman—“state-novel”—used for utopia.

Robert von Mohl came up with it.1

How revealing!

Staatsräson—reason of state—is only one side of the state.

The Staatsroman—the state-novel—is the other.

The state becomes the realm of the pure novel.

Today’s written constitutions are state-novels of this kind.

They begin with the sentence:

“All Germans are equal before the law.”

A beautiful opening sentence for a novel.

Better to leave the rest unwritten.

It would not win the Nobel Prize anyway.

24 June 1951

I remember the wonderful conversations with Tierno and Truyol about the dead point that must arise in every relationship of mutual exchange unless there is a blind first commitment and a blind advance performance.

According to Hobbes (De Cive, Chapter II, §18), this dead point is overcome sola fide—by faith alone.

So there we have sola fides inside legal theory!

I maintain that it can be overcome only by the blind first commitment.

That is human freedom.

“Ubi vero creditur”—

where there is trust—

the contractus, the contract, grows out of the pactum, the agreement.

II §9.

Credit—trust—is the essence of the pactum.

It follows that the foundation of constitutional law is a situation of trust, which means:

peace.

The principle pacta sunt servanda—agreements must be kept—is only the second principle of law.

It is not the foundation.

The foundation is peace.

That is:

a situation.

Law through peace is meaningful and decent.

Peace through law is an imperialist claim to rule.

2 July 1951

Between you and us, on both sides, lie too many desecrated bodies.

Too many dishonored corpses.

The burning of the men hanged at Nuremberg made this condition even worse.

Now they cannot even be buried after the fact.

4 July 1951

Rhyme is to verse what color is to painting.

Ernest Hello says that.

Human beings do not see light.

They see color.1

The German classical writers had a deeply inadequate relationship to color and to painting.

Today we experience color as an element in itself.

Color set free.

Its power to create space is stronger than the illusion of space created by any linear perspective.

We experience Paul Klee as an entirely new world.

Good.

If that is so, then we will also come to understand rhyme as an element in itself.

Rhyme set free.

Its first eruption came during the First World War.

Yes, it really did erupt:

August Stramm.

6 July 1951

Two remarks about the word Raum—space:

  1. Nietzsche’s magnificent sentence:

“With firm shoulders, space stands braced against nothingness. Where there is space, there is Being.”2

So that explains the hatred of the word Raum one finds in people like Hausenstein and Max Picard.

  1. Raum is the same word as Rom—Rome.

So that explains the hatred of the word Raum too.

This hatred is simply a displaced, unanalyzed anti-Roman feeling.

13 July 1951

The tendency to let myself be deceived must lie very deep inside me.

Perhaps it is an inheritance from a proletarian-Christian nature, or from some other source.

In any case, my earliest experiences of life were experiences of deception.

And apparently my latest experiences are too.

Among my most recent experiences of being deceived is the fact that, at sixty years old, I fell for a Caliban because he was able to quote Parmenides.

As though a Caliban who changes masters so often could not also change his vocabulary.

The Calibans of today can read and write.

That is very important.

They can take possession of philosophers and poets as though intellectual history were a brothel and literary history a cheap dive.

They walk in wearing brass knuckles and impress the appropriate ladies.

14 July 1951

Gottfried Benn is a self-tattooer.

Like many German intellectuals of Protestant origin, incidentally.

He tattoos nihilistic horrors all over his decent Pietist skin.

That makes him unrecognizable.

The effect is then combined with his method of chaotically piling up ultra-modern, historical, medical, scientific, asphodel-and-Pyramidon, ultra-fashionable splashes of words.

And he often produces good rhymes too.

Astonishingly good ones.1

But the Pietist core of the whole thing is exposed by his blank verse.

Beneath the five-foot iambic lines of Gottfried Benn there always lurks the rhythm:

Set the fragrant mignonettes upon the table.

Naturally, the mignonettes become orchids.

And the table also becomes fashionable, Berlin-style, Kurfürstendamm.

And yet old Gottlieb always shines through.

So I say:

a Pietist tattooed beyond recognition.

Come to the bar with your green orchid, Bring all of Friedrich Nietzsche with you, And stamp hard on the bourgeois man’s toe, As Franz Blei once did.

19 July 1951

Friedrich Schiller’s Don Carlos:

the genius of a provincial Swabian who did not possess power for a single second of his life and therefore declared power evil for as long as he—and people like him—did not yet possess it.2

He pretends to hope that, by using idealistic phrases, he can persuade those who hold power to hand it over to him—and to people like him—because he is so unbelievably good and humane.3

And yet he is still enough of a genius to recognize that the real issue is access to the king.

That is what the whole drama of Don Carlos is about.

Poor Don Carlos himself is merely an immature young man placed into the game.

The real struggle is a struggle between the king’s advisers and the people in his antechambers.

On one side are the confessor and Alba.

On the other is the Marquis of Posa.

That is where the struggle takes place.

The turning point:

from now on, the Marquis is allowed in without being announced.

Domingo says:

Our time is over.4
