Today the two are the same.)

Something that is valid, and that is successfully made valid—with a real chance of forcing obedience—which means something that can be enforced by coercion.

So what is a jurist?

Someone whose profession is making things legally valid.

A professional enforcer of validity.

These validity-makers are worse than the money-makers.

Get it?

From the positivist point of view—that is, when there is a clearly defined and predictable legal rule—things are still manageable.

But God help us when natural-law infiltration—

Newspaper clippings reporting Stalin’s death.

Written above:

“The death of the ruler; newspapers from 5 March 1953.”

Below:

“March 1954, one year later: the seriously ill Holy Father is suffering from hiccups.

Summer 1954: he has Niehans’s fresh-cell treatment injected into him so that he can live a little longer.”

On the page to the left:

“On this, Khrushchev’s speech at the Twentieth Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, February 1956, and de-Stalinization in spring 1956!!

The revelation of the complete speech at the beginning of June 1956.

And when will de-Rooseveltization follow?

And de-Lincolnization?

And de-Calvinization?

And the Pope’s death in 1958, with Galeazzi-Lisi.

The triumph of medicine.

Thanks to Niehans’s fresh cells, he lived long enough to witness de-Stalinization.

No doubt a miracle through God’s providence and <…>.”

—begins, and broad general clauses start being enforced!

But what am I?

I am a survivor.

I have neither been standardized into a professional validity-enforcer nor infiltrated by natural law.

I am neither a full enforcer nor an empty one.

17 July 1953

I have no insurance of any kind.

I would regard it as an insult to the great universal insurer—the “welfare state”—if I were to permit myself any additional insurance.

I am legal.

That is to say:

I have sworn no oath.

But every status quo wants eternity and demands oaths of eternal loyalty.

By doing precisely that, it reduces the oath itself to mere legality.

Then—

Newspaper clipping from Sonntagsblatt, 19 July 1953.

Written above:

“A sympathetic poem about women, in the manner of Gertrud von Le Fort and Claudel.”

Written on it:

“Sonntagsblatt, 19 July 1953.”

—there finally arise, through terrible torture and persecution, the free oaths, the conjurations, and the new men who are once again capable of oath, of God, and of power.

21 July 1953

Now I am old.

Now I have crossed the age limit.

With the usual farewell music:

I must go away, and you, my darling, stay here.

“Here” means:

on the other side of the age limit.

So now I am old.

And whom do I meet on the far side of the line?

Man and Democracy.

Well, that truly is the opposite of paradise.

Homo homini Radbruch.

Radbruch is man to man.

Absolute Man—not even enlightened absolutism—meets me in the form of a Jewish returning émigré who came back to Germany in 1945 and collected his revenge.

There you have it.

The absolute humanitarian.

Homo homini Radbruch.

Homo homini Leibholz.

But why, exactly, is power supposed to be evil in itself?

The power of God is surely good in itself.

Good in itself and in and of itself.

But poor Jacob of Basel experienced the power of human beings, and concluded that power was “evil in itself.”1

Poor Jacob Burckhardt!

Let us hope that if power had unfortunately fallen into your own hands, you would not have rejected it—and would therefore have considered power at least capable of being good.

God’s power is good.

The Devil’s power is evil.

But what about power when it falls into the hands of a human being like this?

What is it then?

Good?

Evil?

Neutral?

Direct or indirect?

If it falls into the hands of a Swiss man, then naturally it is neutral—which means indirect.

And if it falls into the hands of a Morgenthau Jew in 1948, then God have mercy on us.

Then it appears as the power of the bailiff who flays me with a clear conscience while his employer collects Nobel Peace Prizes.

And now, finally, comes the great front.

Now come all the Antis, the people who reject the friend-enemy distinction as fascist.

So here are the Antis:

The anti-fascists, the anti-alcohol campaigners, the antisemites, against the wine drinkers, against those who defend their homeland, against those who did not emigrate.

The Song of the Totally, Totally Poor German:

I am not an émigré, I was not in the Resistance, I no longer have a chance, I’ll join the Foreign Legion.

27 July 1953

(To Friedhelm Kemp, on the occasion of Simone Weil:)

How much sadness nests inside the Christian first names of the unbaptized!2

Homo homini Deus.

Man can be God to man.

Homo homini Lupus.

Man can be wolf to man.

Both are possible realities and real possibilities.

But:

Homo homini Homo.

Man is man to man.

That is the trap of traps, if Simone Weil’s phrase is to be corrected properly.

(Reference to Gueydan’s essay.)

Therefore:

Homo homini Radbruch.

5 August 1953

Consult the oracles of your senses!

That is advice, and itself an oracle.

And it comes not from Nietzsche, but from Francis Bacon.

Interpret the oracles of your senses.

Bacon called himself the priest and interpreter of these oracles:

a religious priest and no unskilled interpreter of the oracles of the senses.

De augmentis scientiarum, VII.

But Bacon too is already a criminalizer.

He says Plato committed a crime by contaminating natural philosophy with final causes and theology.

“With no lesser crime, you introduced the deification of stupidity,” he tells him.

(Cogitata et Visa de Interpretatione Naturae, IX, p. 173.)

The pleasure of writing down beautiful quotations.

For example:

“An unequal match with Achilles.”

(In Korea, for instance, Achilles was missing.)

Or:

“Nor did your anger last longer than the war.”

(Which has no longer been true since 1945.)1

Or this sentence from de Maistre, Du Pape, p. 259:

“Second-rank powers do what they can. Afterwards they are judged as though they had done what they wanted. Nothing is more common, and nothing more unjust.”

Or:

“With Pompey dead, civil war became a crime, though while he lived it had been loyalty.”

(Pharsalia IX, 248–249.)

6 August 1953

So the criminalizations had already begun in the Middle Ages.

The bull In coena domini is crawling with criminalizations, anathemas, excommunications,2 and the newly created criminals are placed in the same category as pirates:

piratae in mari nostro!

Pirates in our sea!

Compare Mirbt, p. 283.

The connection between theology and criminalization.

The curse against Louis of Bavaria in 1346.

Mirbt, p. 167.

8 August 1953

The Frankfurter Allgemeine calls Heidegger a fascist philosopher.

Jürgen Habermas, article of 25 July 1953.3

At about the same time, a note from the Soviet government describes the Berlin uprising of 17 June as a fascist adventure.

So:

Two souls and one thought. (Two bodies and one desire.) Two souls and one thought. One thought and one level. (Barion adds: Two heads and one record.) Two souls and one level.4

So what is fascism?

Fascism is every attempt to answer the great questions facing the world today in a way that is not Marxist.

This rule governing language is Stalin’s real victory of 1945 over every other victor and profiteer of that year.

And it is only because of this that 1945 became the year of the real decision.

18 August 1953

Homo homini Homo.

To the pure, everything is pure. To pigs, everything is pig. And to man, everything is man.

In war, as in war.

A mark is a mark, and a man is a man.

Meanwhile Moju triumphs, the distinguished specialist in schmonzes—sentimental nonsense.

24 August 1953

The mistake of German Classicism:

looking for the homeland of the soul among the Greeks.

25 August 1953

In the end, he gave up drinking wine.

Wine was no longer a sacrament.

It had become nothing but alcohol.

So instead he drank the pasteurized milk of conformist thought and ate the milk chocolate of the legality of the social welfare state.

29 August 1953

Free is the person who is capable of binding himself by an oath.

But the person who has actually bound himself by such an oath is also free.

Free is the person who can create kinship through an oath.

Loyal means:

bound to a recognizable modus procedendi, a recognizable way of proceeding.

In reality, today:

Freedom is sacred.

Its actual content is determined by the liberation laws.

30 August 1953

After the dangerous attack on me in Das Schwarze Korps at the beginning of December 1936, I wrote this down:

Vestrum scelus, meus somnus.

Your crime, my sleep.

I still stand by it today, faced with the new “Black Corpses” of Germany in 1953:

Vestrum scelus, meus somnus erit.

Your crime will be my sleep.

That is my Christianity.

Psalm 40:6.

Augustine, The City of God, XVII.18.

3 September 1953

The social administrative state turns the private citizen into an official of its own administration.

It does this by simply taking it for granted that private citizens can be put to work carrying out administrative tasks.

It began long ago with sticking contribution stamps into social-insurance books, and with the deductions employers were required to make from wages.

Today every employer is put into government service.

Every bank employee is put into government service.

Every shopkeeper becomes a collector of sales tax.

Even an innkeeper’s actual business of serving guests is now merely the starting point for collecting taxes.

And then there is the blue tax stamp as well.

Compare:

9 September 1953

Being and appearance.

(Sein und Schein—being and seeming; also Sinn und Schein—meaning and seeming.)

Appearance gave being, and being gave appearance, and time slipped away.

Being and doxa—that is, brilliance, shining, radiance.

What a rat king of tangled oppositions:

crossing one another,

confirming one another,

and immediately cancelling one another out again.

The moment I hear the beginning of all this clattering, I would rather switch it off.

11 September 1953

Book title:

I Was There Too.

Better:

In the End, It Makes No Difference.

Even better:

One Was Left.

12 September 1953

I am reading Charles Fourier on the human passions.

Take the tenth passion, for example:

la cabaliste.

The pleasure of cabal, of intrigue.

Its musical note is D.

Its colour is indigo.

Its arithmetic figure is progression.

Its geometric figure is the spiral.

Its metal is silver.1

Is that not brilliant?

Surrealist!

Then I read his description of what happens to human beings when they become caught up in such intrigues:

electoral intrigues,

love intrigues,

the stock exchange,

the family <…>.

“You admire their animated tone, the speed of their actions.”

Look at them beforehand.

How dull and lifeless they are.

Then comes the cabal.

Look how they come alive!

Wonderful.

And finally this sentence:

“Far from that flat calm whose pleasures morality praises to us, the cabalistic spirit is the true destiny of man.”

That is more than Nietzsche.

But if I say this to anyone, I will immediately be pinned down as an advocate of some low intrigue and declared a characterless pig by the great masters of academic cabalism.

Benjamin Constant’s diary is genuine because it was not written for the public.

This whole genre of Jünger’s Radiations becomes more grotesque all the time.

The “radiation diary” stands in relation to Benjamin Constant’s real diary as the marginal notes of Wilhelm II stand in relation to those of Frederick the Great.

In Constant, Napoleon’s Hundred Days are not reflected through the soul of some contemplative idler.

Above all, they appear in his accusations against himself.

His Radiations are still going to cost Ernst Jünger dearly.

18 September 1953

God became man.

Did He therefore accomplish homo homini homo?

Is there now no longer any homo homini Deus—man as God to man?

And no homo homini Lupus—man as wolf to man?

Oh no!

From the standpoint of homo homini homo, God did not become man.

He became subhuman.

Or are we perhaps all supposed to crucify and violate one another and simply trust that resurrection will take care of the rest?

In a country as overcrowded as present-day West Germany, neither Deus nor Lupus applies, nor does that fraudulent escape into the threefold tautology:

“man is man to man.”

Here the rule is simply:

Homo homini Baumwanze.

Man is a stink bug to man.

Or, even more up to date:

Homo homini Radbruch.

24 September 1953

Again and again I think of that conversation on the express train.

The man sitting opposite me puts down his newspaper and says loudly:

“This McCarthy is a genuine scourge of humanity.”

He correctly says Geißel—“scourge”—not Geisel—“hostage”—as one so often hears.

At that moment my dialectical instinct woke up, along with my pleasure in dialogue.

I thought:

Humanity always has two scourges, kept in motion by a dialectically connecting anti.

But that would probably have been too much dialectics.

So I contented myself with saying:

Humanity has two scourges:

McCarthyism

and anti-McCarthyism.

25 September 1953

Important:

an analysis of the writers who use the term petty bourgeois as an insult, especially when defining fascism.

Seen from the German ghetto of the eighteenth century and its long aftermath, the term does indeed describe something deeply contemptible:

people who are not genuine partners in trade and business, which means they are neither princes nor great bourgeois;

but who, on the other hand, are also not the great social nothing represented by the proletarian;

people who cannot even afford to buy a share in a company and yet imagine that they own property;

cannon fodder for usurers and currency reforms;

the small savers who are cheated forever.

At the opening of a high court, a jurist once said:

“Against law there is no law.”

And not one of the jurists present replied:

“But there is the binding finality of a judgment.”

How depressing such talk is.

The real meaning of the statement is something much more depressing:

Against the final legal force of a judgment, there is no law.

Or, in the trivial conceptual language people use today:

Legal certainty takes priority over justice.

29 September 1953

Lenin says there are two kinds of war:

wars of conquest

and wars of liberation.

For wars of conquest, Bruno Bauer’s statement applies:

Only the person who knows his prey better than the prey knows itself can conquer it.

This apparently does not apply to wars of liberation.

The liberator does not need to know his prey.

After all, what he is doing is education.

The Education of Henry Adams.

The Re-education of Carl Schmitt.

21 October 1953

Eternal recurrence.

The eternal cycle.

And then Christianity as the disruption of the cycle.

The world is a cycle.

The Christian is a disruption.

Christian and world.

Today’s conceptual calculating machine works like this:

Power is evil in itself.

Law is good in itself.

Therefore my power is not power.

It is law.

The frauds live off this little game of dominoes.

And so does Homo homini Radbruch, with his humanitarian syllogism.

Compare above.

27 October 1953

I think, therefore I am.

That is:

I am in motion.

I think, therefore I posit myself absolutely.

I think, therefore I am the Absolute in motion.

All of that is perfectly logical.

I think, therefore I posit myself absolutely.

I posit myself absolutely, therefore I am not the “I” of the empirical self—the self that, at the very moment it thinks, is also doing other things:

breathing,

digesting,

living in the biological sense.

Instead I am another, absolute “I.”

Therefore:

I think, therefore I am not the empirical self.

I am the abstract subject of thinking consciousness.

I am.

That means:

I am power.

The essence of God is power.

The Devil’s non-being is the will to power.

The will to power is evil.

Power is good.

A simple litany for simple individuals.

On the Jürgen Habermas campaign against Heidegger in the summer of 1953:1 Theodor Wiesengrund Adorno’s Minima Moralia2 says, word for word, on p. 365 (the passage dates from 1935):

“If the bourgeois class has, since time immemorial, cherished the dream of a savage Volksgemeinschaft—a community in which everyone suppresses everyone else—then children already bearing first names like Horst and Jürgen, and surnames like Bergenroth, Bojunga, and Eckhardt, acted out (sic) that dream before the adults were historically mature enough to make it a reality.”

Bravo! And Jürgen Habermas was the given, predestined name for the Haberfeld-style public shaming campaign against Martin Heidegger.

9 December 1953

(On Petwaidic and Bourdin): The elite are those whose sociology no one dares to write.

22 December 1953

A fine subject: the relationship between the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution (compare Lorenz von Stein’s remark), understood as the historical opposition between land and sea.

26 December 1953

Every name is a Nahme—a taking.3

God is power—and direct power at that: potestas directa.

The Devil is the will to power.

The will to power: the ideology of professional revolutionaries and émigrés; indirect power, potestas indirecta.

Woe to us when they seize power—that is, when they are finally able to take revenge. For revenge is really the only thing they are capable of. See the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 17 December 1953.4

So enough of that!

Carry your uncomprehended heart to the dead!

Stop letting yourself be invited, only to be uninvited again. Stop letting yourself be spat on by windbag intellectuals like Moritz Bonn, and recognize your own Νόμος—your own Nomos!

End of the year 1953.

12 March 1954

God is dead. That means: he is no longer present; he is absent.

There is no God other than the God who is present—the tutela praesens, the protection that is here with us.5

He no longer speaks either.

To someone listening to the radio, anything that is not speaking at that particular moment is absent.

God is good: that means direct power is good. It gives effective protection, and such protection comes from him alone.

But potestas indirecta, indirect power, is evil. It is on the left—izquierda. It is not present; it is not even represented.

Bonald said: society itself—la société, hence socialism! ––––

That means socialism!—cannot declare its belief in God, because society itself, by the very fact of existing, already implicitly contains and presupposes the “presence of God.”1

On this, Robert Spaemann writes (“The Error of the Traditionalist,” Wort und Wahrheit, no. 7, July 1953):

“The concept of presence, as distinct from the mere existence of God, is, incidentally, a very profound one. It prepares us to understand Nietzsche’s ‘God is dead.’”

Yes, Robert Spaemann. That is it. And this remark of yours really is a very profound one.

“A God who is not present is as good as dead.”

Partir, c’est un peu mourir—to leave is to die a little.

Rivarol <…>.

Socialism wants to make God present.

It does so through universal and equal participation: participation in Leviathan itself—the magnus homo, the great man—but also in Leviathan’s banquet.

The two socialist sacraments!

Hegel: the state is God made present.

Marx: the state must be slaughtered for the banquet of Leviathan.

That is the great sacrament of Marxist socialism. It was performed long ago, over there in Russia.

People used to say—the old kitsch word—tableau. Today they say: situation.

Political = Science = Wisdom.

Here in the West, the other sacrament—the sacrament of wine—was destroyed long ago.

The Coal and Steel Community will canalize the Moselle; Moselle wine will be canalized along with it. The Moselle winegrowers will become members of an association of fruit-juice processors.

The cardinals will have to give it their blessing. After all, they took the wine away from the laity long ago.

Tacito rumore Mosella—the Moselle with its quiet murmur; that is, of course, the Moselle before it has been canalized.

15 March 1954

They strum the devastation on harps, And trumpet the Last Judgment. They fiddle away at indignation, And play our nothingness on harpsichords. (Rilke)

16 March 1954

Wine is no longer a sacrament today. Aldous Huxley recommends mescaline instead.

But some magnificent remnants of wine still survive.

Let us drink them before the Moselle is canalized and France is integrated.

Let us drink these beautiful remnants!

Now and then each man took the best; I shall hold fast to these beautiful remnants.

How does an islander, living out of his maritime existence, come to recommend foreign intoxicating drugs when he has probably not tasted even the smallest fraction of Europe’s wonderful wines?

I ought to write to Der Spiegel, which discusses Huxley’s discovery without protest (March 1954):

Why are you spreading false teachings that help uproot today’s Europeans from place?

But there is no point protesting anymore. They would only think it was a joke.

Newspaper clipping. Written above it:

“1) Encyclical 1930: <…> quod Norma renegatur et rejiciatur!!—that the norm is denied and rejected!! Cause: energy, energy of the box. 2) p. 44; the Pope on situation ethics, [(]25 April 1952); 3) 1 June 1954: laicus taceat in et extra ecclesiam nisi acclamat ordinario competenti—the layman must be silent both inside and outside the Church unless he is applauding the competent Ordinary.”

Written below:

“A reasonable compromise: laicus taceat in ecclesia, clericus taceat extra ecclesiam—let the layman keep silent inside the Church, and the cleric keep silent outside it.”

9 June 1954

The age of limitless compatibility is followed by the age of limitless convertibility.

The convert, Herr Hausenstein, as the prototype of German Catholicism: taceat extra ecclesiam—let him keep silent outside the Church.

Treason of the Intellectuals: they recommend mescaline instead of wine. That tells us exactly where they stand. Compare:

15 March 1954 and 16 March 1954 (Aldous Huxley).

9 July 1954

Progress.

I have entrusted my cause to God; Lutheran hymn (used by Schütz for a set of chorale variations, 1624).

I have based my cause on Nothing (Goethe’s answer, eighteenth century).

I am I; nothing stands above Me (Max Stirner, 1845).

A short conversation:

A. These brothers have taken the chalice from us—the wine, and therefore the blood of Christ.

B. Excuse me: on the subject of the word “brothers,” I must insist: no fraternization! Ne joco quidem—not even as a joke.

A. Fine. Then these fathers, these papal sources of the father complex.1

10 July 1954

On my sixty-sixth birthday:

I am old. I have gradually had enough of life—and more than enough of being persecuted.

But I would still like to postpone, for a little while longer, the day when the rabble dances on my grave.

That is a natural wish. It can keep even an old man standing for quite a long time, and hold him firmly on this earth.

15 July 1954

Anni said: “I know my Pappenheimers.”

I replied: “Then you know something old-fashioned. I know my Oppenheimers.”

On 19 July 1954,2 Heinz Weitzel of Frankfurt told me: “I have been saying that for a long time.”

So apparently the thought is an obvious one—and concretely true.

26 July 1954

I discovered an illuminating prediction at the end of a nervous, flickering essay by Anton Kuh:

“The great night of fire, foretold by Nietzsche’s flame, is still to come. Perhaps it will come one day in the future, after the plebeian, bursting strength of the New World has taken possession of the Old and we have all become Americans—when Nietzsche’s work, like Samson, brings the skyscrapers crashing down upon itself.”

(Sic. Published on 25 August 1930 in Neue Rundschau, p. 865.)

27 July 1954

This is how the New World lives, and these are its ideals:

Pleasure without danger.

(Advertisement for Kaffee Hag decaffeinated3 coffee.)

Powerful but harmless.

(Disinfectant, infection-killer B 43, for shaving cream.)

30 July 1954

Why should the name “Israel” in the Psalms bother us during Christian worship?

The “Fiat” in the Paternoster does not bother us either!

1 August 1954

To one particular persecutor of mine, whom I believe to be honest:

Why are you persecuting me?

My situation is very close to yours.

We are jumping from one ice floe to another, and it is childish of you to imagine that your ice floe is somehow more permanent than the one I happen to be drifting on at the moment.

I know perfectly well that you do not really believe this either.

But instead of recognizing how similar our situations are, you appeal to the owners of the ice floe on which you happen to stand.

From status to situs.

Churchill says: anyone who can sit should not stand, and anyone who can lie down should not sit.

So the ideal is: lying down!

The situation—the Lage.

No more standing. No more sitting.

Either flying or lying!

Newspaper clipping from the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 30 July 1954. Written above:

“<…> Poor, brave Werner Schütz! Why not do what Hausenstein did? Or are you not convertible?”

30 August 1954

Un sot trouve toujours un plus sot, qui l’admire.

A fool always finds a greater fool who admires him.

Yes. But today something else is much more relevant:

Un criminel trouve toujours un plus criminel, qui le justifie.

A criminal always finds a greater criminal who justifies him.

12 September 1954

The meaning of every answer depends on the question.

And the question posed by Germany’s situation in the spring of 1933 was correctly raised and correctly formulated only by Konrad Weiß.

You can find it in Der christliche Epimetheus, p. 92.

It is more powerful, and more fateful, than any oracle ever was.

It arises as an antithesis from the division into which we Germans had been placed.

That is where one must begin if one wants to answer the question of justice.

Everything else is either the work of scoundrels or the devilish hatred of foreigners and abortionists.

My situation and my fate are now completely clear to me.

Compared with all the professors and lecturers beside whom I taught from a German university chair for thirty years—jurists, theologians, philosophers, and historians alike—I possess something historically additional, something more.

I owe it to my blind forerunners, and I must neither lose it nor deny it.

1 November 1954

In truth, it is an undeserved piece of good fortune that throughout all these years since Germany’s downfall I have no longer been allowed to practice my profession as a teacher of constitutional law.

Teaching constitutional law in a state that is not sovereign—or, worse still, in a pseudo-sovereign state—can certainly be financially rewarding, rather like the life of a worm inside rotten wood.

But morally it is completely destructive.

It destroys one’s own identity, which cannot be separated from the identity of one’s own people.

Meanwhile Herr L. triumphs as a sujet mixte, a mixed subject, and guards a constitution in which sujets mixtes can themselves serve as guardians of the constitution.

14 November 1954

Who are you?

I read in a diary entry from 3 February 1941:

I am poor Benito Cereno.1

4 December 1954

I am the non-convert in the age of unlimited convertibility.

I am the incompatible one.

He doubts the <Jews’> .2

12 December 1954

L’initié tue l’initiateur—the initiate kills the initiator.

According to Ballanche, this is the formula of every revolution.

But apparently it can happen only once, in the actual history of each historical people.

This is what separates old peoples from young ones:

the old have already committed their regicide; the young still have theirs ahead of them.

According to this measure, we Germans in Central Europe would still be a young people.

The oldest people of all, however, would be the Jews.

But they did not themselves kill the Son of God. They merely had the occupying power kill him—lingua occidistis, as the Good Friday liturgy says.

Or: only one Jew is needed, as Goethe said.

End of the year 1954.

Desecration and slaughter by Carl Linfert on NWDR (22 November 1954).

Memor approbii.

11 January 1955

I can now see the source of the hatred that pursues me and wants to destroy me.

Why do they persecute me, and why do they want to destroy me?

I can tell you:

their plans for destruction shattered against me.

Every foreign idea shattered against me.

That means something in a country occupied by foreigners, subjugated by foreigners, and ruled by foreigners.

12 January 1955

Where does this incredible hatred of me come from?

Why this merciless persecution of a defenseless man?

Because every foreign idea shatters against me.

All the forces of alienation unite against me in a country occupied, divided, and trampled underfoot by foreigners.

Who are you?

Answer: draft of the shortest conceivable biographical note:

I was born on

11 July 1888, and on the occasion of 11 July 1948 I wrote a “Song of the Sixty-Year-Old,” from which everything else can be learned.

24 January 1955

People tell me about the vile things my persecutors are doing.

How do I respond?

I yawn.

One really can say:

I yawn, therefore I am.

30 January 1955, Sunday

Skipped High Mass and instead—or perhaps in return?—had an incredible encounter with St Stephen and with the beginning of Christianity: Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7.

Great excitement.

This is the authentic foundation for every discussion of the relationship between Christians and Jews.

They killed the heir: murderers of the Son, and they remain so.

They killed the heir:

Matthew 21:38–39; Mark 12:7–8; Luke 20:14–15.

(One really can say: I yawn, therefore I am.)

Fourth Sunday after Epiphany.

Quid timidi estis! Et facta est tranquillitas magna.

Why are you afraid?

And there was a great calm.1

14 February 1955

Nothing but world-historical progress:

from (Father of Gymnastics) Jahn to (Brother in Camouflage) John; from (terrorist) Nero to (pacifist) Nehru;2

15 March 1955

At this they look at one another and grin, Thomas’s wife and Thomas Mann, and collect their prizes, large and small.

Peace prizes, war prizes, Schiller prizes, Goethe prizes, East and West, West and East, all serve equally well.

In the end he has to laugh himself.

19 March 1955

Do not speak foolishly about foolish things.

Better to remember your discovery:

The Name points toward the Nahme—the taking—performed by a rightful taker.

He gives a name to what he rightfully takes.

He takes the defeated man’s name away from him and then carries that name himself:

Scipio Africanus, Drusus Germanicus.

Ne simus faciles in nominibus.

Let us not be careless about names.

“In the name of the king” means: in the name of the person who carried out the great taking, to whom we owe the law under whose concrete order we live.

That is the Νόμος Βασιλεύς—the Nomos Basileus, Nomos as king.1

20 March 1955

A declaration placing people hors-la-patrie, outside the fatherland; a program for wiping them out root and branch:

Franz Böhm carries it out.

Anyone who no longer wants to persecute and harass the Nazis is not a German.

You can be German even if you are a criminal.

But you cannot be German if you no longer want to persecute the Nazis.

Because, Böhm says, “German” is a spiritual concept.

Do you see now what the spirit of these persecutors consists of?

The pretext for persecution, the justification of injustice[?]

Do you see how hostility is intensified by making it “spiritual”?

A fine example of this escalation:

spirit used as a means of reaching the true and final distinction between friend and enemy.

The logic of a war of annihilation.

Herr Böhm’s root-and-branch spirit.

Letter by Böhm to the illustrated magazine Quick; reproduced in Frankfurter Hefte, March 1955.

This poor Böhm is clearly losing his way.

Clearly some secret curse is driving him toward the abyss.

Qui vivra, verra.

Whoever lives will see.

3 April 1955

The three intellectuals raised into mythical figures:

Hamlet, Don Quixote, and Faust.

Three bookworms, three compulsive readers, three products of the art of printing.

Hegel’s Gott-Nahme—his taking of God.

Hegel conquers God through Begreifen, through conceptual grasping; com-prendre, to grasp and take together; through reason and for reason.2

Kojève, Introduction, p. 215:

Hegel already sees the ambiguity and double edge of such takings.

Er nahm sich das Leben—he “took his life,” meaning that he killed himself (Phenomenology, p. <…>).

Arbeitnehmer – Arbeitgeber: literally, the work-taker and the work-giver; employee and employer.

The old hidden cunning of the German language:

to “take oneself” can also mean to take oneself away.

So taking and losing become, in a treacherous way, the same thing.

It is like something from a fairy tale.

Similar case:

Aufgabe—a task, but also a giving-up.

Hans-Rudolf Müller-Schwefe:

“Thus eating and drinking can be a form of knowing” (E. Jünger Festschrift, p. 58).

To grasp with the body; to take with the body.

Everything Müller-Schwefe describes as knowing—eating, drinking, experiencing the formative powers of the world, treating something as an object—is a different form of taking.

Through taking, all these things are related.

And therefore:

taking, dividing, pasturing.

We are looking for the primordial taker.

5 April 1955

God is the primordial giver—that is, the primordial distributor.

God gives: he distributes what he has created.

He does not need to take.

Now man is supposed to take his place.

That means giving production priority over distribution, and abolishing taking and Nahme altogether.

Newspaper clipping, cartoon about Yalta. Written above:

“Illustration of Gelimer’s laughter, Die Zeit, Hamburg, 24 March 1955.”

On the right:

“Compare my diary entry, Berlin, Thursday 6 April 1933, 8 p.m., Prinz Leopold Palace, (1 bull in the arena before the toreada2) like the knight, thrust already prepared; at the moment.”

Written underneath:

“The ritual murder of Yalta, February 1945. And this picture can pass without objection in 1955?”

On the right:

“February 1945: this happens.

March 1955: the world learns about it.

February 1956: de-Stalinization begins (Communist Party Congress, Russia; Stalin exposed by Khrushchev as a mass murderer).

December 1958: I sent a copy of my Großraumordnung (3rd ed.), in which this drawing had been pasted, to H. Recknagel, Essen-Stadtwald, Frankenstr. 72.

The Europe curve belongs here, with the hieroglyph of the Western World (from 11 July 1956, V p. 67 [= 349]).”

10 April 1955, Easter Sunday

On the subject of iconography.

A transformation of the icon is itself a form of iconoclasm.3

During the Counter-Reformation, monstrances and images of the Madonna suddenly turned into Gessler’s hats.

Today Thomas Mann is a Gessler’s hat before which everyone must bow if they do not want to be persecuted as neo-Nazis.

And this humanitarian eagerly collects the bows and urges on the organizers who manufacture this kind of fame for him.

(Thoughts during Easter Sunday High Mass.)

The Heine monument as the new Gessler’s hat!

Cor ne edito—do not eat your heart.

With Günther Krauss I really was anthropophagus cordis mei, an eater of my own heart, to borrow a Pythagorean phrase.

16 April 1955

If all distinctions—such as state and society, political and economic—and all incompatibilities dissolve, then only one distinction really remains:

friend and enemy.1

Domestic political order consists in using secondary distinctions to hold down the latent, primary, ultimate distinction.2

The neutral state as katechon—the restraining power.

17 April 1955

The state, as the great distributor, is also the great taker.

It takes what it distributes partly through taxes and levies, and partly through confiscation: by stripping certain inhabitants of its territory of their rights, or by declaring certain people hors la loi, outside the law—or simply treating them that way without formally saying so.3

Utopian society—both the society imagined by the liberal free-market economy and the future society imagined by Marxism—supposedly no longer takes anything.

It only produces.

And it produces infinitely so much that dividing and distributing cease to be problems.

At that point, not only taking but even dividing and distributing effectively disappear.

There is nothing left but production.

Nothing left but creation.

Then the great Gott-Nahme—the great taking of God—is complete.

Human society has become God:

the God who only gives and never needs to take, because he creates everything out of nothing.4

That is political theology.

It is the continuation of the philosophy of work begun by Fichte and Hegel and completed by Karl Marx.

This philosophy of work is the great taking of God.

But the earthly God who creates from nothing, so that he can only give without ever taking, must first create the nothing out of which he creates.

In other words:

he takes.

Who today is capable of understanding this insight into the taking of God?

None of our present-day state-and-society Christians.

No celibate bureaucrat—he only becomes vicious when he hears it—and no Pharisee.

So I suppose I must wait for a Jew.

Perhaps Jacob Taubes.

Perhaps Kojève.5

After all, only Jews recognized the grotesque insolence of this E.[rich] K.[aufmann] and called it by its proper name:

Kurt Hiller, Kempner.

Unfortunately, that does not work either.

19 April 1955

Look reverently at the vibration of leaves, branches, twigs, and the tops of fir trees.

You can practice divination through vibration with them.

You cannot do that with Calder’s mobiles.

Words vibrate just as the tops of fir trees do, or leaves, or the branches and twigs of a tree.

At this very moment, the word vibrating is:

magnus homo—the great man.

Let it vibrate.

Listen.

Suffer.

And then you will recognize the impossibility of a legal order that pretends every micro-being is a makros anthropos, a great human being, and gives the micro-being a fundamental right to be treated as though it were macro.

All human beings are equal.

Yes.

But does that mean equally small or equally great?

The question disappears inside equality itself.

All that remains is:

equal = equal.

Which means:

equal = levelled.

equal = brought into line.

4 May 1955

“The interim is mine”!

Who says that?

I do.

Hamlet (V.2).

Hamlet, son of Mary, the true Jacob, the white raven on every blacklist.

But the interim will be short.

It will be short. The interim’s mine.

Where does that appear?

Only in the 1623 Folio edition of Hamlet (V.2.74), not in the First Quarto of 1603 or the Second Quarto of 1604.

One could become very thoughtful about that.

Because the interim of Christianity has gradually begun to last much too long.

9 May 1955

Perhaps for my sixty-seventh birthday:

Farewell song of the old Moselle man:

Humanity is integrated, The Moselle is canalized. The sacrament is bent around, The layman’s chalice is denied. Dear God remains concealed from sight, The whole world turns to melting pot. Automation becomes global, And the layman gets Veronal.1

That would make a fine poem in memory of Hugo Ball.

30 May 1955, Pentecost

Listen reverently to the oracle of the vowels!

Listen reverently to the sentence of the former theologian Friedrich Nietzsche, answering 1 John 2:17, “The world passes away, and its desire”:

All desire wants eternity!

And now let the vowels of the word Lust—desire, pleasure—begin their merry and cunning game.

For example:

All Lust is lost; that is:

lust is only loss.

All lust is a load.

Throw it off instead of carrying it and falling for it.

All lust is a ruse.

The cunning of the Idea is harmless play compared with the cunning of lust.1

Outwit it!

(On this, 1 John: “Desire conceives and gives birth to sin.”)

1 June 1955

Le microbe n’est rien, le terrain est tout.

The microbe is nothing; the terrain is everything.

That saying of the great Pasteur, a man completely above suspicion, is already almost geopolitics.

Now add:

L’individu n’existe pas.

The individual does not exist.

That is the saying of the great Auguste Comte, likewise completely above suspicion.

Draw the parallel conclusion from the two, and once again you arrive at the thing poor Hausenstein is so terrified of:

space.

In 1945 these worms were suddenly able to turn their claustrophobia and their fear of cramped little rooms into a victory over Hitler—even, in Hausenstein’s case, into a victory over the new problem of space.

After that they could become German chargés d’affaires in Paris.

And that is how postwar Europe came into existence:

without space, and therefore, quite logically, even against space.

For the last four hundred years, Hegel has been the only Christian theologian.

Not Kierkegaard.

Kierkegaard contains no theology of the Trinity.2

Hegel, however, is the theologian of the Trinity.

The greatest since Joachim of Fiore.

Magnificent.

Now the liars of the Peterson type can tremble—the people who tried to persuade us that the doctrine of the Trinity makes political theology impossible.

And the converts of recent decades can start inventing new forms of defamation and drawing up new blacklists.

5 June 1955

In Göttingen, manly professors have been certifying one another’s manliness by bringing down a minister of education who belonged to a very weak political party.

Now, in the press, every one of these Göttingen professors is one of the Göttingen Seven.

Every inch of every Göttingen professor is a Göttingen Seven.

Seventy thousand Göttingen Sevens.

The manliness of the masses.

The victim of this fabulous mass manliness, however, is a sad Herr Schlüter.

The relationship is clear.

The new Göttingen Sevens stand in relation to the old fairy-tale brothers Grimm of 1837 exactly as Herr Schlüter stands in relation to King Ernst August.

3

9 June 1955, Corpus Christi4

An extraordinary second encounter—comparable only to the first, on 30 January 1955, with the story of Stephen in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 7, concerning the killing of the heir by the Jews.

It happened during High Mass, at home in my study, among the books that fell into my hands at precisely this hour while I was staying away from Mass.

Here all the oracles of vibration resonate together.

So this was the second encounter of this kind.

And it makes me certain that Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit is an inspired book of the German faith.

Pages 175–176:

“It seems to it—to self-consciousness that has become reason—when it grasps itself in this way, namely by recognizing that its thought is immediately reality itself, as though the world had only now come into existence for it.

Before this, it does not understand the world. It desires it and works upon it; it withdraws from it and destroys it for itself, and destroys itself as consciousness: both as consciousness of the world as essential being and as consciousness of its nothingness.

Only now, after the grave has lost its truth, after the destruction of its reality has itself been destroyed … does it discover –––– its new real

world.”

So:

first the grave must be lost.

That means the dead God must have risen again.

Therefore this begins with the end of the Crusades, just as Kojève correctly says (Introduction, p. 81).

That is what I read today in Kojève, during the Corpus Christi procession of 1955.

Here, to lose the grave means resurrection:

the destruction of destruction,

the killing of death.

It is all Christian dialectic.

(Yesterday I wrote to Kojève.)

11 June 1955

Several thousand Göttingen Sevens have appeared in Göttingen and gloriously defeated one poor devil.1

What a triumph!

The relationship to 1837 is clear.

These new fairy-tale brothers of 1955 stand in relation to their model of 1837 exactly as their opponent, poor Schlüter, stands in relation to the opponent of 1837, King Ernst August of Hanover.

What a happy age, in which seven thousand Göttingen Sevens can suddenly be found!2

12 June 1955, Sunday

I formulated my opinion on the Schlüter case in Göttingen, June 1955, for Johannes Gross, though in the end I did not send him all of it.

University professors and students forced Schlüter to resign as minister of education through public demonstrations because he had published writings by university teachers who had been removed from their posts.

The whole demonstration against him succeeded because it was directed from left against right and could exploit serious defects in Schlüter’s own character.

So my opinion:

  1. The whole thing: a guaranteed, risk-free way of satisfying the enormous pent-up demand for displays of civil courage!

  2. Its constitutional significance: a minister brought down through action outside parliament; a recall. A test case for mobilizing the plebiscitary elements that cannot be eradicated from any democracy, but which after 1945—especially in the Bonn Basic Law and in the debate over rearmament—were carefully and anxiously suppressed.

  3. Its historical importance: the numerous Göttingen Sevens of 1955 stand in relation to the originals of 1837 exactly as their opponent in 1955, poor Herr Schlüter, stands in relation to the opponent of 1837, King Ernst August of Hanover.

That is a clear and exact measure of their respective historical rank.

  1. The aesthetic quality of the event:

University professors and students, with political permission, manfully throw themselves upon one poor unlucky fool in order to cure him thoroughly of his delusion of grandeur—the idea that he might become the minister responsible for universities.

As a spectacle, this is more a nightmare in the manner of Kafka than a drama of freedom in the manner of William Tell.

  1. Farce:

the wild-boar thief as overthrower of ministers.

(The whole thing: a guaranteed, risk-free way of satisfying society’s accumulated demand for displays of civil courage.)

6 July 1955

Magnus homo / magno homini: magnus homo. Great man to great man: great man.

Magnus homo / parvo homini: Deus. Great man to small man: God.

Parvus homo / parvo homini: Homo. Small man to small man: man.

But where has the wolf gone?!

I think the closest answer is this:

wherever homo homini homo—man is man to man, whether great or small—means equality, man is closer to the wolf than to God.

Otherwise:

Magnus homo / parvus Deus et magnus lupus.

The great man: a little God and a great wolf.

8 July 1955

Progress upon progress:

the Göttingen Seven of 1837 have become the Göttingen Three Thousand of 1955!1

In the July issue of Der Monat, an essay actually describes them under precisely this title:

“The Göttingen Three Thousand.”

The unconscious accuracy of a hack.

But why not simply call them seven thousand?

Or at least three thousand five hundred?

Four-thousandfold resistance to authority.

What an enormous success for re-education!

5 August 1955

And behold:

there is also a Mensch-Nahme—a taking of man!

A man takes a woman, and she knows him.

The slave hunter does not “take” the slave. He robs and sells him, just as the hunter takes wild game.

But Hegel’s taking of God is at the same time a taking of man by the God-taker.

Hic Rhodus! Hic saltat! Hinc illae lacrimae!

Here is Rhodes! Jump here! Hence those tears!

So the only thing left, following Heidegger’s example, is to write in future:

Being, crossed out.

Man, crucified.

9 August 1955

A happy encounter with a remark by James-Hamlet:

when the jurist Sir Edward Coke told the king that he was “defended by the laws,” the king replied that this was “foolish.”

A king, he said, is not protected by laws but by God.

Is that not magnificent?

And place it as the polar—or dialectical—opposite of Rivarol:

L’obscurité protège mieux que la loi.

Obscurity protects better than the law.

Immeasurable depth!

Immeasurable happiness in discoveries and encounters like these.

And who gave me this encounter with James-Hamlet’s remark?

Isaac Disraeli—the father of the famous Disraeli, Lord Beaconsfield—in his Character of James the First, p. 423 (Works of I. D., London 1859, <…>).

It is enough to make one Disraelitic!

Newspaper clipping. Written above:

“6 August 1955. Extra: contemporary-history protectus.”

On the right:

“7 August 1955.”

Below:

“Protection exists only outside contemporary history. L’obscurité protège mieux. Obscurity protects better.”

14 August 1955

So Thomas Mann is dead.

A Gessler’s hat falls from its pole.1

A cloud of fading printer’s ink and radio sound-gas settles over both worlds—East and West, servitude and freedom.

Apparently this industrious master-exploiter, in relation to both worlds, was the higher third term: the fulfillment of their ideal of intellectually elevated comfort.

Now, to begin with, the memory of this product sweated out by the culture industry will itself become a Gessler’s hat.

But as I write the words “Gessler’s hat,” I realize how comfortably old-fashioned and harmless my language still is.

Not Gessler’s hat.

Taboo.

Write:

Taboo.

Today the world resembles a totem clan with taboos more than it resembles a medieval Swiss peasant tribe with an imperial governor named Gessler and a William Tell.

15 August 1955

When I think back to the years 1928–32, and when Adolf Caspary, Leo Strauss, Walter Benjamin—and everyone who belongs with them—ask me today:

Why did you join the other side in 1933?

I must answer:

So that you would still have a partner on the German side.

A partner in thought, a partner in conversation, and—as my fate from 1945 until today demonstrates—even a partner in fate.

Because without sharing that fate, all this partnership in thought and conversation is worthless.

(Thought and written while preparing a lecture on Hamlet, under the impact of Walter Benjamin’s words “sacrifice for the life of the national community that is not yet born,” The Origin of German Tragic Drama, 1930, p. 99.)

22 August 1955

An anticlerical man says to me:

Watch out for the priests.

Every priest is hungry for power and eager to rule, and possesses ancient tricks for subjecting people to himself.

I:

Very good.

But why are you telling me this?

I have known it for a long time.

The only thing I notice, listening to you, is that every human being is a priest.

Perhaps that is the effect of the universal priesthood.

Homo homini Clericus.

Man is a cleric to man.

23 August 1955

Desire conceives and gives birth to sin!

So use contraceptives!

Horrible to imagine that—or to picture it.

But perhaps the will to eternity that Nietzsche places inside desire is precisely this conception of sin.

Just as it is not power itself but the will to power that is sinful.

1 September 1955

Michel Mourre, Lamennais, p. 141:

“Féli, you must surrender! You know it perfectly well, Féli. ‘Society’ means, first of all, your failing bookselling business; it means your creditors …” (p. 172).

Féli the poor.

Féli the defeated.

The cruelty of this method of psychoanalytic-sociological explanation!

No human being can survive it.

The trick is to seize the initiative with this poisonous weapon of psychological and social analysis—to strike first and paralyze the other person before it even occurs to him to defend himself.

Did I not do exactly the same thing to Adam Müller myself?

Michel, this is miching mallecho!

Adam Müller was a successful arriviste.

Lamennais was a poor young man driven mad by faith.

And Michel Mourre places himself on the side of authority, which of course is always right—siempre ragione—on the side of the celibate bureaucracy, which of course can never itself become an object of psychoanalysis and whose sociology not even Max Weber dared to write.

14 September 1955

Under the impact of the news from Adenauer’s trip to Moscow (9–14 September 1955):

The world in which Professor Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines lies behind me now, an insubstantial semblance.

The full-blooded Moju can do it better; He sharpens the ritual-murder knife.

15 September 1955

O God, O God!

Am I supposed to long for the satisfaction promised by the thought of posthumous fame?

Am I supposed to look to posterity for comfort—for some vindication like the one Johann Jacob Reiske of the eighteenth century received from Wilamowitz-Moellendorff at the end of the

Newspaper clipping from 8 September 1955. Written above:

“Compare p. 44 [= 274] and p. 94 [= 306], compare 25 April 1952 (p. 44 l), 21 September 1955. After Michel Mourre’s Lamennais, this highly edifying High-Mass reading for excessively zealous laymen. Sunday, 11 September 1955; poor Donoso.”

nineteenth century?

Am I supposed to flee from these miserable Germans somewhere else—into the future, or into posterity?

How pathetic!

And then, suddenly:

how comforting.

How was I able to discover this passage in Wilamowitz-Moellendorff’s book on Euripides in the first place?

The unfathomable depth of subjective chance!

The hair on the head and the sparrow on the roof!

“Come along, Cohn,” Fontane said.

“Come along, Wilamowitz-Moellendorff,” I say now, in 1955.

17 September 1955

What is the car horn jeering?

God is dead!

But Adenauer is alive—and Pope Pius XII!!!

21 September 1955

How strong the historian Fritz Kern’s anti-Roman feeling was!

How often I noticed it in Bonn during the years 1923–28.1

But this nationalist champion became a member of the League for Human Rights in 1927 and converted to Catholicism after 1945.

He was always looking for security, and he always had a good instinct for knowing where to find it.

A grotesque construction:

a sanatorium—or institution of salvation—in which you are never completely healthy and never completely ill, but merely “wounded.”

You can be healed only as far as necessary to remain inside the institution.

It is impossible to leave the institution as a healed person.

On the other hand, the institution guarantees that you will not die.

A grotesque complexio oppositorum, a combination of opposites, used as neutralization for the purpose of totalization.

A subject for Kafka.

25 September 1955, Sunday

From the Christian point of view, the definition of the Jew would have to be:

A Jew is anyone who takes revenge.

But precisely here one sees most clearly that the Christians have become Jews, and that Karl Marx was right on this point.

30 September 1955

“That is the true taking of land,” says Ernst Jünger (At the Saracen Tower, p. 145):

when a landscape becomes for me “a piece of spiritual homeland.”

He calls this cultural incorporation of another travel experience—a further experience acquired through travel—a Nahme, a taking!

At least the original meaning of nehmen, taking, is still alive in it:

I vernehme—I perceive, I take in—the voices, the beauty, the genius loci, the spirit of the place.

A beautiful confirmation of my interpretation of taking, Nahme, and name.

Naming belongs to the same process.

The two Irishmen climb the highest mountain on a newly discovered island and argue about what the island should be called.

Meanwhile, the two Scots measure it and divide it between themselves.

Ernst Jünger, however, deserves to be transferred from the military class of the Pour le Mérite into its peace class.

Converts everywhere you look!

A whole people of converts.

From Storm of Steel to the tourist trip.

From the false taking of land to the true one.

4 October 1955

“Property entails obligations.”

Today this is a cynical justification for destroying and crushing the old form of private property.

Good old Konrad Beyerle officiously introduced it into Article 153 of the Weimar Constitution.

It serves the social state and the transition toward an order based on distribution.

It was the first blow to strike the sanctuary called “property.”

The second blow no longer struck a sanctuary.

All desire wants eternity.

All reality possesses eternity.

There is only the eternity of time that actually exists here and now.

According to Hegel, that is the Concept.

So in the end it is still thought.

I think, therefore I am.

We think, therefore we are.

Correct thinking is the thinking of a subject that is not individualistic.

5 October 1955

Another kick in the back that I received today deserves to be recorded here.

My cousin André responded to my well-meant gift of a review of his friend Stutterheim’s poems by sending me a picture postcard.

On it he says that he remembers my “collapse in level” during the summer of 1916 in Kiefersfelden.

How charming.

How sensitive.

Apparently all human relationships have been destroyed.

But of course we cannot live without human relationships.

So entirely new and completely different ones will come.

The wholly Other is the God who is coming.

Who is my father?

Who is my brother?

Behold the new Gospel.

After this, perhaps we had better not even ask about cousins.

The phrase “collapse in level” in the mouth of a Frenchman is revealing.

So he still knows that much German, at least.

An instructive experience.

Apparently the fact that he gloriously won two world wars has gone to his head.

The social ideal is victorious war.

The victor is the idealist.

The defeated man either had no ideals at all or—which is worse—had ideals harmful to society.

A closer examination of the defeated man’s past will prove that victorious war is the social ideal, and that the victor is the person entitled to make claims for restitution.

6 October 1955

Listen to the Nobel Prize prophet:

“The fear that nations feel toward one another has always been one of the deep causes of war … The fear I mean … rests on the fact that atomic war has abolished the concept of friend and enemy … War fought with such means, which can hardly still be called weapons, has become absurd … Fear of self-destruction.”

(No longer fear of one another.)

“But trying to settle conflicts of ideas with weapons has always been futile.”

So weapons after all?

Of course.

“Un-spirit” may—and must—be destroyed by every available means.

So exterminate the fascists.

Unite against the defenseless third party, the one who does not possess an atomic bomb.

He can then be declared the embodiment of “un-spirit.”

These natural scientists can imagine only one possible way in which peace can arise:

fear of universal annihilation.

That is Thomas Hobbes’s model for the birth of Leviathan.

This talk of “spirit” is gradually becoming tiresome.

The obviously impatient Max Born handles the word with such reverence precisely so that he can finally drop the bomb on “un-spirit.”

What counts as spirit?

I decide.

Clear enough.

And whatever counts as un-spirit has only itself to blame.

PreviousBook III · 1949–1951NextBook V · 1955–1958

Book V

14 October 1955 – 31 December 1958

14 October 1955

I am too old and too beaten down—too badly beaten down by character assassins and by people who abort everything before it can bear fruit. Otherwise I would have to begin, even today, a book on Hegel’s Marianism and that of Konrad Weiß. I would begin with the passage near the end of the Phenomenology of Spirit where Hegel says that the individual divine man has a Father who exists only in himself, but only one actual, real Mother.1

The Good Friday of Spirit in Hegel and the Mount of Olives of world history in Konrad Weiß are pivotal points that no one can possess. But only the Mother is historically real: she actually gave birth to the divine child.

God is dead. The God-man is dead.

The heir has been killed through the joint action of Jews and Gentiles.

Yes, they killed the heir: Matthew 21:38–39; Mark 12:7–8; Luke 21:14–15; Matthew 24:30; Acts 7, Stephen.

That is the historical beginning of Christianity and of the Christian age.

The first deed was a crime: the murder of Abel. The second was an even more terrible crime: the public killing of the heir, carried out in the forms of justice, through a conspiracy of Jews and Gentiles.

The Christian myth therefore always has the killing of the heir at its center.

Kaspar Hauser is the most recent Christian myth so far. The Romanian shepherd tale of Miorița is Christian.

The pagan myth loves and seeks the victorious hero. Napoleon is the most recent pagan myth so far.

Hamlet seems to be a Christian myth: the killing of the heir. But only in outline.

Benito Cereno: the false liberation.

The heir is the κληρονόμος.

They killed him.

Vigens disciplina, fides moribunda: discipline flourishing, faith dying.

15 October 1955

In Hegel, an awareness of the Christian age is still alive.

But he seems to be saying that this age is now coming to an end. He seems to know it.

World history is approaching a different center from Golgotha, the Place of the Skull.

But that cannot be.

We must break away from the false guardians and beneficiaries of the empty tomb—from the knights of the empty tomb.

26 October 1955

I come to this conclusion: the source of tragedy is a present reality.

Wilhelm Wackernagel, writing in 1838, says that the source of tragedy is historical reality belonging to the past. Present reality, by contrast, belongs to comedy and is the source of the comic!

Is this difference simply the result of the contrast between today and the respectable Biedermeier Basel of his time?

In any case, the distinction is very sharply drawn and deserves further thought.

In my assessment of Adolf Grabowsky’s essay on myth, there is this sentence:

A glissando of quotations, as though straight out of a card index; everything has been put to use, nothing has been worked through.

Who hears everything contained in that sentence?

Who recognizes that an entire type is being disposed of there?

More generally, who does this description fit: putting things to use without working them through?

And what personal passion of mine lies behind it?

Probably the Hegelian struggle between master and servant.

Putting something to use without working it through—is that pure consumption?

Consuming without producing?

The non-worker?

Now, once again, I find myself hunting for a person. I want at any price to meet Pierre Leyris, a French author whose short essay on Benito Cereno I read in Spanish.

The Spanish essay appeared in 1944 as an afterword to a Chilean edition of Melville’s story, in a cheap series of novellas and tales.

Pierre Leyris says that every detail in Melville’s story has a double meaning, and that every reader can find his own path through this bottomless book.

The American literary historians noticed nothing of this, although they did establish the differences between old Amasa Delano’s original report and Melville’s story.

Melville keeps opening up new abysses against his own will.

He does not speak about the problem of the slave trade.

According to Leyris, he turns the slave ship into the condition of original sin: the slave trade itself is original sin.

And the American has fallen under original sin not so deeply, but only weakly—debilmente.

That was not allowed to happen.

Benito leaps from the Navío de las Penas, the Ship of Sorrows, into the little boat of redemption.

An error, my good Leyris.

Melville’s Benito Cereno should have had the subtitle:

or, The False Liberation.

And so Pierre Leyris’s marvelous starting point runs aground in the abstract banality of scholastic theology and all its endless talk.

27 October 1955

These Black men killed the heir, poor Don Alejandro.

Once the heir has been killed, both inheritance and property come to an end.

Who, then, are these vineyard tenants in Matthew 21?

After the workers in the vineyard in chapter 20, who demand a fair wage, come the vineyard tenants of chapter 21, who kill the vineyard owner’s heir.

A beautiful subject for a song by Bert Brecht, with a fiery final effect:

the heir is beaten to death; the leap into the realm of freedom has been made.

Sigmund Freud still knew what it meant that they had killed the prophets—even Moses himself.

He therefore understood more about Christianity than the whole Thomist tradition of the celibate bureaucracy, which deprives precisely this—the killing of the heir—of its concrete presence and thereby becomes an accomplice.

Hamann and Bruno Bauer understood this.

This is the end of the Christian age.

Luther was the great katechon, the great restrainer.

Nietzsche’s rage against Luther and Hegel was justified from Nietzsche’s own point of view.

Hegel too was a great katechon.

The great German emperors were katechontes.

Hence the hatred of Hegel—a hatred that would otherwise be impossible to explain.

28 October 1955

My tables!

Bring me my writing tablets! Bring me my notebook!

Hamlet I.5.

A beautiful title for a diary.

And what drives Hamlet to make his note?

The discovery of a villain—a villain who smiles.

These are the human things worth thinking about and worth writing down.

These are what fill the tables.

This My tables! came to me early this morning, at dawn, when I finally understood what happened to me in May 1953 at Herrenalb and Baden-Baden: the insulting way I was thrown out, and the removal of my lecture on the κατέχων, so that Gerhard Günther could take over the subject.

Schomerus now celebrates that conference in the Linksrheinischer Merkur of 23 September 1955 as his finest conference, precisely because of Gerhard Günther’s lecture—which was in truth nothing more than an unoriginal repetition of the views of his brother Albrecht Erich.

I wanted to carry Albrecht Erich’s thought further.

That was precisely what had to be prevented.

Smiling villains!

So: my tables!

How slow I am to catch on!

How good-heartedly stupid—and stupidly good-hearted—I am!

It took that article in the Linksrheinischer Merkur.

But that article makes it clear.

Who is so stupid he cannot see the fraud? And who so bold as to say that he sees it?

Again and again I have fallen for the fraud.

5 November 1955

Schiller’s Marianism is a subject that could be treated together with Hegel’s Marianism.

The outburst of the exposed traitor Mortimer in Mary Stuart, Act IV, Scene 4, at the end—

“Mary, holy one, pray for me”—

has too much overwhelming force to have been merely invented.

What did these Swabians still have inside them?

And how much did they still know?

Everything!!

Goethe’s Marianism has no martial drive.

In Schiller it becomes a conquering Conquista.

The earthly Mary and the heavenly Mary flow into one another.

For 155 years Germans have been watching and listening to this scene, and no one dares to think about what is being revealed to them there.

Perhaps it will become clear to us on Schiller’s 200th birthday in 1959.

6 November 1955, Sunday

Bring me my writing tablet!

According to Friedrich Glum (Mirror and Distorting Mirror of the Philosophers), Christianity is indispensable to democracy—though only secularized Christianity, of course, a Christianity in which both Christians and non-Christians can make themselves at home!1

Or Rüdiger Altmann, in Civis, November 1955:

in reality, he says, there is no material ethic in the Western cultural world today other than the Christian one.

What a new Christianity!

And it dares to quote Kierkegaard instead of being honest and beating him to death, as he himself demanded.

But even this preacher of repentance, who declared being beaten to death to be the test of whether a preacher of repentance was genuine—even this Christian who called for himself to be beaten to death—disappeared into the universal irony.

People only applauded him all the more enthusiastically.

When a serious individual enters into a race with the public in an atmosphere where every ideology has been swallowed by total irony, that poor individual must eventually collapse from sheer exhaustion and die—naturally to the applause of the very same public he thought he was spitting in the face.

Thanks to the angel who grabbed me by the hair and set me down outside this Christian cultural establishment; who knocked this cup of the murkiest poison out of my hand before it reached my lips; and who showed me the spring from which I am allowed to drink:

the spring of poverty and freedom.

8 November 1955

So first there is the little man, the μικρός ἄνθρωπος, the parvus homo.

That is me, for example.

And that is you.

Then there is the great man, the magnus homo.

That is, for example, the USA or the USSR as directly great powers—or the Pope as an indirectly great power.

In short, the question arises:

what do you, little man, still want at all?

What makes you think that, being little, you have any right to speak about someone great?

The great man has no time for you!

Do you want to become a nuisance to him?

Do you want to disturb the intrigues of his antechamber lackeys?

Shame on you, little man!

Go home!

You, being little, have only little worries.

The great ones, however—Mr. Stalin, for example, or Hitler, or the Holy Father—have only great worries.

Woe to you if one of them should ever get the idea of noticing you at all, in order to prove to himself, to the world, and to democracy that the little people too are equal to the great and enjoy the interest of the great.

Then you will discover the connection between protection and obedience.

And every other great power, which you can no longer obey, will become your enemy.

10 November 1955

“The Christian today, if he still wishes to be called a Christian, must bind himself in the strictest possible way to the original Christian ethic,” Karl Korn said in 1948, in the Berliner Hefte, in his essay “Kyklos.”

Compare this with what Glum and Altmann say above, under 6 November 1955.

Is a person not supposed to go mad listening to all this talk about Christianity?

To one it is ethos, to another it is value; The whole thing is not worth a single shot of powder.

But one can make a living from that too.

It is even a reliable protection against the shot of powder—or against the atom bomb.

La nullité protège mieux.

Nothingness protects better.

L’ambiguïté protège mieux.

Ambiguity protects better.

The shamelessness with which people now, in November 1955, talk about Kierkegaard in newspapers and on the radio overwhelms any remaining thought that mutual understanding might still be possible.

Poor Kierkegaard!

They kill the heir.

You would have no right to be surprised or even to complain—and you do neither.

At last the soul can rest in peace; Just choose the CDU and worries cease. This is Christianity À la Professor Glum.

Give the meekest little mouse a detached house of its own, and the mouse turns into a property rat.

For Hegel, the species are still fixed and are still concepts.

With On the Origin of Species in 1859, the New Age begins—the New World.

Democracy—equalization and leveling—plays only the miserable role of the knacker clearing away the carcass, a role in which Wilson, Stalin, Adolf Hitler, and John Foster Dulles compete to outdo one another.

It serves them right.

The mystery of eating bread and drinking wine: Hegel speaks of it in the Phenomenology of Spirit, pp. 82–83.

Kierkegaard should have read that passage before he opened fire.

It is the passage that exposes the fraud of the celibate wielders of indirect power, who destroyed both forms by constructing themselves as official priests and everybody else as—negatively defined—non-priests.

Many more answers will still be given to this gigantic fraud.

The fraudsters will twist and turn.

They will invent millions of sophisms.

They will lie to millions of fools and clever people.

They will sign a thousand concordats.

They will demand human sacrifices beyond imagining.

They will ally themselves with every restoration and every restitution.

They will always be present whenever something is being collected or taken in.

And despite all of that, the only answers that ever come are the answers of the murdered heir and of the insulted spirit.

Lenin was only the beginning.

Kierkegaard’s greatness lies in the fact that he recognized the great figures of the German awakening, Goethe and Hegel, as brothers made from gently living flesh—as traitors to the spirit, which indeed they were:

the Hegel of the Phenomenology of Spirit—I would like to know whether Kierkegaard ever read it at all—and the Goethe of the Urfaust.

Kierkegaard admittedly had it easy.

It is the hump that builds itself a spirit.

And it is into the hump constructed in this way by the spirit that the psychoanalysts crawl like bedbugs.

The old, experienced brothel madam—wise in her own way, tactful and discreet; she has served kings—is looking for fresh flesh.

She calls this:

the lay apostolate.

Now she is running after the Jews.

11 November 1955

“And powers of delusion, hating without restraint, Begin to disappear, blindly hurling beasts.”

One of these beasts hurled blindly is poor Peter Schneider of Zurich, Switzerland—hurled out in order to refute me quickly, while the powers of delusion that hate one another without restraint are already beginning to disappear.

A fine entry for the hundredth anniversary of Søren Kierkegaard’s death.

A Christian cannot leave this earth as a demigod, or even as a hero.

But suppose this ambitious Peter Schneider really did catch me.

Then all that would be needed would be the decent resolve to make oneself impossible to classify once again for these dogcatchers and distributors of dog tags.

16 November 1955, Day of Repentance and Prayer

We are very slow to catch on.

It took us 150 years to read Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit.

It took us 100 years to understand Hölderlin.

When will we understand lines such as these by Theodor Däubler, from Hymn to Sicily?

And powers of delusion, hating without restraint, Begin to disappear, blindly hurling beasts.

One of these blindly hurled beasts is Simone Weil.

Would I be allowed to write that to Karl Epting?

If I recite a line like that to one of today’s big shots, he smiles and says:

“Very interesting phonetically. The first line is built around the vowel A, the second around I. It also makes sense in terms of the intellectual content.”

Better think about who the beasts blindly hurled by different powers of delusion might be:

Adolf Hitler, Roosevelt—

better stop now, or you will be arrested at once.

I have gone through my whole life without property.

My lack of property corresponded to my lack of illusions.

Psychologically speaking, however, my lack of illusions came first.

Given my profession, I could have become a property owner without much difficulty.

Why did I not?

Out of love of freedom.

Out of contempt for false security.

Out of revulsion at the concrete forms in which property presented itself to me.

So I am the propertyless jurist.

Let someone else try to match that.

Better stop now, or you will be arrested at once.

17 November 1955

Conversation with a wine drinker.

It is about the struggle between intoxicating drugs.

What do you use to intoxicate yourself? I chew clubmoss spores! Then you are a pig! And what do you use to intoxicate yourself? I drink wine! But the priests have taken that away from you! It still tastes good to me!

The fact that it still tastes good to you is irrelevant.

You live in a community where you are allowed to drink wine only under the table—outside the sacrament.

So your pleasure in wine is a private matter.

Apocryphal.

And above the table?

The poor celibate bureaucracy drinks the wine openly.

But it is no longer capable of any intoxicant; of any marriage; of any asceticism.

It lives in its monasteries like people in caves <…>

Down, then, into the underworld with it and all its concubinages-concordats!!

Concordats, yes.

But what about its sacraments?

Do they too fall into the underworld along with this celibate bureaucracy?

Not so fast!

18 November 1955

What makes Simone Weil representative is the superiority of this Jewish girl who managed to escape every effort of the professional makers of converts and left them all standing behind her with stupid looks on their faces.1

That is admirable.

And it is more beautiful than the art of Edith Stein, who allowed herself to be baptized and then became impenetrable inside a religious order.

I wrote this to Karl Epting.

Simone Weil’s horror at the idea of the Corpus Christi, the Body of Christ, is genuine.

But it is also the one decisive test:

anyone who does not want to belong to the Corpus Christi is not a Christian and does not want to be one, even though that person may still want to speak about Christian matters and impress Christians.

Epting thinks the doctrine of the Corpus mysticum, the mystical body, is not Lutheran.

I look it up in Sohm’s Church Law, §34, and find that it is of the highest importance in Luther.

Christ is the head, not the Pope.

According to Sohm, the opposition is:

Corpus versus Corporatio.

And then, naturally:

Corpus Christi versus Corpus Antichrist = Leviathan (= state = Sohm, p. 674).

This economic miracle is only a miracle of repentance; when repentance ends, the miracle ends.

This state is only a state of repentance, or, as [Franz] Böhm says, a reparations state; when repentance ends, the state ends with it.

And then surely morality as well:

when repentance ends, morality ends with it.

And then none of it is true anymore—including the Christianity of the C-parties and all the established and officially recognized values, together with those who assign those values and those who cash them in:

the preachers of repentance who persecute others instead of supplying the only proof of truth of which, according to Kierkegaard, a preacher of repentance is capable:

allowing himself to be beaten to death.

“For to be the great preacher of repentance means to be beaten to death.” (The Concept of the Chosen One, p. 303.)

But they live in the economic miracle which, as I said, is a miracle of repentance—and vice versa.

23 November 1955

Of course the song is not finished yet.

Certainly:

when repentance ends, the miracle ends.

Quite right.

That is how they threaten us Germans.

But we threaten them back:

when the miracle ends, repentance ends,

and with it the whole beautiful Caux co-existence!

Then the preachers of repentance will no longer be able to travel around in their Mercedes Apostolorum and will turn back into honest black-market petrol dealers.

24 November 1955

  1. Where are you?

Bombers above my cap, both my feet deep inside the camp. Around me, the ugliness of the victors, and the sound-wave hell of their radio hits.

  1. What are you doing?

I am losing the time that loses itself and gaining the time that exists.

For I experience and shape concrete concepts.

And powers of delusion, helplessly hating one another, Begin—blindly hurling beasts—to disappear.

Hitler was one such blindly hurled beast, but he was not the only one and not the last.

And before he disappeared, he in turn blindly hurled beasts of his own and bound his enemies to his shadow.1

To speak about this without falling oneself into the unrestrained hatred of those powers of delusion; without oneself being turned into one of those blindly hurled beasts; without theological-demonological cozy talk and without some hidden motive concerning reparations—that is difficult and dangerous.2

For the moment, the blindly hurled, the blind haters and avengers, still control the field and allow no objective word to be spoken.

One need only look at the disgusting falsifications that dominate Baron von der Heydte’s article in Hochland, January/February 1951.

Above all there is the central and revealing falsification in his quotation of my sentence about prayer as the final refuge, from Ex Captivitate Salus, p. 61.

He silently leaves out the crucified God.

He simply suppresses Him.

(Hochland, p. 289.)
