The level at which the two sides finally meet will be the lowest and most comfortable one:

universal lay status.

Not universal priesthood.

That is the path of democracy.

Democracy is universal kingship.

Everyone his own sovereign.

The democratic way of life.

It is the road forced upon us by the logic of concepts of this kind.

20 June 1957

The final result of a jurist’s existence:

I do not want to have power.

But I want even less to be in the right.

So my heartfelt condolences on your constitutional state!

1 July 1957

The steel bells that call a person to church in this country—

those are no longer my bells.

Everything else follows by itself:

those are no longer my songs;

those are no longer my wines;

not even my schnapps anymore.

It is Coca-Cola-coalition music.

21 July 1957

In Heidelberg I quoted to Carl-Joachim Friedrich the line:

Those bells were never yours, and they are no longer mine.

At that very moment the bells for Vespers were ringing.

He said:

In America you rarely hear church bells ringing.

30 July 1957

In Wiesbaden, at Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, we laughed at Adorno’s revealing remark about Hegel’s “grandiose peasant cunning.”

In that remark you can see a cloven hoof that may turn into a boomerang and, as Hans Barion added, strike an Achilles heel.

How amusing these self-revelations of the great revealers are.

10 August 1957

How disgusting the whole philosophy of work then becomes:

with its servant undermining the master,

its serva padrona—the servant who becomes mistress,

its successful private tutor,

and all the social climbers who marry aristocratic girls and eventually create in Darwinism their grand myths of the ambitious survivor who compensates for his physical weakness through intelligence.

So that was the European nineteenth century.

Perhaps I will live to see its end.

How magnificent, by contrast, was Hans Freyer’s reply to Arnold Gehlen’s birthday speech:

What we have gained is:

progress in the mode of failure.

The defeated man writes history.

The infiltrator writes sociology.

And Samuel Pepys crawls into his diary.

Switzerland is certainly no katechon.

12 August 1957

When I was talking with A. Kojève about the falsification of the sacrament and complained about the withholding of the wine, he replied:

The layman has too much blood anyway.

At that moment I noticed that he was a cleric and I was a layman.

And yet no Iron Curtain fell between us.

Nor did the speaking grille of a confessional.

17 August 1957

In Wiesbaden, in his speech for Hans Freyer’s seventieth birthday, Arnold Gehlen declared:

we are passing from one age, the age of history, into another—the age of sociology.

The age of history is over.

According to Kojève’s interpretation, Hegel had already said the same thing.

But Hegel did not yet know what Gehlen knows:

that the age—one presumably must no longer say time—of sociology is now beginning.

Excellent.

And how pleasant to hear and believe.

The end of time has arrived.

History was never the ground of happiness.

But now sociology is coming.

And the social is coming.

The pure consumer society.

That, presumably, will be the ground of happiness.

Wars will cease.

Class struggles will cease.

Socialism ends in sociology.1

21 August 1957

The real explosive force of the atomic bomb strikes the very concept of the human being.

It drives homo homini homo out of its comfortable hiding place and blows apart the threefold neutrality of this threefold tautology.

Human beings drop atomic bombs made by human beings onto the heads of other human beings.

That is the reality of homo homini homo.

Here human beings are completely among themselves.

So where is the true human being?

And what becomes of the other person, who by consequence is no longer a true human being?

I really ought to start thinking about a Song of the Seventy-Year-Old, an antistrophe to my Song of the Sixty-Year-Old.

Perhaps like this:

Listen and suffer! Listen and suffer?

That is still too grand.

I listen and hear nothing anymore. I suffer and feel nothing anymore. What am I still doing in the world? Waiting until the atomic bomb is hurled?

Spare yourself the death of an insect that threatens from Nobel Prize clouds.

Leave this establishment before the brothel owner throws you out and has his police arrest you as an enemy of the constitutional state.

Should I sing like that?

Or rather with the cheerfulness of an all-knowing old man who knows that he has passed beyond the line and nothing can happen to him anymore, because neither a declaration of enmity nor the decoration of some order can still reach him?

Vedremos.

We shall see.

Perhaps you should sing of progress?

Yes indeed!

2 September 1957

Yes indeed!

Progress of every kind:

Progress in the consciousness of freedom, with Hegel.

Progress in the consciousness of the distinction between friend and enemy.

Progress in the consciousness of defeat.

Progress from taking land to taking sea, and from there to taking industry,

taking space,

taking the world.

Progress in the methods used to liquidate whoever disturbs the cleansing.

Progress in the mode of failure.

Come into your own where you inherit your failure!!

And carry out progress in the mode of failure!

That would make a fine antistrophe to the many forms of terror in the Song of the Sixty-Year-Old!

13 September 1957

The Catholic lay intellectual who speaks publicly is normally a comic figure—and in great cases, such as Donoso, a tragicomic one.

Who exactly is he talking to?

Inside the domain of the celibate bureaucracy he has nothing to say.

Outside it, people must take him for an altar boy.

A just punishment for this idiot of an intellectual layman.

Why does he insist on speaking when all he is allowed to say is Yes and Amen?

A naked, unclothed intellectual standing among prelates decked out in pomp!

A very comic role.

One cannot ignore the saying

Ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis

—where you have no power, desire nothing—

without being punished for it.

If a person starts preaching instead of dutifully acclaiming—that is, instead of saying Yes and Amen—he merely causes embarrassing attention.1

But look:

atheist rationalists and Marxists such as Georg Lukács suddenly find themselves in exactly the same tragicomic situation and are instructed by their own headquarters about their true function.

So perhaps we could all quite happily philosophize together about knowledge and power, sagesse et tyrannie—wisdom and tyranny—without insulting one another and criminalizing one another as traitors to the spirit.

4 October 1957

By creating the world out of nothing, God thereby made Nothing into Something it had not been before:

Something from which a world can be created.1

And that is quite something.

What?

This whole beautiful world was created out of nothing?

Out of nothing?

Ex nihilo?

Ex nihilo, yes indeed!

Well, it certainly looks like it.

Yes indeed.

It certainly looks like it.

Which only makes this Nothing from which it was created more and more interesting.

5 October 1957

The problem of the order:

wine—woman—song.

Material for a new world war.

I find it unbelievable that wine comes before woman.

Woman is the first stage.

6 October 1957

Carl Schmitt—

connaisseur of Chaos.

Tu quis es?

Who are you?

To my friend George Schwab:

The identity formula homo homini homo lies at the core of the identity between rulers and ruled—that is, at the core of democracy itself.2

Anyone who denies it cannot be a democrat.

Yesterday I became agitated for a moment when George Schwab read the note at the end of my opinion of 25 August 1945 on aggressive war:

How can Hitler’s scelus infandum—his unspeakable crime—be atoned for?

Surely not through a judicial process!

That would strip it of its unbelievable character and standardize it.

It would turn the crime into a procedure, into a precedent, and place it inside the realm of what can be foreseen—and reviewed afterward.

Hugo Ball criticized my Political Romanticism with the remark:

To hunt one rabbit—Adam Müller—an entire province is sealed off.3

I replied:

Fine.

But that sealing-off produced the first map of the province.

28 October 1957

Three grim prophecies for the Germans:

  1. To reach your Reich, Germans, you struggle in vain.

  2. To form yourselves into a nation, Germans, you hope in vain.

    (With , the Jew has backing; see Karl Kraus.)4

  3. To become a people, Germans, you wish in vain.

  4. Like Rome.

  5. Like the French.

  6. Like the Poles and Czechs.1

29 October 1957

Why exactly did Ernst Bloch become so furious when I spoke of the “proletarian consciousness of having been cheated”?2

I said it as a proletarian myself.

Admittedly, a different kind of proletarian from his.

Not a proletarian hungry for loot.

All I have left is progress in the consciousness of having been cheated.

From time to time I change the kind of person I allow to cheat me.

Then the discarded swindler rages after me and calls me a characterless traitor.

31 December 1957

Good Werner Becker expects Rome to make a confession of guilt because of the Renaissance popes.

Rome will gladly give him one.

It does not matter anymore.

And are today’s dollar-and-rejuvenation popes really better and more Christian than those genuine sinners?

Those genuine sinners at least still held the trump card of pecca fortiter—sin boldly—and by their very existence could refute Luther eo ipso.

Today’s popes, by contrast, are merely normativists and righteous peacemakers.

Peacemakers with retirement insurance and a right to a long, edifying earthly life.

That is:

a right to die of old age.

We should not envy them for it.

If I had the power, I would gladly guarantee every one of them death from old age.

4 January 1958

Today human beings use technology to create their own environment.

They cease to be endangered living creatures and attain an improbably advanced age in complete security, with well-organized provision for every need.

But in doing so, they cease to be the endangered living creature that remains “open” and is bound to no fixed environment.

They become animals, like other animals.

No wonder there has never been so much talk about Man and humanity as there is today.

[6 April 1958], Easter 1958

And your race is ’89!

(Michelet)

[25 May 1958], Pentecost 1958

Aubrey Beardsley seems to be proving right:

Protestantism ends as Hamlet.

Sons of Puritans become Jesuits.

The entire Western world is Hamlet and will give its dying voice to a Fortinbras.

Constitutional-Theory Pentecost Festival, 1958

A picture of the state of the concept of the constitution in Western Europe.1

In Germany In France
De-legalization
Democratic legitimacy

Adolf Arndt in the Bundestag (proceedings, 25 April 1958, pp. 1495–1502): “We should spare ourselves the discussion of legality and illegality” (p. 1502). “We think in the category of the legitimate.” The popular referendum is legitimate and democratic (SPD press, 23 May 1958).

Happy constitutional Pentecost, 1958!
Legitimate Pentecostal joy for us all!
Your race is ’89!		 Republican legality

Paris, 19 May 1958. De Gaulle demands extraordinary powers, but “within the framework of republican legality.” The Committee of Public Safety in Algiers wants to “remain within republican legality.”

At the margin:
Ulm trial against the principal SS [defendant] Böhme: he admits that the shootings were not legal in the sense of the liberal constitutional state (FAZ, 23 May 1958).

Germany de-Hamletized, 1933–45.

A very nice addition on 2 June 1958 from Hans Fleig in Die Tat (FAZ, 3 June 1958):

Seen through the lens of “legality and legitimacy,” much that appears confused falls into order.

“France will never give up Algiers.”

Pflimlin in the National Assembly, Paris, 20 May 1958.

“Germany will never give up Alsace-Lorraine.”

State Secretary Kühlmann in the German Reichstag, 1917.

A Kunde comes with a Kunde—

a customer comes bearing news.

He even comes with an Ur-Kunde—an original document.

Urkunde:

it has already been written down, and yet it still calls itself Ur—original, primordial—and all the more exclusively “original.”

Meanwhile other scribes are writing.

The Roman scribes in Rome, who for a thousand years deceived Europe with pseudo-Isidorian original documents, now find themselves facing unfair competition.

At least these customers notice that every painter who paints abstractly today also be-ur-kundet—certifies, documents, bears witness.

They experience that as unfair competition.

Naturally, it has to be stopped.

And any stoppage will do.

First Adolf Hitler.

Then Stalin and Roosevelt—par nobile fratrum, a noble pair of brothers.

Then someone else who will eventually conclude another concordat with the old producers of “original documents” in Rome.

A customer came bearing news!

Einstein was one such customer!

But the producers of original documents in Rome could issue their documents only in the pseudo-Isidorian style.

For that purpose Holy Scripture was good enough for them as the holy Ur-Urkunde—the original original document—

complete with primordial fresh-cell interpretations.

1 June 1958

After reading C. F. von Weizsäcker’s discussion of “the present prospects for limiting the danger of atomic war”:

So the final impression is one of uncertainty—the uncertainty that now dominates precisely those circles in the United States that take the most intense political interest in European problems.

Poor Delano. Poor Melville.

The result is Hamlet.

The whole West ends as Hamlet.

It begins as a revenge drama—revenge on Hitler’s Germany—and will end as a murder ballad in which, at last, every character lies dead on the stage and Fortinbras inherits everything, legitimized by the dying Hamlet and his dying voice.

3 June 1958

There are, after all, two Carl Schmitts:

the exoteric one—who therefore calls himself Carlo—and the esoteric one.

On Otto Weininger’s hatred of the Viennese waltz: hatred of the Leviathan, hatred of chthonic life. Compare my Leviathan, p.1

5 June 1958, Corpus Christi

Gentlemen!

A seventy-year-old looks back and divides his life into periods according to the succession of his masters—that is, according to the regimes he has lived through:

  1. Childhood, 1888–1900: an Eifel-Moselle family Catholicism transplanted into the Sauerland and shaped by rebellion against the state.

  2. Boyhood, 1900–1907: the clericalism of the Catholic boarding school, stripped of its claim to total authority and made relative by a humanist education.

  3. Youth, 1907–1918: a Greater Prussianism of the Wilhelmine kind, stripped of Hegel, together with Neo-Kantianism.

  4. Manhood, 1919–1932: German identity stripped of Prussianism, combined with Weimar-style liberal democracy and strong nationalist reactions, especially anti-Versailles feeling.

  5. Mature years, 1933–1945: unleashed Greater German nationalism in the style of Brother Straubinger, accompanied by an inward retreat.

  6. Later years, 1945–1958: unleashed antifascism, with a charity pension under Article 131.

And the corresponding masters:

  1. Good-natured older priests with memories of the Kulturkampf.

  2. Boarding-school directors and patriarchal factory owners.

  3. Wilhelmine officials and officers—basically quite easy-going people.

  4. Genuine pluralism, with a great deal of freedom.

  5. Party bosses, colossal careerists, and lunatics.

  6. Shylocks and persecutors who have been superficially “Nathanized.”

And that is enough.

Thank you, gentlemen!

An anxious question from the seventy-year-old:

Will I live to see the de-Nathanization of Germany?1

July 1958, in Casalonga

A great encounter with land and sea at Cape Finisterre.

A great encounter with the Vandals through Christian Courtois’s book Les Vandales (1955).

Gelimer’s laughter, la carcajada de Gelimer,2 and the smiles of Daniel and the Evangelist John in the Pórtico de la Gloria at Santiago.

Perhaps nothing remains to us but Gelimer’s laughter.

But the smiles of Daniel and the Evangelist follow me into my dreams.

Two attempts were suppressed and quickly smothered:

1950: The Nomos of the Earth and Ex Captivitate.

1954: the dialogue on power and the new edition of Constitutional Theory.

And now, in 1958, the third attempt:

the collected essays and the commemorative volume.3

Only a born counterfeiter could have come up with the idea of the three rings in Nathan the Wise.

16 August 1958

The key sentence—which also applies to the whole invasion of Wilhelmine Germany by people coming out of the declining Habsburg [Monarchy], people such as Reinhardt, Freud, Schnitzler, Werfel, Rilke, and Däubler—is found quite near the beginning of Hitler’s Mein Kampf, on p. 57, in the second chapter, “Years of Study and Suffering in Vienna”:

“In proud admiration I compared the rise of the Reich with the slow decline of the Austrian state.”

1908!!

4

22 August 1958

Indocilis privata loqui—incapable of speaking of private things—Lucan V, 539.

Everything is secret language.

Everything is secret knowledge.

Secret religion.

The greatest insights are overrun by false prophets.

Do you finally understand where you live and who you are?

Et mortem sentire juvat.

And there is joy in feeling death.

Lucan’s religion, without those who exploit it and falsify it.

The religion of a young man who had access to Nero.

25 August 1958

Once again, a Sunday morning full of good ideas.

The night before: an encounter with the princeps religiosissimus, the most religious prince, Sisebut; with the Lecto de la validez—the validity of a baptism once it has been carried out—and with the validez del Lecto.

Vitoria later treated the matter in exactly the same way.

The scandal has already happened.

To undo it would create a new scandal.

So the baptism performed by force remains valid.

Coactus voluit.

He was forced, but he willed it.

Long live the pious King Sisebut!

Long live Innocent III and his decretal Maiores!

Long live Canon 57 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and Gratian’s gloss on C. 5 D. XLV!

Long live Vitoria!!

The concept of scandal as the great back door of jurisprudence based on the concrete situation!

À corsaire, corsaire et demi!

Against a pirate, a pirate and a half!

À Juif, Juif et demi!

Against a Jew, a Jew and a half!

Secundum occasionem et veritatem coactus sive condicionaliter, sive absolute voluit.

According to the circumstances and the truth of the matter, although he was forced, he nevertheless willed it—whether conditionally or absolutely.

Here lies the true source and practical end result of all Vitoria’s beautiful arguments in De Indis, and of his supposed founding of modern international law.

I have discovered another seed as well:

No. 39 of Quevedo’s Sueños, La hora de todos, is the seed from which The Protocols of the Elders of Zion grew.

But who were the Monopantones then?

And who are they today?

26 August 1958

No human being has ever spoken to his persecutors more calmly and reasonably than I have.1

Through gentleness—practice this duty— You will defeat your enemy. Oh, do not rob your soul Of this heavenly pleasure.2

27 August 1958

On the note from the end of 1956, at the top of p. 80 [= pp. 353 ff.]:

De Gaulle is only an interlude.

He is catching up with Germany.

Much will still be repeated elsewhere that we in Germany got ahead of everyone in doing first.

Until then, we remain the people of collective shame, and we introduce Days of Shame as paid public holidays:

Hiroshima, for example, in August;

the Morgenthau Plan;

a Devil’s Calendar instead of a Calendar of Saints.

3 September 1958

So God is the Wholly Other.

Correct.

The totally Other.

Total alienation, in other words.

Wonderful!

That is exactly what human beings need in order to become human.

Alienation, then, is not an objection and it is not a refutation.

Human beings need something of this kind in order to estrange themselves from the animal and become human.

But there are also false forms of alienation.

And those, naturally, are deadly.

Then begins the hopeless struggle over what is genuine and what is false—which means friend and enemy—with all its satanic violence and all its Nathan-like fraud.

7 September 1958, Sunday

“The genuine ring was presumably lost.”

Ecco!

There it is!

The fraud reveals itself.

The destruction of genuineness as such!3

9 September 1958

Today, survivors are reproached for having survived.

Ernst Jünger reproached me for exactly this in January 1950.1

What does that mean in legal terms?

It means that certain people claim the right to survive for themselves while denying that same right to others.

A delightful state of affairs.

Why did you not throw yourself onto the tyrant’s knife?

Well, did you throw yourself onto his knife?

But I did not support him!

Everyone who lived through the period supported him in some way—even everyone who tried to assassinate him.

I am eager to read Jünger’s new diary from the occupation years.

I reread what he wrote in 1950, in his letters of 10 and 16 January:

“Had you followed my advice and example in this matter, you might no longer be alive today, but you would have the right to pass final judgment on me.”

So that is his court-of-last-resort relationship to me!

A contemptible death sentence.

Horrifying.

And yet he has not read a single one of my legal works. Encased in his own armor, he has never even felt the slightest impulse to find out what I actually wrote in that field.

And now I am supposed to send him my collection of essays on constitutional law?

So that I can be told that I had no right to survive?

That would amount to submitting to his claim to pronounce death sentences simply by treating a person’s survival as something to hold against him.

No.

It cannot go on.

Gelimer’s laughter is still the mildest possible answer to insults as deadly as these.

16 September 1958

Consensus follows power.

Power does not follow consensus.

Barion puts it very nicely:

My convictions do not follow power.

On the contrary, they set themselves against power.

Very good.

But perhaps that is simply his clerical existence speaking.

The state theory of money is a state theory of power.

Knapp, Sohm, Below—all post-Hegelians.

Imperium rationis: the rule of reason.

All human beings are equal.

Correct.

But only in the sense that, for example, all strings tuned to D are equal.

On one of them, someone plays a beautiful melody.

On another, some dreadful incompetent scratches away.

21 September 1958

Consensus follows power and thereby becomes genuine consensus.

Power that follows consensus, however, ceases thereby to be genuine power.

“What does blood cost?”

Pribićević asked this in the Yugoslav parliament in 1925, in response to the <…> Corfu legend and its use in claims for reparations.

Sava told me this when I told him about the legends of today.

The uncanny intelligence of the Serbian people.

The point grows sharper and sharper:

A welfare state is a state in which the socially weaker person is politically and legally the stronger person.

The question, therefore, is who can get control of the monopoly possessed by the socially weak.

The trade unions have succeeded in doing so.

22 September 1958

When Hegel says “God is dead,” there is still something of the magic of Good Friday in it.

With Heidegger, it means something else.

It is most dangerous of all in Bonald:

“God is dead” means:

God is absent.

27 September 1958

Bismarck’s Reich had two components.

It was National-Liberal.

The national element was the political component.

The liberal element was the economic component.

After the defeat of 1918, these two components came apart, producing a kind of nuclear fission.

That was the critical period of the Weimar Constitution, 1919–1933.1

In 1933, the national element was unleashed as an independent force and grew far beyond all proportion until it finally burst apart in 1944/45.

Today, in the so-called Economic Miracle, the economic element has likewise grown far beyond all proportion.

The two elements split apart and each grew without restraint until it burst.

Fermentation instead of breathing.

From Crooke to the rain. Citizen, outside baptism, you come, Christian, by wet roads from the rain beneath the eaves.2

Jünger’s new diary.3

His friend and chief witness is Ernst Niekisch.

Let him stick with him now.

The social ideal is Jünger’s war.

10 October 1958

Yesterday morning, at around four o’clock, God Almighty summoned the Roman Pope, who had sat upon the Holy See, before His own throne—the judgment seat of the Almighty and All-Knowing.4

No fresh-cell injection can help him now.

Nor can friendship with the rulers of today’s Western world.

Ready or not to go, before his Judge he now must stand—

after prolonging matters for so long and so often, and after so long playing the highest judge himself.

The sentimental newspaper, radio, and television chatter that poured out in streams over this death now flows into the scale on the left.

God have mercy on the poor diplomat’s soul.

30 October 1958

Let us found an organization for the timely criminalization of any possible inhabitants of the Moon and Mars!5

ORKEMM!

Otherwise the conquest of the Moon and Mars might possibly turn out to be the same kind of thing as the Spanish conquest of America.

And surely that cannot be allowed!

Columbus, Cortés, and Pizarro neglected to do this.

Let us summon any possible natives before a tribunal whose president would, of course, have to be Mr. Henry Morgenthau.

Let us heap the burning coals of collective guilt and collective shame onto their criminal heads!

And then, in the name of humanity:

hit them hard!

Only in this way can our departure into the cosmos be fully prepared and made morally acceptable.

It is infamous, the way these people who award the Nobel Prize are playing with the life and fate of poor old Pasternak: hanging their prize around his neck and thereby turning him into a target for persecution in his own country.

Infamous, this method of stirring people up—calling on them to resist while remaining safely far from the line of fire.

Exactly as people did against Hitler from 1933 to 1945.

It shows what awaits the Russians if they are ever defeated.

Perhaps they will then receive their just punishment for having taken part at Nuremberg—and, in the main trial, for having been there as the true masters of the court.

Then their successful antifascist trick will fall back onto their own heads.

Reflections by an Article 131 pensioner on the Pasternak affair.

Of the interesting parallel from the Hitler period—the Nobel Prize awarded to Ossietzky—we hear nothing.

What tact!

What disciplined use of language!

What consistency of method and line!

What identity!

I had better say no more, “out of consideration for the society in which I live.”

4 November 1958

All Jews come to grief against me.

But as long as I, Carl Schmitt, remain alive, the Jews still have a chance.

Feast day of Saint Charles Borromeo.

9 November 1958

Why don’t you get yourselves some ERP [European Recovery Program] money!

And why, exactly, is God supposed to be dead?

He is so willing—and so easy—to bring into line!

How old-fashioned, all this effort over “God is dead.”

We have now entered the second half of Hamlet.

No more ghosts appear.

Now begins the hard hand-to-hand struggle for survival.

It is no longer about revenge.

It is only about power.

I wanted to send Montherlant’s Le Maître de Santiago back to Hans-Joachim Arndt with these words:

What has become of this Montherlant!

An anticolonialist d’Annunzio!

Here I return to you this older form of Romanticism.

I return the Christian-Cathar-Buddhist bouillabaisse of an old, incurable Romantic. Even the seasoning of a Romero Santiago has not made it any easier for me to digest, despite my considerable weakness for that particular flavor.

I prefer the leyenda negra, the Black Legend, to the white snow of the sublime néant, the sublime nothingness.

The white ceremonial cloak, purified of colonialism, belongs in the Technicolor magazine of a Hollywood converted to Christianity.

Give me the honest conquistador a thousand times over rather than this white snowman of sublime nothingness—even if that conquistador is the heroic swineherd Pizarro from poor Extremadura.

The whole thing is a niaiserie sublime, a sublime piece of silliness.

You will find its key phrase in the naïve confession on p. 148:

“du moins dans l’art”—

“at least in art!”

Only on the stage is the purity of the Perfect achieved.

Escape into the theater.

There is only one concrete question still worth asking:

Is the soil of Algeria the sol natal—the native soil—of France, or is it not?

I can imagine who helped this propaganda piece become a literary success.

The one personal gain I have taken from it is this clear realization:

At that time, the Christian Church of the West finally failed.

It withdrew into a wretched potestas indirecta, an indirect power, because it no longer possessed the religious strength required for sacred consecration and sacred naming—the strength with which, a thousand years earlier, it had still been able to bind and consecrate the wild conquerors of the Germanic migrations.

Europe’s entire conquest of the world:

une tragédie sans issue—

a tragedy with no way out.

On p. 70:

Alvaro shows Spain to his daughter Marianna in the same way that the Spartans showed their sons a drunken Helot.

These drunken Helots also appear in Annette, in The Spiritual Year, on the twenty-fifth Sunday after Pentecost.

I think the deliberately drunken Helot is Europe today.

And Montherlant imagines himself to be a Spartan because, with the permission and applause of the masters, he helps mix the drink.

11 November 1958

Today we are Pasternakized.

Tomorrow we will be de-Pasternakized.

Entung and Ententung.

De-ing and de-de-ing.

It would take the pen of a Pasternak to describe all this adequately—that is, in a manner worthy of the Nobel Prize.

On the Spiegel interview, no. 46, dated 12 November 1958, with “Cassandra,” the journalist Mr. Connor of the Daily Mirror:

The particular achievement of Der Spiegel, in my view, is that it exposed a false costume—the mask of Cassandra.

The tragedy of Cassandra, the Trojan woman, includes the fact that Troy lost the war.

But here, in the Daily Mirror, we have someone from the side that won the war roaring for hatred and revenge and calling himself Cassandra.

That is grotesque.

But people of this kind are dangerous.

They can no longer climb down from the exaggerations that brought them success.

They remain trapped inside the simplest possible dilemma:

If the Germans are not what he (Connor) says they are—what is he?

12 November 1958

An important proposal for relieving our burden:

The name Germany has been discredited.

It brings with it shameful memories which, on the one hand, we are not permitted to forget and which, on the other hand, we understandably wish to erase.

Given this divided condition, the compelling necessity arises to abolish the old name and introduce a new one.1

Fortunately, today we have an effortless way out of this delicate situation.

The name of a great martyr for freedom comes to our aid: a brilliant poet whose novel Doctor Zhivago is now spontaneously bought by every German and—so far as the progress made in organizing our leisure still permits it—also subjected to an attempt at reading.

We have therefore found the correct symbol for our progress in the consciousness of freedom.

Until now, we had tried to read Kafka and thereby justify the name Kafkania for our country.

We are now entering a further stage of our development.

For this reason I propose the name:

PASTERNAKISTAN

Under the banner of this name, recognition of our ascent into humanity will be made much easier, and our chances of admission to the United Nations will be greatly improved.

Erich Strauss.

16 November 1958

Please listen to this:

“Here too we see confirmed the instructive observation, typical of the entire course of the revolution, that theory always fails precisely where the situation seems entitled to expect the decisive word from it.”

Who could have said that?

It dates from 1909.

And it was said in Germany!

Who was so intelligent and so experienced?

By that time, German legal positivism in constitutional law had long since declared:

“Count me out.”

It had solemnly announced:

Constitutional law ends here.

Count me out—that is, precisely in the situation where people expect constitutional law to provide the decisive answer.

So who in Germany, as early as 1909, could have been this intelligent and experienced?

Go on.

Search diligently!

You will find it on p. 351 of a book on constitutional theory.1

My own experience, admittedly, was rather different.

In 1932 I found the decisive word.

But the moment the decisive situation actually arrived, my theory received a kick in the teeth.

Later, after everything had gone wrong, the theory was declared to have paved the way for the disaster.

In cases like this, theory serves as the scapegoat.

And for human beings it is more important to have a scapegoat than to have a theory.

Cassandra is particularly well suited to that purpose.

Someone says to me, as a German:

You started it!

I answer:

And you did not stop!

How disgusting, this endless tug-of-war over aggression and the question of guilt.

Only parasites can live off such things.

No honest person can.2

Aggression is supposed to be a crime in an age of unleashed progress!

7 December 1958, Sunday

In the West German newspaper whose business pages reflect the Economic Miracle and whose cultural pages serve as a well-furnished pied-à-terre for the supposedly homeless Left, Ernst Niekisch is now declared to be a historical source.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 6 December 1958.

Ernst Jünger serves as Niekisch’s guarantor.

That is the situation.

Do not forget it because of your friendship with Ernst Jünger.

I wrote to Jünger that I already feel sufficiently humiliated for ever having allowed myself to enter into a conversation with Niekisch—a man who, thirty years later, now presents such “reports” of his conversations with me.

Conversations with people like Niekisch were interrogations on the steppe.

They end with someone being shot.

Anyone who knows that 2 × 2 = 5 simply knows too much.

Machiavelli already knew too much.

But with Hobbes it became a matter of life and death, because he knew that all knowledge is too much.

And yet he still hoped—as a former tutor to princes, he could never stop hoping—that he might teach those in power.

Until finally he realized:

doceo, sed frustra.

I teach, but in vain.

When I read Theodor Haecker’s afterword of 1918, I understand Thomas Hobbes’s fury against theological agitators and troublemakers.

And yet Theodor Haecker was my friend at the time!

A crocodile wearing clerical neckbands—neckbands that he later exchanged for a rosary.

Who says that during the thousand-year kingdom it must always be the same chosen people—that is, the same beneficiaries—sitting at the top?

Perhaps there too a rapid circulation of elites takes place while the thousand-year epoch itself remains unchanged.

We experienced such a replacement in 1945.

We must be prepared for more.

Novalis thought that the Last Day would not be an eternal day but an entire epoch—and specifically that epoch we call the thousand-year kingdom.

Obviously no individual human being, and no human group, can endure a thousand years of prosperity.

It is too much.

We Germans did not even manage twelve years.

And we were particularly resilient.

The Economic Miracle will not last a thousand years either.

But the age of enormously increased production, and therefore enormously increased possibilities of consumption, will remain.

In other words:

the thousand-year kingdom began long ago.

It continues unchanged, with the elites circulating through it.

8 December 1958

Irony will never become popular.

Yes, Kierkegaard is right about that.

More than that:

it will become dangerous to one’s life.

Not among the masses, who will never even sense that irony is there.

But among the ruling class and the creatures who serve it.

In the early stages of a totalitarian system, irony still has a certain amount of room to move.

In Germany this lasted until around 1936/37.

Then amusement, jokes, and irony came to an end.

Eventually they themselves began to seem stupid and childish.

With Kierkegaard—especially in his work on Adler—you can still see how comfortable his existence basically remained, how thoroughly Biedermeier his situation still was.

And the fiercely polemical Theodor Haecker never understood the situation either—first because he was too busy preaching, later because he was too busy playing the sacristan.

He understood neither the First World War nor the Second.

“An abyss of mendacity among degenerate Furche Pietists.”

Who said that?

Perhaps Joseph Goebbels?

Or Ilya Ehrenburg?

No.

It was Theodor Haecker, in his 1918 afterword to The Concept of the Chosen One.

Nothing more occurs to you when you think of Hitler?

When I think of Hitler, all of you occur to me!

28 December 1958

The story—the short story, or rather the lightning-fast story—of the three men can also be told like this:

Three men are riding across the prairie.

One asks:

How much is 2 × 2?

The second answers:

2 × 2 = 5.

The first man immediately shoots him.

The third asks:

Why did you shoot him?

The first replies:

He knew too much.1

Three men are riding across the prairie.

One says:

When I think of Hitler, nothing occurs to me.

The second says:

When I think of Hitler, all kinds of things occur to me.

The first immediately shoots him.

The third asks:

Why did you shoot him?

The answer:

Because something occurred to him when he thought about Hitler.

“He knows too much.”

Ludwig Feuchtwanger, Ernst Bloch, and Paul Joachimsen had already confirmed that to me in a letter from October 1923, in connection with Political Romanticism and my book on parliamentarism.

30 December 1958

At Christmas I received a Christmas greeting from Otto Kirchheimer:

an engraving by Baldung Grien, jument ruant étalon—a mare kicking a stallion.

A horrifying Christmas greeting.

Kirchheimer certainly has no idea what he is doing.

Nor what he is doing to me by sending it.

And yet I still prefer him to Nathan the Wise and Satan the Quiet.

But:

Those were never your bells.1

31 December 1958

Peaceful as my intentions are, I sit in my room and, suspecting nothing bad, leaf through the Frankfurter Allgemeine, which until now had seemed not yet to have been infiltrated by the poisonous vindictiveness of our ambitious present age.

Suddenly someone hits me over the head with a rubber truncheon.

What happened?

Our venerable head of state—may God preserve him until the Last Judgment—gave a speech on 10 December to mark the tenth anniversary of the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights.

At the end of it, he says that the political friend-enemy thesis, topical some years ago, was certainly flirtatious, but intellectually and psychologically poor and limited.

Those are his exact words:

flirtatious, psychologically poor and limited.

A hint delivered with a rubber truncheon.

I know what it means when a seventy-five-year-old pouvoir neutre, a “neutral power,” makes such an effort to morally defame and destroy the reputation of a defenseless seventy-year-old who has been completely dismissed from public life and is sitting peacefully in some corner of the Sauerland.

Flirtatious and psychologically poor.

Murder of the soul in a speech about human rights.

An obiter dictum and an obiter factum from a Federal President.

A fine occupation for the head of state in a democracy.

A special solution to the problem of how a talkative pouvoir neutre can fill his excessively abundant leisure hours.

Am I really supposed to end the year 1958 with this horror?

Certainly not!

But what should I end it with?

With the observation that Gottfried Benn’s 1952 speech on Else Lasker-Schüler and Thomas Mann’s story The Blood of the Walsungs from 19[06] must be placed beside one another and compared?

The problem of the years 1832–1933?

The fusion of the German and Jewish spirit?

No.

Not that either!

Absit!

Far be it from me!

But I actually did have one great New Year’s Eve pleasure:

reading Odo Marquard’s essay on the question:

Is Kant’s metaphysics reality or a substitute?

It is wonderful.

The new language of these young Germans!

For example:

“decisionism without decision” (p. 81 n.);

transcendental dialectic as the ironic destruction, by means of parody, of a metaphysics governed by controlling reason (p. 89 n.);

and Adam—the human being—in Kleist’s The Broken Jug as defendant and judge at the same time (pp. 106–107 n.).

All three concern me:

me, the decisionist;

me, the parodist;

and me, the propagator of the principle:

I do not compare the victims. I compare only the judges!

And then there is the motto to the intermediate remark on p. 52, with which I would like to end this year:

The philosophers have changed the world in various ways.

The point, however, is to spare it.

Looking ahead to the coming year 1959 from the end of 1958 (predictions):

  1. After the national component of Bismarck’s National-Liberal Reich became independent under the Hitler regime and was driven to explosion, the liberal component of that Reich is now becoming independent in its turn and being driven ad absurdum.

Perhaps this will happen as early as the coming year.

  1. In Germany, Gelimer’s laughter will spread ever more irresistibly and become impossible to extinguish.

  2. The next bestseller, which will replace Pasternak—and which it will be an unmistakable sign of neo-Nazism not to buy—would be best given the name Rafo Konforti.

  3. This year, many gravediggers will themselves be buried.

  4. Fishing in troubled waters will prove to be child’s play compared with fishing in the hour before the Maelstrom, when the fish are paralyzed by fear.

Khrushchev’s ultimatum has produced just such a paralysis.

Above all, the paralysis consists in no longer wishing to distinguish between friend and enemy.

  1. Wonders upon wonders!

First the miracle of the Rentenmark in 1923.

Then the miracle of the seizure of power in 1933.

Then the Economic Miracle of 1950.

Truly, as Germans we can now sing the chorus sung by the Jews in besieged Bethulia in Nestroy’s farce Judith:

We’ve had miracles enough in our history; We can do without miracles of bravery.

  1. In the coming year 1959, I too will remain what I have already been for years:

the chief defendant in a trial being conducted simultaneously from Moscow and Zurich, with Georg Lukács and Peter Schneider walking arm in arm as the prosecutors.

Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? Quem jutorem rogaturus?

What shall I, poor wretch, say then?

Whom shall I ask to defend me?

  1. According to the classical rules of the political cycle—as seen in the model case of France—restorations following long coalition wars last fifteen years.

The model:

France, 1815–1830.

Applied to Germany today, this would mean that the present period continues until 1960.

Or, if we begin counting from 1948 or 1949, until 1963/64.

So for the moment we still have a reprieve before the hanging.

We shall thoroughly enjoy the condemned man’s last meal and diligently butter our Nuremberg gallows.

  1. So many political trials will be conducted in the Federal Republic of Germany that some just people will finally understand my thesis:

that a trial changes the very object being tried.

Some will also understand why I so often quote the sentence:

I do not compare the victims. I compare only the judges.

And the few who are initiated will understand where the development is heading—a development that does not yet fully take the form of justice being killed by political overburdening, but which already reveals precisely that tendency.

Out of homo homini homo—

man is man to man—

out of the complete humanization of law, there arises:

judex homini lupus.

The judge is a wolf to man.

  1. Gelimer’s laughter does not stop.

But that does not have to prevent us from seeing our reality.

On the contrary:

it can and should shake the scenery and stage sets of deception.

In that way, it becomes a form of appeal appropriate to the situation:

J’en appelle de ta justice à ta réalité.

I appeal from your justice to your reality.

End of Gelimer’s laughter.

in Arist[otle], Athenaion politeia 39.6.

Busolt-Swoboda, Griechische Staatskunde, 1926, p. 917.

forgetting commanded of everyone— the citizens.

μηδενὶ πρὸς μηδένα μνησικακεῖν ἐξεῖναι—

with the exception concerning the Thirty <…> intentions.

the concept of the political;

concerning the state:

Asylum and Location.

  1. Location

All roads lead to Rome.

The problem of Roma aeterna, Eternal Rome.

An indissoluble connection—in law, even if not always in fact—between the universal episcopate and the Roman episcopate:

Charles Journet, L’Église du Verbe incarné, I, La hiérarchie apostolique, Paris 1941, p. 522.

The Pope always remains Bishop of Rome, even if he moves his residence somewhere else.

Siège de Rome / résidence.

Péronne:

“Wherever he resides, the true successor of Saint Peter must necessarily remain Bishop of Rome.”

Praelectiones theologicae, Paris 1856, vol. IV, p. 257.

Ch. Journet agrees.

Dissoluble:

Jean de Saint-Thomas:

“It is a matter of divine faith that the papacy and the See of Rome were united in the past and remain united today; nevertheless, this union is temporary.”

It is not irrevocable.

The bond can be changed under Church law; it is not indissoluble under divine law.

The “Roman Church” would therefore be such a <soul?> only in name.

Indissoluble:

in law and in fact.

It is impossible for Rome ever to exist without clergy or faithful people.

Thus Bellarmine, De Romano Pontifice, Book IV, ch. 4.

Even the very soil of Rome cannot disappear:

Billot, De Ecclesia Christi, p. 596.

Roma aeterna.

A Swiss scholar, R. M. Schultes, states this explicitly in De Ecclesia Catholica, Paris 1925, p. 455.

  1. Ancient Rome

a) Pompey failed because the senator would not leave Rome.

Pompey thought dictatorially.

Like Sulla, he wanted to defend the law in <?> a province.

The senators follow.

Ed. Meyer, Principat.

These Romans were incapable of separating themselves from the city-state.

In 43 the fili <…> had to leave Rome and go to the army.

Cicero stays!

<…>

Tacitus, Histories I:

arcanum imperii Romae <…> alibi quam—

[Folio 3r]

<…>

c) pomerium;

d) Places of pilgrimage.

e) The problem of transportation.

Asylum and amnesty = renunciation of human justice.

Its meaning for all human knowledge and understanding:

giving up the insistence on being right.

A sense for the “demonic.”

Gerhard Ritter, Machtstaat und Utopie, 1940:

the insoluble of good and evil, p. 53.1

Erasmus:

“For the Christian there is no just war” (p. 52).

In real political struggles there is rarely a case of clear right standing against clear wrong (p. 53).

The mostly rather primitive teachings of late-medieval theologians on “just war” (p. 83).

War as an expression of vital energies.

Correct, gl<..?>, but the doctrine of war is one too, only more refined!!

All the more vital, the more just!!

<…>

Thesis:

There are just wars, but only in the sense of wars conducted according to proper form.

There are no just wars except formally regular wars.

There is the justus exercitus, the lawful army, and the justus hostis, the lawful enemy.

Here too, law depends entirely on form.

Lucan, Pharsalia X, 436:

Procul e [recte: a] muris acies non sparsa maniplis Nec vaga conspicitur, sed iustos qualis in [recte: ad] hostes Recta fronte venit.

Far from the walls, the battle line is not seen scattered into separate units or straggling at random; it advances in a straight front, as it would against lawful enemies.

East—West.

Max Weber, p. 483.

Tocqueville.

Michelet, la loi.

The Vistula as the boundary.

Suddenly I am afraid of these one-idea abolitionist prosecutionists.

They are probably the worst totalitarians of all, whether they want to abolish alcohol, war, or brothels.

Henry Adams, The Education of Henry Adams, p. 145:

“In 1858 the whole plain of northern Europe, as well as the Danube in the south, bore evident marks of being still the prehistoric highway between Asia and the Ocean. The trade-route followed the old routes of invasion, and Cologne was a resting-place between Warsaw and Flanders. Throughout northern Germany, Russia was felt even more powerfully1 than France. In 1901 Russia had vanished, and not even France was felt;

[Folio 4r]

hardly England or America.2 Coal alone was felt – its stamp alone pervaded the Rhine district and persisted to Picardy – and the stamp was the same as that of Birmingham and Pittsburgh. The Rhine produced the same power, and the power produced the same people, the same mind, the same impulse.”

For a sixty-three-year-old man, he says, these were the hardest months of his Education.

1901!

“and Russia was the most indigestible morsel he ever met; but the sum of it, viewed from Cologne, seamed reasonable.3 From Hammerfest to Cherbourg on one shore of the Ocean, from Halifax to Norfolk on the other, one great empire was ruled by one great emperor – Coal.4 Political and human jealousies might tear it apart or divide it, but the power and the empire were one. Unity had gained that ground. Beyond lay Russia, and there an older, perhaps a surer, power, resting on the eternal law of inertia, held its own.”

Niebuhr.

Tocqueville, 1835.

Europe suddenly growing strong again.

an expression of this European superiority.

13 August 1947

The verses by Lenau from the Travel Pages—“The Log Cabin,” 1833 [recte: 1839]—and sentences in the log cabin in the .

Look at the burning logs:

These trunks are burning here upon the hearth To keep me warm for one brief hour, Though soon enough I too must grow cold, And I myself will sink into ash.

Perhaps there is no loneliness at all? Am I myself only a burning log?

And while I warm myself beside the oak, Perhaps an unseen guest is warming himself In secret at my consuming flame of life, Stirring and fanning the fever of my thoughts?

His constant wavering between belief in God, moods, despair, nihilism, engagements, and ridiculous adventures.

All of it amounts to so little.

And finally, madness.

And yet this is the greatest poet of the period before 1848.

How secure and courageous Annette seems by comparison.

She was challenged just as deeply, and she was every bit as lovely, but infinitely stronger.

How firmly she keeps both her reason and her moral bearing!

But where does the lasting force of Roman words and concepts come from?

Caesar.

Politics.

26 August 1947

Law is eternal.

Only form is eternal.

Ê and Ewe, marriage and property—the same thing:

form.

Form means deliberately looking away from the interest, mood, and plan of the moment.

A leap into eternity.

Holding back and holding down immediate interest.

The katechon, the restrainer, is present here too.

Only in this way does form become possible.

A reach from what cannot be understood into what cannot be grasped.

That is the legal concept.

Legal form is therefore an angling, a folding together of the eternal and the temporal:

within temporal material, an eternal moment.

It appears as an institution rooted in a place:

the enclosed Thing-site where the assembly meets;

the judge’s seat;

the defendant’s bench;

the crown of the land of Hungary, Bohemia, Castile and León, England.

Location is this angling:

the folding of the eternal into something temporal.

Law depends entirely on this form.

(Consequence:

the angle in which x temporal and <…> x earthly and unearthly concepts meet.)

That is why the jurist has a theological origin.

And that is why he displaces the theologian when the theologian is no longer capable of creating such institutions and instead crawls into a potestas indirecta, an indirect power.

That is also why legal science comes to an end when the jurist becomes a technician.

At that point he is no longer even capable of forming a concept.

Punishment then becomes:

security;

hygiene;

pest control;

the extermination of bedbugs.

And its great form, the criminal trial, accordingly becomes a technical measure carried out by police officers, doctors, propagandists, and the chemists of wars of annihilation.

26 August 1947

The distinction often made between jurisprudence and legal science—for example by Karl Renner—rests entirely on the assumption of a positivist, natural-scientific idea of what “science” means.

Once that assumption is made, legal science becomes a wretched technical science.

Theology and legal science, however, are sciences of a particular kind.

An internal tension is essential to both of them.

Only this tension sets thought in motion.

In that respect they resemble the opposing tensions from which genuine natural sciences begin and toward which they move:

positive and negative;

full and empty;

particles and waves;

and so on.

In theology this tension can take forms such as:

Infinite — finite.

Natura naturans — natura naturata.

Constituent power — constituted power.

Compare Dictatorship, p. 142.

Substitution — decision.

Charisma — office.

Pneuma — tradition.

Compare the marvelous essay by Hans Barion on Rudolf Sohm, Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft, January 1942.

But is the infinite not precisely the absence of form?

Does the formless not break through at this point?

This is where jurisprudence touches theology and finds in theology the support without which jurisprudence sinks.

Correct.

Theology does not find that support in another science.

It finds it directly in “revelation.”

Legal science therefore presupposes a constituted theology—not merely a “religion.”

It is a science modeled on theological science.

Jurisprudence in general is possible when it can lean on a constituted religion.

Law and religion.

Legal science and theology.

Pity = selfhood and its apparent opposite.

One only ever feels pity for oneself.

What is pity?

Identification with another person.

So the other person becomes identified with me—but even more importantly, my own self becomes identified with the other.

Therefore all pity is self-pity.

And I am ashamed of the accusation made against Germans that they feel sorry for themselves.

When things are going this badly for someone, and pity is supposed to be the first humanitarian virtue, is the wretched German really forbidden to feel pity for himself?

The shameless Phariseeism of these smug little guardians of humanitarian virtue!

Rousseau stands at the beginning of all such lies.

But at least he himself was still a poor tormented devil, a helpless bohemian.

Now, by contrast, along come the fat, overfed gluttons and declare our starving corpses morally disgusting.

[Folio 8r]

I do not barricade myself inside a conclusion.

I do not bury myself in an achievement.

That means I do not die and I do not look backward.

I continue to serve, and therefore I continue to live.

I do not stop at any thought.

I do not remain with any conclusion.

I keep going and keep pushing onward.

That is why only a few people can follow me.

Most run out of breath.

They stop at some particular point in my process of thought and try to pin me down there.

In other words, they declare me dead because they themselves are dead.

They want to fix me in place and make me rigid, just as they themselves are fixed and rigid.

Anyone who wants to hold me to my <yesterday’s> thought will find that I am already in the beyond.

I am no longer there.

I have disappeared into what cannot be grasped.

And this is why they become furious when they discover that physically I am still alive, however modestly and secretly, somewhere in some miserable refuge.

Their hatred only grows stronger.

Their desire to persecute me bursts into flame at the thought that I am still alive not only intellectually, but physically as well.

These people belong to the past.

For that reason they are dead.

But they do not know death.

I have known it for a long time.

It is constantly reborn from the spirit and from thought:

life as the great festival of , in whose constant transformation physical death is only one moment among many.

I have already died many times.

And I am still alive.

As for what there is to fear in physical death, and what there is not to fear, I have considerable experience.

I have tested it.

I fear physical death less than I fear the filthy meanness of those shades who tried to drag me down onto the level of their own corpses:

those poor fat caterpillars trying to glue a butterfly in flight with their slime.

(Form = distance;

= perspective;

and precisely that is supposed to disappear early!)

26 August [1947], evening

Again and again:

“the prey of the mighty moment,” which tears me upward and downward.

The tutor of Friedrich Wilhelm IV used the expression “the prey of the mighty moment” in front of his pupil.

But we are all prey to it.

Annette above all.

Her letters affected me profoundly.

How charmingly she speaks, in her language and her surroundings:

a girl;

a bright and intelligent, wisely foolish virgin;

one could imagine nothing more beautiful.

Then she falls in love twice.

First with Heinrich Straube.

Then with Levin Schücking.

Each time with a bourgeois literary man who probably won her heart only because he offered her the literary understanding she could not find among people of her own estate, class, and caste.

These infatuations were intense.

But they never reached the core of her being.

She remained a virgin.

Amazon-like.

An intelligent girl, intelligent even in a practical domestic sense.

Nothing decadent about her.

Levin Schücking’s “little mother.”

In an age that was coming apart, she remained unstupid, indestructible right down to the heart.

And yet she was obedient, as every good woman was expected to be, obedient to her time.

She went along with its currents.

She dutifully participated in the literary business of her age.

At times she verses together in a Schillerian , in the of this <…> and of this dissolved Lenau.

The doubts of The Spiritual Year are the recoil back into herself after those foolish infatuations with literary men.

The imperfect nun.

The faithless Druidess.

Her accusations against herself become so terrible because she carries a great standard within herself.

At the beginning of the age of l’art pour l’art, she certainly participates in the literary world—but no more than is proper for a well-brought-up, respectable, obedient girl.

At the deepest level she knows the nihilism of her age.

And it shatters her.

That is the meaning of The Spiritual Year.

Her aversion to the schoolmaster Julius Schering.

That is why the greatest <…> of the young girl;

the first half of the poems of The Spiritual Year, the Holy Week poems;

the second part of The Spiritual Year already laments consciously, already becomes a hand-wringing cry over what is being lost;

while the first part is still a lament.

She could not look upon the Virgin Mary.

Mary was too “bright” for her.

She could think of Mary’s purity only with terror.

Oh, poor Annette.

[Folio 9r]

27 August 1947

The infatuations were literary mutations of love.

She was not a saint.

But her sadness came from knowing that she was not a saint.

La tristesse de ne pas être des saintes.

The sadness of not being saints.

That sadness lies closer to holiness than any other human condition, including <…>.

Anyone who does not know this has no choice but to become a schoolmaster, whether he gives The Spiritual Year a good grade, as Kreiten did, or a bad one, as Julius Schering did.

A saint with a laurel wreath:

the poetry business of the time,

publishers’ theatrics,

pseudo-fame.

The most successful and famous poet of the time was Lenau.

Yes, he fishes pearls and jewels, And they cost nothing but his soul.

The genuine pearls are tears of repentance.

The Spiritual Year, fourth Sunday after Pentecost, p. 121.

The core of her work is the poems of The Spiritual Year.

What is this foolish historiography with its endless “if only” and “what if”?

If this or that had not happened, everything would have turned out differently.

The horrifying madness of these unreal fantasies.

All this “if only” and “what if” is a symptom.

These historians are merely the exhaust pipe for an activism that was prevented, obstructed, or defeated.

Prometheus raging on paper.

The worst example is Mommsen’s portrayal of Julius Caesar.

Here <…>, not Caesar, but an example in vers<…> secures all his wish-dreams:

the symbol of nerve and spirit,

mens sana in corpore sano—

a healthy mind in a healthy body—

<…>.

The other possibility is the contemplative one:

the Christian Epimetheus.

He does not want to think the already-thought all over again.

You cannot walk through the same river twice.

You cannot think the same thought twice.

The second time, it will be either more correct or more false.

Anyone who does not know that cannot really think at all.

Above all, he cannot reflect.

To reflect means to think differently.

But then the thought is no longer “genuine.”

This dreadful obsession with authenticity among historians, art historians, and legal historians!

Everything withers miserably under their sterility.

They want to think everything again:

how everything was;

how it happened;

how it came about that it happened.

Everything all over again, and this time more correctly.

That is not merely a ridiculous claim.

It is an impertinent one.

To claim that one has found an “authentic” image of the Middle Ages on the basis of extremist art-historical categories <?>—

what inwardly falsified authenticity!

The authenticity and purity of these zealots.

What does this whole myth of the Worker actually mean?

The technologization of soldiers.

The <…> of the Saint-Simonian, Comtean, Spencerian antithesis:

the opposition between the military and industry.

Democratized industry?

The activated Promethean.

The bride earns herself more with one kiss for God than all the half-breeds do through labor unto death.

But according to Ernst Jünger’s The Worker, even a kiss is “work”!!!

[On the right:]

The whole mythology of the Worker comes from this.

So at its core all this Promethean noise surrounds a nothing:

everything is supposed to become <…>, and tomorrow my graves <?>, when we create the world.

Yes indeed, Professor.

We’ll take care of that.

Then the great Gustav Klemm:

Here matters become clearer.

Either protection among active and passive races, <…>.

Everything else follows automatically once the framework of the inherited Christian churches falls away and the restraints people still feel come to an end.

[Folio 79v]

Amnesty.

An ordinary clause of peace treaties <…>.

Fauchille § 1700.

Art. A.[mnestie] <…>.

Verdross.

Strupp, Wörterbuch des Völkerrechts, I, p. 38.

<…>

oubli général—

general forgetting.

W. E. Hall, International Law, 8th ed., edited by Pearce Higgins, Oxford 1924, p. 677:

“oblivion.”

Grotius III, 10, §§ 3–4.

Gudelin:

in amnestia consistit substantia pacis et absque illa nequit esse pax.

The substance of peace consists in amnesty, and without amnesty there can be no peace.

Rogge, <…>, Nationale Friedenspolitik, 1934, p. 55.

<…>

Charte Constitutionnelle, 4 June 1814, art. 11:

Toutes recherches des opinions et votes émis jusqu’à la restauration sont interdites. Le même oubli est commandé aux tribunaux et aux citoyens.

All investigations into opinions expressed and votes cast before the Restoration are forbidden.

The same forgetting is commanded of the courts and the citizens.

<…>

Asylum:

Ferdinand von Martitz, Internationale Rechtshilfe in Strafsachen, II, Leipzig 1897.

Article 120 of the Jacobin Constitution of 1793:

The French Republic <?> grants asylum to all foreigners driven from their homeland because of liberty, and refuses it to tyrants.

Compare Juristische Wochenschrift, 1933, p. 1639, on political crimes.

“Exchange forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet,” says the dying Laertes.

<…>

V.2.

Amnesty.

Every peace treaty contains an amnesty.

After a peace treaty, war <?> crimes can no longer be punished.

Lauterpacht explicitly says so in International Law, 6th ed. (1940), p. 476:

“All amnesty is implied in every peace treaty.”

<…>

Versailles.

O my poor soul.

Commentary

28 August 1947

Noble simplicity — J. J. Winckelmann’s highly influential definition of classical art.

trahison des clercs — Julien Benda, La trahison des clercs, Paris 1927; German: Der Verrat der Intellektuellen, Munich 1978.

King Peter — Schmitt is presumably referring to Peter II Karađorđević (1923–1970), King of Yugoslavia from 1934. In November 1945 the Communists forced him to give up the throne.

God transforms the lie — Allusion to Romans 1:22 ff.

Enrico Corradini — Italian nationalist writer and journalist (1865–1931); became a minister in 1928.

Sallust contra pecuniam — In his Bellum Iugurthinum (The Jugurthine War), Sallust describes how King Jugurtha was able to bribe the Roman nobility with money.

bellum externum … — Quattuor principes ferro interempti: trina bella civilia, plura externa ac plerumque permixta.

“Four emperors were killed by the sword. There were three civil wars, more foreign wars, and most of them were mixed together.”

Tacitus, Histories I.2. Tacitus is speaking here about the bloody Year of the Four Emperors, AD 69, which was disastrous for Rome.

Otto Brunner — Otto Brunner, Land und Herrschaft, 1973. The first quotation (lines 5–7) is on p. 145; the second (“that the problem of sovereignty …”) is on p. 144, n. 1; and the third (“As long as …”) is also on p. 144. Schmitt’s quotation, however, includes the second word aber (“but”), which is missing here.

Ganahl — Karl-Hans Ganahl (1905–1942), Austrian legal historian.

Willy Haas — Willy Haas, “Eine neue politische Lehre,” in Die literarische Welt (Berlin), vol. 8, no. 12, 20 May 1932, pp. 1–2.

The habilitation thesis by the SS man Lemmel — Herbert Lemmel, Die Volksgemeinschaft, ihre Erfassung im werdenden Recht, Stuttgart/Berlin 1941. Berlin habilitation in law and political science, dated 14 July 1939. Submitted under the title Die Erfassung der Gemeinschaft im lebensgesetzlichen Recht. Reinhard Höhn was the first examiner and Carl Schmitt the second.

See Carl Schmitt, report on the habilitation thesis of Dr. jur. Herbert Lemmel, RW 265 no. 19074; Christian Tilitzki, “Carl Schmitt – Staatsrechtler in Berlin. Einblicke in seinen Wirkungskreis anhand der Fakultätsakten 1934–1944,” in Etappe 7, 1991, pp. 62–117, especially pp. 65–66 and 72–74.

In his habilitation thesis, Lemmel criticized Schmitt’s concepts because they had no connection with “race” or with the “blood-structure of the people.”

The SS officer Lemmel (1911–1990), after returning from Soviet captivity, became a commercial judge in Frankfurt am Main in 1950, and later a businessman and factory owner in Bad Homburg.

Schmitt’s papers contain seven letters and two postcards from Lemmel dating from 1948 to 1978 (RW 0265 nos. 8724–8732), in which Lemmel unsuccessfully tried to establish a closer relationship with Schmitt.

28 August 1947

as Ortega told me — Schmitt spoke with the Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset (1885–1955) in Lisbon on 20 May 1944. See Christian Tilitzki, “Die Vortragsreisen Carl Schmitts während des Zweiten Weltkriegs,” in Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 249.

Tacitus — Quotations from Tacitus, Histories:

I.1: magna [illa] ingenia cessere — “Those great minds have disappeared.”

I.2: opus adgredior optimum casibus, atrox proeliis, discors seditionibus, ipsa etiam pace saevum — “I approach a work rich in reversals of fortune, savage in battle, divided by sedition, terrible even in peace.”

29 August 1947

nefasque mixtum — Conquerar, an moneam mixtum fas omne nefasque?

“Should I lament, or should I warn that good and evil have become completely mixed together?”

Ovid, Ars amatoria, Book I, 739–740.

Barion essay — Hans Barion, “Der Rechtsbegriff Rudolph Sohms. Zur 100. Wiederkehr von Sohms Geburtstag,” in Deutsche Rechtswissenschaft 7, 1942, pp. 47–51; reprinted in H. Barion, Kirche und Kirchenrecht. Gesammelte Aufsätze, ed. Werner Böckenförde, Paderborn 1984, pp. 115–119.

plenitudo potestatis … — “Immediate absolute power over everyone and over each individual.” This was the formula used from the High Middle Ages onward for the pope’s claim to power. Compare Dictatorship, pp. 42–43.

a Deo excitatus — In Protestant historical writing, Luther was said to have begun his Reformation a Deo excitatus: “called forth by God.”

31 August 1947

Berlin lecture — James T. Shotwell (1864–1965), American historian and politician, and a leading promoter of the Kellogg Pact.

The lecture was “Stehen wir an einem Wendepunkt der Weltgeschichte?” (“Are We at a Turning Point in World History?”), given on 1 March 1927 at the German Academy of Politics in Berlin as part of the newly established Carnegie chair. In it, Shotwell called for the renunciation of war.

Published in Henri Lichtenberger / James Shotwell / Max Scheler, Ausgleich als Schicksal und Aufgabe, Berlin 1929, pp. 15–28.

Jäckh — Ernst Jaeckh (1875–1959), journalist, founder and lecturer at the German Academy of Politics; emigrated in 1933.

2 September 1947

M. J. Bonn — Moritz Julius Bonn (1873–1965), political economist. In 1919, as director of the Munich School of Commerce, he secured a lectureship there for Carl Schmitt; in 1928 he brought Schmitt to the Berlin School of Commerce.

In his memoirs Bonn wrote very negatively about Schmitt. See M. J. Bonn, So macht man Geschichte. Bilanz eines Lebens, Munich 1953, pp. 330–332, with a note in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 25938.

Spiritus malignus, magnus deceptor — “The evil spirit, the great deceiver.” In Cartesian philosophy, our ability to know is threatened if we mistake what is false for what is true.

Castor-Pollux offer — Refers to the poem “An Levin Schücking” by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, final stanza:

Pollux and Castor—alternating glow and pallor, The light of one taken only from the other, And yet the sign of the most faithful loyalty. So give me your hand, my Dioscurus! And may the lovely myth renew itself, Where the twin flame burned above the helmet.

Tout ce qui arrive est adorable — “Everything that happens is worthy of adoration.”

Léon Bloy used the sentence repeatedly, for example in letters to Julien Leclercq dated 31 July 1894 and to Heinrich de Groux dated 8 June 1895, published in L. Bloy, Le mendiant ingrat.

The sentence confirmed Schmitt’s view of history, which had been shaped by Konrad Weiß. Schmitt also liked to quote it as a way of expressing his dislike of unreal “if only” statements about things that had already happened.

3 September 1947

Gerhard Günther — (1889–1976), conservative journalist, brother of Albrecht Erich Günther.

The Leviathan has spat me out three times — Namely in 1936, when Schmitt survived an attack by the SS; in 1946, when he was released from the American camp at Berlin-Lichterfelde; and in 1947, when he was released from detention as a witness at Nuremberg.

Quiesco, exsul in patria mea … — “I remain quiet, an exile in my own country.”

The phrase ex[s]ul in patria mea appears often in these years. See the entries for 4 June 1948, 16 September 1949, and 25 November 1949; BW Forsthoff, p. 52; BW Mohler, p. 67; FoP, p. 590.

Its importance to Schmitt’s understanding of himself is clear from the fact that he placed it at the head of Book III of the Glossarium. See the appendix.

Bernanos — Georges Bernanos (1888–1948), French Catholic writer. He was discussed as a possible French ambassador to Rome, but was never appointed. On the speech, see the entry for 13 March 1949.

4 September 1947

Castruccio Castracani — (1281–1328), Italian mercenary commander.

Machiavelli writes of him:

As he was walking through a street, he saw a young man coming out of a prostitute’s house. The young man blushed deeply when he realized Castruccio had seen him.

Castruccio said:

“Do not be ashamed when you come out. Be ashamed when you go in.”

Niccolò Machiavelli, Das Leben des Castruccio Castracani von Lucca, German-Italian edition, Cologne/Vienna 1969, p. 81.

“Let us make man” — Genesis 1:26.

5 September 1947

“creeping softly” — From Annette von Droste-Hülshoff’s Geistliches Jahr. In the poem “Am zehnten Sonntag nach Pfingsten”:

And let me only look upon A feather, trembling secretly, Remembering that behind its black trace Death and life creep softly.

7 September 1947

Pinder — Wilhelm Pinder (1878–1947), art historian; professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin from 1935 to 1945.

Fumet — As part of the twenty-volume collected edition of L. Bloy, Stanislas Fumet edited Léon Bloy, Le mendiant ingrat, Paris 1948.

When Schmitt writes “likewise the new edition 1928,” he apparently means this edition.

Claudel — Paul Claudel, Introduction au “Livre de Ruth.” Texte intégral de l’ouvrage de l’Abbé de Moidrey, Paris 1938, pp. 109–110.

Cor Jesu, saturatum opprobriis — “Heart of Jesus, filled with reproaches,” from the Catholic Litany of the Sacred Heart.

9 September 1947

Hauriou — Maurice Hauriou (1856–1929), French jurist.

already in Bodin — Jean Bodin, Les six livres de la république. Rev. corrigée & augm. de nouveau, Paris 1580 (RW 265 no. 22687).

10 September 1947

Bellarmin — Roberto Bellarmino (1542–1621), Jesuit controversial theologian and important cardinal. He developed the doctrine of the Church’s potestas indirecta, its indirect power.

His Autobiografia, written in 1613, was not published until 1751 in Ferrara.

relatiuncula, scriptiuncula, breviculum, notila — Dismissive Latin terms for a “work” or piece of writing: roughly, “little report,” “little writing,” “little brief,” “little note.”

13 September 1947

aquae [correctly: aqua] et igni interdictus — “Someone denied water and fire,” meaning denied hospitality. A Roman formula of outlawry.

There is no evidence at all that Schmitt was unwelcome in Dr Schranz’s house in Siedlinghausen in 1947. It is possible, however, that some of the other guests treated him with reserve.

18 September 1947

Visit from Paul Adams — Paul Adams (1894–1961), editor of the cultural supplement of the Centre Party newspaper Germania. From 1934 he worked in radio in Munich and belonged to the Siedlinghausen circle. Schmitt regarded him as one of his closest friends. See p. 125.

Knappe — Karl Knappe (1884–1978), sculptor and stained-glass artist in Munich, and a friend of Konrad Weiß.

Rikus — Josef Rikus (1923–1989), sculptor. In January 1946 he moved to Siedlinghausen to work with the sculptor Eugen Senge-Platten (1890–1972). From 1947 he continued his training under Karl Knappe.

Möllenbrock — Klemens Möllenbrock, Die religiöse Lyrik der Droste und die Theologie der Zeit. Versuch einer theologischen Gesamtinterpretation und theologiegeschichtlichen Einordnung des “Geistlichen Jahres”, Berlin 1935; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Münster 1934.

Westemeyer — Dietmar Westemeyer, Donoso Cortés. Staatsmann und Theologe. Eine Untersuchung seines Einsatzes der Theologie in die Politik, Münster 1940; Spanish translation published in 1957.

Joseph Westemeyer (1908–1997) took the religious name Dietmar when he entered the Franciscan order.

The published book was based on his 1940 Catholic-theology dissertation at Münster.

Veit — Otto Veit, Die Flucht vor der Freiheit. Versuch zur geschichtsphilosophischen Erhellung der Kulturkrise, Frankfurt am Main 1947.

Memories of Walther Rathenau — On Schmitt’s relationship with Rathenau, see his account in Schattenrisse, as well as Tb 1912–15, pp. 333–335, and Tb 1921–24, pp. 103–107, 116–119.

Goethe, “We live …” — Probably Schmitt’s paraphrase of Goethe’s maxim:

“We all live from the past, and we perish from the past.”

Goethe, Maximen und Reflexionen, 167.

paradisiacal little chambers — A phrase used by the Catholic pastoral theologian Johann Michael Sailer (1751–1832), which Schmitt may have known through Eschweiler.

See Karl Eschweiler, Die katholische Theologie im Zeitalter des deutschen Idealismus. Die Bonner theologischen Qualifikationsschriften von 1921/22. Aus dem Nachlaß hrsg. und mit einer Einl. vers. von Thomas Marschler, Münster 2010, p. 163.

20 September 1947

Coclicus — Adrien Petit Coclico (1499/1500–after September 1562), composer and music theorist.

Huber’s dissertation — Kurt Huber (1893–1943), musicologist and member of the White Rose resistance group.

Kurt Huber, Ivo de Vento (ca. 1540–1575), Lindenberg im Allgäu 1918; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Munich 1918.

in my essay on the taboo — Not identified.

Kalijarvi — Thorsten V. Kalijarvi, “Die Neutralität Amerikas,” in Europäische Revue 11, 1935, p. 721.

Kalijarvi (1897–1980) was professor of political science at the University of New Hampshire in the United States.

21 September 1947

Lewis — Wyndham Lewis, The Enemy. A Review of Art and Literature, London 1927 ff.; idem, Hitler und sein Werk in englischer Beleuchtung, Berlin 1932; idem, Time and Western Man, London 1927.

In the second edition of Die geistesgeschichtliche Lage des heutigen Parlamentarismus, Schmitt had already referred in 1926 to Wyndham Lewis, The Art of Being Ruled, London 1926: GL, p. 11, n. 1.

The text here is in shorthand. It probably reads:

“did not arouse the hostility that I aroused.”

Essay by Hennecke — Hans Hennecke, “Wyndham Lewis. Vision und Satire,” in Europäische Revue 14, 1938, pp. 205–214.

Rosenbaum — Eduard Rosenbaum (1887–1979), Schmitt’s fellow student and friend from Strasbourg. See Tb 1912–15, pp. 404–405.

On 25 November 1950 he wrote against Schmitt in the Rheinischer Merkur under the title “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.”

It is unclear whether he had already expressed criticism of Schmitt in 1947.

“I do not know that I did well, but I did honestly” (Grey) — The British Foreign Secretary Edward Grey (1862–1933) wrote this sentence to his wife in 1906.

See Viscount Grey of Fallodon, Twenty Five Years, vol. 1, Toronto 1923, p. 79.

Film — Schmitt’s attitude toward film here was completely different from his attitude in the 1920s and 1930s. Compare his diaries.

22 September 1947

“All I inherited was my own body …” — Richard Wagner, Götterdämmerung, Act I, Scene 2.

23 September 1947

Podszus — Friedrich Podszus (1899–1971), literary scholar and editor, and co-editor of the two-volume Benjamin edition of 1955.

See Helmut Peitsch, “Wolf von Niebelschütz, Walter Benjamin und ihre Leser im ‘Dritten Reich’. Zur Erinnerung an Friedrich Podszus,” in LiLi. Zeitschrift für Literaturwissenschaft und Linguistik 16, 1986, pp. 170–178.

Binaris numerus infamis — “Two is an evil number.” Meister Eckhart.

See Wouter Goris, Einheit als Prinzip und Ziel. Versuch über die Einheitsmetaphysik des Opus tripartitum Meister Eckharts, Leiden/New York/Cologne 1997, pp. 106 ff.

25 September 1947

Drucker, “For Jews always remain Jews …” — Peter F. Drucker (1909–2005), Austrian economist. He emigrated to England in 1933 and became a US citizen in 1943. He later became an influential writer and teacher on management.
