Schmitt, who had been his friend, dedicated Ex Captivitate Salus to him in 1950 and also contributed to the 1951 memorial volume for Ahlmann.

In Hermann Kasack’s novel Die Stadt hinter dem Strom (1947), Ahlmann appears as the “Lübeck merchant Dr. Hahn.” Kasack also contributed an essay under that title to the memorial volume.

See Tymbos für Wilhelm Ahlmann, Berlin 1951, pp. 127–134 for Kasack and pp. 244–251 for Schmitt. Schmitt’s copy, containing annotations, inserted material, and pasted-in newspaper clippings, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 28355.

Pascual Jordan — (1902–1980), theoretical physicist. Three letters survive in Schmitt’s papers.

2 April 1948

δός μοι ποῦ στῶ — Δός μοι ποῦ στῶ καὶ τὴν γῆν κινήσω: “Give me a fixed point outside the earth, and I will move the earth.”

A saying attributed to Archimedes, used to illustrate his law of the lever.

Stare decisis — “Stand by earlier decisions.” A principle of Anglo-American case law.

Heinrich Weinstock — (1889–1960), philosopher and educator.

my lecture of February 1941 — “Staatliche Souveränität und freies Meer.” Most recently published with an extensive commentary by G. Maschke in SGN, pp. 401–430.

Introduction to Thucydides — Schmitt owned the following edition: Thucydides, Der große Krieg, translated and introduced by Heinrich Weinstock, Kröner pocket edition 150, Stuttgart 1938.

3 April 1948

“annihilated in nothing” — “Defenseless, but in no way destroyed.”

From the opening poem titled “1933” in Konrad Weiß, Der christliche Epimetheus, Berlin 1933.

Dominus litis — “Master of the proceedings,” a legal term.

A Nation can only be condemned out of her own mouth — A reference to the English documentation of German war crimes during the First World War: H. W. Wilson, Convicted out of her own mouth. The record of German crimes, London 1917. German edition: Durch das Zeugnis des eigenen Mundes überführt, no place or date, c. 1918.

Schmitt probably became familiar with the book, in effect as part of his professional duties, while working for the Bavarian military command.

5 April 1948

pèlerin de l’Absolu — Le Pèlerin de l’Absolu (“The Pilgrim of the Absolute”), the title of a volume of diaries by Léon Bloy.

6 April 1948

CIC — Civil Internment Camp, the Allied camps established from 1945 onward for suspected or potential war criminals.

7 April 1948

Günther Krauss’s diary, Captivitas — Unpublished.

“Hic jacet” is the finishing part of his [correctly: their] history — Daniel Defoe, The Instability of Human Glory.

The ashes will not rest; they scatter through every land — After Jan Hus was burned as a heretic at Constance in 1415 and his ashes were thrown into the Rhine, a song arose among his followers. It begins:

The ashes will not settle down, They scatter through every land; No stream or pit or grave can help— They bring the enemy to shame!

Schmitt quotes this song in a letter to Jünger in connection with a funeral ceremony in Rome at which ashes were thrown into the Tiber.

See BW EJ, pp. 394 f.

8 April 1948

my περίψημα-existence — See the note above to p. 23.

my work of 1932 — LuL.

9 April 1948

Arnold Toynbee (Int. Affairs, Nov. 47) — Arnold Toynbee (1889–1975), British historian and theorist of civilization. Schmitt is referring to Toynbee’s article in The International Outlook, Vol. 23, No. 4, October 1947, pp. 463–476.

10 April 1948

Claudel discovers … — Paul Claudel, “Quelques réflexions sur l’Allemagne,” in A présent, 19 March 1948.

Biographical introduction — To: Thomas Hobbes, The Moral and Political Works Of Thomas Hobbes Of Malmesbury. Never before collected together. To which is prefixed, The Author’s Life, Extracted From That said to be written by Himself, As Also From The Supplement to the said Life by Dr. Blackbourne [Richard Blackburne]; and farther illustrated by the Editor, with Historical and Critical Remarks on his Writings and Opinions, London 1750.

Schmitt owned this edition, RW 265 No. 24285.

11 April 1948

Blötz — Ferdinand Blötz (1901–1967), Hamburg jurist, later a senior judge at the Regional Court there.

Eugen Ott — (1889–1977), general and diplomat. As an adviser to the Schleicher government in 1932–33 he worked closely with Schmitt. In 1933 he first became military attaché; from 1938 he served as ambassador to Japan. In 1942, in connection with the affair surrounding the spy Richard Sorge, he was recalled from his ambassadorial post and withdrew to Beijing. From 1951 onward he lived in retirement in Tutzing.

Spiegel on Sorge — A multi-part series on the spy Richard Sorge in Der Spiegel, 1951, issues 24–40.

13 April 1948

To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 222 f.

15 April 1948

Sohm II — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Rudolf Sohm, Kirchenrecht (= Systematisches Handbuch der deutschen Rechtswissenschaft, ed. Karl Binding, Vol. 8), anastatic reprint, Munich/Leipzig 1923.

Vol. 1: Die geschichtlichen Grundlagen. Vol. 2: Katholisches Kirchenrecht.

Copies survive in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 Nos. 25085 and 25336.

17 April 1948

Conde — Francisco Javier Conde (1908–1974), Spanish political scientist who moved politically from socialism to Francoism. Conde studied under both Hermann Heller and Carl Schmitt and translated Schmitt’s The Concept of the Political and Leviathan.

Schmitt is probably referring to their meeting in Madrid in 1943, where Conde had been a professor since 1942.

Conde died while serving as Spanish ambassador in Bonn.

20 April 1948

Naturales deos colere cupis, civiles cogeris — “You wish to worship the gods of nature, but you are compelled to worship the gods of the state.”

Augustine, De civitate Dei, Book 6, ch. 6. Translation based on the German edition: Augustine, Vom Gottesstaat, translated from the Latin by Wilhelm Thimme, Vol. 1, Munich 1977, p. 295.

your essay — Helmut Rumpf, “Deutschlands Anschluß. Voraussetzungen für die Einigung,” in Volk und Zeit. Monatszeitschrift für Demokratie und Sozialismus 3, 1948, pp. 58–60.

what E. Troeltsch said about it —

“The Christian theory of natural law is, as a scientific theory, wretched and confused. Within it, the pure natural law of humanity’s original state constantly collides with the completely opposite relative natural law of the fallen state; with positive law, which often includes the worst atrocities; and with a supreme theocratic authority which, despite everything, claims that true goodness can only be communicated through itself. But as a practical doctrine it is of the highest importance in cultural and social history …”

Ernst Troeltsch, Die Soziallehren der christlichen Kirchen und Gruppen, third reprint of the Tübingen 1922 edition, Aalen 1977, p. 173.

Schmitt is referring to the first edition, Tübingen 1912. His annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22087.

Léon Bloy answers this way —

“Someone pointed out to me that the highest point of the Redeemer’s suffering, after the Agony in the Garden, must have been not the spitting, not the blows, not the scourging, not the crowning with thorns, not the carrying of the Cross, not even the Crucifixion, but simply appearing before a judge.”

Léon Bloy, Méditations d’un solitaire en 1916, 5th ed., Paris, c. 1920, p. 105.

21 April 1948

“Pope Aenea Sylvio …” — This is not Aenea Sylvio Piccolomini, Pope Pius II, but his successor Pietro Barbo, who reigned as Pope Paul II from 1464 to 1471.

See Franz Xaver Seppelt, Das Papsttum im Spätmittelalter und in der Zeit der Renaissance (Geschichte des Papsttums IV), Leipzig 1941, p. 345.

Hefele — Karl Joseph Hefele, Conciliengeschichte. Nach den Quellen bearbeitet, continued by J. Hergenröther, 2nd improved ed., Vol. 1, Freiburg im Breisgau 1873.

22 April 1948

Otto Veit — (1898–1984), ordoliberal economist, banker, and professor of economics and public affairs at the University of Frankfurt am Main.

Hauriou — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Maurice Hauriou, Principes de droit public. A l’usage des étudiants en licence et en doctorat ès-sciences politiques, 2nd ed., Paris 1916. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 27583.

with the Three Types and the Leviathan blurb — Carl Schmitt, Über die drei Arten des rechtswissenschaftlichen Denkens (On the Three Types of Juristic Thought), Publications of the Academy for German Law, Hamburg 1934.

The typed publicity sheet or blurb for Schmitt’s 1938 Leviathan book was circulated by Schmitt among various acquaintances after 1945 and has been reprinted several times, for example in Leviathan, pp. 243 f.

Whether it was actually written in 1938 is unclear.

23 April 1948

an ambitious student of Thoma — Karl Schultes (1909–1982), Der Niedergang des staatsrechtlichen Denkens im Faschismus. Die Lehren des Herrn Prof. Carl Schmitt, Kronjurist der Gegenrevolution (Bausteine unseres neuen Weltbildes, 2), Weimar 1947.

Schmitt’s copy, containing annotations, inserted material, and pasted-in newspaper clippings, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 28043.

Radbruch, Röpke, Böhm — Schmitt wrote to Radbruch on 13 September 1928:

“My engagement with you will proceed very slowly, because this is not a matter of cheap debate but of differences in our very modes of being.”

Quoted in FoP, p. 952.

Schmitt later liked to sum up this difference—for example in his letters to Mohler—with the mocking phrase Homo homini Radbruch: “Man is a Radbruch to man.”

Material concerning Radbruch also survives in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 No. 21288.

Wilhelm Röpke (1899–1966), neoliberal economist, held Schmitt—and Smend—responsible for the collapse of the Weimar Constitution in his book Die deutsche Frage, 2nd ed., Zurich 1945, pp. 77 f.

Franz Böhm (1895–1977), jurist, economist, and politician, said at a Pestalozzi memorial event in 1946 that Pestalozzi’s attitude was completely different

“from that of almost every modern thinker of the state, beginning with Machiavelli and ending with the German constitutional lawyer Carl Schmitt and his power-worshipping disciples.”

Karl Geiler/Franz Böhm, Pestalozzi als Erzieher und Staatsdenker, p. 22.

See also the note below to p. 311.

24 April 1948

Justus Koch — (1891–1962), lawyer and defense counsel in the Wilhelmstrasse Trial.

my memorandum from the summer of 1945 — Angriffskrieg (War of Aggression).

Dix — Rudolf Dix (1884–1952), criminal-defense lawyer. At Nuremberg he represented Hjalmar Schacht and Friedrich Flick. Schmitt had written the legal opinion mentioned above for Flick.

See Quaritsch’s afterword there: Angriffskrieg, p. 142.

27 April 1948

Sciendum vero est … — “It must be understood that Satan’s will is always evil, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself, whereas his power comes from God.”

Gregory the Great, Moralia in Iob, Book 2, ch. X, on verse 17.

Burckhardt’s opposite thesis — “And now power is evil in itself.”

Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, Kröner pocket edition 55, Stuttgart 1978, p. 97.

What Peterson says about clothing — Erik Peterson, “Theologie des Kleides,” in Benediktinische Monatsschrift 16, 1934, pp. 347–356. Also in Peterson, Ausgewählte Schriften, Vol. 2, Würzburg 1995.

Kempski — Jürgen von Kempski (1910–1998), philosopher. He studied under Carl Schmitt in the 1930s and repeatedly worked on Bruno Bauer.

Schmitt is probably referring to J. von Kempski, “Das kommunistische Palimpsest,” in Merkur, No. 7, 1948, pp. 53–68, where Kempski stresses Bruno Bauer’s decisive importance for Marx.

according to Barnikol — Ernst Barnikol (1892–1968), theologian. Schmitt is referring to E. Barnikol, Das entdeckte Christentum im Vormärz. Bruno Bauers Kampf gegen Religion u. Christentum u. Erstausg. seiner Kampfschrift, Jena 1927. Schmitt’s copy, with inserted material, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25529.

See also Barnikol, “Bruno Bauers Kampf gegen Religion und Christentum und die Spaltung der vormärzlichen preußischen Opposition,” in Zeitschrift für Kirchengeschichte 46, New Series 9, 1928, pp. 1–34.

Günther Krauss’s Captiva captivitas — See above, note to p. 93.

28 April 1948

Maurice de Gandillac — (1906–2006), French philosopher, editor, and translator of the works of Nicholas of Cusa.

Schmitt owned Maurice de Gandillac, Nikolaus von Cues. Studien zu seiner Philosophie und philosophischen Weltanschauung, Düsseldorf 1953. Here, however, he is probably referring to the French edition first published in 1941.

Mittite me in mare … — Vulgate, Jonah 1:12.

In Luther’s translation:

“He said to them: Take me and throw me into the sea, and the sea will become calm for you. For I know that this great storm has come upon you because of me.”

a saying of Hegel — The quotation from Hegel’s Lectures on the History of Philosophy can be found in Nomos, p. 299.

30 April 1948

Found the motto in E. Jünger — Ernst Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 9, Stuttgart 1979, p. 115.

my remark to Smend —

“The year 1948 will give rise to many backward looks and renewed connections. The soil of German idealism seems to have contained something potent, and the rubble left behind by the skeptical break with it now seems to be turning into a field of ambiguous, rumbling beginnings of new theogonies.”

Schmitt to Rudolf Smend, 6 January 1948, in BW Smend, p. 121.

E. Rothacker — The philosopher Erich Rothacker (1888–1965) had known Schmitt since becoming a professor in Bonn in 1928. Their acquaintance probably deepened through Rothacker’s membership in the Academy for German Law and his role as a co-founder of the Committee for Philosophy of Law in 1934.

The handwritten draft of Schmitt’s letter to Rothacker survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 13429. The original is held by the Bonn University and State Library, Department of Manuscripts and Rare Books, Rothacker Papers.

Hans Barion wrote to Schmitt on 4 February 1948:

“Rothacker … spoke of you with great affection.”

RW 265 No. 701.

conversation with Fr. Meinecke — Friedrich Meinecke had tried in 1922 to bring Carl Schmitt to the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik. See Tb 1921–24, p. 39. The attempt failed.

Nebel’s reflections on the elements — Gerhard Nebel, Von den Elementen, Wuppertal 1947. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22280.

the little book Land and Sea — Carl Schmitt, Land und Meer. Eine weltgeschichtliche Betrachtung, Leipzig 1942.

1 May 1948

Froude’s biography — James Anthony Froude, Lord Beaconsfield, Freeport 1971, reprint of the London 1890 edition.

The quotation containing the phrase “social sorcery,” which Schmitt repeated several times, does not actually come from the letter mentioned here, but from B. Disraeli, Tancred or the New Crusade, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1847, p. 252.

To Frau von Schnitzler — See Schmittiana, New Series I, 2011, pp. 182 f.

an overwhelming sentence from Saint-Martin — In the original:

“Pour prouver qu’on est régénéré, il faut régénérer tout ce qui est autour de nous.”

“To prove that one has been regenerated, one must regenerate everything around us.”

L. C. de Saint-Martin, Oeuvres Posthumes, Vol. 1, Tours 1807, p. 102.

See also Karl Epting, “Die politische Theologie Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin’s,” in Epirrhosis. Festgabe für Carl Schmitt, ed. Hans Barion et al., 2nd ed., Berlin 2002, pp. 161–184.

the speech written by Sallust — When the Roman Senate was debating what to do with the arrested Catilinarian conspirators, Caesar, in the speech recorded by Sallust, urged the senators to free themselves “from hatred and affection, anger and pity.”

“When a man exerts his rational judgment, it can achieve something; but when passion takes possession of him, passion rules, and reason is powerless.”

Gaius Sallustius Crispus, Die Verschwörung des Catilina, Latin and German, translated and annotated by Josef Lindauer, Reinbek 1964, pp. 64 ff.

lex Porcia — In his speech, Caesar cites the Porcian law, which forbade Roman officials to flog or execute a Roman citizen while ignoring his right to appeal to the popular assembly.

Ibid., p. 66.

ne plus valeat apud vos illorum scelus … — In the original:

… ne plus apud vos valeat P. Lentuli et ceterorum scelus quam vostra dignitas, neu magis irae vostrae quam famae consulatis.

“… so that the crime of Publius Lentulus and the others does not carry more weight with you than your own dignity, and so that you do not pay more attention to your anger than to your good name.”

Ibid., pp. 64–65.

Don Capisco’s Pocket Oracle — Schmitt seems first to have used the name “Don Capisco” for himself in 1943.

On 24 January 1943, Ernst Jünger recorded a conversation with Carl Schmitt in which he “admired, or perhaps doubted, his expertise.”

Schmitt replied:

“Don’t you know that I am Don Capisco?”

E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, Vol. 2, p. 487.

The manuscript originally contained the word “Gracián’s,” which was crossed out and replaced with “Don Capisco.” This indicates that Schmitt was placing himself in the tradition of the Spanish neo-Stoic writer Baltasar Gracián, who published his maxims under the title Handorakel und die Kunst der Weltklugheit—The Pocket Oracle and Art of Worldly Wisdom.

In Gracián’s novel The Criticón, the rational and discerning figure of Critilo was probably Schmitt’s model for Don Capisco.

4 May 1948

to Scheffer — Paul Scheffer (1883–1963), journalist. On Schmitt’s long relationship with him, see Tb 1921–24, p. 71 and passim.

After leaving for the United States in 1937, Scheffer never returned to Germany.

Poor Jünger — Apparently refers to Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen, which Schmitt had received in manuscript from Gerhard Nebel, as well as Jünger’s plans for Heliopolis.

See BW EJ, pp. 226 f.

5 May 1948

Sent Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 226 f.

6 May 1948

Hamburg conference of German law professors — This means the meeting of the German Society for International Law, which had been dissolved in 1934 and re-established in 1947.

The 1948 meeting dealt with fundamental questions of international law, including the question of whether Germany had continued to exist as a subject of international law.

See Michael Stolleis, Geschichte des öffentlichen Rechts in Deutschland, Vol. 4, Munich 2012, pp. 76 ff.

Machiavelli says — Niccolò Machiavelli, Discorsi. Gedanken über Politik und Staatsführung, Kröner pocket edition 377, 3rd improved ed., Stuttgart 2007, p. 262.

Schmitt used the Testina edition of Tutte le opere from 1550, which is why the wording does not match.

7 May 1948

Theodor Haecker said in 1917 … — Haecker actually wrote this as early as 1915: Theodor Haecker, “Der Krieg und die Führer des Geistes,” in Brenner-Jahrbuch 1915, pp. 130–188, here p. 170.

Schmitt probably gives the year as 1917 because the text was republished in Haecker’s Satire und Polemik in 1922 with an afterword dated 1917.

Haecker’s essay was a fierce attack on the intellectuals who supported the First World War. It was so sharp that it became a subject of debate in the Reichstag, and Der Brenner was subsequently banned.

Among other people, Haecker attacked Theodor Wolff, editor-in-chief of the Berliner Tageblatt. Wolff had written of the “sincere grief” felt by educated Germans over the destruction of cathedrals during the war.

Haecker replied:

“The silent stones must surely groan for fire and conflagration. They must surely long to be destroyed. They must surely beg to be delivered from the touching and gawking of the educated Wolff and his companions.”

Carl Schmitt read these lines with great approval when they appeared. At the same time, however, as part of his service with the deputy general command in Munich, he was himself required to order the confiscation of anti-war literature.

Of Theodor Haecker, whom he also met personally during this period, Schmitt said:

“Haecker […] is one of my kind.”

Tb 1912–15, p. 74.

Schmitt later became more critical of Haecker. See below, pp. 131 f., entry for 2 July 1948.

8 May 1948

good old Hall — Schmitt is referring to William Edward Hall, A Treatise on International Law, 8th ed., ed. A. Pearce Higgins, Oxford 1924. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25814.

Strupp — Karl Strupp (1886–1940), scholar of international law.

Lauterpacht — Hersch Lauterpacht (1897–1960), scholar of international law.

something I noticed years ago while reading Westlake — John Westlake (1828–1913), British scholar of international law. Schmitt is probably referring to Nomos, pp. 203 and 210.

“impatience of justice” — See BW EJ, p. 232.

Ernest Nys — (1851–1920), Belgian scholar of international law.

Cardinal Mercier’s Christmas pastoral letter of 1914 — The Primate of Belgium was regarded, especially because of his pastoral letter Patriotisme et Endurance, as the intellectual leader of resistance to the occupation of his country.

See Désiré Mercier, Patriotisme et Endurance. Lettre pastorale de S. É. le Card. Mercier, Archevêque de Malines, The Hague 1914. German edition: Vaterlandsliebe und Ausdauer, Lausanne 1915.

Schmitt thought very highly of Cardinal Mercier. See RK, p. 11.

10 May 1948

L’initié tue l’initiateur — “The initiate kills the initiator.”

The sentence comes from the French writer and philosopher of history Pierre-Simon Ballanche (1776–1846).

See Ballanche, Oeuvres de M. Ballanche, Vol. 4, Paris/Geneva 1830, p. 487.

See also the note below to p. 309 and BW Sombart.

W. Fraenger’s Grand Master of the free brotherhood — See Wilhelm Fraenger, Hieronymus Bosch. Das Tausendjährige Reich. Grundzüge e. Auslegung, Coburg 1947.

Schmitt assisted Fraenger with his Bosch research during the war.

See Wilhelm Fraenger, “Korrespondenz mit Hans Arp, Carl Schmitt und Franz Roh,” in Sinn und Form 57, 2005, pp. 303–330.

15 May 1948

Mirko Jelusich — (1886–1969), National Socialist writer and author of popular historical novels.

the millennium of the new Ewe — In Stefan George’s private vocabulary, Ewe means “age” or “era.”

Hail to me that I see those who have been seized — From poem II, written at the outbreak of war in 1914, in Rainer Maria Rilke’s cycle Fünf Gesänge.

See R. M. Rilke, Werke. Kommentierte Ausgabe in vier Bänden, ed. Manfred Engel et al., Vol. 2, Frankfurt am Main 1996, p. 107.

“At last, a god!” — Rilke, ibid.

the “Stahl” affair — The constitutional lawyer Friedrich Julius Stahl (1802–1861), originally named Jolson, was a Jewish convert to Christianity who explicitly grounded his conservative legal and political theory in Christianity.

Schmitt attacked him sharply as “Stahl-Jolson.”

On Freisler, see the note above to p. 74.

16 May 1948

Barbey d’Aurevilly — Jules Amédée Barbey d’Aurevilly (1808–1889), French anti-modernist writer greatly admired by Schmitt.

17 May 1948

Hadamovsky — Eugen Hadamovsky (1904–1945), specialist in National Socialist propaganda.

His book Propaganda und nationale Macht. Die Organisation der öffentlichen Meinung für die nationale Politik, Oldenburg 1933, was extensively used by Hannah Arendt for the section “Totalitarian Propaganda” in her book The Burden of Our Time, London 1951—later published in German as Elemente und Ursprünge totaler Herrschaft.

Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22551.

On p. 352 Arendt writes:

“The advantages of a propaganda that constantly ‘adds the power of organization’ to the feeble and unreliable voice of argument …”

18 May 1948

Youth Without Goethe — Max Kommerell, Jugend ohne Goethe, Frankfurt am Main 1931.

In his own copy, Schmitt added the handwritten words “but with Hölderlin” to the title. The copy is privately owned.

Norbert von Hellingrath — (1888–1916), Germanist who discovered Hölderlin’s late hymns and published them in 1916.

23 May 1948

Hans Buchheim — (born 1922), political scientist.

meeting with Joachim Schoeps — Hans-Joachim Schoeps (1909–1980), conservative German-Jewish historian of religion.

In 1951 there was a brief exchange of letters between Schoeps and Schmitt.

See Frank-Lothar Kroll, Geschichtswissenschaft in politischer Absicht. Hans-Joachim Schoeps und Preußen, Berlin 2010, Appendix IV, pp. 92 f.

Cramer von Laue — Constantin Cramer von Laue (1906–1991), jurist. He studied under Schmitt during the 1930s and from 1951 onward worked for the Federal German government in a variety of roles.

Blüher’s debate about Israel — Hans Blüher/Hans-Joachim Schoeps, Streit um Israel. Ein jüdisch-christliches Gespräch, Hamburg 1933.

Gundolf — Friedrich Gundolf (1880–1931), Germanist and poet.

Rosenzweig — Franz Rosenzweig (1880–1929), philosopher.

read Kafka — See Schmitt to Mohler, 26 December 1953, BW Mohler, p. 147:

The German has no time just now, He has to Kafka read; He strains himself and stands prepared For Kafka to cure him instead.

24 May 1948

Gerhard Hess — (1907–1983), scholar of Romance languages. In 1938 he completed his habilitation at Berlin University with a study of Gassendi, discussed below, and then taught there as a lecturer.

In the early 1940s, while working for the Leibniz Commission of the Prussian Academy, Hess helped Schmitt verify quotations from Leibniz.

See F.-R. Hausmann in Romanistische Zeitschrift für Literaturgeschichte 23, 1999, p. 410.

After 1945 Hess became an influential figure in German academic administration, serving as president of the West German Rectors’ Conference and of the German Research Foundation.

edition of the Anti-Lucretius — Melchior de Polignac, Anti-Lucretius, sive de deo et natura, libri novem. Opus posthumum, Vols. 1–2, Paris 1754.

At Christmas 1968 Schmitt gave this edition to Rainer Specht with the dedication:

“with reference to Epirrhosis II, p. 699 ff.”

Shortly before this, R. Specht had published the essay “Über Polignacs ‘Antilucretius’” in the Schmitt Festschrift Epirrhosis, Berlin 1968, Vol. 2, pp. 697–707. The essay also discusses the physical phenomena mentioned here and Polignac’s relationship to Cartesianism.

Eripuit fulmen Jovi — “He wrested the thunderbolt from Jove.”

The idea ultimately goes back to Lucretius’s De rerum natura, which in turn refers to Epicurus. The phrase itself, however, probably first took this form in the Roman poet Marcus Manilius’s Astronomica, around 12 BC:

Eripuitque Jovi fulmen, viresque tonandi, Et sonitum ventis concessit, nubibus ignem.

“And he took from Jove the thunderbolt and the power to thunder, leaving sound to the winds and fire to the clouds.”

De Polignac quotes an altered version of the line in the first book of his Anti-Lucretius, where it refers to Epicurus:

Coeli tonitralia templa lacessens, Eripuit, fulmenque Jovi Phoeboque sagittas.

“Challenging the thundering temples of heaven, he took the thunderbolt from Jove and the arrows from Phoebus.”

During the eighteenth century the phrase became a familiar slogan of the Enlightenment, usually in altered form.

It appeared, for example, on the bust of Benjamin Franklin made by Houdon. Franklin, the inventor of the lightning rod, was celebrated there with a reference to In tyrannos—“against tyrants”—joining the conquest of lightning to a militant hostility toward traditional authority and religion.

Schmitt was suspicious of this celebration of humanism and Promethean reason.

See his letter to Ernst Jünger of 23 August 1955, BW EJ, pp. 284 and 723 f.

His skepticism reaches its clearest form at the end of Political Theology II, where eripuit fulmen Jovi is once again taken up critically.

See C. Schmitt, Politische Theologie II. Die Legende von der Erledigung jeder Politischen Theologie, Berlin 1970, p. 126.

your Gassendi — Gerhard Hess, Pierre Gassend. Der französische Späthumanismus und das Problem von Wissen und Glauben, Berliner Beiträge zur romanischen Philologie 9, 3/4, Jena/Leipzig 1939; also submitted as Hess’s habilitation thesis at Berlin University in 1938.

Schmitt owned a presentation copy inscribed to him by the author: RWN 260 No. 218.

Gassendo amatus surculus erroris — “The offshoot of error loved by Gassendi.”

This refers to lines 389 ff. of Polignac’s Anti-Lucretius:

… metuo, ne surculus ille Letiferi erroris, Gassendo nuper amatus Defensore novo speret se posse tueri.

“I fear that this branch of deadly error”—the atheism of Epicurus—“which Gassendi once loved, may hope to flourish again under this new defender”—Isaac Newton.

27 May 1948

Th. Däubler, At the Sea — From Th. Däubler, Der sternhelle Weg, Leipzig 1919, p. 64.

The water demon dies … — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Die Alexandrinische Phantasie (“Christmas Triptych”), p. 346.

29 May 1948

Mythology of the dwarf — See Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Der äthiopische Totentanz, pp. 160–168.

30 May 1948

Whom you do not abandon, Genius! — Quotation from Goethe, “Wanderers Sturmlied.”

Konrad Weiß with his poem “1933” — This does not mean the opening poem titled “1933” from Der christliche Epimetheus; see p. 149.

Here Schmitt means the poem “Justitia,” written in 1933 and dedicated to Carl Schmitt.

See Weiß, pp. 665 f.

deeply moved by the sentence from Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen — Correctly:

“The good boy. From childhood onward, his aim was to follow his father’s example. Now, on his very first attempt, he has done it better and surpassed him beyond measure.”

E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke 3, p. 360.

See also Martin Tielke, Der stille Bürgerkrieg, Berlin 2007.

31 May 1948

Gabba — Carlo Francesco Gabba (1835–1920), Italian jurist. See Nomos, p. 180.

whereas Hall — William Edward Hall (1835–1894), American scholar of international law.

Schmitt is referring to W. E. Hall, A Treatise on International Law, 8th ed., ed. A. Pearce Higgins, Oxford 1924. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25814.

See Nomos, p. 235.

1 June 1948

the feast of the Leviathan — See Leviathan, p. 18.

Köppelsbleek, the Schinderkuhle — Terms from Ernst Jünger’s story Auf den Marmorklippen (On the Marble Cliffs).

3 June 1948

Touching, Gerhard Ritter — Schmitt is referring to Gerhard Ritter, Machtstaat und Utopie. Vom Streit um die Dämonie der Macht seit Machiavelli und Morus, 3rd and 4th ed., Munich/Berlin 1943.

Schmitt’s copy, inscribed by the author, survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 24136.

4 June 1948

this Californian radio hero — Schmitt is targeting Thomas Mann and his broadcasts Deutsche Hörer! (“German Listeners!”), in which Mann regularly addressed the German people over the BBC from October 1940 to May 1945.

5 June 1948

the creature of the Word in Konrad Weiß — See Konrad Weiß, “Kreatur des Wortes,” in Der Ring 4, 1931, pp. 901–903.

Th. Haecker’s attack on my Concept of the Political — Haecker criticized Schmitt for speaking of the enemy but not of the friend.

See Theodor Haecker, Was ist der Mensch, Leipzig 1933, pp. 71 ff.

the weakling Maritain and his hate-filled Raïssa — Jacques Maritain (1882–1973), French Thomist philosopher, had been a friend of Schmitt during the 1920s.

Their friendship ended because of Schmitt’s involvement with National Socialism. Schmitt placed much of the blame for the break on Maritain’s Jewish wife, Raïssa.

On the relationship between Schmitt and Maritain, see Piet Tommissen, “Neue Bausteine zu einer wissenschaftlichen Biographie Carl Schmitts,” in Schmittiana V, 1996, pp. 210–213.

“Now you stand naked, naked as at birth, in barren expanses” — From Theodor Däubler’s poem “Perseus.” The original has “Now” in the sense of Nun rather than Jetzt.

See Theodor Däubler, Der sternhelle Weg, Leipzig 1919, p. 71.

6 June 1948

everything has already been accomplished, and you only answer — A passage frequently quoted by Schmitt after 1945, from Konrad Weiß’s poem “Klage über die Schöpfung.”

See Weiß, p. 408.

The stanza reads:

So the mind, the more it searches for itself, leads the soul from dark captivity into the world. Do what you must: it has always already been accomplished, and you only answer.

8 June 1948

Magnificent, Gueydan … — The quotations come from a manuscript by Gueydan titled Pensées d’un dékan. The manuscript is not preserved in Schmitt’s papers.

See below, p. 122, entry for 11 June 1948.

10 June 1948

reply concerning the state secretaries — Schmitt’s written answer to the question “Why did the state secretaries follow Hitler?”, which had been put to him by Robert Kempner, deputy chief prosecutor in the Nuremberg Wilhelmstrasse Trial.

It was first published under the title “Das Problem der Legalität” in Die neue Ordnung 5, 1950, pp. 270–275.

The planners rule — As early as 1933, in the essay “Machtpositionen des modernen Staates,” Schmitt had referred to Hans Freyer, Herrschaft und Planung. Zwei Grundbegriffe der politischen Ethik, Hamburg 1933.

The passage was later reprinted in Freyer, Herrschaft, Planung und Technik. Aufsätze zur politischen Soziologie, ed. Elfriede Üner, Weinheim 1987, p. 31:

“Where there is to be planning, there must be rule. It is not the planners who rule—that was the mistake of utopia. Rather, those who rule do the planning.”

Eduard Heimann — (1889–1967), social scientist. On the basis of his book Freedom and Order, New York 1947—German edition: Freiheit und Ordnung. Lehren aus dem Kriege, Berlin-Grunewald 1950—he gave lectures in several European countries during the spring and summer of 1948.

11 June 1948

Däubler’s two brother-sonnets — In his collection Attische Sonette, Theodor Däubler dedicated the poem “An Phaidros” to Rudolf Pannwitz and “Pegasus” to Carl Schmitt.

See Gedichte, pp. 4 f.

Iranian Rhapsody — A cycle of poems in Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, pp. 265–341.

Kelsen’s reasoning … — In Kelsen’s view, the German state ceased to exist with the surrender of 8 May 1945 because state authority was thereafter exercised by the condominium of the Allied victors.

According to this view, every institutional connection between any future German state and the “Third Reich” was to be excluded once the Allied-dominated interim period had ended.

A broad counter-position developed against this doctrine of discontinuity. According to this opposing view, the German state had not ceased to exist but had merely become temporarily incapable of acting.

From 1947 onward this position was defended by Rolf Stödter, Wilhelm Grewe, Ulrich Scheuner, and others.

See Hans Kelsen, “The International Legal Status of Germany to be established immediately upon Termination of the War,” in American Journal of International Law 38, 1945, pp. 689 ff.; Kelsen, “The Legal Status of Germany According to the Declaration of Berlin,” ibid. 39, 1945, pp. 518 ff.; Rolf Stödter, Deutschlands Rechtslage, Hamburg 1948; Ulrich Scheuner, “Die staatsrechtliche Kontinuität in Deutschland,” in Die Öffentliche Verwaltung, 1950, No. 10, pp. 481 ff.

The paragraph corresponds to a section, though not an identical one, in Schmitt’s letter to Ernst Jünger of 11 June 1948.

See BW EJ, pp. 228 f.

the primal dissonance of nothing’s chirping — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Der äthiopische Totentanz, pp. 160 f.:

“Dwarf, whirling runt,” I cried, “amuse yourself freely; cheat Death in the dance of whatever you rise to gain, and grow fat and lusty:

Let the primal dissonance of nothing’s chirping sound loudly in you; let it come from your own breast! Dance, dance, delouse the world, rid it of bedbugs; hey, black dwarf, tar-greasy and soot-thick, covered in the black shine of coal, your head shrivels up, your body grows crusted, and around you rolls a masked dance!”

Humbert Clérissac — (1864–1914), Dominican priest, author of Le mystère de l’église, published in 1914.

German edition: Das Geheimnis der Kirche, ed., trans., and annotated by Rudolf Michael Schmitz, Studi tomistici 23, Vatican City 1984.

Denis de Rougemont — (1906–1985), Swiss essayist. D. de Rougemont, La part du diable, New York 1942 and later editions. German edition: Der Anteil des Teufels, Munich 1999.

Gueydan, pensées d’un Dékan — Not identified.

13 June 1948

that Nietzsche had fathered Hitler — See Ernst Niekisch, Deutsche Daseinsverfehlung, Aktuelle Kulturreihe, Berlin 1946.

Schmitt owned two copies, RW 265 Nos. 23051 and 23052.

Leon Trotsky wrote in 1923 … — Schmitt quotes inaccurately from Trotsky’s Literatur und Revolution, in Frida Rubiner’s German translation, Vienna 1924, RW 579 No. 1118.

The relevant passage, pp. 177–179, correctly reads:

“Human beings first drove blind elemental forces out of production and ideology, replacing barbaric routine with scientific technology and religion with science.

Then they drove the unconscious out of politics: first by overthrowing monarchy and the estates through democracy and rationalist parliamentarism, and finally through the transparently clear dictatorship of the soviets.

Blind elemental force weighs most heavily on economic relations—but human beings are driving it out there as well through the socialist organization of the economy. This makes a radical transformation of traditional family life possible.

Finally, in the deepest and darkest corner of the unconscious, elemental self, human nature itself lies asleep.

Is it not obvious that the greatest efforts of scientific thought and creative initiative will eventually be directed there?

Surely humanity did not stop crawling on its belly before God, kings, and capital only to surrender afterward to the blind laws of heredity and blind sexual selection!

Liberated humanity will want to achieve a greater balance in the functioning of its organs, a more even development and use of its tissues, and thereby confine fear of death within the limits of a useful biological response to danger.

For there can be no doubt that the extraordinary disharmony of the human being—both anatomical and physiological—the extraordinary unevenness in the development and wearing-out of organs and tissues, gives the instinct for life that cramped, pathological, hysterical form we call the fear of death: a fear that clouds reason and feeds stupid and degrading fantasies about an afterlife.

Human beings will set themselves the task of becoming masters of their own feelings, of raising their instincts to the highest level of consciousness and making them transparently clear, of extending the guiding threads of the will beneath the threshold of consciousness, and in this way of raising themselves to a higher level of awareness.

In other words, humanity will create a higher social-biological type—or, if one prefers, a superhuman.

[…]

The average human being will rise to the level of an Aristotle, a Goethe, a Marx.

Above that mountain ridge, new peaks will rise.”

“Hail to you, resplendent earth” — From Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Act III, Scene 3. A piano reduction survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 26258.

In Dostoevsky, Kirillov says … — Schmitt quotes Dostoevsky from Walter Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche. Symbolik ihres Lebens, Lucerne 1939, p. 47.

In Dostoevsky, according to E. K. Rahsin’s translation, the sentence reads:

“Man will be God and will change physically.”

Fyodor M. Dostoevsky, Die Dämonen, trans. E. K. Rahsin, Frankfurt am Main, c. 1992, p. 155.

15 June 1948

Renan said — Ernest Renan (1823–1892), French scholar of religion and historian.

Renan made this often-repeated remark to the nationalist politician Paul Déroulède in 1883.

15 June 1948

To Hans Beyer — Hans Joachim Beyer (1908–1971), historian and active National Socialist. He was an SS-Hauptsturmführer and a close associate of Reinhard Heydrich.

In 1940 he became a professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin, in 1941 at Posen, and in 1943 at Prague.

After the war he became press spokesman for the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Schleswig-Holstein, and from 1951 he was a professor at the teacher-training college in Flensburg.

For more on him, see Stephan Linck, Neue Anfänge? Der Umgang der Evangelischen Kirche mit der NS-Vergangenheit und ihr Verhältnis zum Judentum. Die Landeskirchen in Nordelbien, Vol. 1, 1945–1965, Kiel 2013.

Beyer’s letter of 12 June 1948, to which Schmitt was replying, survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 1318.

16 June 1948

“Haecker’s thought … a more genuinely Catholic sharpening” — The correct passage reads:

“On closer examination, however, Haecker’s thought now belongs essentially to the Catholic literary movement as well.

It did not arise from that movement, because Haecker entered it as an outsider. Nor did it take part in the movement’s earlier opposition between a ‘classicist’ neutralization and a ‘Gothic’ realization.

But it is now struggling toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.

The movement itself is in many places turning, out of a barrenness in its creaturely and historical understanding, from the Word to language, from particularity to universality, and from a neutralized form of life to political confession. Much the same can also be said more generally about the intellectual and artistic decisions of the older generation.

Haecker’s thought now takes part in this struggle toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.”

Konrad Weiß, “Die Kreatur des Wortes,” in Der Ring (Berlin) 4, 1931, No. 48, p. 902.

Reprinted in Literaturwissenschaftliches Jahrbuch der Görres-Gesellschaft, New Series 12, 1971, pp. 311–315.

17 June 1948

On Güllich — Hans Güllich, a first lieutenant on the Eastern Front during the Second World War.

Schmitt is referring to Güllich’s text titled “Lagebeurteilung,” which Güllich sent to Jünger and Jünger passed on to Schmitt.

See BW EJ, pp. 224–227 and 655.

Wilhelm Schmitz — (1912–?), jurist and industrialist who supported Schmitt after 1945.

See W. Schmitz, “Zur Geschichte der Academia Moralis,” in Schmittiana IV, 1994, pp. 119–156.

G. Radbruch’s favorable review of this book — Karl Schultes’s Der Niedergang des staatsrechtlichen Denkens im Faschismus, Weimar 1947; see the note above to p. 103.

Gustav Radbruch praised it in the Süddeutsche Juristenzeitung, Vol. 3, No. 5, 1948, pp. 223 f., as

“a work much needed for the cleansing of political thought. Heine’s phrase ‘No talent, but character’ could be applied here in reverse.”

Quoted from van Laak, p. 36.

18 June 1948

“Idea and Reality of the Free German League” — Ernst Rudolf Huber, Idee und Realität eines Freideutschen Bundes, typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 20250.

See Schmitt’s letter to Huber of 18 June 1948, BW Huber, pp. 327–332.

20 June 1948

Robert Brasillach — (1909–1945), French writer, executed for collaboration on 6 February 1945.

21 June 1948

Gebhard — Klaus Gebhard (1896–1976), Wuppertal manufacturer and art collector, and a friend of Ernst Jünger and Gerhard Nebel.

Iskar — Heading: “Judas.” Iskar = Iscariot.

22 June 1948

Ernst Jünger often says … — Jünger does not write this under 9 December, but under 14 December 1943 in Strahlungen:

“Of all the minds I have known, Carl Schmitt is the one who can define things best.”

Privy Councillor am Zehnhoff — Hugo am Zehnhoff (1855–1930), jurist and politician, Prussian minister of justice from 1919 to 1927.

During his time as a lawyer at the Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf, Carl Schmitt served his legal traineeship under him.

Before moving to Berlin in 1928, Schmitt also stayed at am Zehnhoff’s ministerial residence when visiting Berlin.

See also Tb 1912–15, pp. 405–409.

23 June 1948

Poor in deeds and rich in thought — From Friedrich Hölderlin’s poem “An die Deutschen” (“To the Germans”), second version.

In Hölderlin, Gedichte, based on the historical-critical edition of F. Zinkernagel, Leipzig, no date, p. 125:

Never mock the child when, foolish still, astride its wooden horse, it thinks itself glorious and great. O good people! We too are poor in deeds and rich in thought!

Genoveva’s realm of sorrows — Robert Schumann’s opera Genoveva.

24 June 1948

Kaete Eisler — (1898–?), first wife of Schmitt’s friend Georg Eisler.

See Reinhard Mehring, Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt, Plettenberger Miniaturen 2, Plettenberg 2009.

Lucan’s atheism —

Sunt nobis nulla profecto Numina — “For us, there are certainly no gods.” Pharsalia VII, 445 f.

sed victa Catoni — See the note above to p. 79.

Sanctus Cato = nec sancto caruisset vita Catone — “nor would holy Cato have lost his life.” Pharsalia VI, 311.

surdae aures Coelicolum = Inpia tot populis, tot surdas gentibus aures Coelicolum dirae convertunt carmina gentis — “The godless spells of this accursed people reach the ears of the gods, though those ears are deaf to so many nations.” Pharsalia VI, 443 f.

Quis labor sit Superis cantus herbasque sequendi — “Why do the gods above take such trouble to obey incantations and herbs?” Pharsalia VI, 492.

Mortalia nulli Sunt curata Deo. Cladis tamen huius habemus vindictam, quantam terris dare numina fas est — “No god concerns himself with the fate of mortals. Yet the gods have paid for this catastrophe, as far as gods are able to make payment to mortals.” Pharsalia VII, 454–456.

Mentimur regnare Jovem — “We lie when we say that Jupiter rules.” Pharsalia VII, 447.

Hellingr., Vol. VI, p. 120 — Friedrich Hölderlin, Sämtliche Werke, begun by Norbert von Hellingrath and continued by Friedrich Seebass and Ludwig von Pigenot, Vol. 6, Berlin 1923.

The quotation appears at the beginning of Pharsalia.

25 June 1948

But I will cultivate within myself the seed of freedom … — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Leipzig 1922, Vol. 2, Die Auferstehung des Fleisches, p. 495.

26 June 1948

Jamjam hiscit flammeus — “At once the flames blaze up.”

Ibid., p. 496.

27 June 1948

Nicolaus Sombart’s Capriccio — N. Sombart, Capriccio Nr. 1. Des Wachsoldaten Irrungen und Untergang, Frankfurt am Main 1947.

Walter Fuchs — (1888–1966), diplomat and friend of Schmitt from his Munich years.

See P. Tommissen, “Bausteine zu einer wiss. Biographie,” in Complexio oppositorum. Über Carl Schmitt. Vorträge und Diskussionsbeiträge des 28. Sonderseminars 1986 der Hochschule für Verwaltungswissenschaften Speyer, ed. H. Quaritsch, Berlin 1986, p. 79.

See also Tb 1921–24, p. 113.

28 June 1948

I know the dear Germans already, etc. —

“I know the dear Germans well enough: first they keep quiet, then they carp, then they push you aside, then they steal from you and keep silent about you.”

Goethe to Riemer, 29 August 1819.

In J. W. Goethe, Gedenkausgabe der Werke, Briefe und Gespräche, ed. Ernst Beutler, 2nd ed., Vol. 22, Zurich 1964, p. 863.

Schmitt quoted the passage repeatedly. See, for example, BW Mohler, p. 182; Tb 1930–34, p. 427.

29 June 1948

omnia cedunt in favorem et jus justum bellum gerentium — “Everything gives way to the advantage and the rights of the one who wages a just war.” Francisco de Vitoria, Escuela Española de la Paz. Primera generación 1526–1560, Madrid 1981, p. 336. See also the notes below on pp. 148 and 154.

si licite sunt capta, puto quod non sunt obnoxia restitutioni — “If something has been lawfully seized, I do not think there is any duty to return it.” F. de Vitoria, cited above.

J’ai montré la porte … — Antoine de Rivarol, Maximen, Frankfurt am Main 1956, p. 117. Ernst Jünger translates it as: “I shall therefore not point out the secret entrance to that remote sanctuary where the most delicate and difficult questions of law and morality are decided—all those problems too subtle for the scales of Themis. For if that gate were shown, greed and all the sophistries of passion would soon force their way inside and violate conscience in its last refuge.” E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 14, p. 302. See also Schmitt’s letter to Ernst Jünger of 20 August 1948, in BW EJ, p. 231.

The letter to Forsthoff mentioned here is not included in BW Forsthoff.

Valléry-Radot — Robert Valléry-Radot (1885–1970), French writer and friend of Georges Bernanos and François Mauriac.

Höffner’s book — Joseph Höffner, Christentum und Menschenwürde. Das Anliegen der spanischen Kolonialethik im goldenen Zeitalter, Trier 1947.

Rossini being booed — Rossini’s most famous opera, The Barber of Seville, was booed at its premiere in Rome in 1816.

1 July 1948

Golombek — Walter Golombek (1914–?), Schmitt’s assistant at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin. Two letters from him and one from his father survive in the papers; RW 265, nos. 5065–5067.

collaboration with Frank — Hans Frank (1900–1946), lawyer, Reich Minister under the Nazis, and Governor-General of occupied Poland, supported Schmitt during the early years of the Third Reich. Frank was sentenced to death at the main Nuremberg war-crimes trial and executed in 1946.

2 July 1948

Richard Seewald — (1889–1976), painter and writer who belonged to Schmitt’s circle of acquaintances in Munich; see Tb 1915, pp. 524–527.

2 July 1948

Si tacuisset, magnus Ironicus mansisset — “If you had remained silent, you would have remained a great ironist.”

Irregularität ex defectu corporis propter deformitatem — The Corpus Iuris Canonici provided for the exclusion from ordination of people with serious physical or mental disabilities (Canon 984.2). In 1983 this was restricted to mental disability (Canon 1041).

“Only where there are graves are there resurrections” — Friedrich Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra. In: Nietzsche, Werke, ed. Karl Schlechta, vol. 2, 8th ed., Munich 1977, p. 369.

Walter Schubart — (1897–1941), writer and philosopher whom Ernst Jünger brought to Schmitt’s attention; see BW EJ, p. 181 and elsewhere. Schmitt is quoting from Walter Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche. Symbolik ihres Lebens, Lucerne 1939. The first quotation (“Für die Wiedergeburt …”) is on p. 79; the second (“Aber in unsere Hand …”) on p. 35.

“Life draws strength from the source of evil …” — This is not a quotation from Nietzsche but from Schubart. Schubart’s actual wording is: “Life draws strength from the source of evil, but morality drains it away into death.” W. Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche, cited above, p. 73.

8 July 1948

“Song of the Sixty-Year-Old” — Beginning on 9 July 1948, Schmitt sent this poem to numerous friends and acquaintances. It was first published in 1950 in ECS, pp. 92–93.

10 July 1948

εἰς ἄλλο γένος — From μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, “transition into another kind or category”; Aristotle, Posterior Analytics, Book I, chapter 7, 75a38.

14 July 1948

Herbert Guthjahr — Correctly: “Gutjahr” (1911–1944), Nazi student leader and Schmitt’s assistant at the University of Berlin from 1935 to 1939; from 1939 onward he served as a soldier. Although Gutjahr supplied information to Schmitt’s rival Reinhard Höhn, was also a member of the SS, and worked for the SS Security Service, Schmitt included him in a memorial to the dead delivered on his birthday in 1953, alongside Popitz, Jessen, Ahlmann, and others; see Schmittiana NF II, p. 291.

Prof. Trainin — Ilja Pavlovič Trajnin (1887–1957), Soviet lawyer, at Moscow University from 1921 onward, and one of the architects of Soviet criminal law. The initiative to indict representatives of German industry and business at the Nuremberg trials also came from him.

Walter Lippmann’s Atlantic “greater space” — Walter Lippmann (1889–1974), American journalist who wrote mainly on US foreign policy.

London Charter of August 1945 — The charter signed by the four principal Allied powers of the Second World War that laid down the legal basis and rules of procedure for the Nuremberg trials. Trainin was one of its signatories.

19 July 1948

resistance through cooperation — See Schmitt’s letter of 25 August 1948 to E. R. Huber; BW Huber, pp. 339–342.

Weizsäcker trial — The Nazi-era diplomat Ernst von Weizsäcker (1882–1951) played a contradictory role during the Third Reich and later had to answer for his conduct in a highly publicized trial at Nuremberg. In 1949 he was sentenced to five years in prison.

Maquis — Apparently a reference to the maquis as a shorthand term for the French Resistance.

20 July 1948

Henry Adams (The Education of Henry Adams) — Schmitt owned two editions, one of which—Cambridge 1927, RW 265, no. 24954—contains his annotations.

The importance of the book to Schmitt can be seen from two passages in his letters. On 26 January 1956 he wrote to Rolf Stoedter:

“Do you have The Education of Henry Adams in your library, the book from which I quoted a sentence for you in our conversation about power? I have been reading this Education since 1930, when Professor Carl Joachim Friedrich gave it to me as a gift. For me it is the finest and most important American book there is, and I knew exactly what I was doing when I quoted it at the end of my Nomos of the Earth (p. 299).” (RW 265, no. 13549.)

On 19 August 1972 he wrote to Marianne Kesting:

“For my own part, from 1933 onward I had every reason to reflect on my own situation, and this became even more intense from 1939 onward, continuing through the American camp and Nuremberg, where, as an object of American reeducation, I was reminded often enough of the well-meaning Delano. There I resolved that, in my old age, if I ever had enough time, I would write down my experiences under the title and from the perspective: Education of Henry Adams — Reeducation of Carl Schmitt.” (Publication forthcoming.)

22 July 1948

Pareto — Vilfredo Pareto (1848–1923), Italian economist and sociologist.

23 July 1948

“From your hands the meteor emerges …” — From R. M. Rilke, Werke, vol. II/2, Frankfurt am Main 1974, p. 132.

the famous passage about Christianity — Rilke’s letter was written not on 7 December but on 17 December 1912, from Ronda. It includes the following passage:

“[…] ever since Córdoba I have been in an almost violently anti-Christian mood. I am reading the Koran, and in places it speaks to me in a voice that I enter into with all my strength, like wind entering an organ. […] In any case, Mohammed was the closest to the source: like a river breaking through ancient rock, he forces his way through to the one God, with whom one can speak so magnificently every morning, without using the ‘Christ’ telephone into which someone is constantly shouting: Hello, who’s there?—and no one answers.”

Rainer Maria Rilke/Marie von Thurn und Taxis, Briefwechsel, vol. 1, Zurich 1951, pp. 245–246.

25 July 1948

cum subtristes homines sunt, aut aliquantulum morosi … — “Since people are somewhat sad, or a little ill-tempered, it is time to become angry.”

27 July 1948

Quantum arma hominum … — Correctly:

quantum enses et sclopeti, arma hominum, superant arma brutorum, cornua, dentes, aculeos, tantum homo lupos, ursos, serpentes, qui ultra famem rapaces non sunt, nec nisi lacessiti saeviunt, rapacitate et sevitia superat, etiam fame futura famelicus.

“For just as swords and firearms, the weapons of human beings, surpass horns, teeth, and stings, the weapons of animals, so human beings surpass wolves, bears, and snakes in greed and cruelty. Animals do not prey beyond what their hunger requires and become savage only when provoked; human beings can be made hungry even by the thought of future hunger.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 17.

1 August 1948

Werner Kaegi — (1909–2005), Swiss lawyer. On 10 May 1947 he delivered his inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich under the title “Widerstandsrecht und Rechtsstaat (Zur Erneuerung des abendländischen Rechtsdenkens)” [“The Right of Resistance and the Constitutional State: Toward a Renewal of Western Legal Thought”].

Monsieur Béguin — Albert Béguin (1901–1957), Swiss literary scholar who wrote on the role of academics in the rise of National Socialism; see Albert Béguin, Faiblesse de l’Allemagne, Paris 1946.

2 August 1948

**Today I discover § 247 in Hegel’s Philosophy of Right*** — See C. Schmitt, *Land und Meer, 6th ed., Stuttgart 2008, afterword.

3 August 1948

birthplace of modern Bethlehem — Andrew Carnegie’s steelworks were located in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, and formed the basis of his wealth.

letter from Mr. Andrew Carnegie — Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919), American industrialist, one of the richest men of his time, philanthropist, and pacifist. Schmitt quotes from the following book: Henri Chardon, L’organisation de la République pour la paix (Publications de la Dotation Carnegie pour la Paix Internationale / Section d’Economie et d’Histoire. Histoire économique et sociale de la guerre mondiale. Série française), Paris and elsewhere, 1926.

a German oaf — Adolf Hitler.

K. Marx, Rjasanow I, p. 131 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Karl Marx/Friedrich Engels, Historisch-kritische Gesamtausgabe. Werke, Schriften, Briefe, commissioned by the Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow and edited by D. Rjazanov, section 1, half-volume 1, Frankfurt am Main and elsewhere, 1927. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 25161.

5 August 1948

Propos d’Alain — Émile-Auguste Chartier (1868–1951), French philosopher who, under the pseudonym Alain, created the literary form known as the Propos.

9 August 1948

Karl Eschweiler — Catholic theologian, Schmitt’s colleague in Bonn and a friend of his; in 1933 he became an outspoken supporter of National Socialism. See Thomas Marschler, Karl Eschweiler (1886–1936). Theologische Erkenntnislehre und nationalsozialistische Ideologie (Quellen und Studien zur neueren Theologiegeschichte 9), Regensburg 2011.

Schildgenossen, vol. 13, no. 1 — Konrad Weiß, “Die politische Spannung von Inbegriff und Geschichte,” in Die Schildgenossen 13, no. 1, 1933. A copy with Schmitt’s annotations survives in his papers.

11 August 1948

quoted in Duhourcau — François Duhourcau, La Voix intérieure de Maurice Barrès. D’après ses cahiers, Paris 1929.

15 August 1948

Genitum, non factum — “Begotten, not made,” a quotation from the Christian Creed. Schmitt is turning against the positivists a formula that had been used at the Council of Nicaea to exclude the Arian sect.

17 August 1948

hohoho through RoRoRo — To be understood as: homo homini homo through Rowohlt’s Rotations-Romane. Publisher Ledig-Rowohlt had picked up in America the idea of printing inexpensive books using rotary presses.

18 August 1948

Niebel — Fritz Niebel (1913–1998), legal adviser in private industry; from 1950 managing director of the FDP parliamentary group in the German Bundestag; from 1958 onward he held various posts in the government of North Rhine-Westphalia and in the federal government.

Wilke — Not identified.

20 August 1948

χωριζόμενος του κυβερνήτου — “Separated from the helmsman.” From Plato’s Statesman, where the withdrawal of the divine ruler causes the cosmos to fall into disorder (273b3).

To Ernst Jünger — See BW EJ, pp. 231 ff., 659 ff. “If you had been sitting with us at the table” refers to Jünger’s absence from Schmitt’s sixtieth-birthday gathering.

the little Rivarol volume you gave me in Paris seven years ago — Antoine de Rivarol, Notes, maximes et pensées (Collection des moralistes), Paris 1941. See BW EJ, p. 136.

cup bearing the inscription “To justice—always” — A pewter cup Schmitt gave to guests at his fiftieth birthday.

25 August 1948

Qui veut faire l’ange fait la bête — “Man is neither angel nor beast, and the misfortune is that anyone who tries to act like an angel ends up acting like a beast.” Pascal, Pensées (Brunschvicg), fragment 358. Schmitt owned both Brunschvicg’s modern edition (RW 265, no. 24340) and an annotated edition from 1670 (RW 265, no. 24343).

1 September 1948

Dahm — Georg Dahm (1904–1963), National Socialist scholar of criminal and international law.

2 September 1948

Versari in re illicita — “To place oneself in an unlawful situation.” This Latin principle was formerly used for a doctrine in criminal law according to which anyone who committed a forbidden act could automatically be held responsible for all consequences arising from it, even in cases involving negligence.

4 September 1948

Omnia cedunt in favorem gerentibus bellum iustum — See the note above on p. 130.

Versanti (or versato) in re illicita omnia nocent … — “Everything works against the person who is—or has been—in an unlawful situation. Everything works against the person defeated in a just war. The person defeated in a just war is in an unlawful situation; everything therefore works against him.”

5 September 1948

Walz — Gustav Adolph Walz (1897–1948), scholar of international law. See the note below on p. 159.

8 September 1948

In Monarchia is qui latere vult … — Correctly:

In monarchia igitur, is qui latere vult, qualiscunque sit qui regnat, extra periculum est.

“Therefore, under a monarchy, anyone who wishes to live quietly and out of sight is safe, whoever may be ruling.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 180.

Minus saepe damnantur cives immerito … — Correctly:

Minus tamen saepe damnantur cives immerito, regnante homine, quam populo.

“Moreover, innocent citizens are less often condemned under the rule of one person than under the rule of the people.”

Hobbes, M/B, p. 179.

16 September 1948

Ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant — “So that no harm may come to them through contact.” The passage refers to people regarded by the Gauls as godless or criminal and therefore avoided.

Hans Schneider — Hans Schneider (1912–2010), constitutional lawyer and student of Schmitt.

21 September 1948

Sir Henry James Sumner Maine — Henry Sumner Maine, Ancient Law. Its Connection with the Early History of Society and Its Relation to Modern Ideas, London 1861, chapter IV. In the second edition of 1870, the quotation appears on p. 87.

23 September 1948

poems such as “Der Nachtwandler” or “Lauschender auf blauer Au” — Theodor Däubler, Der Flammende Lavabach, in Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, pp. 549–605; the two poems appear on pp. 583 and 584–585.

“And from attempts, miraculous flowers would spring” — Quotation from the poem “Die Verneinung,” in Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, p. 556.

28 September 1948

beautiful definition of law in the young Hegel — “Before the law, the criminal is nothing but a criminal; but just as the law is only a fragment of human nature, so too is the criminal. If the law were a whole, an absolute, then the criminal too would be nothing but a criminal.”

G. W. F. Hegel, Der Geist des Christentums und sein Schicksal, in Hegel, Frühe Studien und Entwürfe 1787–1800, Berlin 1991, p. 509.

30 September 1948

l’homme surpasse l’homme — “Man surpasses man.” B. Pascal, Pensées (Brunschvicg), fragment 434.

8 October 1948

“Si j’avais la disgrâce d’être Allemand …” — Correctly: “… les deux Bigs de ce temps-là — bigre de Bigs! — j’aurai été tenté …”

16 October 1948

Henri Murger — (1822–1861), French writer whose novel Les scènes de la vie de bohème provided the basis for Puccini’s opera La Bohème.

**Henry Miller’s Tropique du Cancer*** — Here and in the quotations that follow, Schmitt is referring to Henry Miller, *Tropique du Cancer, translated by Paul Rivert, preface by Henri Fluchère, Paris 1945. Schmitt obtained the book, which did not appear in German until 1953, with Ernst Jünger’s help; see BW EJ, pp. 234–235.

Salus ex Judaeis — Vulgate, John 4:22: vos adoratis quod nescitis nos adoramus quod scimus quia salus ex Iudaeis est. “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation comes from the Jews.”

Bes uswika — Title of a poem by the Serbian poet Milutin Bojić (1892–1917), translated by Schmitt in 1923 together with his future wife Duška Todorović; see Tb 1921–24, pp. 203–204 and elsewhere. See also Carl Schmitt, “Illyrien — Notizen von einer dalmatinischen Reise,” in SGN, pp. 485–490.

the brilliant essay by Herbert Krüger — Herbert Krüger, “Das Janusgesicht der Nürnberger Prozesse,” in Die Gegenwart 3, 1948, no. 66, pp. 11 ff. See also Kempner’s reply, ibid., no. 68, pp. 9 ff.

in jus et favorem bellum justum gerentis — “… si iure belli factum est, omnia cedunt in favorem iustum bellum gerentis.” “If something has been done under the law of war, everything gives way in favor of those who wage a just war.”

“At last time turns Saul …” — From Johann Christian Günther’s poem “Trostaria”; J. Chr. Günther, Gesammelte Gedichte, ed. H. Heckmann, Munich 1981, pp. 291–292.

animus hostilis — hostile intent or disposition.

18 October 1948

les êtres humains font une faune et une flore étranges … — Henry Miller, Tropique du Cancer, cited above, p. 349.

21 October 1948

as Heraclitus says — “War is the father of all things and king of all things. Some he makes gods, others men; some slaves, others free.” Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, ed. Hermann Diels, Berlin 1903, p. 74, fragment 53.

27 October 1948

Annie Kraus — (1900–1991), cousin of Georg Eisler, who had worked as Schmitt’s secretary in 1928–1929. Schmitt also went walking with her and visited cafés and cinemas with her. In his diary from this period he usually speaks positively of her, though he occasionally calls her “stupid.”

Kraus, who was also friends with Paul Adams and Eduard Rosenbaum, survived in Germany as a Jewish woman. She converted to Catholicism in 1942 and studied philosophy, among others, with Heidegger. See Andreas Mix, “Hilfe im katholischen Milieu,” in Überleben im Dritten Reich. Juden im Untergrund und ihre Helfer, ed. Wolfgang Benz, Munich 2003, pp. 131–142.

Her 1948 book Über die Dummheit, which is strongly influenced by Thomas Aquinas, says on p. 38:

“Freedom of the will takes shape through its bond with true Being, with God. When the will abandons this bond, there emerges the abstract un-boundness of arbitrary choice, which is therefore stupid in its very essence. The recent past has provided no shortage of drastic examples of this groundless ‘presence’ presenting itself as ‘the existential’ (Carl Schmitt).”

And on p. 42:

“Sin begins in the mind: all these intellectually gifted creators of heretical philosophical doctrines bear a profound share of responsibility for the final degradation of their people—a degradation that may even surprise them themselves, so thoroughly have they already become ‘stupid’ …”

In 1983 Annie Kraus helped bring about a reconciliation between Schmitt and Georg Eisler. See Reinhard Mehring, “Annie Kraus, der Würgeengel des Carl Schmitt,” in FAZ, 20 July 2007, p. 35; and Mehring, Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 2), Plettenberg 2009, pp. 18 and 27–28.

Con-versanti in re illicita / co-existentibus in re illicita — “Those who together find themselves in evil circumstances must live together in evil circumstances.” See the note above on p. 148.

7 November 1948

Rolf Stödter — (1909–1993), lawyer and shipowner.

2 December 1948

Hannes — Hans Schneider.

at Ostermann’s — An inn in Plettenberg-Eiringhausen.

“The serpent, it is said …” — Jeremy Bentham, The Works of J. Bentham, Edinburgh 1838, vol. 1, part 2, p. 325.

protestatio factis et actis contraria — Refers to the following rule of Roman law: protestatio facto contraria non valet. A reservation or declaration has no validity if it contradicts one’s own actual conduct.

4 December 1948

“l’obscurité protège mieux que la loi” — Rivarol: “We live in an age in which obscurity protects better than the law and gives greater reassurance than innocence.”

Schmitt did not begin quoting this maxim only after his exclusion from academic life. He had already used it during his period of service in the Volkssturm. He and Jünger discussed at length how obscurité should be translated.

Jünger initially proposed “Nichtigkeit” (“insignificance” or “nothingness”), then “Niedrigkeit” (“lowliness”), both of which Schmitt rejected. See BW EJ, pp. 279–292.

Jünger eventually translated the maxim as: “We live in an age in which insignificance offers more protection than the laws and gives a better conscience than innocence.” E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 14, p. 274.

Even this probably did not capture what Schmitt understood Rivarol to mean. Jünger discussed the difficulty of translating obscurité in the appendix to his Rivarol edition, cited above, pp. 322 ff. See also BW Forsthoff, p. 114.

12 December 1948

Bible de l’humanité — Jules Michelet, Bible de l’humanité, Paris 1864.

The Yogi and the Commissar — Arthur Koestler, Der Yogi und der Kommissar. Auseinandersetzungen, Esslingen 1950.

14 December 1948

Nohl, pp. 347–348 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Hegels theologische Jugendschriften, edited from the manuscripts in the Royal Library in Berlin by Dr. Herman Nohl, Tübingen 1907. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 24647.

16 December 1948

“For as thou urgest justice be assured …” — Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act IV, Scene 1.

Ave consilescens in arcano — “Greetings, fellow keeper of silence in the secret.”

the pack of Korah — Korah and his followers rose in rebellion against Moses; Numbers 16–17.

18 December 1948

“So Christ has already been dead for our sins for so long …” — Quoted in Karl Rosenkranz, G. W. F. Hegels Leben, facsimile reprint of the Berlin 1844 edition, Darmstadt 1969, p. 541.

is supposed to become Lukács’s star witness (Lukács, p. 590) — Georg Lukács, Der junge Hegel. Über die Beziehungen von Dialektik und Oekonomie, Zurich and Vienna 1948, p. 590. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 24641.

20 December 1948

news of poor Gustav Adolf Walz’s death — Walz, who had been dismissed from his university position in 1945 and interned by the French occupying authorities, died on 17 December 1948.

On 10 January 1949 Schmitt wrote to E. R. Huber:

“Will anyone have the courage to do justice to Walz in public? […] This is how we are being finished off—Walz at fifty.”

BW Huber, p. 349.

Ecce quomodo moritur iustus, et nemo considerat — “Behold how the just man dies, and no one takes notice.” From the medieval liturgy for the death of John the Baptist.

but I will remember him — The depth of Schmitt’s reaction to the death of his colleague can be seen from the fact that he still commemorated Walz in his speech on his sixty-fifth birthday in 1953; see Schmittiana NF II, 2014, p. 291.

Konrad Weiß — The quotations that follow are from Weiß’s drama Konradin von Hohenstaufen.

25 December 1948

William Ebenstein — (1910–1976), Austrian-American political scientist. Schmitt believed that Ebenstein had misrepresented him in his book Man and the State (New York 1947); see BW Mohler, p. 25.

14 January 1949

Le combat spirituel est plus brutal que la bataille des homes — Correctly:

Le combat spirituel est aussi brutal que la bataille d’hommes; mais la vision de la justice est le plaisir de Dieu seul.

“The spiritual struggle is as brutal as battle between men; but the vision of justice is God’s pleasure alone.”

Arthur Rimbaud, Sämtliche Dichtungen. Französisch und Deutsch, ed. and trans. Walther Küchler, 6th ed., Heidelberg 1982, p. 324.

18 January 1949

“Now the laws, seen through to their primal depths, will shatter” — Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, poem “Neumond,” p. 544.

22 January 1949

Gottfried Benn: “I am not of the opinion …” — Gottfried Benn, Drei alte Männer, in Sämtliche Werke, vol. VII/1, Stuttgart 2003, p. 121; first published in Wiesbaden in 1949.

26 January 1949

Etat postiche — “artificial” or “fake state.” Schmitt probably borrowed the term from Georges Sorel, Réflexions sur la violence (Études sur le devenir social, 4), 4th ed., Paris 1919. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 25175.

27 January 1949

To Mrs. Jünger — See BW GJ, pp. 112 ff.

on the subject of Chaopolites — Schmitt wrote to Ernst Jünger on 25 November 1949: “As you know, I am a Chaopolite, not a Heliopolite.” BW EJ, p. 241.

13 February 1949

Ohle — Village near Plettenberg.

15 February 1949

**the Ludus de Antichristo*** — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Gottfried Hasenkamp, ed., *Das Spiel vom Antichrist, translated into German with an afterword on the Ludus de Antichristo, its performance, and its translation, Münster 1932. Schmitt’s copy, with a dedication from the editor, survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24532.

19 February 1949

“In the spell of this luxuriant paradise-air …” — Correctly:

“In the spell of luxuriant paradisal delight, every claim upon life and every hope for the hereafter finds satisfaction.”

Johann Jakob Bachofen, Der Mythus von Orient und Occident. Eine Metaphysik der Alten Welt, with an introduction by Alfred Baeumler, ed. Manfred Schroeter, Munich 1926, p. 402. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24846.

“A scarcely greeted, lost, unspeakable moment” — Nikolaus Lenau, poem “Frage,” in Lenau, Sämtliche Werke und Briefe, vol. 1, Frankfurt am Main and Leipzig 1970, p. 120:

“Human heart, what is your happiness? A moment born as a mystery, scarcely greeted and already lost, never to be repeated!”

22 February 1949

En quelque façon nul … — See Hans Peter Ipsen, “Deutsche Gerichtsbarkeit unter Besatzungsmacht (Einwirkungen der Besatzung auf den gerichtlichen Rechtsschutz gegen deutsche Hoheitsakte in der britischen Besatzungszone),” in Festschrift zu Ehren von Prof. Dr. jur. Rudolf Laun, Rektor der Universität Hamburg, 1948, pp. 68–96.

Schmitt discusses Montesquieu’s formula, which referred to the judiciary, in his Verfassungslehre; VL, pp. 184–185.

Venire contra factum proprium — “To act contrary to one’s own previous conduct”; a formula from German law of obligations.

Rolf Stödter in his otherwise very thorough book — Rolf Stödter, Deutschlands Rechtslage, Hamburg 1948.

C. M. O. van Nispen tot Sevenaer — Carel Marie Otto van Nispen tot Sevenaer, L’occupation allemande pendant la dernière guerre mondiale. Considerations sur le caractère du pouvoir de la puissance occupante et de ses mesures selon les principes généraux du droit et selon la 4e convention de La Haye, The Hague 1946.

Barandon’s Hamburg radio lecture — Paul Barandon (1881–1971), German diplomat who at this time was a private lecturer in international law at the University of Hamburg.

24 February 1949

Otto Veit, speeches — 29. Dezember 1948. Ansprachen von Ernst Beutler und Otto Veit, Frankfurt am Main 1948, commemorative publication for Otto Veit’s fiftieth birthday.

25 February 1949

“In you I see the God …” — Stefan George, “Kunfttag,” in George, Werke. Ausgabe in zwei Bänden, 3rd ed., Düsseldorf and Munich 1976, vol. 1, p. 279. Correctly: “… whom I recognized with a shudder …”

Kurt Hiller’s enemy-flailing — Kurt Hiller (1885–1972), pacifist writer. Schmitt regarded his article “Ewiger Friede in Gänsefüßchen” (Die Weltbühne, year 28, 4 October 1932, pp. 498–500) as “one of the many examples of documentary value in which the word and concept ‘annihilation’ are attributed to me”; BW Mohler, p. 48.

against Paetel — Karl Otto Paetel (1906–1975), writer and leading representative of National Bolshevism.

1 March 1949

“The men of the German National Assembly in Frankfurt …” — Quotation from Bruno Bauer. Correctly:

“The men in Frankfurt wanted to found a Reich whose existence would have amounted to a general European revolution, and they calculated the future on the basis of the illusions in which the revolutionary excitement of the moment was living.”

B. Bauer, Der Untergang des Frankfurter Parlaments. Geschichte der deutschen constituirenden Nationalversammlung, Berlin 1849, p. 94.

Schmitt also uses this sentence to open the essay on Donoso mentioned below.

Donoso essay — [C. Schmitt], “Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation,” in Die neue Ordnung 3, 1949, no. 1, pp. 1–15, published without the author’s name.

The essay originated in a lecture delivered in Spanish in Madrid on 31 May 1944 and was anonymously published in 1949 under the title “Donoso Cortés y las revoluciones de 1848,” in Revista de la Faculdad de derecho y ciencias sociales de la Universidad de Buones Aires 4, 1949, no. 17, pp. 13–26. In 1950 it appeared as chapter 4 of the book published under the same title.

the refuge offered by the Dominicans — During these years Schmitt received support at the Dominican monastery of Walberberg, especially from its prior, Father Eberhard Welty, who edited the journal Die neue Ordnung.

7 March 1949

P.[asserin] d’Entrèves — Alessandro Passerin d’Entrèves (1902–1985), Italian philosopher of law.

8 March 1949

“Above my cap only the stars” — See Goethe, West-östlicher Divan, in Goethes Werke, ed. Erich Trunz, Hamburg edition, vol. 2, p. 9:

“Let me count for something only in my saddle! Remain in your huts and in your tents! And I ride happily into the distance, Above my cap only the stars.”

I wish to be thought, I who am wholly thought — From the New Testament apocrypha, Acts of John 95. See Die Apokryphen Schriften zum Neuen Testament, trans. and annotated by Wilhelm Michaelis, Bremen 1956, p. 251, where the wording is: “I wish to be thought, for I am thought through and through.”

10 March 1949

“The Man in the Cell” — Refers to Nicolaus Sombart, “Der Mann in der Zelle,” in Nordseezeitung (Bremen), 2 March 1949.

On 10 March 1949 Schmitt wrote to Sombart:

“‘The Man in the Cell’ has rekindled my old affection for you. There are moments in it that reveal your own distinctive genius. For me, one example is the passage on Goethe’s line ‘above my cap only the stars.’ Other parts seem too psychological to me, too much like topical conversation and reflections that lie too close at hand. Every paragraph, indeed every sentence, keeps me occupied.”

BW Sombart, pp. 22–23.

12 March 1949

Hans Zehrer — (1899–1966), journalist and leading figure of the Tat circle; editor-in-chief of the Sonntagsblatt from 1948 to 1953 and of Die Welt from 1953 to 1966. He had known Carl Schmitt since 1931.

13 March 1949

letter from Gottfried Benn — G. Benn, “Ein Berliner Brief,” in Merkur 3, 1949, pp. 203–206. This letter, written in July 1948 to the editor of Merkur, marked the beginning of Benn’s postwar comeback. See G. Benn, Gesammelte Werke in vier Bänden, ed. D. Wellershoff, vol. 4, 3rd ed., Wiesbaden 1977, pp. 280–285.

14 March 1949

the German judges on trial in Luxembourg — Trials were held in Luxembourg in 1948–1949 against German judges who had served on special and emergency courts during the war. Most of the charges proved impossible to sustain. See Matthias Herbers, Organisationen im Krieg (Beiträge zur Rechtsgeschichte des 20. Jahrhunderts, 71), Tübingen 2012, pp. 24 ff.

Donoso essay, anonymous — See the note above on p. 168.

15 March 1949

the depressing discussion about democracy and elites — At 9:15 p.m. on 15 March 1949, Radio Frankfurt’s evening program broadcast a debate entitled “Masse und Elite” [“Mass and Elite”]. The participants were Heinrich Gremmels (“son of a secondary-school teacher”), Friedrich Minssen, Gerhard Nebel (“former secondary-school teacher”), and Nicolaus Sombart (“son of a sociologist”). See Schmittiana VII, 2001, p. 92, note 6, and BW Sombart, p. 20.

18 March 1949

remark by Danzenbrinck — Franz Danzenbrinck (1899–1960), lawyer and local politician. Schmitt wished he had made the remark himself; see BW Mohler, p. 52.

22 March 1949

“The trend from unanimity to majority” — Schmitt is referring to Paul Guggenheim, Lehrbuch des Völkerrechts. Unter Berücks. d. internat. u. schweizer. Praxis, installments 1–3, Basel 1947–1948. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, nos. 22936–22938.

In note 141, the sentence is sourced as follows: Cromwell A. Riches, Majority Rule in International Organization. A Study of the Trend from Unanimity to Majority Decision, Baltimore 1940.

3 April 1949

friend Barth — Karl Barth (1886–1968), Swiss Reformed theologian who understood God as the “wholly Other” and whose thinking therefore stood in a tense relationship with Carl Schmitt’s. See Mathias Eichhorn, Es wird regiert! Der Staat im Denken Karl Barths und Carl Schmitts in den Jahren 1919 bis 1938 (Beiträge zur politischen Wissenschaft, 78), Berlin 1994. See also above, pp. 277–278.

10 April 1949
