“Heidegger on thinking” — Correctly:

“The word of thinkers has no authority. The word of thinkers has no authors in the sense in which writers have authors. The word of thinking is poor in images and without charm. The word of thinking rests in a sobering return to what it says.”

Martin Heidegger, Gesamtausgabe, vol. 7, section 1, Frankfurt am Main 2000, p. 234.

“Poor in deeds and rich in thoughts” — See above, note to p. 127.

“Gliding on sultry dactyls …” — Published in: Die neue Gesellschaft. Bemerkungen zum Zeitbewußtsein, ed. Rüdiger Altmann and Johannes Gross, Stuttgart 1958, p. 99. Now also in: Gedichte, p. 26.

15 October 1951

“We arrive at the way we behave more by acting against ourselves than by acting out of ourselves.” — Quotation from Ludwig Raiser (1904–1980), jurist. In the Deutsche Universitätszeitung (1951, no. 9, p. 7), Raiser published an article entitled “Carl Schmitt — kein Bundesgenosse” (“Carl Schmitt — No Ally”).

“all righteous comb-makers” — See above, note to p. 41.

“I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.” — See Schmitt’s letter to G. Jünger, 24 February 1948:

“I do not think about the future, because I know how powerless we are. Nor do I seek the past, because I do not want, by reflecting on myself, to outlive myself. So what am I looking for, and what am I doing? I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.”

BW GJ, p. 105. Schmitt wrote something similar to E. R. Huber on 2 June 1948; BW Huber, p. 322. See also above, p. 73.

ἀναγκαζόμενος — See above, note to p. 18.

Rud. Fischer — Rudolf Fischer (1900–1961), journalist, who publicly but anonymously defended Schmitt. See X [= R. Fischer], “Hexenverfolgung. Der Fall Carl Schmitt. Charaktermord.” In: Der Fortschritt, 25 January 1952; see BW Mohler, pp. 115–16, 119; BW Forsthoff, pp. 84, 387.

Don Capisco (et obmutesco) — When Jünger criticized Schmitt for his conduct in 1933, Schmitt replied on 5 February 1950 with the sentence: “Capisco et obmutesco” — “I understand and fall silent.” BW EJ, p. 248. He later responded in the same way to criticism from Nicolaus Sombart; see Schmitt’s letter to Sombart of 7 January 1978, BW Sombart, p. 129.

“namesake of Carlo Schmid” — See above, note to p. 52.

17 October 1951

V. Leemans — Victor Leemans (1901–1971), social scientist and politician, author of Carl Schmitt. Bijdrage tot de sociologie van Staat en Politiek, Antwerp 1933; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 28380.

21 October 1951

“The body is the outward expression” —

“This outward element initially makes the inward visible only as an organ, or gives it a being for others at all; for the inward, insofar as it is in the organ, is the activity itself.”

G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes. In: idem, Werke, vol. 3, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, Frankfurt am Main 1970, pp. 234–35.

23 October 1951

The character assassination as one of the fine arts — A reference to Thomas De Quincey, On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts, 1827 and later editions. See also the caption to the illustration on p. 257.

25 October 1951

“to Mohler, 12 November” — See BW Mohler, p. 108.

Lilian Winstanley — The English author Lilian Winstanley (1875–1960) made one of the first attempts, in her 1921 book Hamlet and the Scottish Succession, to interpret Shakespeare’s Hamlet against the political and historical background of the Elizabethan period. The book was translated into German by Anima Schmitt as L. Winstanley, Hamlet, Sohn der Maria Stuart, Pfullingen 1952. Carl Schmitt wrote a substantial foreword.

“to M. F.” — In his history of the English Revolution, Die große Revolution in England (1951), Michael Freund portrays James I as a grotesque figure. Schmitt commented on this in a letter to Freund dated 7 March 1953; RW 265 no. 13003. In March 2015, the antiquarian-book market ZVAB listed a copy of the 1956 edition of Hamlet oder Hekuba bearing a dedication to M. Freund.

6 November 1951

Forrestal — James Vincent Forrestal (1892–1949), United States Secretary of Defense. Doubts were raised about whether his death was really suicide.

28 November 1951

“Rest. Board at Herford” — The “Restitution Board” was an international court that decided claims for restitution arising from the period 1933–1945. It existed from 1955 to 1990 and was based in Herford until 1984. Schmitt must therefore have added this entry later, something also suggested by the different handwriting.

“Smend wrote this to me as early as 1938” — This refers either to Smend’s letter of 10 July 1938 or to a letter that has been lost; see BW Smend, pp. 99–100, note 333.

“the passages on p. 86 of my Leviathan” — Schmitt means Hobbes’s distinction between an outward “profession of the tongue” and inward belief, which Spinoza transfers from religion to philosophy:

“Only a few years after the publication of the Leviathan, the first liberal Jew fixed his attention on this barely visible fracture. He immediately recognized it as the great point through which modern liberalism could break in, and from which the entire relationship Hobbes had established and intended between outward and inward, public and private, could be turned into its opposite. Spinoza carried out this reversal in the famous chapter 19 of his Tractatus theologico-politicus, published in 1670.”

Leviathan, pp. 86–87.

Bakunin: il n’y a rien de plus borné … —

“Germany itself, moreover, cured me of the philosophical disease that prevailed there. After looking more closely into metaphysical problems, it did not take me long to become convinced of the emptiness and vanity of all metaphysics. I looked for life in it, but found only death and boredom. I looked for action, but found nothing but absolute inactivity. This discovery was greatly helped by my personal relations with German professors, because there is nothing more narrow-minded, more contemptible, or more ridiculous than the German professor — or the German in general!”

M. Bakounine, Confession (1857), reissue of the edition published in 1932, Paris 2001, pp. 61–62.

29 November 1951

Populus Romanus victam Pompejo … —

“Although, for example, the Roman people once governed the land of Judaea through a governor, Judaea was not therefore a democracy, because the people were not governed by an assembly that every one of them had a right to enter; nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by an assembly that any elected person among them might enter.”

Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, trans. Jutta Schlösser, ed. Hermann Klenner, Hamburg 1996, p. 163.

22 December 1951

Ceterum censeo Romam esse liberandam (a Romanitate) — “For the rest, I believe that Rome must be liberated — from Romanness.” A variation on the famous sentence with which Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches in the Senate:

Ceterum censeo Carthaginem esse delendam.

“For the rest, I believe that Carthage must be destroyed.”

12 January 1952

Eulenburg Affair — The dispute between Philipp, Prince of Eulenburg-Hertefeld, and the journalist Maximilian Harden. Harden accused the circle around Eulenburg, which exercised considerable influence over the Kaiser, of homosexuality, and the affair grew into a major public scandal.

“Parallel: Kortner — W. Krauss” — The director Fritz Kortner considered Werner Krauss a great actor, but reproached him for his closeness to National Socialism. Schmitt said that he had once met Krauss on a train and spoken with him.

20 January 1952

“A professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt!” — From a note by Colonel General Werner von Fritsch dated 1 February 1938 concerning the Blomberg Affair, which led to his removal as commander-in-chief of the Army:

“In the autumn, the Party once again intensified its campaign against me. It was driven above all by the Gestapo and related circles. They succeeded in largely convincing Göring that I was planning a coup. Himmler claimed to know that this coup would be carried out on 10(?) January 1935, or on some other day in January 1935. For this reason, Blomberg invited the commanding generals and many other senior officers to an evening of beer at the Kaiser Wilhelm Academy on the first date in question, I believe 10 January 1935. Himmler gave a lecture.

“The incriminating point against me was supposedly that I had invited a professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt, to give a lecture on constitutional law on a Thursday at the Tirpitzufer. Göring claimed that the lecture was intended to prove that a coup was permissible under constitutional law. In the presence of the minister and numerous officers!

“The invitation had been issued by Department 4. The man was and remains completely unknown to me. The lecture was cancelled.”

Friedrich Hoßbach, Zwischen Wehrmacht und Hitler 1934–1938, 2nd rev. ed., Göttingen 1965, p. 61.

“Süsterhenn in the Parliamentary Council” — Correctly:

“We are not afraid of the danger of what has been called a ‘judicialized politics,’ which the namesake of our colleague Carlo Schmid — whose name is spelled with two t’s — has painted on the wall.”

See also VA, pp. 105–6.

3 February 1952

“This sentence by Karl Marx” —

“The Jew has emancipated himself in a Jewish manner, not only by acquiring the power of money, but because through him, and also without him, money has become a world power, and the practical Jewish spirit has become the practical spirit of the Christian peoples. The Jews have emancipated themselves to the extent that the Christians have become Jews.”

K. Marx, “Zur Judenfrage.” In: Marx/Engels, Werke, vol. 1, Berlin 1971, p. 373.

Blasius blessing — On 3 February, the feast day of St. Blaise, this blessing is given by holding two consecrated candles in the form of a St. Andrew’s cross before the face and throat.

5 February 1952

“everything becomes a set of brass knuckles in his hands” — An allusion to Gerhard Nebel’s boxing career and his fights; see above, p. 242.

Drath & Leibholz — The constitutional lawyer Martin Drath (1902–1976) dealt critically with Schmitt in his unpublished habilitation thesis at Jena in 1946. In 1951 he became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court. See van Laak, pp. 166 ff.

The Schmitt critic Gerhard Leibholz (1901–1982) became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court in 1951 and later one of the most influential judges in the Court’s history.

“poor Kriesenhahn” — Schmitt means Ernst Friesenhahn, who in the 1950 Festschrift for Richard Thoma had, in Ernst Forsthoff’s words, “perfidiously disowned” his teacher, and who criticized Schmitt when he took office as rector in Bonn in November 1950. See van Laak, pp. 154–55; BW Huber, pp. 331 and 377.

1 March 1952

quod licet Jovi, non licet bovi — “What Jupiter is allowed to do, the ox is certainly not allowed to do.” Roman saying.

6 March 1952

“Miorița fate” — See above, note to p. 201.

8 March 1952

animus procreandi — “the intention to procreate.”

In his essay “Die Einheit der Welt,” Schmitt writes:

“For in the end it would be a sorry state of affairs if the dualism of the present world amounted to nothing more than the contrast between birth control and animus procreandi, so that every newborn child entered the world as an aggressor and was immediately drawn into the modern system of criminalization.”

C. Schmitt, “Die Einheit der Welt.” In: Merkur 6, 1952, p. 8. Reprinted in SGN, pp. 496–512.

“Hans Peters, director of studies at the Nazi Academy of Administration …” — Although Peters was a member of the Kreisau Circle, before 1945 he published writings that conformed to the National Socialist regime. Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff about him on 3 September 1949:

“What you write about Hans Peters agrees with the experiences I have had with him since 1945: intellectually as well as morally, a specimen of the ruling third-rate set.”

BW Forsthoff, p. 53; see also BW Huber and above, note to p. 204.

9 March 1952

“Serge Maiwald died on 22 February …” — This note was expanded into the obituary; see above, note to p. 212.

20 March 1952

Miching mallecho — Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 3, Scene 2. Hamlet to Ophelia:

“Marry, this is miching mallecho; it means mischief.”

See Schmitt’s reference in Hamlet oder Hekuba, Stuttgart 1985, p. 68, note 1, to Laura Bohannan, “Miching Mallecho. That Means Witchcraft.” In: The London Magazine 1, 1954, no. 5, pp. 51–60.

8 April 1952

“Power is evil in itself” and “God is dead” —

“And now power is evil in itself.”

Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen, Kröners Taschenausgabe 55, Stuttgart 1978, p. 97.

“God is dead!”

Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, section 125.

“You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well” — Schmitt ended his 1955 radio “Conversation on the New Space,” broadcast by Hessischer Rundfunk, as follows:

“You surely know how the second part of Goethe’s Faust begins. Faust awakens after a night filled with terrible dreams and feels the happiness of a new earthly morning, which gives him comfort and strength, the happiness of a new beginning. And so he greets the new world now opening before him with the magnificent line:

You, Earth, remained steadfast through this night as well.

“In the same way, I believe that after a terrible night threatened by atomic bombs and similar horrors, mankind will one morning awaken and gratefully recognize itself once again as the child of the firmly grounded Earth.”

C. Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber. Gespräch über den neuen Raum, Berlin 1994, p. 64.

“Conclusion of my Duisburg lecture” — As part of the Lower Rhine University Weeks, Schmitt gave a lecture in Duisburg on 21 April 1952 entitled “Die Einheit der Welt.” It was largely identical to the essay of the same name published in Merkur, no. 47, 1952, pp. 1–11. It ends:

“But just as the Earth remains greater than the dilemma posed by this dualistic question, so history remains stronger than every philosophy of history. For that reason, I do not regard the present division of the world into two as a preliminary stage on the way to unity, but as a passage toward a new plurality.”

See also G. Maschke’s note to the republication in SGN, pp. 510–12.

27 April 1952

“Wonderful passage in Buffon” — Georges-Louis Leclerc de Buffon, Histoire naturelle, générale et particulière, avec la description du Cabinet du Roy, vols. 1–15, Paris 1749–1767.

The quotation in Rousseau reads, in Heinrich Meier’s German edition:

“Since plants draw far more of the substance they need for nourishment from air and water than from the earth, it follows that when they decay, they return more to the earth than they took from it …”

J. J. Rousseau, Diskurs über die Ungleichheit, ed. H. Meier, Paderborn 1984, p. 285.

renegatur et rejiciatur Norma — “The norm is denied and rejected.”

In his encyclical Summi Pontificatus of 20 October 1939, Pope Pius XII lamented the “denial and rejection of the norms of natural law,” which he identified as one of the causes of the war.

“Norma, Norma, you have vanished” — An allusion to Friedrich von Flotow’s opera Martha, oder der Markt zu Richmond. In Act 3, Scene 4, the aria “Ach! so fromm, Ach! So traut” contains the line:

“Martha! Martha! You have vanished.”

“Interjections by H. Heller and A. Arndt” — Hermann Heller, counsel for Prussia in the Prussia v. Reich case before the State Court in Leipzig in 1932, interrupted Schmitt’s plea by calling out “situational jurisprudence.” See Preußen contra Reich vor dem Staatsgerichtshof. Stenogrammbericht der Verhandlungen vor dem Staatsgerichtshof in Leipzig vom 10. bis 14. und vom 17. Oktober 1932, Berlin 1933, p. 464.

“CDU deputy Nellen” — On 3 July 1956, Bundestag deputy Peter Nellen raised objections to provisions governing conscientious objection in the Conscription Act, arguing that in his view they restricted a fundamental right. See Der Spiegel, 1956, no. 29, pp. 9–11. After repeated disagreements with his party, Nellen moved to the SPD in 1959.

3 May 1952

“Letter from Rabbi Jacob Taubes” — To Armin Mohler, 14 February 1952. The religious philosopher Jacob Taubes (1923–1987), a friend of Mohler, was at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem from 1951 to 1953. The letter, in which Taubes describes his tense and complicated relationship with Carl Schmitt, is printed in BW Taubes, pp. 130–37. Schmitt received the letter from Mohler and circulated copies among acquaintances; see BW Mohler, pp. 116, 119.

17 May 1952

“Hans Zehrer: All disaster comes from the Renaissance” — See Hans Zehrer, Der Mensch in dieser Welt, Hamburg 1948.

18 May 1952

“Bacon of Verulam’s buccinatores” — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Francis Bacon, Fr. Baconi De Verulamio Sermones fideles …, Lugduni Batavorum 1644; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23412. The passage is not on p. 248, however, but on pp. 241–42:

Attamen, sine controversia, hujusmodi ingeniis, in Civilibus, aliquando uti prodest. Si fama excitanda sit, vel opinio late spargenda, sive virtutis, sive potentiae, istiusmodi homines Buccinatores egregii sunt.

“There is, without question, sometimes a certain use for people of this kind in public affairs. When a reputation must be stirred up, or an opinion about someone’s virtue or power spread far and wide, such people make excellent trumpeters.”

“Machiavelli, thou art an Ass” (1640) — A quotation from The Distracted State by the Elizabethan author John Tatham, though the work dates not from 1640 but from 1641. The line is regarded as an early example of people mocking Machiavelli. See John Tatham, The Dramatic Works of John Tatham, New York 1967, p. 46.

“Dio Chrysostom: Christ died as a Haman” — This apparently refers not to Dio Chrysostom but to John Chrysostom and his anti-Jewish work Adversus Judaeos, written around 390. The Codex Theodosianus XVI, 8.18, in 408 prohibited Jews from mocking Christianity by burning an image of Haman on a cross during the festival of Purim. In the Book of Esther, Haman is the highest official at the Persian court and seeks to exterminate the Jews of the Persian Empire.

Sacaea — Festival in honor of the Babylonian goddess Saco.

“white mouse” — Colloquial expression for a police officer.

“Letter from Dr. Kleine” — The lawyer Dr. Heinz Kleine was one of five editors of the Juristenzeitung. In its issue of 9 May 1952, under the heading “Constitutional Law,” pp. 269–72, the journal discussed the danger posed to legislative authority by an expansion of the Federal Constitutional Court’s power of judicial review. The Court is described there as the “guardian of the constitution,” without any mention of Carl Schmitt.

11 June 1952

fame futura famelicus — See above, note to p. 179.

Fiat Justitia Pereat Mundus — “Let justice be done, even if the world perishes.” Motto of Emperor Ferdinand I, who reigned from 1556 to 1564.

18 June 1952

“Reply to Klug and Klein” — Klein = Kleine; see above, note to p. 275. Klug is probably the jurist Ulrich Klug (1913–1993).

“Konradin, Act 3, Scene 2” — Refers to Konrad Weiß’s drama Konradin von Hohenstaufen.

3 July 1952

Deus Venter — quorum deus venter, “whose god is their belly,” Vulgate, Philippians 3:19.

“Bibliography by Mr. Piet Tommissen” — Piet Tommissen (1925–2011), Belgian economist and sociologist, produced the first Carl Schmitt bibliography: Piet Tommissen, Versuch einer Carl-Schmitt-Bibliographie, Düsseldorf 1953; compiled in 1952, with a typescript in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 20492. It later appeared in expanded form in Festschrift für Carl Schmitt zum 70. Geburtstag dargebracht von Freunden und Schülern, ed. Hans Barion, Ernst Forsthoff, Werner Weber, 2nd unchanged ed., Berlin 1989, pp. 273–330.

“If Eduard Spranger confronts me with the questionnaire answer” — See C. Schmitt, “Gespräch mit Eduard Spranger.” In: ECS, pp. 9–12. The question “Are you a Christian?” does not appear there. On the relationship between Schmitt and Spranger, see Schmittiana V, 1996, pp. 205–7; Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 146–52.

13 July 1952

“Whoever says God means to deceive” (Proudhon) — Schmitt may be referring to Proudhon’s statement Dieu c’est le mal — “God is evil” — which Schmitt usually renders in the form “Whoever says humanity means to deceive.” See BdP, p. 55.

“Magnificent, what Günther Krauss says” — Günther Krauss, Homo homini homo. Zwölf Kapitel zur Relectio de Indis des Francisco de Vitoria, typescript habilitation thesis, n.d.; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 27110. Krauss’s attempt to qualify as a professor at the University of Bonn with this work failed; van Laak, p. 248, note 46. Schmitt wrote to Forsthoff in 1956 “that Krauss was bound to fail because of his own stubbornness.” BW Forsthoff, p. 127.

28 July 1952

“the zeal of Karl Thieme and Romano Guardini for persecution and compensation” — K. Thieme (1902–1963), historian and theologian. For the criticism of Schmitt by Thieme, a friend of Waldemar Gurian, see K. Thieme, “Carl Schmitts Apologie.” In: Deutsche Universitätszeitung, 17 November 1950, p. 18; see also BW Mohler, p. 123; van Laak, pp. 147–48.

R. Guardini (1885–1968), Catholic theologian, held the chair in Philosophy of Religion and Christian Worldview at the University of Berlin from 1923 until his forced retirement in 1939. Schmitt met him in Sombart’s house in 1930; see Tb. 1930–34.

“the grand seigneur of Pasel” — Peterheinrich Kirchhoff; see above, note to p. 75.

Jup — Josef Schmitt (1893–1970), physician and Carl Schmitt’s brother.

29 July 1952

Würmeling — Franz-Josef Würmeling (1900–1986), conservative politician and influential member of the CDU. In 1952 he introduced a bill in the Bundestag proposing the adoption of a first-past-the-post electoral system.

30 July 1952

“Jehovah, I mock you forever …” — Freely adapted from Heinrich Heine’s poem “Belsazar”:

Jehovah! I mock you forevermore — I am the King of Babylon!

“Nasses Brot, p. 137” — Richard Hasemann, Nasses Brot, Pfullingen 1952, an account of Russian captivity as a prisoner of war.

Pepysm — After Samuel Pepys; see above, note to p. 72.

5 August 1952

“A Caliban who knows Greek …” — Schmitt is speaking about Gerhard Nebel; see above, note to p. 269.

14 August 1952

“the old Marius’s seventh consulship” — Gaius Marius, c. 156–86 BC, died shortly after beginning his seventh consulship, which he assumed after returning from exile in Africa and taking revenge on his enemies.

13 September 1952

“Saint-Just on 13 November 1792” —

“There are noble souls who, in another age, would have said that a king should be put on trial not for the crimes committed during his rule but simply for the crime of having been king. For nothing in the world can legitimize this usurpation. Whatever illusions and conventions monarchy may wrap itself in, it is an eternal crime, against which every human being has the right to rise up and take arms.

“It is one of those outrages that not even the blindness of an entire people can justify. Such a people is guilty before nature because of the example it has set, and from nature all human beings receive the secret mission to exterminate domination in every country.”

Antoine L. de Saint-Just, Opinion concernant le jugement de Louis XVI. Séance du 13 novembre 1792, l’an premier de la République française. In: idem, Oeuvres de Saint-Just, Paris 1834, p. 7.

A. Koestler, Darkness at Noon — Schmitt read the book in French translation: Arthur Koestler, Le zéro et l’infini, Paris 1945. The first German translation appeared in 1946 under the title Sonnenfinsternis.

Rubashov — Nikolai Rubashov is the main character in Koestler’s Darkness at Noon. Schmitt is not quoting literally here, but only paraphrasing.

ecclesia non militans sed intrigans — “a Church that does not fight, but intrigues.”

“He was a man who noticed such things” — Correctly: “He was a man who used to notice such things.” Thomas Hardy, “Afterwards.” In: idem, The Collected Poems of Thomas Hardy, Ware 2002, p. 521.

“see Michel Mourre, Lam[ennais], p. 184” — Michel Mourre, Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes, Paris 1955. Since the book was not published until 1955, the remark must have been added later. This is also suggested by the fact that it appears on the verso in different ink. Schmitt did not meet the French historian Mourre (1928–1977) until 1954, through Mohler, who also sent him Mourre’s 1955 book on Lamennais. See the index to BW Mohler.

17 September 1952

“see Der Spiegel, 38/52” — The issue contains an article about Frank Lloyd Wright under the title “Der amerikanische Ausdruck.”

21 September 1952

“A note from the summer of 1914” — Tb 1912–15, p. 193.

“Guardini is a person” — Schmitt may be referring to Romano Guardini, Die Macht. Versuch einer Wegweisung, Würzburg 1951. Schmitt understood “power” differently; see BW Mohler, p. 161.

30 September 1952

Godenholm — Title of a story by Ernst Jünger.

5 October 1952

“Hobbes, De Cive, X § 3, note on Prometheus” — In the chapter Schmitt quotes, Hobbes compares different forms of government in order to argue for the superiority of monarchy. All other forms, according to Hobbes, are pieced together afterward from the wreckage of monarchy destroyed by human beings. He then adds this note:

“The ancients seem to have had this point in mind when they created the myth of Prometheus. They tell us that Prometheus, after stealing fire from the sun, formed man out of earth; and that as punishment from an enraged Jupiter he was condemned to have his liver continually eaten away.

“This means that human ingenuity, represented by Prometheus, borrowed laws and justice from monarchy by imitation; and that through them, like a fire taken away from its natural source, the multitude — the dirt and dregs of mankind — was given life and united into a civil person called aristocracy or democracy.

“But the authors and accomplices who might have lived securely and comfortably under the natural rule of kings must, once discovered, suffer the punishment of being placed in high office and tormented there by constant worries, suspicions, and disputes.”

Hobbes, M/B, pp. 176–77.

6 October 1952

“God can raise up from these stones …” — Matthew 3:9.

“Gneiß” — probably an old spelling of Gneis, gneiss, a rock composed of feldspar, quartz, and mica.

5 November 1952

“Without having shared the guilt of his contemporaries …” — Correctly:

“Live with your century, but do not become its creature. Give your contemporaries what they need, not what they praise. Without sharing their guilt, share their punishment with noble resignation, and freely submit to the yoke that they are equally incapable of doing without or of bearing.”

F. Schiller, Schriften, in Schillers Werke, vol. 4, Frankfurt am Main 1966, p. 217.

12 November 1952

“From a poem by Fontane” — Not Fontane, but from August Kopisch’s poem “Blücher am Rhein”:

The armies stopped beside the Rhine: Should we march into France this time? They pondered this and pondered that, until old Blücher simply said:

“Bring me the general map! Getting into France is no great task. Where is the enemy?” — “The enemy? Here!” “Put your finger on him! We’ll beat him there! Where is Paris? — Paris? Here!” “Put your finger on it! We’ll take it there! Now build the bridges across the Rhine! And I imagine the champagne wine tastes best of all where grows the vine!”

15 November 1952

“You are appointed by the strength of the center …” — From Konrad Weiß’s poem “Klage über der Schöpfung.” In: Weiß, p. 407.

16 November 1952

Conscientia vulnerata vulnere crescit; nomen vulneratum — Approximately:

“You can wound what is within a person, the spirit, and it will only grow through the wound. But once a name is damaged, it remains damaged.”

The saying cannot be found in Tertullian.

“And these Germans …” — Konrad Weiß, Konradin von Hohenstaufen. Ein Trauerspiel, Leipzig 1938, p. 115.

“in the presence of the Merkur from the left bank of the Rhine” — The reference is to the weekly newspaper Rheinischer Merkur, published in Bonn.

23 November 1952

“I do what I want …” — Weiß, p. 595.

25 November 1952

“the three-and-a-half-billion Böhm” — Under the Luxembourg Agreement of 10 September 1952, the Federal Republic of Germany undertook to pay 3.5 billion Deutsche Marks in reparations to Israel and the Jewish Claims Conference. The German side of the negotiations leading to the agreement was headed by the jurist, economist, and later CDU member of the Bundestag Franz Böhm.

11 December 1952

Michael Thomas — (1915–1995), born in Berlin as Ulrich Hollaender to a Jewish father. He began studying law there and attended lectures in 1933–34, including lectures by C. Schmitt. He later moved to Tübingen intending to complete a doctorate under Carlo Schmid, but abandoned his studies and emigrated to England in 1939. There he took the name Michael Thomas and joined the army.

After taking part in the invasion of continental Europe, he served as an occupation officer in Germany until 1950, after which he worked for the Hamburg trading company Coutinho, Caro & Co.

At a farewell gathering for Thomas at the Weinhaus Streng in Bonn in early 1951, he also invited Schmitt. Thomas found Schmitt’s antisemitic remarks unpleasant, but this evidently did not lead him to break off contact. See Michael Thomas, Deutschland, England über alles. Rückkehr als Besatzungsoffizier, Berlin 1984, pp. 268–69.

7 January 1953

“An actor could teach a pastor” — Goethe, Werke, Hamburg edition, vol. 3, p. 24.

“Who holds me when I am tired …” — Source not identified.

“Hegel, 1820: the uneducated person thinks abstractly” — In his essay “Wer denkt abstrakt?” Hegel describes the uneducated person as someone who sees everything only one-sidedly and from a restricted point of view — that is, abstractly. Hegel, Werke, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, Frankfurt am Main 1970, vol. 1, pp. 578–81.

“J. P. Sartre, December 1952 — Peace Congress in Vienna” — At the end of 1952, Sartre prohibited a performance in Vienna of his anti-communist play Dirty Hands, in breach of contract, because he intended to attend the Peace Congress then taking place in Vienna and did not want to anger the communists. See Der Spiegel, 1952, no. 48.

5 February 1953

“the Constitutional Court in a sad dilemma …” — This sentence sums up Schmitt’s criticism of the institution of constitutional review. He first formulated the argument in 1929 in “Das Reichsgericht als Hüter der Verfassung”; with an addition addressing the situation in Bonn, it was republished in 1958 in VA, pp. 63–109.

“Mr. Pringsheim” — Fritz Pringsheim (1882–1967), jurist, who was forced to emigrate to England because he was Jewish. Pringsheim had attacked Schmitt in 1933 over his position toward the Jews, and in 1950 he expressed outrage at Schmitt’s new publications with Greven-Verlag. See Schmittiana III, 1991, p. 50, note 1.

Schmitt wrote to Gretha Jünger on 15 May 1952:

“Professor Pringsheim in London — probably a maternal uncle of Golo Mann — is one of my worst persecutors …”

BW GJ, p. 164, with note 6 on p. 165. See also BW Mohler, pp. 291 ff.

Guido Vernani da Rimini — Correctly:

Ego autem credo, quod gens Iudeorum, et ratione situs terre … et ratione religionis … magis de iure debebat principari gentibus quam romani.

“I, however, believe that the Jewish people, both because of the location of their land … and because of their religion … had a greater right to rule over the gentiles than the Romans did.”

Guido Vernani da Rimini, Il più antico oppositore politico di Dante. Testo critico del “De Reprobatione Monarchiae”, ed. Nevio Matteini, Padua 1958, p. 106.

17 February 1953

“Desecration of my name” — See below, note to p. 309.

Tiso — Jozef Tiso (1887–1947), Catholic priest and, from 1939 to 1945, president of the First Slovak Republic, which collaborated with Hitler. After the war he was sentenced to death by a people’s court as a war criminal and executed. Schmitt’s claim that the Pope showed no interest in his case is false; an appeal for clemency by Pius XII was rejected.

Julius Rosenberg — (1918–1953), executed in the United States as a Soviet spy. Pope Pius XII unsuccessfully appealed on his behalf.

19 February 1953

“Black-market work is my delight! …” — A parody of the fourth stanza of Eichendorff’s poem “Heimweh.” See Joseph von Eichendorff, Gedichte Versepen, ed. Hartwig Schultz, Frankfurt am Main 1987, p. 253:

Morning is my delight! In the quiet hour I climb to the highest mountain and look into the distance, and from my heart I greet you, Germany!

Error in persona — “mistake about the identity of the person”; a term used in criminal law.

22 March 1953

“Heraclitus says this” — Fragment 54. In: Hermann Diels, ed., Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, Berlin 1903, p. 74.

Le secret de l’église catholique … — An allusion to Villiers de l’Isle-Adam; see above, note to p. 251. Schmitt wrote the sentence in Armin Mohler’s guest book in Paris on 9 May 1960; see BW d’Ors, p. 146.

21 May 1953

Bodin: de ne jamais braver la fureur populaire — “never to defy popular fury.” Schmitt quotes from Jean Bodin, Oeuvres philosophiques, text established, translated, and published by Pierre Mesnard, Corpus général des philosophes français: Auteurs modernes, 5/3, Paris 1951; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 26970.

17 July 1953

Galeazzi-Lisi — Dr. Roberto Galeazzi-Lisi (1891–1968), personal physician to Pius XII. Among other treatments, he used the fresh-cell therapy developed by Paul Niehans and supplied tabloid newspapers with reports about the Pope’s final agony.

21 July 1953

“in the form of a Jewish remigrant” — The reference is to Karl Löwenstein (1891–1973), who in 1945, as a legal adviser to the American military government, pushed for Schmitt’s arrest and the confiscation of his library. See Martin Tielke, “Die Bibliothek Carl Schmitts.” In: Schmittiana NF I, 2011, pp. 294 ff.

27 July 1953

Simone Weil — (1909–1943), French philosopher and mystic. Born Jewish, she moved toward Catholicism without formally converting. Schmitt is probably referring to her book Das Unglück und die Gottesliebe, translated by Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1953; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23477. See also Karl Epting, Der geistliche Weg der Simone Weil, Stuttgart 1955; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23454.

Epting — Karl Epting (1905–1979), scholar of Romance languages, active in National Socialist cultural policy in occupied France and head of the German Institute in Paris from 1940 to 1945. From 1946 to 1949 he was imprisoned in the French military prison Cherche-Midi. From 1949 to 1951 he worked as an editor at Greven-Verlag in Cologne, where he was responsible for Carl Schmitt’s works.

“Gueydan’s essay” — William [Guillermo] Gueydan de Roussel, “Leviathan et Homo. Hommage à Carl Schmitt.” In: Epirrhosis. Festschrift zum 65. Geburtstag am 11. 7. 1953, unpublished and inconsistently paginated typescript; Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 21368.

5 August 1953

“Bacon called himself …” — Correctly:

Quare existimamus nos sensus (a quo omnia in naturalibus petenda sunt, nisi forte libeat insanire) antistites religiosos, et oraculorum ejus non imperitos interpretes, nos praestitisse: ut alii professione quadam, nos re ipsa, sensum tueri ac colere videamur.

“For this reason I consider myself, as it were, a faithful priest of the senses — from which all knowledge of natural things must be drawn unless one wishes to go mad — and no unskilled interpreter of their oracles.”

Francis Bacon, Neues Organon, Latin-German ed. Wolfgang Krohn, Hamburg 1990, part 1, pp. 48–49.

Deinde etiam, tu scelere haud minore stultitiae apotheosin introduxisti, et vilissimas cogitationes religione munire ausus es.

“Then, in an offense no less serious, you introduced the deification of stupidity and dared to protect the vilest thoughts with religion.”

Francis Bacon, The Works of Francis Bacon, collected and edited by J. Spedding, R. L. Ellis, and D. D. Heath, vol. 3, London 1870, p. 531.

impar congressus Achilli —

Parte alia, amissis Troilus armis, Infelix puer atque impar congressus Achilli.

Virgil, Aeneid, Book 1, lines 474–75. In Voss’s translation:

“There too is Troilus, fleeing after losing his armor, an unhappy boy, unequal when he met Achilles.”

Nec tibi quam bellum longior ira fuit — From a distich by Marco Antonio Casanova on Pope Julius II:

Una dedit bellum, bellum lux sustulit una, Nec tibi quam bellum longior ira fuit.

“One day gave the war, one day brought the war to an end, and your anger lasted no longer than the war.”

Quoted in Joseph de Maistre, Du Pape, 9th ed., Lyon and Paris 1853, p. 192.

Pompeio scelus est bellum civile perempto / Quo fuerat vivente fides —

“After Pompey’s death, civil war is a crime; while he lived, it had been a proof of our loyalty.”

Pharsalia, IX, 248–49.

6 August 1953

“see Mirbt” — Schmitt is referring to Carl Mirbt, Quellen zur Geschichte des Papsttums und des römischen Katholizismus, 3rd rev. and expanded ed., Tübingen 1911; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 26089.

8 August 1953

“Essay by Jürgen Habermas” — J. Habermas, “Mit Heidegger gegen Heidegger denken.” In: Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 25 July 1953. In this review of Heidegger’s Einführung in die Metaphysik, Habermas protested against the unannotated republication of a Heidegger text dating from the 1930s. See BW Forsthoff, p. 97; van Laak, p. 89.

“Two souls and one thought …” — Inspired by Friedrich Halm, Gedichte, Stuttgart and Tübingen 1850, p. 165:

My heart, I want to ask you: what is love? Tell me true. “Two souls and a single thought, two hearts that beat as two.”

18 August 1953

Moju — Moritz Julius Bonn; see 26 December 1953. The words “has meanwhile triumphed” probably refer to the publication of M. J. Bonn, So macht man Geschichte, Munich 1953.

30 August 1953

“Attack in Das Schwarze Korps” — The SS sharply attacked Schmitt twice in its journal at the end of 1936: “Eine peinliche Ehrenrettung,” Das Schwarze Korps, 3 December 1936; and “Es wird immer noch peinlicher,” ibid., 10 December 1936.

Vestrum scelus, meus somnus — Augustine, De civitate Dei, Book 17, chapter 18:

Quid agitis vani? Quod vestrum scelus erit, meus somnus erit.

“What are you doing, vain men? What is your crime will be only my sleep.”

Aurelius Augustine, Vom Gottesstaat, trans. Wilhelm Thimme, Munich 1978, vol. 2, p. 405.

“Ps. 40:6” — This follows the numbering of the Vulgate. In modern numbering: Psalm 41:6.

9 September 1953

“Being and appearance …” — After Ferdinand Hardekopf, “Zwiegespräch.” In: idem, Gesammelte Dichtungen, Zurich 1963, p. 169:

Dialogue became a magic text, a necromancer’s play; from both sides there was conjured forth whatever pleased the spirit, whatever seemed an appearance to the senses, whatever appearance itself devised. Appearance gave meaning, and meaning gave it appearance, and time passed away.

δόξα — “opinion,” in the sense of mere opinion, illusion, or appearance.

12 September 1953

“I am reading Ch. Fourier” — Charles Fourier, Théorie de l’unité universelle, Oeuvres complètes, vol. 4, Paris 1841, pp. 407 ff.

Loin de ce calme plat … — Ibid., p. 399.

24 September 1953

“this McCarthy” — Joseph McCarthy (1908–1957), Republican senator from Wisconsin whose name became associated with the anti-communist campaign in the United States in the early 1950s. Schmitt also described the episode on the train in a letter to Walter Petwaidic dated 10 September 1953, printed in Kai Burkhardt, ed., Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013, p. 121.

29 September 1953

“Only he who can conquer …” — See above, note to p. 236.

“re-education of Carl Schmitt” — See above, note to p. 136.

27 October 1953

“In Theodor Wiesengrund Adorno’s Minima Moralia” — Th. W. Adorno, Minima Moralia, Frankfurt am Main 1969, p. 255.

9 December 1953

Petwaidic — Walter Petwaidic (1904–1978), who wrote under the pseudonym Walter Fredericia, journalist at the weekly newspaper Die Zeit.

Bourdin — Paul Bourdin (1900–1955), editor-in-chief of Die Welt and commentator for the weekly newspaper Die Zeit.

22 December 1953

“Statement by Lorenz von Stein” — Schmitt refers to Lorenz von Stein, Geschichte der sozialen Bewegung in Frankreich von 1789 bis auf unsere Tage, ed. Gottfried Salomon, Munich 1921, vol. 2, p. 11; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 25087. See C. Schmitt, “Die Stellung Lorenz von Steins in der Geschichte des 19. Jahrhunderts.” In: SGN, pp. 156–65.

26 December 1953

“Federal Constitutional Court judgment of 17 December 1953” — The judgment held that all civil-service employment relationships had ended on 8 May 1945.

Le Pal — Title of a weekly newspaper written entirely by Léon Bloy, of which four issues appeared in 1885. A fifth issue was assembled in 1935 from texts Bloy had intended for it. A new annotated complete edition appeared in 1979: L. Bloy, Le Pal, notes and prefaces by Daniel Habrekorn, complete edition revised and corrected against the originals, Vanves 1979.

Das Brandmal — Emmy Hennings, Das Brandmal. Ein Tagebuch, Berlin 1920; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 22103. Emmy Hennings was the wife of Hugo Ball.

temerataque jura relinquo — “Here I leave peace behind, and violated law.” Pharsalia, I, 225. The words are spoken by Caesar after crossing the Rubicon. Schmitt quoted the line repeatedly; see Dirk Blasius, Carl Schmitt. Preußischer Staatsrat in Hitlers Reich, Göttingen 2001, pp. 69–70; Gespräch, pp. 171–72; BW EJ, p. 446. As late as the end of 1983, he used it as a dedication to Christian Meier; see Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte, IV/3, 2010, p. 104.

“Carry your incomprehended heart to the dead” — Friedrich Schiller, Demetrius, Act 1:

Go down in silence, and carry to the dead your undiscovered, incomprehended heart.

“Do not let yourself be invited and then disinvited again” — Hans Schomerus, director of the Evangelical Academy in Herrenalb, had invited Schmitt to a conference on “Conservatives and Reactionaries” scheduled for 7–10 May 1953 and asked him to give a lecture on “The Antichrist and Creation.” The invitation went back to a discussion Schmitt had had with Wilhelm Stapel in 1942 about the katechon.

Schomerus also asked him to speak at a conference on the island of Mainau from 16–18 May on the theme “A New Approach to Shakespeare.”

Schmitt immediately accepted, but wanted the title of the first lecture changed to “The Antichrist and What Holds Him Back,” and the title of the second to “Hamlet, God’s Player.”

After protests from Adolf Arndt, Gustav Heinemann, Walter Strauss, and others, Regional Bishop Julius Bender ordered that Schmitt be disinvited.

On 5 May, Schmitt received a telegram from Schomerus:

“Both lectures prohibited by bishop.”

See Schomerus’s letters to Schmitt, RW 265 nos. 14493–14498; Schmitt’s letters to Schomerus, RW 265 nos. 13505–13506; BW Forsthoff, pp. 396–97.

12 March 1954

tutela praesens — “present protection.” Refers to Horace, Carmina IV, 14.43. In: idem, Sämtliche Werke. Lateinisch und deutsch, 10th ed., Munich and Zurich 1985, p. 206.

For Schmitt, tutela praesens was an essential part of political representation:

“Representation is nothing if it is not tutela praesens.”

Leviathan, p. 53.

“Bonald said” —

Dieu existe avant la société des hommes intelligents, et la création n’a fait que le produire à l’univers. Donc Dieu existe avant l’homme; donc Dieu est cause, et l’homme est effet.

“God exists before the society of intelligent human beings, and creation merely brought him forth into the universe. Therefore God exists before man; therefore God is the cause, and man the effect.”

L. G. A. de Bonald, Oeuvres complètes, published by Migne, vol. 1, Paris 1859, col. 481.

tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata — “the Moselle flowing with a quiet murmur — namely, the Moselle before it had been canalized.”

With tacito rumore Mosella, Schmitt, whose ancestors came from the Moselle region, quotes the poem Mosella by the late Roman poet Decimus Magnus Ausonius. See ECS, p. 10.

When plans to canalize the Moselle were being considered in the 1950s, Schmitt added the qualification. For example, in a letter to E. Jünger dated 30 December 1955, he wrote:

“In the ‘Conversation with Spranger’ in Ex Captivitate Salus it should read: tacito rumore Mosella sc. nondum canalisata. I am therefore your uncanalizable Moselle man.”

BW EJ, pp. 288–89.

15 March 1954

“They harp away at the devastation …” — Possibly a parody of Rilke’s poem “Das jüngste Gericht.”

16 March 1954

“Aldous Huxley recommends that we …” — Der Spiegel, no. 10, 3 March 1954, reviewed Aldous Huxley’s book The Doors of Perception, in which Huxley describes his experience with mescaline, under the title “Ersatz für Alkohol” — “A Substitute for Alcohol.”

1 June 1954 — newspaper clipping

“Encyclical 1930” — Correctly: 1939; see above, note to p. 274.

Laicus taceat in et extra ecclesiam … — “The layman shall remain silent both inside and outside the Church, unless he is cheering the competent ecclesiastical superior.” An allusion to 1 Corinthians 14:34.

9 June 1954

“The convert, Mr. Hausenstein” — Wilhelm Hausenstein converted to Catholicism in 1940. Schmitt was generally suspicious of converts:

“[…] I cannot stand converts.”

Gespräch, p. 56. See also above, pp. 99–100, on Helmut Rumpf, and below, p. 330, on Simone Weil and Edith Stein.

9 July 1954

“I have founded my cause on nothing” — Opening line of Goethe’s poem “Vanitas! Vanitatum vanitas!”, written in 1806 as a parody of a hymn by Adam Reußner. See J. W. Goethe, Gedichte. Vollständige Ausgabe, Stuttgart, n.d. [c. 1959], p. 98.

Ne joco quidem — “I am certainly not joking.”

Anton Kuh — (1890–1941), Austrian writer and feuilletonist. Schmitt is probably referring to A. Kuh, Juden und Deutsche. Ein Résumé, Berlin 1921, reprint Hamburg 2012, in which Kuh describes the Jews as marked by a “guilt of lineage.”

15 July 1954

“But I know my Oppenheimers” — A large and widely branched German-Jewish family. Schmitt probably means above all the liberal economist Franz Oppenheimer (1864–1943), who was hostile to the state. See BdP, p. 75; BW Mohler, p. 343; BW Forsthoff, pp. 205, 458.

Heinz Weitzel — (1902–1990), lawyer at the Hengeler-Müller firm, in which several members of the Oppenheimer family had worked until 1933. Weitzel had known Schmitt since the proceedings concerning the nationalization of the Buderus works; see BW Forsthoff, pp. 212, 462.

26 July 1954

“for 25 August 1930” — The thirtieth anniversary of Nietzsche’s death.

1 August 1954

“We jump from one ice floe to another” — Schmitt wrote in 1922 in Der Schatten Gottes:

“I live in a raging current, on a melting ice floe. Perhaps I can save myself onto the next one and, by jumping from one to another, keep myself above water for a while. But no shore is in sight, no shore.”

Tb 1921–24, pp. 406–7.

Schmitt wrote in 1930 in “Staatsethik und pluralistischer Staat”:

“Perhaps there are a few agile and mobile individuals who manage the trick of keeping themselves free beside the many powerful social groups, as one jumps from one ice floe to another. But this acrobatic kind of freedom cannot be demanded from the mass of ordinary citizens as a normal ethical duty.”

PuB, p. 157.

Werner Schütz — (1900–1975), jurist and CDU politician, Minister of Education and Cultural Affairs in North Rhine-Westphalia from 1954 to 1956 and again from 1958 to 1962.

30 August 1954

Un sot trouve toujours un plus sot … — “A fool always finds a greater fool …” Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, L’Art poétique, Canto I. In: idem, Oeuvres de Boileau Despréaux à l’usage des collèges royaux et des écoles secondaires, Tours 1838, p. 167.

12 September 1954

“the question as it stood in the spring of 1933” — In his book Der christliche Epimetheus, Konrad Weiß discusses in 1933 what he calls the “pairing of a conservative German spirit with the actual current of the new German party movement”:

“The more a person, in the certainty of a fruitful and wide-ranging contemplation, feels history resting within itself, the less hurried and compliant he will be in action.

“And yet the age now stands within an antithesis, in the most tangible division imaginable, defined at this moment by inner tension and by contrary meanings opposed to the more ‘objective’ tendencies and emphases on values. From within this division, one is led to ask, at a higher level: what will now contribute more to meaning and to the inner image — the more conservative political style, or the fanatical and limitless commitment thrown wholly onto a single point?

“What once determined the growth of the inner image: the maturity of a world-form that knows what it is and finds expression within conservatism, or the future approaching through the speechlessness of barbarians who act under a continual pressure of necessity?”

K. Weiß, Der christliche Epimetheus, Potsdam 1933, p. 92.

1 November 1954

“Meanwhile, however, Mr. L. has triumphed” — Karl Löwenstein.

14 November 1954

“I read in a diary entry of 3 February 1941: I am Benito Cereno” — Gretha Jünger reports on 2 February 1941 on conversations with Schmitt about Benito Cereno. G. von Jeinsen [= G. Jünger], Die Palette, Hamburg 1949, pp. 46–47.

12 December 1954

L’initié tue l’initiateur — “The initiate kills the initiator.” See above, p. 112.

On 30 November 1954 Schmitt sent his “Gespräch über die Macht” to Nicolaus Sombart and inscribed this sentence from Ballanche as a dedication.

As Sombart’s relationship with Schmitt became increasingly critical in the 1960s, Schmitt repeatedly returned to the sentence and saw in it an explanation for Nicolaus Sombart’s behavior toward him. See BW Sombart, pp. 64–65, note 150, and p. 127.

lingua occidistis — This does not occur in the Good Friday liturgy. It comes instead from St. Augustine’s commentary on the Psalms:

Et vos, o Iudaei, occidistis. Unde occidistis? Gladio linguae.

“And you, O Jews, have killed. With what did you kill? With the sword of the tongue.”

See also Tb 1930–34, p. 421.

“It takes only one Jew” — Correctly:

“It is certainly difficult to remain patient; but one must remember that it takes only one beggar Jew to mock a God on the cross.”

Goethe, letter to Carl Ludwig von Knebel, 12 January 1814. In: Goethe, Werke, Weimar edition, section IV, vol. 24, p. 99.

“Desecration and slaughter by Carl Linfert on NWDR” — On 22 November 1954, Nordwestdeutscher Rundfunk repeated Schmitt’s “Gespräch über die Macht,” which Hessischer Rundfunk had already broadcast on 22 June, now under the title “Macht — so gefährlich wie immer, so verdächtig wie nie” — “Power — As Dangerous as Ever, As Suspect as Never Before.”

Carl Linfert (1900–1981), head of NWDR’s late-night educational programming, introduced the broadcast with a very cautious disclaimer. Schmitt commented on this to Mohler:

“The NWDR broadcast of my conversation was introduced by Carl Linfert, with endless apologies, as though something were about to follow that God had forbidden.”

BW Mohler, p. 183. Schmitt made a similar remark in a letter to Rolf Hinder; see Schmittiana V, 1996, p. 173.

See also G. Giesler’s afterword, p. 80, in C. Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber, Stuttgart 2008, and Monika Boll, Nachtprogramm. Intellektuelle Gründungsdebatten in der frühen Bundesrepublik, Münster 2004, p. 103, note 39.

Memor approbii — “I keep the applause in my memory.”

30 January 1955

homicidae , et manent — Vulgate, Acts 7:52: “You were murderers.” The early Christian preacher and first martyr Stephen accuses the Jews of murdering the prophets. The addition et manent — “and they remain so” — is not in the Bible and was added by Schmitt.

The biblical passages that follow contain the parable of the workers in the vineyard who kill the vineyard owner’s son in order to seize the inheritance.

Quid timidi estis! Et facta est tranquillitas magna — Vulgate, Matthew 8:26:

et dicit eis quid timidi estis modicae fidei tunc surgens imperavit ventis et mari et facta est tranquillitas magna.

“And he said to them: Why are you afraid, you of little faith? Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.”

14 February 1955

“Tarnbruder John” — Otto John (1909–1997), first president of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, from 1950 to 1954. On 20 July 1954 he went to East Germany, probably under duress, and criticized the Federal Republic for the growing influence of former National Socialists.

In 1955 he escaped back to West Berlin, was charged with treason, and sentenced to four years in prison. He was later pardoned. According to current historical understanding, he was innocent.

19 March 1955

Ne simus faciles in nominibus — See above, note to p. 15.

Νόμος Basileus — For an explanation of the concept, see Nomos, pp. 42 ff.

20 March 1955

“The stump-and-style spirit of Mr. Böhm” — Franz Böhm wrote in the letter mentioned:

“An end to denazification? Good. I would never have started it in the first place.

“But anyone who understands ‘an end to denazification’ to mean the rehabilitation and restoration of the Nazis, their ways of thinking, and their political methods will have to accept that there is a gulf between him and the other Germans greater than the gulf separating us from even the most foreign inhabitants of any country on this planet — indeed, even from enemies of Germany who think justly.

“German is not a biological concept but a spiritual one. It includes sinners and dubious characters of every kind, including criminals. But it does not include people who concern themselves with integrating National Socialism, in any form, into our historical and political tradition …”

In: Frankfurter Hefte 10, 1955, p. 167.

3 April 1955

“Kojève, Introduction” — Schmitt is referring to Alexandre Kojève, Introduction à la lecture de Hegel. Leçons sur la phénoménologie de l’esprit professées de 1933 à 1939 à l’École des hautes-études, collected and published by Raymond Queneau, Paris 1947; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 24734.

“he took his own life” — Schmitt gives no page reference, but he is probably referring to the following passage:

The individual “experiences the double meaning contained in what it did, namely that it took its life; it took its own life, but in doing so it rather seized death.”

G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes, Sämtliche Werke, ed. H. Glockner, vol. 2, p. 282.

“So eating and drinking can be called a form of knowing” — H.-R. Müller-Schwefe, “Erkenntnis und Wort Gottes.” In: Freundschaftliche Begegnungen. Festschrift für Ernst Jünger zum 60. Geburtstag, ed. Armin Mohler, Frankfurt am Main 1955, pp. 56–74; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23095.

“Taking, dividing, pasturing” — See C. Schmitt, “Nehmen / Teilen / Weiden. Ein Versuch die Grundfragen jeder Sozial- und Wirtschaftsordnung vom Nomos her richtig zu stellen.” In: VA, pp. 489–504; first published in 1953.

“Gelimer’s laughter” — Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals, was decisively defeated in 533 by the Byzantine general Belisarius, bringing the Vandals’ historical existence to an end. Gelimer responded to the destruction of his kingdom with grim laughter.

Schmitt identified with this reaction as the laughter of a defeated man to such an extent that he gave Book V of the Glossarium the heading “Gelimer.” See the appendix; see also above, p. 371. See BW EJ, pp. 353, 454–55; Reinhard Mehring, “Das Lachen der Besiegten. Das Lachen Gelimers.” In: Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte 4, 2012, no. 1, pp. 32–45; Martin Tielke, “Habent sua fata libelli et balli.” In: Sinn und Form 64, 2012, pp. 466–67.

“see my diary entry of 6 April 1933” —

“… at 7:45 by taxi to Popitz for the press reception. Saw Hitler and Goebbels. Saw both clearly. Great excitement. Hitler like the greedy bull in the arena. Shaken by that look.”

Tb 1930–34, p. 279. See also Gespräch, p. 105.

H. Recknagel — The commercial lawyer Heinz Recknagel asked Schmitt for the work because the German consul in Malmö, Dr. Meyer, had advised him to read it so that he could better understand the policies of the Soviet Union, where Recknagel had contacts. See his letter to Schmitt of 8 December 1958; RW 265 no. 11334.

10 April 1955

Cor ne edito — “Do not eat your heart out”; a proverb meaning: “Don’t worry.” anthropophagus cordis mei — “The devourer of my own heart.”

16 April 1955

to E. Forsthoff — Not in BW Forsthoff!

17 April 1955

to Kojève, 9 May 1955 — In: Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 101. Kojève, his letter of 2 May 1955 — In: Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 100. Jews who recognized the grotesque insolence of this E. K. — See Kurt Hiller, “Der Fall Erich Kaufmann.” In: idem, Köpfe und Tröpfe, Hamburg 1948, pp. 74–80.

During Kempner’s interrogation of Schmitt, Schmitt’s mention of E. Kaufmann was a tactical chess move. In the Wilhelmstrasse Trial, Kempner later called Kaufmann as a witness and tried to discredit him as a nationalist and militarist; see Carl Schmitt – Antworten in Nürnberg. Edited and annotated by Helmut Quaritsch, Berlin 2000, pp. 42 ff.

9 May 1955

Farewell song of the old Moselle man — Under the title “Gesang des alten Mosellaners 1957” (“Song of the Old Moselle Man, 1957”), Schmitt also sent this poem to A. Kojève (see Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 123) and to A. Mohler (BW Mohler, p. 232). See also the note above on p. 305.

Törwang — A village in Upper Bavaria where E. Forsthoff had a holiday home and where Schmitt visited him in May 1955.

5 June 1955

In Göttingen, manly professors have … — When the right-wing nationalist Leonard Schlüter, representing the FDP in the Lower Saxony state government, was appointed Minister of Education and Cultural Affairs at the end of May 1955, the University of Göttingen mounted a major protest. As a result, Schlüter submitted his resignation on 9 June. See Heinz-Georg Marten, Der niedersächsische Ministersturz. Proteste und Widerstand der Georg-August-Universität Göttingen gegen den Kultusminister Schlüter im Jahre 1955, Göttingen 1987. See also Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 108 f.; BW Forsthoff, pp. 502 f.; BW Mohler, p. 200.

9 June 1955

“It is for it …” — Correctly:

“As it thus grasps itself, it is as though the world were only now coming into being for it. Before this, it does not understand the world; it desires it and works upon it, withdraws from it into itself, and destroys it for itself, while also destroying itself as consciousness—as consciousness of the world as essence, and as consciousness of its nothingness. Only here, after the grave of its truth has been lost, and after the destruction of its reality has itself been destroyed … does it discover the world as its new real world.”

G. F. W. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 179.

yesterday I wrote to Kojève — Correctly: on 7 June; see Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 108 ff.

11 June 1955

to Wirsing — Giselher Wirsing (1907–1975), journalist. In the 1920s he belonged to the Tat circle around Hans Zehrer and, until 1945, served as an editor of various periodicals. In 1948 he was a co-founder of the weekly newspaper Christ und Welt, which he edited as editor-in-chief from 1954 to 1970. During the 1950s, Wirsing was an important supporter of Schmitt in the press. See Kai Burkhardt (ed.), Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013.

9 August 1955

when the jurist Sir Edward Coke told the king … —

“…when Coke said before the king, that ‘his Majesty was defended by the laws,’ James, in anger, told him he spoke foolishly, and he said he was not defended by the laws, but by God (alluding to his ‘divine right’).”

Isaac Disraeli, The Literary Character or, The History of Men of Genius. Drawn from Their Own Feelings and Confessions. Literary Miscellanies; and an Inquiry into the Character of James the First. A new ed. (The Works of Isaac Disraeli, [4]), London etc. 1859, p. 423.

15 August 1955

Adolf Caspary — (1898–1953), jurist, emigrated to the United States in 1942. Schmitt had contact with him in 1932 (see Tb 1930–34, p. 184) and refers approvingly above, p. 63, to Caspary’s 1927 book Die Maschinenutopie.

Leo Strauss — (1899–1973), political philosopher. On his relationship with Schmitt, see Heinrich Meier, Carl Schmitt, Leo Strauss und „Der Begriff des Politischen“. Zu einem Dialog unter Abwesenden, 3rd ed., Stuttgart/Weimar 2013.

Walter Benjamin — (1892–1940), philosopher, literary critic, and translator. See Susanne Heil, „Gefährliche Beziehung“. Walter Benjamin und Carl Schmitt, Stuttgart/Weimar 1996; Michael Rumpf (ed.), “Briefwechsel Michael Rumpf – Carl Schmitt.” In: Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 275–285.

under the impact of the words “sacrifice for life …” — Schmitt repeatedly worked through Benjamin’s book on German tragic drama with great intensity; see Reinhard Mehring, “Geist ist das Vermögen, Diktatur auszuüben. Carl Schmitts Marginalien zu Walter Benjamin.” In: idem, Kriegstechniker des Begriffs. Biographische Studien zu Carl Schmitt, Tübingen 2014, pp. 132–152; Jürgen Thaler, “Genial. Carl Schmitt liest Walter Benjamin.” In: Marcel Atze/Volker Kaukoreit (eds.), Lesespuren – Spurenlesen oder Wie kommt die Handschrift ins Buch? Von sprechenden und stummen Annotationen, Vienna 2011, pp. 246–251.

23 August 1955

Pleasure conceives and gives birth to sin — 1 John 2:16; see above, p. 315.

1 September 1955

Michel Mourre, Lamennais p. 141 — Michel Mourre, Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes, Paris 1955.

Have I not done exactly the same myself with Adam Müller — In: PR.

14 September 1955

The world in which Prof. Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines — Grewe, who from 1950 onward advised Adenauer in negotiations with the victorious powers of the Second World War, took part in the 1955 trip to Moscow. There he was less willing than Adenauer to make concessions to the Soviets. He is regarded as the originator of the Hallstein Doctrine.

The full-blooded Moju can do that better — This refers to Moritz Julius Bonn, who took part in the negotiations over the Treaty of Versailles as a member of the German delegation in 1919 and was appointed adviser to the Reich Chancellor on reparations in 1920.

15 September 1955

Johann Jacob Reiske — (1716–1774), German scholar of Greek, Arabic, and Byzantine studies. In his works, Wilamowitz-Moellendorff repeatedly drew attention to Reiske’s philological achievements, which went unrecognized for many years.

15 September 1955

Come along, Cohn — From Theodor Fontane’s poem “An meinem Fünfundsiebzigsten” (“On My Seventy-Fifth Birthday”), which ends:

I was something to everyone, They all read me, They had all known me for ages, And that is the main thing … “come along, Cohn.”

21 September 1955

the anti-Roman feeling of the historian Fritz Kern — Kern (1884–1950) became Schmitt’s colleague at the University of Bonn in 1922. On 5 May 1923 Schmitt wrote about him in his diary: “I dislike him; a Protestant professor.” (Tb 1921–24, p. 192). Kern converted to Catholicism in 1949.

30 September 1955

“That is the true taking of land” —

“Again and again, from the tangled outlines of the Littorale, the Saracen tower emerged, gradually growing smaller as the perspective changed, a pale shape amid the solitude of rock and sea. At every bend I was glad to see it again, the guardian of a southern territory that had become for me a piece of spiritual homeland. That is the true taking of land.”

E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 6, p. 315.

4 October 1955

Konrad Beyerle — (1872–1933), jurist and politician, co-author of the Weimar Constitution. Article 153 of the Weimar Constitution—corresponding to Article 14 of the German Basic Law—guaranteed property, but also stated:

“Property entails obligations. Its use should also serve the common good.”

This led to a debate lasting several years over the expropriation of the former princely houses. A popular initiative supported expropriation in 1926, but the referendum that followed did not. The attempted expropriation of the princes therefore failed.

5 October 1955

My cousin André — André Steinlein (1891–1964), son of the younger brother of Schmitt’s mother, whom Schmitt had known since their school days. On 16 December 1954, Schmitt wrote to Nicolaus Sombart about his ambivalent relationship with him:

“…But I still have to coordinate matters with my Lorraine cousin, an aging bon vivant who, after a typically bourgeois life as a notary, has retreated into a rural backwater on the Seille. Yet, from old habit—we have somehow kept running into one another ever since our youth—I am very fond of him; if only because the old saying applies to him in a typical way: il n’y a pas de notaire qui n’ait rêvé de sultan—there is no notary who has not dreamed of being a sultan.”

(BW Sombart, pp. 67 f.)

6 October 1955

Hear the Nobel Prize prophet — This refers to Max Born (1882–1970), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1954. Schmitt is quoting M. Born, “Das entscheidende Motiv. Eine Erwiderung.” In: Merkur, 1955, no. 92, p. 999.

14 October 1955

Alfons Adams — (1899–1973), philosopher, brother of Paul Adams.

Good Friday of the spirit — See G. F. W. Hegel, Glauben und Wissen. In: idem, Werke, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 2, p. 432. Hegel’s spelling of Karfreitag has been modernized here.

Mount of Olives of world history — See Konrad Weiß, Zum geschichtlichen Gethsemane, Mainz 1919, reprint Bigge n.d. [1945], pp. 185 ff.

κληρο-νόμος — “the heir.”

Vigens disciplina, Fides moribunda — “The discipline [of the Church] flourishing, faith dying.” Vigens ecclesiae disciplina is a term from canon law.

26 October 1955

Wilhelm Wackernagel says — W. Wackernagel (1806–1869), Germanist and art historian, professor in Basel from 1835. Schmitt is referring to Wilhelm Wackernagel, Über die dramatische Poesie, Basel 1838. See Carl Schmitt, Hamlet oder Hekuba, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 51, with note 21 on pp. 72 f. (first published 1956).

report on Adolf Grabowsky — A. Grabowsky (1880–1969), geopolitician, lecturer at the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik from 1921 to 1933, published Gott und der Zauberer. Ein Mythos, Berlin 1912. Schmitt’s report on it is in his papers, RW 265 no. 19394.

Pierre Leyris — (1907–2001), translator and literary critic. Schmitt means: H. Melville, Benito Cereno (Biblioteca Zig Zag, 19), Santiago de Chile 1944. On pp. 130–142 appears P. Leyris, “Reflexiones sobre ‘Benito Cereno’.” Leyris had already published an annotated French translation of Benito Cereno, with a preface, in 1937.

28 October 1955

May 1953 in Herrenalb — See the note above on p. 304.

It took that article in the Linksrheinischer Merkur — Eduard Rosenbaum, “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.” In: Rheinischer Merkur no. 48, 25 November 1950.

Again and again I fell for the deception — Schmitt is quoting himself here: ECS, p. 88; see also the entries above for 11 February 1948 and 11 August 1950.

6 November 1955

Friedrich Glum — F. Glum, Philosophen im Spiegel und Zerrspiegel. Deutschlands Weg in den Nationalismus und Nationalsozialismus, Munich 1954.

Rüdiger Altmann — (1922–2000), jurist, political writer, and political adviser. At the end of the war he studied under Schmitt, later under Wolfgang Abendroth. Schmitt quotes the essay “Was heißt christliche Demokratie?” by Friedrich Grund, probably a pseudonym for Rüdiger Altmann. In: Civis. Zeitschrift für christlich-demokratische Politik 2, 1955, no. 11, pp. 57–58. The sentence:

“In fact, today there is no substantive ethic in the Western cultural sphere other than the Christian one”

appears on p. 57.

10 November 1955

Karl Korn — K. Korn, “Kyklos. Zu F. G. Jüngers neuen Gedichten.” In: Berliner Hefte für geistiges Leben 3, 1948, pp. 42–55.

La nullité protège mieux. L’ambiguité protège mieux — “Nothingness protects better. Ambiguity protects better.” A variation on Rivarol’s frequently quoted maxim, L’obscurité protège mieux—“Obscurity protects better.” See the note above on p. 158.

With The Origin of Species in 1859 — Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favored Races in the Struggle for Life, London 1859.

The secret of eating bread … —

“…those who affirm the truth and certainty of the reality of sensory objects [can] be told that they must be sent back to the lowest school of wisdom, namely the ancient Eleusinian mysteries of Ceres and Bacchus, and must first learn the secret of eating bread and drinking wine…”

G. W. F. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 91.

Brothers of the gently living flesh — Thomas Müntzer called Luther “the soft-living flesh of Wittenberg.”

It is the hump … — See above, p. 131.

11 November 1955

And powers of delusion … — Theodor Däubler, “Hymne an Sizilien.” In: idem, Dichtungen und Schriften. Edited by Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1956, p. 86.

Peter Schneider — (1920–2002), Swiss jurist, assistant to Carlo Schmid. In 1955 he completed his postdoctoral qualification with the study Ausnahmezustand und Norm. Eine Studie zur Rechtslehre von Carl Schmitt, Stuttgart 1957. Schmitt first learned of Schneider in 1953 through A. Mohler; see BW Mohler (index) and BW Huber, pp. 374 ff.

16 November 1955

Simone Weil, Karl Epting — See the note above on p. 299.

17 November 1955

The poor celibate bureaucracy — Schmitt coined the term “celibate bureaucracy” in 1923; see RK, p. 6; Gespräch, p. 57.

18 November 1955

Edith Stein, who had herself baptized and became impenetrable within the religious order — E. Stein (1891–1942), philosopher and women’s rights advocate. She converted from Judaism to Catholicism in 1922 and entered the strict Carmelite order. She was murdered at Auschwitz and canonized in 1998.

concept of the chosen one — See the note above on p. 208.

23 November 1955

Caux — Swiss resort town, known from 1946 onward as an international conference center for Moral Re-Armament.

24 November 1955

Above my cap … — Parody of Goethe; see the note above on p. 170.

Rolf Schroers — (1919–1981), writer; see van Laak, pp. 251–255.

article by Baron von der Heydte in Hochland — Friedrich August von der Heydte, “Heil aus der Gefangenschaft? Carl Schmitt und die Lage der europäischen Rechtswissenschaft.” In: Hochland 43, 1950/51, pp. 288–294; see also the note above on p. 210.

28 November 1955

Julian Huxley — (1887–1975), English biologist and researcher of animal behavior. Schmitt is referring to J. Huxley, Entfaltung des Lebens (Fischer Bücherei, 61), Frankfurt am Main/Hamburg 1954. A copy containing annotations is in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 26715.

all the Walter Ottos and all the Schadewaldts — Walter F. Otto (1874–1958), classical scholar; Wolfgang Schadewaldt (1900–1974), classical scholar. Both studied the continuing influence of Greek mythology and religion.

4 December 1955

in an article in Junge Wirtschaft — Winfried Martini, “Ein gefährliches Provisorium.” In: Junge Wirtschaft. Zeitschrift für fortschrittliches Unternehmertum, 1955, no. 11, pp. 404–405.

19 December 1955

a poisonous Morgenthau type — This refers to Franz Borkenau (1900–1957), Marxist sociologist and philosopher of history. Schmitt is referring to F. Borkenau, “Spengler – Weitergedacht. Eine Antwort an seine Kritiker.” In: Der Monat 8, 1955, pp. 46–55. The quotation beginning “The malice …” appears on p. 48.

… non canalisata, non canalisabilis — “…not channeled, not capable of being channeled”; see the note above on p. 305.

miching mallecho. It means mischief — See the note above on p. 271.

We Christian folk now have joy — Opening line of a Christmas hymn by Kaspar Füger (1521–1592), also used as an organ chorale by J. S. Bach.

26 December 1955

to Sombart, to Jünger — Schmitt’s letter of 26 December 1955 to Nicolaus Sombart ends with the sentence:

“I wish you and your wife happiness and good health in the New Year and remain, on this side and beyond every boundary of age and market, your eternally unchannelable Moselle man.”

(BW Sombart, p. 85). Similar wording in BW EJ, p. 289.

4 January 1956

lecture by Hermann Heimpel — The historian Heimpel (1901–1988), professor at the Reich University of Strasbourg from 1941 to 1944 and a friend of E. R. Huber, spoke on NDR—not NWDR—at 6:25 p.m. on 1 January 1956 under the title “Was verlangt das neue Jahr?” (“What Does the New Year Demand?”).

No longer the Jews … — The 1906 Catechism of the Catholic Church stated that Jesus was condemned to death because Pilate “cowardly gave in to the threatening pressure of the people of Jerusalem.” In the 1955 catechism the wording became:

“The Son of God was rejected by the leaders of the chosen people.”

(Kath. Katechismus der Bistümer Deutschlands, Freiburg 1955, p. 53). In the revised catechism of 2005, this became “some leaders.”

Sovereign is he who decides on the state of exception. — Schmitt formulated this not in 1921 but in 1922, in Political Theology. The problem of the exception had, however, already been discussed systematically in 1921 in Carl Schmitt, Die Diktatur. Von den Anfängen des modernen Souveränitätsgedankens bis zum proletarischen Klassenkampf, 6th ed., Berlin 1994, pp. XVII f. and passim.

Exceptions do not count — Not a literal quotation; see Hans Freyer, Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters, Stuttgart 1955, pp. 157 ff.

about the conversation with Hans Freyer after Wiesbaden — On 6 January 1956, a colloquium on Hans Freyer’s Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters was held in Wiesbaden.

the passage from 1921 … —

“The formal feature [of a justification of dictatorship] lies in the authorization by a supreme authority that is legally capable of suspending the law and authorizing a dictatorship—that is, permitting a concrete exception whose content, compared with the other case of a concrete exception, the granting of a pardon, is enormous. Abstractly speaking, the problem of dictatorship would be the problem of the concrete exception, a problem that has so far received little systematic treatment in general legal theory.”

C. Schmitt, Die Diktatur, 6th ed., Berlin 1994, p. XVIII.

1 February 1956

Küster — Otto Küster (1907–1989), jurist.

W. Strauss — Walter Strauss (1900–1976). As State Secretary in the Federal Ministry of Justice, he was the driving force behind the withdrawal of Schmitt’s invitation to the Evangelical Academy of Baden conference in Herrenalb in May 1953; see the note above on p. 304.

2 February 1956

Banquet of the slaughtered Leviathan — See Leviathan, p. 18.

4 February 1956

Dombois — Hans Adolf Dombois (1907–1997), theologian and jurist, a student of Smend. In 1950 he published a book on denazification that Schmitt studied intensively: Hans Dombois, Politische Gerichtsbarkeit. Der Irrweg der Entnazifizierung und die Frage des Verfassungsschutzes. Mit e. Nachw. von Hermann Ehlers, Gütersloh [1950]. The copy held at the Institute for Political Science and Sociology at the University of Bonn contains the dedication:

“Respectfully dedicated to Prof. Dr. Schmitt with gratitude, Hemer 14/5/1953, Dr. Dombois.”

Klaus Ritter — (born 1918). Schmitt is referring to K. Ritter, Zwischen Naturrecht und Rechtspositivismus. Eine erkenntnistheoret. Auseinandersetzung mit den neueren Versuchen zur Wiederherstellung e. Rechtsmetaphysik. Mit e. Vorw. von Hans Dombois, Witten 1956.

Emil Wiener — Not identified.

Coing — Helmut Coing (1912–2000), jurist, Rector of the University of Frankfurt in 1955/56.

16 February 1956

Ernst Jünger (6 March 1956) — BW EJ, pp. 295 f.

Neesse — Gottfried Neeße (1911–1987), National Socialist jurist specializing in civil-service law and a colleague of Schmitt at Berlin University. He dedicated the following work to Schmitt: Geheimnis mitten im Licht: Das ist Naxos. Carl Schmitt zum 80. Geburtstag, n.p. 1968. Typescript, RW 265 no. 27664.

Peter Diederichs — (1904–1990), publisher. In 1949 he re-established in Cologne the Diederichs publishing house his father had run in Leipzig. Schmitt’s Hamlet oder Hekuba appeared there in 1956.

Millions of heads and one record — A variation on the poem “Himmel und Hölle” by Franz von Paula Huber, which says:

Millions of souls, one thought, Millions of hearts and one beat!

Schlagintweit — Several brothers who published accounts of their travels and research in the nineteenth century.

1 March 1956

Three premiums, three premiums … — After the folk and soldiers’ song:

Three lilies, three lilies, I planted on my grave; Then came a proud horseman And broke them off.

On the “three premiums attached to the legal possession of power,” see LuL, pp. 32 f., with the later note in VA, p. 348. Schmitt also used this “political surplus value” attached to the legal possession of power to explain his own conduct in 1933; see Gespräch, pp. 68 ff.

On obéissance préalable—“prior obedience”—see the note above on p. 25; on the “application of general clauses,” see C. Schmitt, Über die drei Arten des rechtswissenschaftlichen Denkens, 3rd ed., Berlin 2006, pp. 48 f.

16 March 1956

jus primae noctis — “The right of the first night.” In the period of serfdom, the lord exercising judicial authority was said to have the right to spend the first night with a bride. Whether, and to what extent, this was ever actually practiced is unclear.

30 March 1956

Whoever does not work shall not eat — The saying comes from Paul (2 Thess. 3:10) and appears in Article 12 of the Constitution of the Soviet Union of 5 December 1936.

1 April 1956

Caduca culmina vagi saeculi contemnens — Correctly: caduca vagi contemnens culmina saecli, “despising the decaying heights of this restless age”; from the Carmen paschale of the Christian Latin poet Caelius Sedulius, fifth century.

Novalis: The Jew must perish —

“The fundamental difference between the Old and New Testaments. Why Palestine and the Jews were chosen for the founding of the Christian religion. Just as the Jews perished through it, so the French in the present Revolution.”

Novalis, Teplitzer Fragmente. In: idem, Schriften. Edited by Paul Kluckhohn and Richard Samuel, vol. 2, Stuttgart etc. 1981, p. 616.

Positionen und Begriffe, p. 113, note — PuB, p. 128, note 2.

It lives on as a ghost … — See the note above on p. 207.

They have Niehans-style fresh cells injected into themselves — This refers to Pope Pius XII; see above, p. 297.

see Lucan (sed victa Catoni) — Pharsalia, I, 128; see also the note above on p. 79.

2 April 1956

Henri Lévy-Bruhl — H. Lévy-Bruhl (1884–1964), sociologist of law and professor of Roman law at the University of Paris.

7 April 1956

Pascal’s “human condition” (fr. 139) — Schmitt is using Brunschvicg’s numbering. The fragment says:

“all the unhappiness of men comes from one thing: their inability to remain quietly alone in their room.”

B. Pascal, Über die Religion und über einige andere Gegenstände (Pensées). Translated and edited by Ewald Wasmuth, 8th ed., Heidelberg 1978, p. 77.

Hobbes’s sociology of competition — Schmitt is referring to Chapter 13 of Leviathan.

13 May 1956

pp. 511/12 PhdG — See G. W. F. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Eva Moldenhauer and Karl Markus Michel, vol. 3, p. 571.

18 May 1956

Hans Graß — (1909–1994), Protestant theologian.

29 May 1956

Mr. von Sedlmayer — Hans Sedlmayr, Verlust der Mitte. Die bildende Kunst des 19. und 20. Jahrh. als Symbol der Zeit, Salzburg 1948.

31 May 1956

Ernst Bloch: the fascist Carl Schmitt … —
